body.text: samādhipādaḥ
body.translated_text: The Chapter on <s>Samādhi</s> (Concentration).

body.text: yastyaktvā rūpamādyaṁ prabhavati jagato'nekadhā'nugrahāya prakṣīṇakleśarāśirviṣamaviṣadharo'nekavaktraḥ subhogī। sarvajñānaprasūtirbhujagaparikaraḥ prītaye yasya nityaṁ devo'hīśaḥ sa vo'vyātsitavimalatanuryogado yogayuktaḥ ॥ 1 ॥
body.translated_text: He who, having abandoned his primordial form, manifests in manifold ways for the benefit of the world, with the mass of afflictions destroyed, bearing various poisons, many-headed, with beautiful coils, the source of all knowledge, with serpent-attendants for whose constant delight—may that god, the lord of serpents, of pure white body, the bestower of <s>yoga</s>, absorbed in <s>yoga</s>, protect you! // 1 //

body.text: atha yogānuśāsanam ॥ 1 ॥
body.translated_text: Now, the teaching of <s>yoga</s>. // 1 //

body.text: athetyayamadhikārārthaḥ।
body.translated_text: "Now" (<s>atha</s>)—this word has the meaning of commencement (<s>adhikāra</s>).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yasminna staḥ karmavipākau yata āstāṁ kleśā yasmai nālamalaṅdhyā nikhilānām । nāvacchinnaḥ kāladṛśā ya: kalayantyā lokeśastaṁ kaiṭabhaśatruṁ praṇamāmi ॥ 1 ॥
yaḥ sarvavit sarvevibhūtiśaktiḥ vihīnadoṣopahitakriyāphala: । viśvodbhavāntasthitiheturīśo namo'stu tasmai gurave gurorapi ॥ 2 ॥
[athe] tyādipātañjalayogaśāstra[sūtrabhāṣya]vivaraṇamārabhyate । tatrānākhyātasambandhapraye.ājanaṁ na puruṣapravṛttinivṛttibhyāṁ paryāpnotīti, sūtrakārābhiprete puruṣapravṛttinimittabhūte sambandhaprayojane pūrvaṁ prakaṭīkriyete ॥
tatra prayojanaṁ tāvat - cikitsāśāstre taccaturvyūhatvapradarśanadvāreṇa vyākhyātam । tadyathā-cikitsāśāsraṁ caturvyūhaṁ, rogaḥ, rogahetuḥ, ārogyaṁ, bhaiṣajyam iti । vidhipratiṣedhaniyamadvāreṇa [ca tat] caturvyūhāviṣayavyākhyānaparam । evamihāpi “pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraduḥkhairguṇavṛttivirodhācca duḥkhameva sarvaṁ vivekina:“ ityārabhya caturvyūhatvaṁ śāstrasya pradarśitam । tadyathā-duḥkhapracuraḥ saṁsāro heyaḥ । tasyāvidyānimitte draṣṭṛsaṁyogo hetuḥ । vivekakhyātiraviplavā hānopāyaḥ । vivekakhyātau ca satyāmavidyānivṛttiḥ, tannivṛttāvātyantiko draṣṭṛdṛśyasaṁyogoparamo hānam, tadeva kaivalyamiti । ārogyasthānīyakaivalyaprayuktatvādasya tadeva kaivalyaṁ prayojanam ॥
nanu ca heyataddhetū na prastotavye, niṣprayojanatvāt । hānaprayuktaṁ hi śāstraṁ, tadupāyabhūtā vivekakhyātireva vaktavyā । na hi kaṇṭakaviddhacaraṇatalasya tadapanayanaṁ muktvā duḥkhataddhetū codyete । naitadevaṁ-heyatatkāraṇāpekṣatvāddhānopāyasya । yāvadidamanenopāyena hātavyaṁ saṁsāracakram asya cāvidyānimitto draṣṭṛdṛśyasaṁyogo hetu: iti nākhyāyate, tāvannāvidyāpratipakṣabhūtā vivekakhyātirākhyātuṁ śakyate । heyataddhetumato hānopāyārthino rogiṇo bhaiṣajyārthitvadarśanāt । na hi rogaṁ rogahetuṁ cānapekṣya cikitsāśāsramupadiśyate ॥
sambandho'pi-vivekakhyāterhānameva phalaṁ sādhyaṁ hānasyāpi vivekakhyātireva sādhanamiti sādhyasādhanayoritaretaraniyama eva, nānyasaṁbandhaḥ । tadyathā-bhaiṣajyasyārogyameva phalam ārogyasyāpi bhaiṣajyameva sādhanamiti itaretaraniyamaḥ, sa ca śāstrāditi । tasmāt sasaṁbandhaprayojanaṁ yogānuśāsanam ।
nanu ca yadi hānaṁ prayojanaṁ tadupāyaśca vivekakhyātiriti, tatra vaktavyam ‘atha vivekakhyātyanuśāsanam‘ iti । kimartham 'atha yogānuśāsanam‘ iti sūtritam ?
tadupāyatvādyogasya । upāya eva vaktavyaḥ syāt । upeyopapradarśane hi upeyamupāyaṁ prati sākāṅkṣamevetyupāyaḥ sāṅgakalāpaḥ punarapi vaktavyaḥ syāt । tasmiṁścābhihite sarvamabhihitamiti । ﻿
kathaṁ tadupāyatvam ? yata āha sūtrakāraḥ-- ‘yogāṅgānuṣṭhānādaśuddhikṣaye jñānadīptirāvivekakhyāteḥ‘ iti । ‘nirvicāravaiśāradye'dhyātmaprasādaḥ‘ ‘ṛtaṁbharā tatra prajñā‘ iti ca । tathā bhāṣyakāro'pyāha--‘yastvekāgre cetasi sa bhūtamarthe pradyotayati‘ iti । bhūtārthāvagatiśca vivekakhyātiḥ । tasmādyuktaṁ tadupāyayogānuśāsanamevādau sūtritamiti ॥
nanu ca yogāṅgānuṣṭhānādvivekakhyātiḥ, tatra vaktavyaṁ 'atha yogāṅgānuśāsanam iti-na-phalenopakramāt । yogāṅgānuṣṭhānasya hi phalaṁ yoga iti tadupakramo yuktaḥ ॥
yadyevaṁ hānenopakramyeta-na-tasyopeyatvāt-upeyameva hi tat । yogaḥ punaḥ svāṅgānāmupeyaśca, upāyaśca vivekakhyāteraṇimādiprāpteścetyabhyarhitataraḥ । phalatadupāyarūpatvāt (phalapayanimittatvāt) ॥
uttarasūtrārthavācca । na hi 'atha yogāṅgānuśāsanam । ' ityukta ‘yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ' iti yuktaṁ vaktum । tadā hi ‘yamaniyayama'disūtrameva paṭhitavyaṁ syāt ॥
atha tadeva paṭhitavyamiti cet-na-yogope(pā)yayā hānopāyabhūtāyā vivekakhyāte:, phalasya ca hānasya, saṁbandha[pra]darśanārthatvāt ‘yogaścittavṛtinirodhaḥ‘ ityasya ॥
(sa)kathaṁ punaretatsaṁbandhapradarśanārtham ? yāvatā nirbījasamādhilakṣaṇābhidhānametat । satyamevaṁ, tathāpi hānatadupāyasaṁbandhamavadyotayadeva sūtraṁ nirbījasamādhilakṣaṇatāmāpadyate ॥
na hi nirodhalakṣaṇāt samādherarthāntaraṁ hānam । kiṁ tvetāvatā viśeṣa:, nirodhalakṣaṇasamādhai (dherne) punaḥ pravṛtiḥ, hāne tvātyantitikī nivṛttiriti । samādhyavasthāyāṁ tu hānāviśeṣa eva । tathā cāha-‘‘tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam‘‘ [iti] ॥ ‘‘svarūpapratiṣṭhā ca citiśaktiḥ kaivalyam‘‘ iti svarūpapratiṣṭhatvaṁ(ṣṭhaṁ) hi kaivalyamāha । tataśca nirbījasamādhinā kaivalyameva śāstrārthapratyayadraḍhimne sākṣākriyate ।
tasmādyaducyate kaiścit sabījasamādhiḥ kaivalyasādhanamiti-tanna ! kiṁ tarhi? khyātireva sādhanamavidyānivṛtidvāreṇa । avidyānimitto hi bandhaḥ । tasmādyadyapi yogānuśāsanaṁ sūtritam, tathāpi khyātyarthavādyogasya taddvāreṇa khyātihānasaṁbandhamapi darśayatīti, suṣṭhūcyate uttarasūtrasaṁbandhārthaṁ ca yogānuśāsanamiti sūtrayitavyamiti ॥
yadyapi phalārthināṁ tatphalasādhanaṁ pratyutpannākāṅkṣāṇāṁ sādhanopadeśo'pyāsti । tathāpi na tatprayojanam , sarvasya phale.oddeśena pravṛttestadeva prayojanamiti ॥
[yogānuśāsanamiti] । yathā-śiṣyo'nuśiṣyate viśiṣṭapravṛttinivṛttiniyamadvāreṇa, tathā viśiṣṭasādhyasādhanatadaṅganiyamamātrasādṛśyādantevāsyanuśāsanavadyogānuśāsanamityucyate । anuśiṣṭiranuśāsanaṁ, yoge'nuśiṣyate'nenāsminniti vā yogānuśāsanaṁ śāstram ॥
[athetyayamadhikārārthaḥ] । adhikāra ārambhaḥ prastāvaḥ, artho'bhidheyo'sya ; śiṣṭasmṛtiprāmāṇyāt । nanu cānantaryārthasyāthaśabdasya smaranti śiṣṭāḥ । tathā cāha-“vṛttādanantarasya prakriyārthe dṛṣṭaḥ” iti । na-sarvatrārambhārthatvāt । ānantaryasya ca gamyamānatvāt । yathā putra ityukte pitā gamyate, na ca putraśabdasyārthaḥ pitā, tathehāpyārambha evābhidhīyate, ānantaryaṁ tu pratīyate ॥
ata eva ca ‘vṛttādanantarasya prakriyārtho dṛṣṭaḥ‘ ityucyate । yadi cānantaryārtho'bhaviṣyattadā ‘vṛttādānantarye'rthe prakriyāyāḥ‘ ityavadiṣyat । anantarasyeti cānantarabhāvina evābhidhānam ।
api caivaṁ hi smṛtiḥ-‘‘kiñcidavyaṁ vibhaktyarthapradhānaṁ kiñcitkriyāpradhānam । ucainīcairityādi vibhaktyarthapradhānam, hiruk pṛthagilyādi kriyāpradhānam' [iti] । na caitadvyatirekeṇāvyayānāmarthoṁ vidyate । tatrāthaśabdasyānantaryārthatve sati vibhaktya(kti)śravaṇamayuktam, sattvapradhānatvāt । ārambhakriyārthatve tu na vibhaktyartha)śravaṇamayuktam, asattvapradhānatvāditi ॥
tasmādathaśabdaḥ prastāvārthe eveti yuktamathelyadhikārārthe iti । svarūpāvadyotanārtha itiśabdaḥ । yathā gaurityāheti । prasiddho'pyathaśabdārtho'dhikriyamāṇaviṣaye śiṣyabuddhisamādhānārtha kīrtyate । siddhe hyayaṁ nyāyaḥ śrutau ‘vyākhyāsyāmi te vyācakṣāṇasya tu me nididhyāsasva' iti ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
In whom the fruitions of <s>karma</s> exist, from whom the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) arose, whom the entirety of beings cannot transgress, who is not delimited by the gaze of <s>Kāla</s> (Time) even as she reckons [all things]—to that Lord of the world, the enemy of <s>Kaiṭabha</s>, I bow. // 1 //
He who is omniscient, whose power is all sovereignty, free from faults, whose actions and their fruits are well-established, the Lord who is the cause of the origination, dissolution, and sustenance of the universe—to that teacher of even the teacher, homage! // 2 //
The <s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Exposition) on the <s>Pātañjala Yogaśāstra</s> [Sūtra and Bhāṣya] is hereby commenced. Since one who does not know the relation (<s>sambandha</s>) and purpose (<s>prayojana</s>) of a text not yet explained is not motivated to engage or disengage, the relation and purpose—which serve as the occasion for a person's engagement—as intended by the author of the <s>sūtras</s>, are first made manifest.
As for the purpose: it has been explained in the science of medicine (<s>cikitsāśāstra</s>) by means of demonstrating its fourfold structure. Namely, the science of medicine has a fourfold structure: the disease, the cause of the disease, health, and the remedy. And it is devoted to explaining the domain of that fourfold structure through injunction, prohibition, and regulation. Similarly here too, beginning with "suffering alone is everything for the discerning, due to the pain of transformation, anguish, and latent impressions, and due to the conflict of the <s>guṇa</s>-activities," the fourfold structure of the teaching has been demonstrated. Namely: <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence), replete with suffering, is to be abandoned (<s>heya</s>). Its cause is the conjunction of the seer with the seen, occasioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). Unwavering discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the means of abandonment (<s>hānopāya</s>). And when discriminative knowledge is present, <s>avidyā</s> ceases; upon its cessation, the absolute cessation of the conjunction of seer and seen is the abandonment (<s>hāna</s>)—that itself is <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). Since this teaching is directed toward <s>kaivalya</s>, which corresponds to health, <s>kaivalya</s> itself is the purpose.
Objection: The thing to be abandoned and its cause need not be discussed, since that would be purposeless. The teaching is directed toward abandonment, and only discriminative knowledge, which is the means thereof, need be taught. For one whose foot is pierced by a thorn is not interrogated about the suffering and its cause, apart from the removal of the thorn. Reply: This is not so—because the means of abandonment depends on knowledge of the thing to be abandoned and its cause. Until it is explained that this wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s> is to be abandoned by this means, and that the conjunction of seer and seen, occasioned by <s>avidyā</s>, is its cause, discriminative knowledge, which is the antidote to <s>avidyā</s>, cannot be explained. For we observe that it is the sick person, knowing the disease and its cause and desiring the means of abandonment, who desires the remedy. For the science of medicine is not taught without reference to the disease and its cause.
As for the relation: the fruit to be accomplished by discriminative knowledge is abandonment alone, and the means to abandonment is discriminative knowledge alone—thus the mutual restriction of means and end, and no other relation. Just as the fruit of medicine is health alone, and the means to health is medicine alone—this mutual restriction comes from the teaching. Therefore the teaching of <s>yoga</s> comes with its relation and purpose.
Objection: If abandonment is the purpose and discriminative knowledge is its means, then the <s>sūtra</s> should read "Now, the teaching of discriminative knowledge." Why was it composed as "Now, the teaching of <s>yoga</s>"? Reply: Because <s>yoga</s> is the means to that. It is the means itself that should be taught. For in demonstrating the goal and the means, the goal creates expectation toward the means, and so the means with all its limbs must be further taught. And when that has been stated, everything has been stated.
How is <s>yoga</s> the means to that? Because the author of the <s>sūtras</s> says: "Through the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>, upon the destruction of impurity, the light of knowledge [shines] up to discriminative knowledge" (YS 2.28). And: "Upon the clarity of <s>nirvicāra</s> [meditation], there is inner serenity" (YS 1.47); "The <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom) there is truth-bearing" (YS 1.48). Likewise the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> also says: "He whose mind is one-pointed illuminates the real nature of things." And the apprehension of the real nature of things is discriminative knowledge. Therefore it is fitting that the teaching of <s>yoga</s>, which is the means thereto, was composed first.
Objection: Since discriminative knowledge arises from the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>, the <s>sūtra</s> should read "Now, the teaching of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>." Reply: No—because one begins with the fruit. For <s>yoga</s> is the fruit of the practice of its limbs, so beginning with that is fitting.
If so, one should begin with abandonment. Reply: No—because that is the ultimate goal. It is indeed the ultimate goal. But <s>yoga</s> is both the goal of its own limbs and the means to discriminative knowledge and to the attainment of powers such as <s>aṇimā</s>, and so it is the most worthy. Because it has the nature of both fruit and means to fruit.
And because of the meaning of the subsequent <s>sūtras</s>. For if it had been said "Now, the teaching of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>," it would not be fitting to say "<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind" (YS 1.2). In that case, the <s>sūtra</s> on <s>yama</s>, <s>niyama</s>, and so forth should have been recited directly.
Objection: That very thing should be recited. Reply: No—because "<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind" serves to demonstrate the relation between the means to abandonment, which is discriminative knowledge attained through the method of <s>yoga</s>, and abandonment, which is the fruit.
How is this a demonstration of the relation? Insofar as it is a definition of <s>nirbīja samādhi</s> (seedless concentration). Truly so, but even so, the <s>sūtra</s> arrives at the definition of <s>nirbīja samādhi</s> precisely by illuminating the relation between abandonment and its means.
For abandonment is not something other than <s>samādhi</s> characterized by cessation. But the distinction is just this: in <s>samādhi</s> characterized by cessation, there is re-emergence, whereas in abandonment, there is absolute and final cessation. But in the state of <s>samādhi</s>, there is no difference from abandonment. Thus it says: "Then the seer abides in its own nature" (YS 1.3). And: "The power of consciousness established in its own nature is <s>kaivalya</s>" (YS 4.34)—for it calls establishment in one's own nature <s>kaivalya</s>. Therefore, through <s>nirbīja samādhi</s>, <s>kaivalya</s> itself is directly realized for the firm conviction in the meaning of the teaching.
Therefore, the claim of some that <s>sabīja samādhi</s> (seeded concentration) is the means to <s>kaivalya</s> is wrong. Rather, discriminative knowledge alone is the means, through the cessation of <s>avidyā</s>. For bondage has <s>avidyā</s> as its occasion. Therefore, although "the teaching of <s>yoga</s>" was composed, since <s>yoga</s> speaks for the purpose of discriminative knowledge, through that it also demonstrates the relation between discriminative knowledge and abandonment—thus it is well said that "the teaching of <s>yoga</s>" should be composed for the purpose of connecting with the subsequent <s>sūtras</s>.
Even though for those who desire the fruit, teaching the means to that fruit addresses their present expectation, still that is not the purpose, because everyone engages with reference to the fruit—that alone is the purpose.
["The teaching of <s>yoga</s>"] Just as a pupil is instructed through the regulation of specific engagements and disengagements, so by virtue of the mere similarity to such instruction—being the regulation of the specific goal, means, and their components—it is called "the teaching of <s>yoga</s>." Instruction (<s>anuśiṣṭi</s>) is the teaching (<s>anuśāsana</s>); it is the <s>śāstra</s> by which one is instructed in <s>yoga</s>, or in which one is instructed.
["'Now' (<s>atha</s>)—this has the meaning of commencement."] <s>Adhikāra</s> means commencement, introduction; its meaning (<s>artha</s>) is its expressed sense—on the authority of the usage of the learned. Objection: The learned remember <s>atha</s> as meaning "immediately after." Thus it is said: "It is seen in the sense of succession after something completed." Reply: No—because it is used everywhere in the sense of commencement. And because succession is understood implicitly. Just as when one says "son," the father is understood, yet "father" is not the meaning of the word "son"—so here too, commencement alone is expressed, while succession is implied.
For this very reason it is said: "It is seen in the sense of succession after something completed." If it had the meaning of succession, it would have been said: "In the sense of succession after something completed." And "of the succeeding" (<s>anantarasya</s>) designates only that which follows.
Moreover, there is this grammatical tradition: "Some indeclinables have case-meaning as primary, some have action-meaning as primary. <s>Ucaiḥ</s>, <s>nīcaiḥ</s>, etc. have case-meaning as primary; <s>hi</s>, <s>ruk</s>, <s>pṛthak</s>, etc. have action-meaning as primary." And there is no meaning of indeclinables beyond these two. Therefore, if <s>atha</s> had the meaning of succession, hearing a case-ending would be inappropriate, since it would be entity-primary. But if it has the meaning of the action of commencement, then not hearing a case-ending is appropriate, since it is not entity-primary.
Therefore, the word <s>atha</s> is in the sense of introduction—thus it is fitting that "<s>atha</s> is in the sense of commencement." The word <s>iti</s> is for the purpose of elucidating the intrinsic nature, as in "<s>gauḥ</s> (cow)—thus he said." Although the meaning of <s>atha</s> is well-known, it is stated in the context of the subject being commenced for the purpose of settling the student's understanding. For this is the method in established [traditions], as in the Śruti: "I shall explain to you; as I explain, attend closely."

body.text: yogānuśāsanaṁ śāstramadhikṛtaṁ veditavyam। yogaḥ samādhiḥ। sa ca sārvabhaumaścittasya dharmaḥ। kṣiptaṁ mūḍhaṁ vikṣiptamekāgraṁ niruddhamiti cittabhūmayaḥ। tatra vikṣipte cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhirna yogapakṣe vartate।
body.translated_text: The <s>śāstra</s> (teaching) on the teaching of <s>yoga</s> has been commenced and should be understood. <s>Yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (concentration). And that is a universal property of the mind. The states of the mind are: scattered (<s>kṣipta</s>), torpid (<s>mūḍha</s>), distracted (<s>vikṣipta</s>), one-pointed (<s>ekāgra</s>), and arrested (<s>niruddha</s>). Of these, when the mind is distracted, the concentration that is subordinate to distraction does not belong to the domain of <s>yoga</s>.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kaḥ punaryogo yasyānuśāsanaṁ prastutamiti-aha-- [yogaḥ samādhiriti] ॥ samādhigrahaṇāt 'yujiyoge' iti nivartya, 'yuja samādhau' ityayaṁ gṛhītaḥ । yogaḥ samādhānam । nanu ca ‘yogaḥ samādhiḥ‘ ityevamantena vyākhyāte sūtre ‘sa ca sārvabhaumaḥ‘ ityādibhāṣyamasaṁbandhaṁ dṛśyate । naiṣa doṣaḥ । iha samādhirityukte, samādhīyamānāpekṣatvāt, samādhīyamānānāṁ ca bahutvāt, kimātmā samādhīyate ? thā kiṁ vā śarīram, āhosvidindriyāṇi, iti bahu(vidāṁ)dhā vipratipate:, svaviśeṣaṇākāṅkṣatvācca samādhe:, kasyāyam? kiṁviśeṣaṇakaḥ? ityanuṣakte praśne, idamāha- [sa ca sārvabhaumaścittasya dharma] iti । cittasya dharmo nātmādīnām । tacca cittaṁ svayameva samādhīyate [samādhātra]ntaranirapekṣatvāt ॥
kāḥ punarbhūmaya ityata āha- [kṣipta mūḍhamityādayo bhūmaya] iti । kṣiptamiti karmakartari niṣṭhā । yathā bhinnaḥ kusūlaḥ svayameveti । kṣiptamaniṣṭaviṣayāsañjanena stimitam । mūḍhaṁ nirvivekam । vikṣiptaṁ nānākṣiptam । karmakartaryeva । vivekākṣamaṁ ca vikṣiptatvādeva । ekāgraṁ tulyapratyayapravāham । niruddhamiti pratyayaśūnyaṁ cittam ॥
nanu ca bhūmiṣu dharmeṣu vivakṣiteṣu, kimarthaṁ kṣiptamityādinā dharmyucyate ? naiṣa doṣaḥ, dharmiṇā dharma evopadiśyate । dharmāṇāṁ dharmiviṣayatvāt । yathā gotve kiṁ liṅgamiti pṛṣṭe, viṣāṇī kakudmān prāntavālādhiriti dharmiṇā dharma evopadiśyate । tasmāt kṣepādayaścittasya bhūmayo dharma ityarthaḥ ॥
nanu ca bhūmīnāṁ cittadharmatve samādheśca, kathaṁ bhūmibhiḥ samādhirādhāratvena viśeṣyata sārvabhauma iti ? sāmānyabhūtatvāt samādheḥ । bhūmīnāṁ ca viśeṣatvāt । yathā kṣiptaṁ tiṣṭhati, mūḍhaṁ tiṣṭhati, vikṣisamakāgraṁ ceti, kṣiptādibhūmiṣu sthitiranuvartate sāmānyam । sthitiśca samādhiḥ । tasmāt sāmānyarūpaṁ sarvāsu bhūmiṣu prādhānyena vartata iti । ‘sarvabhūmipṛthivī' ityaiśvaryārthīyo'ṇpratyayaḥ । anuśatikāditvādubhayapadavṛddhiḥ ॥
anye punarbāhmādhyāmikān saṁyamaviṣayān bhūmaya ityācakṣate । teṣāṁ ‘vikṣipte cetasi‘ iti sāmānādhikaraṇyānupapattiḥ । svavacanavirodhaśca katham ? kṣipyate'sminniti kṣiptam , muhyate'sminniti mūḍhaṁ, yadā caivaṁ na tadā saṁyamaviṣayatā । tatra kṣepādyasaṁbhavāt । ekāgrāvasthāyāṁ hi saṁyamo bhavati ॥
kiṁ cānyat-kṣipeśca dhrauvyādyarthābhāvādadhikaraṇe niṣṭhāpratyayābhāvaḥ । kiṁ ca-niruddhe cetasi saṁyamasyāpi tatrābhāvāt vṛttiśūnyatvāt saṁyamaviṣayābhāvaḥ । na hi nirodhe viṣayaviśeṣe cittaṁ nirudhyate । tadā hi viṣayitvānnivartate । parigaṇanānupapattiśca । na hi kṣiptādayaḥ pañcaiva saṁyamasya viṣayāḥ । teṣāmānantyāt ॥
nanu cānyathā yogaṁ kecidicchanti । tathā cāhuḥ--‘‘indriyamano'rthasannikarṣāt sukhadu:khe, tadanārambha ātmasthe manasi, saśarīrasya sukhadu:khābhāva: prāṇamanevinigrahāpekṣaḥ saṁyogo [yoga] iti‘‘ । taditi prakṛtāpekṣam । yo'sau sukhaduḥkhayorātmendriyamano'rthasannikarṣo hetuḥ, tasyānārambhaḥ tadanutpattiḥ । sa kathaṁ bhavati ? ātmasthe manasi, nendriyasthe । saśarīrasya aviśīrṇaśarīrasya । tadā kāraṇābhāvāt kāryābhāva iti, sannikarṣābhāve sukhaduḥkhayorapyabhāvaḥ, tasyāmavasthāyāṁ yo'sau vibhorātmano manasā saṁyogaḥ sa prāṇamanovinigrahāpekṣaḥ saṁyogaviśeṣo yoga iti ।
atrocyate-ātmasthe manasītyayuktam, sarvadā atmasthatvānmanasaḥ । indriyādisanniṣkarṣānārambhāpekṣayā ātmasthe iti cet, tadanārambha ityeva siddhatvādātmasthe manasītyanarthakaṁ syāt ॥
kiṁ cānyat-muktasyāpi manasa ātmasthatvādindriyasannikarṣābhāvācca yogaḥ prāpnoti । tasyāpi hi sarvagatatvāt manasaśca nityatvāt sarvadātmasthatvameva ॥
kiṁ ca-ātmanaḥ pradeśābhāvādātmastha ityayuktam । na cāpyupacaritātmapradeśasaṁyogaḥ paramārthasya yogasya hetuḥ syāt । upacaritasya mithyātvāt ॥
kiṁ cānyat-mano'rthasannikarṣābhāva ityeva siddheḥ(ddhaṁ)indriyagrahaṇamanarthakaṁ syāt । athendriyairvinā mano'rthasannikarṣābhāvāttadanārabhbha iti prāptyabhāve pratiṣedho na yukta iti cet । naitadevam, vinendriyairmano'rthasannikarṣo nāstītyarthātsannikarṣapratiṣedhaṁ kurvatā viṣayaprāptirindriyadvārā pratipāditā syāt ।
kiṁ cānyat-sarvaprāṇabhājāmindriyamano'rthasannikarṣāt sukhaduḥkhapratilambhasya prasiddhatvādātmanaḥ sambandhasya ca nityatvāt sukhaduḥkhābhāvo yoga ityeva siddheḥ, tatra [sūtra] śeṣo'narthakaḥ syāt ॥
athāpi syādindriyamano'rthasannikarṣagrahaṇādṛte sukhaduḥkhābhāva ityetāvati sati muktasyāpi sukhaduḥkhābhāvādyogitvaprasaṅga iti tannivṛttyarthaṁ sūtraśeṣagrahaṇamiti । tacca na, muktasya sukhaduḥkhaprāptyabhāvāt, prāptipūrvapratiṣedhasya nyāyyatvāt, yasya sukhaduḥkhaprāptiḥ, tadviṣayaḥ sukhaduḥkhābhāva eva yoga iti sūtraśeṣapratyākhyānaṁ yujyate ॥
kiṁ cānyat – upātte'pi saśarīragrahaṇe muktādvinivṛttirna śakyate kartum, niṣprayojanatvāt । sukhaduḥkhābhāvaścedyogaḥ, vidyamānamapi śarīraṁ kāryākaraṇādanarthakaṁ syāt । kāryānapekṣāyāṁ hi muktāmuktayoraviśeṣa eva ॥
kiṁ cānyat – prāṇamanovinigrahāpekṣa ityapi na ghaṭate । vidhārakasya prayatnasyātmasamavetatvādavidyamāne'pi manasaḥ kriyāvattve indriyeṇāsaṁjya manaḥ prāṇa [mano]nigrahau na kartuṁ paryāpyate । indriyasaṁyoge ca manasaḥ, tadanārambha ityayuktam । manasaśca prāṇanigrahe vyāpṛ(vṛ)tatvādanārambhānupapattiḥ ॥
na cāsati indriyavāyusannikarṣe prāṇanigrahaḥ । na cānigṛhīte prāṇe yogaḥ, ātmasthavidhārakaprayatnadvārā manogatakriyāsaṁbandhahetutvāt prāṇanigrahasya । athāpi syādyogaḥ samādhiriti । tacca na, niṣkriyatvādātmano nityasamādhānameva । sthitiśca samādhirityucyate । tasmādyuktamabhidhīyate - ‘ [sa ca sārvabhaumaścittasya dharmaḥ‘ iti ॥]
yadyevaṁ samādhiścedyogaḥ, sa ca sārvabhaumaścittadharmaḥ, sa ca sarvajanānāmayatnasiddhaḥ, kṣiptādyanugatatvāt । tathā ca sati, yathaiva śvāsapraśvāsādīnāṁ prayatnādṛte siddhatvāttatkaraṇama(llakṣaṇama)narthakam, evaṁ yogānuśāsanamapyanarthakaṁ prāptamityata āha – [tatra] [vikṣipte (anavikṣipte) cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhirna yogapakṣe vartate iti] ॥ kṣiptādyanugatasya yogapakṣe'nabhipretatvāt । na hi kṣepādyanugataḥ samādhirbhūtārthāvadyotanādikṣamaḥ, kṣepādipradhānatvāt । vikṣepaniṣedhenaiva hi pradhānamallanibarhaṇanyāyena kṣaptamūḍhayorapi niṣedhaḥ kṛtaḥ । pradhānatā ca vikṣepasamādheradhikārayogyatvāt । vikṣepasthaṁ hi cittamapakṣapātādiṣṭaṁ viṣayamupanetuṁ śakyate । na hi viṣayāsañjanādinā kṣiptamiṣṭaviṣayaviyogādinā vā mūḍhamanyathāpanetuṁ pāryate ॥
[yogapakṣa iti ॥] samādhitve satyapi kāryākaraṇāta pakṣa ityucyate । yathā gacchataḥ pratipadaṁ vidyamānāpi sthitiḥ sthitikāryākaraṇānna sthitirityucyate । vikṣepopasarjanībhūtatvaṁ vikṣepasthaikasamādhivyaktyabhiprāyeṇa । sārvabhauma iti tu prādhānyaṁ, sāmānyena sarvabhūmiṣu vṛttaḥ ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
What then is the <s>yoga</s> whose instruction is being set forth? To this he says: [<s>yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (concentration)]. By the use of the term <s>samādhi</s>, the root '<s>yuji yoge</s>' (to yoke) is set aside, and the root '<s>yuja samādhau</s>' (to concentrate) is adopted. <s>Yoga</s> is <s>samādhāna</s> (settling of the mind). Now, if the <s>sūtra</s> is explained as meaning '<s>yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s>,' then the subsequent commentary '<s>sa ca sārvabhaumaḥ</s>' (and it pervades all stages) and so forth appears unconnected. This is not a fault. Here, when <s>samādhi</s> is stated, since it requires specification of what is being concentrated, and since the things that can be concentrated are many—is it the self that is concentrated? Or the body? Or the sense-faculties?—when there are many divergent opinions, and since <s>samādhi</s> requires its own qualifier—'Whose is this? What is its qualifier?'—when the question arises, he states: [And it is a property of the mind that pervades all stages (<s>sārvabhaumaḥ cittasya dharmaḥ</s>)]. It is a property of the mind, not of the self and so forth. And that mind itself is concentrated, since it does not depend on any external concentrator.
What then are the stages (<s>bhūmis</s>)? To this he says: [The distracted (<s>kṣipta</s>), the deluded (<s>mūḍha</s>), and so forth are the stages]. '<s>Kṣipta</s>' has the past participle used in the agent-for-object sense (<s>karmakartari niṣṭhā</s>), like 'the granary that has broken apart of its own accord.' <s>Kṣipta</s> means stagnated through attachment to undesirable objects. <s>Mūḍha</s> means devoid of discernment. <s>Vikṣipta</s> means scattered in various directions—also in the agent-for-object sense—and incapable of discrimination precisely because of its scattered nature. <s>Ekāgra</s> (one-pointed) means a flow of homogeneous cognitions. <s>Niruddha</s> (arrested) means a mind devoid of cognitions.
Now, when the properties (<s>dharmas</s>) that are the stages are intended, for what purpose is the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>) mentioned by means of '<s>kṣipta</s>' and so forth? This is not a fault: it is the property itself that is taught through the property-bearer. For properties have the property-bearer as their subject. Just as, when asked 'What is the defining mark of cow-hood?', one teaches the property through the property-bearer: 'having horns, having a hump, having a tail with a tuft at the end.' Therefore the meaning is: the states of distraction and the rest are the stages that are properties of the mind.
Now, if the stages are properties of the mind, and <s>samādhi</s> too [is a property of the mind], how is <s>samādhi</s> qualified by the stages as its substrate, being called '<s>sārvabhauma</s>' (pervading all stages)? Because <s>samādhi</s> has the nature of a universal. And the stages are particulars. Just as: the distracted persists, the deluded persists, the scattered and the one-pointed persist—persistence pervades all stages beginning with the distracted, and this is what is universal. And persistence is <s>samādhi</s>. Therefore, being of the nature of a universal, it primarily operates across all stages. '<s>Sarvabhūmipṛthivī</s>' uses the <s>aṇ</s> suffix in the sense of sovereignty. Being of the <s>anuśatikādi</s> type, there is <s>vṛddhi</s> in both members of the compound.
Others, however, declare that the stages are the external and internal objects of restraint (<s>saṃyama</s>). For them, the co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) in 'when the mind is scattered (<s>vikṣipte cetasi</s>)' would be untenable. And how is there a contradiction with their own statement? '<s>Kṣipta</s>' means 'that in which [the mind] is cast about,' '<s>mūḍha</s>' means 'that in which [the mind] is deluded'—and when it is so, there is no restraint-object status, since distraction and the rest cannot occur there. For restraint occurs only in the one-pointed state.
Furthermore, since for '<s>kṣip</s>' (to cast) and the like there is no sense of location and so forth, the past participle suffix in the locative sense is untenable. Moreover, when the mind is arrested (<s>niruddha</s>), since even restraint is absent there—the mind being devoid of activity—there is no restraint-object. For the mind is not arrested with respect to some particular object of cessation; for at that point, it withdraws from being a subject [of objects]. And the enumeration would be untenable, for the objects of restraint are not merely these five beginning with the distracted, since they are infinite.
Now some desire <s>yoga</s> in a different way. Thus they say: 'From the conjunction of the sense-faculties, mind, and objects arise pleasure and pain; the non-initiation of that, when the mind abides in the self, is the absence of pleasure and pain for the embodied being, dependent on the restraint of breath and mind—this conjunction is <s>yoga</s>.' 'That' refers to what is under discussion. The conjunction of self, sense-faculties, mind, and objects that is the cause of pleasure and pain—its non-initiation means its non-arising. How does this occur? When the mind abides in the self (<s>ātmasthe manasi</s>), not when it abides in the sense-faculties. 'Of the embodied being' means of one whose body has not disintegrated. Then, due to the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect: when conjunction is absent, pleasure and pain too are absent. In that state, the conjunction of the all-pervading self with the mind, dependent on the restraint of breath and mind—this special conjunction is <s>yoga</s>.
To this we reply: 'When the mind abides in the self' is untenable, since the mind always abides in the self. If one says 'abiding in the self' is said with reference to the non-initiation of conjunction with sense-faculties and the rest, then since it is already established by 'the non-initiation of that,' the phrase 'when the mind abides in the self' would be purposeless.
Furthermore, <s>yoga</s> would follow even for the liberated self, since its mind also abides in the self and there is no conjunction with sense-faculties. For that [self] too, being all-pervading, and the mind being eternal, there is always abiding in the self.
Moreover, since the self has no spatial parts, 'abiding in the self' is untenable. Nor could a figuratively-ascribed conjunction with a location of the self be the cause of ultimate <s>yoga</s>, since what is figurative is false.
Furthermore, since the result is already established by 'the absence of conjunction of mind and objects,' the mention of sense-faculties would be purposeless. If one says that without sense-faculties there is no conjunction of mind and objects, hence 'the non-initiation of that' is a prohibition where there is no possibility—this is not so, for by saying that without sense-faculties there is no conjunction of mind and objects, and thereby prohibiting conjunction, the reaching of objects through the door of the sense-faculties would be implicitly established.
Furthermore, since for all living beings the attainment of pleasure and pain through the conjunction of sense-faculties, mind, and objects is well-known, and since the self's connection is eternal, the absence of pleasure and pain being <s>yoga</s> is already established; the remainder [of the definition] would be purposeless.
Even if one were to say that without the inclusion of 'conjunction of sense-faculties, mind, and objects,' if the absence of pleasure and pain alone were sufficient, then even the liberated would be a <s>yogin</s> due to having no pleasure and pain—and the remainder is included to exclude that—this too is untenable, since the liberated does not attain pleasure and pain, and since a prohibition presupposes a prior attainment; for one for whom there is attainment of pleasure and pain, the absence of pleasure and pain directed toward that is <s>yoga</s>—thus the rejection of the remainder of the definition is appropriate.
Furthermore, even if 'of the embodied being' is accepted, the exclusion of the liberated cannot be accomplished, since it would be purposeless. If the absence of pleasure and pain is <s>yoga</s>, the body too, even though present, would be purposeless since it produces no effect. For when no effect is required, there is no distinction between the liberated and the unliberated.
Moreover, 'dependent on the restraint of breath and mind' also does not work. Since the effort that sustains is inherent in the self, and since even when the mind's activity does not exist, one cannot accomplish the restraint of breath and mind without conjunction with the sense-faculties. And when the mind is conjoined with the sense-faculties, 'the non-initiation of that' is untenable. And since the mind is engaged in the restraint of breath, the non-initiation would be untenable.
Nor is there restraint of breath without conjunction with the sense-faculties and <s>vāyu</s> (vital air). Nor is there <s>yoga</s> without the restraint of breath, since the restraint of breath is the cause of the connection with the activity residing in the mind through the effort of sustaining that abides in the self. If one were then to say: '<s>yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s>'—this too is untenable, since the self being inactive, there would be eternal concentration. And persistence is called <s>samādhi</s>. Therefore it is rightly stated: ['And it is a property of the mind that pervades all stages.']
If this is so—if <s>samādhi</s> is <s>yoga</s>, and it is a property of the mind pervading all stages, and it is accomplished effortlessly for all people, since it accompanies the distracted and the rest—then just as the performance of breathing and the like, being accomplished without effort, renders teaching about them purposeless, so too the instruction of <s>yoga</s> would be rendered purposeless. Therefore he says: [In the scattered mind, <s>samādhi</s> that has become subordinate to distraction does not belong to the category of <s>yoga</s>]. Since what accompanies distraction and the rest is not intended in the category of <s>yoga</s>. For <s>samādhi</s> accompanied by distraction and the rest is not capable of illuminating the true nature of things, since distraction and the rest are predominant. By the negation of distraction alone, the negation of the distracted and deluded is also accomplished, by the principle of defeating the chief wrestler. The predominance [of the scattered state] is because it is suitable for being the domain of practice. For a mind in the scattered state can be led toward a desired object free from partiality and the like. But a mind that is distracted by attachment to undesirable objects, or deluded by separation from desired objects, cannot be redirected otherwise.
[The category of <s>yoga</s>]: Even though <s>samādhi</s> exists [in all states], it is called a 'category' (<s>pakṣa</s>) because of its non-performance of the function. Just as for one who is walking, even though standing exists at every step, it is not called 'standing' because it does not perform the function of standing. 'Subordination to distraction' is said with reference to the single instance of <s>samādhi</s> in the scattered state. '<s>Sārvabhauma</s>' refers to predominance, having generally operated across all stages.

body.text: yastvekāgre cetasi sadbhūtamarthaṁ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśānkarmabandhanāni ślathayati nirodhamabhimukhaṁ karoti sa saṁprajñāto yoga ityākhyāyate। sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato'smitānugata ityupariṣṭānnivedayiṣyāmaḥ। sarvavṛttinirodhe tvasaṁprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ ॥ 1 ॥
body.translated_text: But the <s>samādhi</s> that, when the mind is one-pointed (<s>ekāgra</s>), illuminates the true nature of an object, attenuates the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), loosens the bonds of <s>karma</s> (action), and directs [the mind] toward <s>nirodha</s> (cessation)—that is called <s>saṃprajñāta yoga</s> (cognitive <s>yoga</s>). And it is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation), accompanied by <s>vicāra</s> (reflection), accompanied by <s>ānanda</s> (bliss), accompanied by <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness)—this we shall set forth later. But when all mental modifications (<s>vṛttis</s>) are ceased, it is <s>asaṃprajñāta samādhi</s> (non-cognitive concentration). (Sūtra 1)

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yadyupasarjanībhāvaḥ samādhipakṣāvṛttau kāraṇam , ihāpyekāgre ekāgratopasarjanatvaṁ syāt । tataśca yogapakṣāvṛttiriti cedata āha- [yastvekāgra] iti । naikāgratāyāṁ bhūmyupasarjanatvam । kutaḥ ? kleśakarmāprabalatvāt । kleśakarmāprabalatve na hi vikṣepādīnāmudayaḥ ।
ekāgratābhūmau samādhiryaḥ sa bhūtamarthaṁ yathātmānaṁ pradyotayati avagamayati । ayogyathaijñānamayathābhūtatvagandhitameveti bhūtagrahaṇam । kṣiṇoti, kṣapayati, pañcaparvaṇo'vidyādīn kleśān । karmabandhanāni, karmāṇyeva bandhanāni, dharmādharmavimiśrakarmajātāni janmādinibandhanāni, ślathayati, śithilīkaroti, nirodhamāmukhīkaroti, abhimukhīkaroti । sa samprajñāta ityākhyāyate ācārye: ॥
[sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ityādibhāṣyam] । samprajñātasya prāthamyāllakṣaṇābhidhāne prāpte, abhyarhitatvādasamprajñātasyaiva lakṣaṇaṁ yuktamiha vaktumiti samprajñātamupariṣṭāt pravedayiṣyāma ityucyate ।
itaścāsamprajñātasya lakṣaṇamihaiva vaktavyaṁ, samprajñātanirapekṣo'pyasamprajñātaḥ para(prakṛṣṭa)vairāgyavirāmapratyayābhyāsābhyāṁ sidhyatītyetatpradarśanārtham । iha samprajñātalakṣaṇābhidhāne taduttarakāle cāsamprajñātalakṣaṇābhidhāne samprajñātāpekṣayaiva asamprajñātasamādhāvadhikāra ityāśaṅkā syāt, tasmādupariṣṭāt pravedayiṣyāma ityāha ॥ 1 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
If subordination is the cause of non-inclusion in the category of <s>yoga</s>, then here too, in the one-pointed [state], there would be subordination to one-pointedness, and consequently non-inclusion in the category of <s>yoga</s>—to address this he says: [But that which is one-pointed]. There is no subordination to the stage in one-pointedness. Why? Because the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and <s>karma</s> (action) are not powerful [in that state]. When the afflictions and action are not powerful, there is no arising of distraction and the rest.
The <s>samādhi</s> that is on the stage of one-pointedness illuminates—makes known—the true nature of an object (<s>bhūtam artham</s>), as it really is. The inclusion of 'true' (<s>bhūta</s>) is because knowledge that is not of this type is tainted by being-not-as-it-really-is. It attenuates—diminishes—the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) beginning with <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), which have five divisions. 'Bonds of <s>karma</s>' means actions that are themselves bonds—the assemblage of actions constituted by <s>dharma</s> (merit), <s>adharma</s> (demerit), and mixed [karma], which are the fetters of birth and the rest. 'Loosens' means makes slack. 'Directs toward <s>nirodha</s> (cessation)' means turns toward, faces toward. That is designated by the teachers as <s>saṃprajñāta</s> (cognitive).
[And it is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s>, accompanied by <s>vicāra</s>, and so forth—this is the commentary text]. Since <s>saṃprajñāta</s> comes first [in order], it would be natural to state its definition [first]; but since <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> is more worthy of elaboration, it is appropriate to state its definition here—therefore it is said 'we shall set forth <s>saṃprajñāta</s> later.'
And for this further reason the definition of <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> should be stated here: even without dependence on <s>saṃprajñāta</s>, <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> is accomplished through the practice of supreme <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion) and <s>virāma-pratyaya</s> (the cognition of cessation)—this is to demonstrate that. If the definition of <s>saṃprajñāta</s> were stated here and the definition of <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> thereafter, the apprehension might arise that qualification for <s>asaṃprajñāta samādhi</s> depends on <s>saṃprajñāta</s> alone. Therefore he says 'we shall set forth later.' (Sūtra 1)

body.text: tasya lakṣaṇābhidhitsayedaṁ sūtraṁ pravavṛte-
body.translated_text: With the intention of stating its definition, this <s>sūtra</s> has been set forth:

body.text: yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ ॥ 2 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ</s> (<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the modifications of the mind). (Sūtra 2)

body.text: sarvaśabdāgrahaṇātsaṁprajñāto'pi yoga ityākhyāyate। cittaṁ hi prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlatvāttriguṇam।
body.translated_text: Since the word 'all' is not used [in the <s>sūtra</s>], <s>saṃprajñāta</s> (cognitive) too is called <s>yoga</s>. For the mind (<s>citta</s>) is constituted of the three <s>guṇas</s>, since its nature is that of luminosity (<s>prakhyā</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[sarvavṛttinirodhe tvasaṁprajñāta] iti । tuśabdo'vadhāraṇārthaḥ । [tasya] evaṁvidhasya samādherasaṁprajñātasyaiva kevalasya lakṣaṇābhidhitsayedaṁ [sūtraṁ pravavṛte] pravṛttaṁ ‘yogaścittavṛttinirodha:‘ i[tī]ti vaktavyam ॥
nanu ca tasya lakṣaṇamabhidhātumetat sūtraṁ pravṛttaṁ, tathā ca sati ‘yogasya cittavṛttinire.odhaḥ‘ iti vaktavyaṁ, sāmānādhikaraṇyaṁ na yuktam । na hi lakṣyameva lakṣaṇaṁ syāt । cittavṛttinirodhalakṣaṇa iti vā vaktavyam । naiṣa doṣaḥ । lakṣye । lakṣaṇādhyāsāt । yathā'yaṁ piṇḍo devadatta iti lakṣye lakṣaṇamadhyasyate (pratyasyate) ॥
nanu ca sarvavṛttinirodhe tvasamprajñātaḥ, tasya cedaṁ lakṣaṇaṁ, tataśca ‘yogaḥ sarvacittavṛttiniredhiḥ‘ iti vaktavyam । na coktam । ato'tivyāpi lakṣaṇam । sarvaśabdāgrahaṇe tāvatkāraṇamucyate-yadi sarvagrahaṇaṁ kriyate, tadaikadeśanirodhanimittasya saṁprajñātasya yogatvaṁ nivartitaṁ syāt । tanmābhūditi sarvaśabdāgrahaṇam ॥
astu tarhi saṁprajñātāsaṁprajñātayoḥ sāmānyalakṣaṇaṁ, viśeṣānupādānāt । naiṣa doṣaḥ । yoge prakṛte punaryogagrahaṇāt । viśeṣāvivakṣāyāṁ hi yogagrahaṇaṁ nārthavat syāt ॥
nanu cānuśāsane nyagbhūtatvādyogasya iha yogagrahaṇe asati cittavṛttinirodha ityukte'nuśāsanārthatā bhavet sūtrasya-naivaṁ-yogānuśāsanasya prastutatvāt । ye.āgānuśāsanaṁ hi prārabdhaṁ, nāyogānuśāsanaṁ, tallakṣaṇābhidhāne hyatiprasaṅgaḥ, . padārthāsaṅgatiśca । na hi cittavṛtinirodho yogānuśāsanamiti padārthaḥ saṅgacchate ॥
evamapi yogagrahaṇāt kuto'saṁprajñātasyaiva lakṣaṇaṁ, na punaḥ saṁprajñātasya lakṣaṇaṁ syāt, yogagrahaṇasyāviśiṣṭatvāditi ?
﻿ ucyate--avyabhicārāt । vyabhicarati na tattasya lakṣaṇaṁ, nirodhastvasaṁprajñāte'pi vartata iti saṁprajñātaṁ vyabhicarati । na hi viṣāṇitvaṁ gorliṅgaṁ, mahiṣyādibhirvyabhicārāt ॥
nanu cāsaṁprajñātamapi vyabhicarati, saṁprajñātasyāpi heyavṛttinirodhatvāt । satyamevaṁ, kiṁ tu na nirodhādanyena lakṣayitumasaṁprajñātaḥ śakyate । nirodha eva tu tasya lakṣaṇam, anyasyābhāvāt । saṁprajñātasya tvasādhāraṇavitarkādilakṣaṇalakṣyatvāt । yathā sparśalakṣaṇamityukte vāyurevāsādhāraṇyāllakṣyate sparśavatvena, atha ca vidyata eva sparśavatvaṁ tejaḥ:prabhṛtiṣvapi ॥
evaṁ ca sati yogagrahaṇamanuvādamātram । ata eva ca sarvagrahaṇaṁ na kṛtaṁ sūtre । nirodhagrahaṇenaivāsaṁprajñātalakṣaṇatve siddhe yadi sarvagrahaṇaṁ kriyeta, tatsaṁprajñātasya yogatāṁ nivārayet । tasmādasaṁprajñātasyaivedaṁ lakṣaṇam । tathā copasaṁharati bhāṣyakāraḥ-’na tatra kiṁcit saṁprajñāyate ityasaṁprajñātaḥ, sa yogaścitavṛttinirodha' iti ।
cittatadvṛttitannirodhavyācikhyāsayā cittaṁ hītyādi bhāṣyam । kimātmakaṁ punastacittaṁ, yasya vṛttinirodho yoga ityata āha- [cittaṁ hi prakhyāpravṛtti.āsthitiśīlatvāt triguṇamiti] । tatra cittaṁ triguṇamiti vyākhyāyate, prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlavāditi hetuḥ । prakhyā prakhyānaṁ prakāśanaṁ, sa hi । sattvaguṇasya dharmaḥ । pravṛttiḥ pravartanaṁ vyāpāraḥ, sa hi rajodharmaḥ । sthitiḥ sthānaṁ varaṇaṁ pratibandha iti, sa ca tamodharmaḥ । evaṁśīlāḥ hi sattvādayo guṇāḥ, cittaṁ ca prakhyādiśīlaṁ, tasmāt trayāṇāṁ guṇānāṁ pariṇāmaścittaṁ bhavitumarhati ।
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
"But when all activities (<s>vṛttis</s>) are ceased, it is <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive)." The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) is for the purpose of restriction. It should be said that this <s>sūtra</s> "<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind" was set forth with the intention of defining that very kind of <s>samādhi</s>—<s>asaṃprajñāta</s> alone, in isolation.
Objection: If this <s>sūtra</s> is set forth to define that, then it should read "The cessation of mental activities belongs to <s>yoga</s>" (in the genitive), and coordinate predication would be inappropriate. For the characterized thing itself should not be the characteristic. Or it should read "characterized by the cessation of mental activities." Reply: This is not a fault, because the characteristic is superimposed on the characterized—just as in "This body is <s>Devadatta</s>," the characteristic is superimposed on the characterized.
Objection: "But when all activities are ceased, it is <s>asaṃprajñāta</s>"—if this is its definition, then the <s>sūtra</s> should read "<s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of all mental activities." But it does not say so. Therefore the definition is too broad. The reason for not using the word 'all' is stated: If 'all' were included, it would negate the <s>yoga</s>-nature of <s>saṃprajñāta</s> (cognitive concentration), which involves the cessation of only some activities. To prevent that, the word 'all' is not included.
Objection: Then let it be the general definition of both <s>saṃprajñāta</s> and <s>asaṃprajñāta</s>, since no particular qualification is adopted. Reply: This is not a fault, because the word '<s>yoga</s>' is used again when <s>yoga</s> is already the topic. If no particular specification were intended, the word '<s>yoga</s>' would serve no purpose.
Objection: Since <s>yoga</s> is subordinated to the teaching (<s>anuśāsana</s>), if the word '<s>yoga</s>' were absent here and only 'cessation of mental activities' were stated, the <s>sūtra</s> would become a teaching about the teaching—but this is not so, because the teaching of <s>yoga</s> has been established as the topic. For the teaching of <s>yoga</s> has been commenced, not the teaching of non-<s>yoga</s>, and defining that would lead to over-extension and inconsistency of subject matter. For 'the cessation of mental activities is the teaching of <s>yoga</s>' does not cohere as a sentence.
Even so, given the use of the word '<s>yoga</s>,' how is this the definition of <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> alone and not also of <s>saṃprajñāta</s>, since the word '<s>yoga</s>' is unspecified?
Reply: Because of non-deviation. A characteristic that deviates is not a valid characteristic. Cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) is present in <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> but deviates from <s>saṃprajñāta</s>. For 'having horns' is not the defining mark of a cow, since it deviates to she-buffaloes and the like.
Objection: But it also deviates from <s>asaṃprajñāta</s>, since <s>saṃprajñāta</s> too involves the cessation of activities to be abandoned. True, but <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> cannot be characterized by anything other than cessation. Cessation alone is its characteristic, since nothing else is available. But <s>saṃprajñāta</s> is characterized by its distinctive marks of <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation) and the like, which are not shared. Just as when one says 'characterized by touch,' it is wind alone that is characterized specifically by touch, yet touch does exist in fire and the rest as well.
This being so, the use of the word '<s>yoga</s>' is merely a reiteration. For this very reason, the word 'all' (<s>sarva</s>) was not used in the <s>sūtra</s>. Since the definition as characterizing <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> is established by the use of '<s>nirodha</s>' alone, if 'all' were added, it would exclude the <s>yoga</s>-nature of <s>saṃprajñāta</s>. Therefore this is the definition of <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> alone. And thus the <s>Bhāṣya</s>-author concludes: 'Nothing is cognized therein, hence it is <s>asaṃprajñāta</s>; that <s>yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind.'
With the desire to explain the mind (<s>citta</s>), its activities (<s>vṛttis</s>), and their cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), the <s>Bhāṣya</s> beginning with 'For the mind...' is given. What is the nature of that mind whose cessation of activities is <s>yoga</s>? To this he says: "For the mind, being of the nature of illumination, activity, and stability, is composed of the three <s>guṇas</s>." Here 'the mind is composed of the three <s>guṇas</s>' is being explained, and 'being of the nature of illumination, activity, and stability' is the reason. Illumination (<s>prakhyā</s>) is manifestation, making known—that is the property of the <s>sattva guṇa</s>. Activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>) is engagement, operation—that is the property of <s>rajas</s>. Stability (<s>sthiti</s>) is fixation, obstruction, resistance—that is the property of <s>tamas</s>. Such are the natures of <s>sattva</s> and the other <s>guṇas</s>, and the mind has the nature of illumination and the rest; therefore the mind can be a transformation of the three <s>guṇas</s>.

body.text: prakhyārūpaṁ hi cittasattvaṁ rajastamobhyāṁ saṁsṛṣṭamaiśvaryaviṣayapriyaṁ bhavati। tadeva tamasā'nuviddhamadharmājñānāvairāgyānaiśvayopagaṁ bhavati। tadeva prakṣīṇamohāvaraṇaṁ sarvataḥ pradyotamānamanuviddhaṁ rajomātrayā dharmajñānavairāgyaiśvaryopagaṁ bhavati।
body.translated_text: For the <s>sattva</s> of the mind, whose nature is illumination, when mixed with <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, becomes fond of sovereignty and sense-objects. That same [mind], when pervaded by <s>tamas</s>, inclines toward <s>adharma</s> (demerit), ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty. That same [mind], when the covering of delusion is diminished, shining forth in all directions, pervaded by only a trace of <s>rajas</s>, inclines toward <s>dharma</s> (merit), knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tasya ca prakhyādihetorasiddhimāśaṁkyāha- [prakhyāsvarūpaṁ hi cittasatvamiti] । hiśabdaḥ prasiddhāvadyotanārthaḥ । prasiddhaṁ hi loke śāsre ca sarvavabhāsakatvaṁ cittasya । cittameva satvaṁ cittasatvaṁ sattvapradhānaguṇapariṇāmatvāt ॥
athavā anyasaṁsargaviyogābhyāmanekavṛtti khyātimātraṁ ca cittaṁ spaṣṭaṁ darśayituṁ śakyta iti bravīti- [prakhyāsvarūpaṁ hi cittasattvamiti] ॥
idānīṁ vṛttayo vyākhyāyante । tāsāṁ cānekatvaṁ rajastamasorudbhavābhibhavanimitte viruddhatvaṁ cetyāha- [rajastamobhyāṁ saṁsṛṣṭaṁ] samapradhānābhyāṁ yadā saṁsṛṣṭaṁ tadānīṁ [aiśvaryaviṣayapriyaṁ bhavati] ॥ prītiḥ rāgaḥ, aiśvaryaviṣayarāgayuktā vṛttayo bhavantītyarthaḥ ।
[tattamasānuviddhaṁ ॥] tadeva prakhyāsvarūpaṁ cittaṁ yadā guṇabhūtarajaskenodbhūtena tamasānuviddhaṁ, tadānīmadharmadicatuṣṭayaviṣayā vṛttayaḥ kliṣṭā jāyante ॥
[tadeva prakṣīṇamohāvaraṇamiti ॥] nyagbhūtatamaskaṁ tamaḥkṣayādeva jaladharāpagamādiva (pari)ravibimba sarvataḥ pradyotamānaṁ [rajomātrayā] rajoleśena [anuviddhaṁ] yadā tadā dharmādyupagataṁ । dharmādicatuṣṭayaviṣayā vṛttayo'kliṣṭā bhavanti ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
Anticipating the objection that the cause—namely illumination and the rest—is unestablished, he says: "For the <s>sattva</s> of the mind, whose nature is illumination..." The word 'for' (<s>hi</s>) is for indicating what is well-known. For it is well-known both in the world and in the <s>śāstra</s> that the mind illuminates everything. The <s>sattva</s> of the mind is the mind-<s>sattva</s>, because it is a transformation of <s>guṇas</s> with <s>sattva</s> as predominant.
Alternatively, he says "For the <s>sattva</s> of the mind, whose nature is illumination" in order to clearly show that the mind, through association and dissociation with other [<s>guṇas</s>], has multiple activities and is in essence mere cognition (<s>khyātimātra</s>).
Now the activities (<s>vṛttis</s>) are being explained. Their multiplicity and their conflicting nature, caused by the emergence and suppression of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, are stated: "When mixed with <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>"—when mixed with these two in equal predominance—"it becomes fond of sovereignty and sense-objects." Fondness (<s>prīti</s>) means attachment (<s>rāga</s>); the meaning is that activities endowed with attachment to sovereignty and sense-objects arise.
"That same, when pervaded by <s>tamas</s>"—that same mind whose nature is illumination, when pervaded by <s>tamas</s> which has emerged while <s>rajas</s> is subordinate—then afflicted (<s>kliṣṭa</s>) activities arise with the fourfold domain of <s>adharma</s> and the rest.
"That same, when the covering of delusion is diminished"—when <s>tamas</s> is subordinated, by the very diminishing of <s>tamas</s>, like the sun's orb when the clouds have departed, shining forth in all directions, "pervaded by only a trace of <s>rajas</s>"—when pervaded by a mere remnant of <s>rajas</s>—then it inclines toward <s>dharma</s> and the rest. Activities with the fourfold domain of <s>dharma</s> and the rest become unafflicted.

body.text: tadeva rajoleśamalāpetaṁ svarūpapratiṣṭhaṁ sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātraṁ dharmameghadhyānopagaṁ bhavati। tatparaṁ prasaṁkhyānamityācakṣate dhyāyinaḥ। citiśaktirapariṇāminyapratisaṁkramā darśitaviṣayā śuddhā cānantā ca sattvaguṇātmikā ceyamatoviparītā vivekakhyātiriti। atastasyāṁ viraktaṁ cittaṁ tāmapi khyātiṁ niruṇaddhi। tadavasthaṁ saṁskāropagaṁ bhavati। sa nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ। na tatra kiṁcitsaṁprajñāyata ityasaṁprajñātaḥ। dvividhaḥ sa yogaścittavṛttinirodha iti ॥ 2 ॥
body.translated_text: That same [mind], when freed from the stain of even a trace of <s>rajas</s>, established in its own nature, consisting merely of the cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>, inclines toward the meditation called <s>dharmamegha</s> (cloud of <s>dharma</s>). The contemplatives call that the supreme <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (discernment). The power of consciousness (<s>citiśakti</s>) is non-transforming, non-transferring, has its objects displayed [to it], is pure, infinite, and has <s>sattva-guṇa</s> as its nature—discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the opposite of this. Therefore, the mind, detached even from that discriminative knowledge, restrains even that cognition. In that state, it is accompanied only by latent impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>). That is seedless (<s>nirbīja</s>) <s>samādhi</s>. Nothing is cognized therein, hence it is <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive). That twofold <s>yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind. // 2 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yadā tadeva [rajo[leśa]malopetaṁ svarūpapratiṣṭhaṁ] kevalena svena prakhyārūpeṇāvasthitaṁ, tadā [sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātimātraṁ] bhavati । sattvaṁ cittaṁ puruṣo bhoktā tayoranyatā viviktatā tatkhyātiḥ tadavagamaḥ, tanmātragrahaṇaṁ kleśādyabhāvapradarśanārtham । [dharmameghadhyānopagaṁ bhavati] dharmamegho nāma samādhiḥ ॥
tadeva prasaṁkhyānabalādrajastamasī tiraskṛtya kevalena khyātyātmanā puruṣasvarūpamātradarśanena avasthānaṁ dhyānaṁ [prasaṁkhyānamityācakṣate] , dhyāyino yoginaḥ ॥
evaṁ vṛttisvarūpe vyākhyāte tannirodhapradarśanārthamāha-- [cittaśaktirityādi] ॥ citireva śaktiḥ [citiśaktiḥ] । yathā pacyādayaḥ śaktayaḥ śaktimadapekṣāprāpaṇīyajanmāno na svayaṁśaktayaḥ । citiḥ punaḥ svayameva śaktiḥ, nārthāntaramapekṣate । tena nilyāvasthitatvam । citiśabdasya cinmātrābhidhāyinaḥ śaktiśabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyaṁ avikṛtarūpāyā eva citerviṣayitvapradarśanārtham ॥
yasmādevamato ['pariṇāminī ।] vyavasthite dharmiṇi dharmāntaratirobhāvena dharmāntaraprādurbhāvaḥ pariṇāmaḥ । na pariṇamituṁ śīlamasyā ityapariṇāminī । ata eva [apratisaṅkramā] , pariṇāmina eva cittāderviṣayādau pratisaṅkramadarśanāt ॥
ata eva [darśitaviṣayā] darśito'ntaḥkaraṇena viṣayo'syā iti । tenaiva [śuddhā] । ata eva [anantā] deśataḥ kālataśca । pūrvapūrvamuttarasyottarasya hetutvena draṣṭavyam । vaidharmyadṛṣṭāntaḥ cittamindriyāṇi ca । [sattvaguṇātmikā] sattvameva guṇaḥ sattvaguṇaḥ tasyevātmā svarūpamavabhāso yasyāḥ seyaṁ sattvaguṇātmikā avabhāsasvarūpetyartha: । vṛtyaviśiṣṭavṛttitvādvā satvaguṇātmikepyucyate ॥
yadi vā khyātyā saṁbadhyate khyātiḥ sattvaguṇātmiketi । ata: citiśakteruktalakṣaṇāyā viparītā vilakṣaṇā vivekakhyāti: pariṇāmādimatī ॥
yasmāt puruṣādutkṛṣṭāt pariṇāmādiguṇavirahitānnikṛṣṭā pariṇāmādiguṇayuktā, ataḥ svarūpadoṣadarśanāt [tasyāṁ viraktaṁ] aparaktaṁ [tāmapi khyātiṁ] ātmano niruṇaddhi ॥
[tadavasthaṁ] nirodhāvasthaṁ, [saṁskāropagaṁ] , saṁskāramātrāvaśeṣam । niruddhāsu vṛttiṣu vṛttijanitāḥ saṁskārā evāvaśiṣyante । etasyāṁ nirodhabhūmau yaḥ samādhiḥ [sa nibajaḥ] । nirgataṁ bījamatra kleśādibījaṁ sarvamutsannamasminniti । tasmādasaṁprajñātasamādhilakṣaṇārthameva sūtramityupasaṁharati-- [sa yogaścittavṛttinirodha iti] ॥ 2 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
When that same [mind], "freed from the stain of even a trace of <s>rajas</s>, established in its own nature"—abiding solely in its own form of illumination—then it "consists merely of the cognition of the difference between <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>." <s>Sattva</s> is the mind; <s>puruṣa</s> is the experiencer; their difference (<s>anyatā</s>) is their distinctness; its cognition (<s>khyāti</s>) is its apprehension. The word 'merely' (<s>mātra</s>) indicates the absence of <s>kleśas</s> and the rest. "It inclines toward the meditation called <s>dharmamegha</s>"—the <s>samādhi</s> called <s>dharmamegha</s>.
That same [mind], having thrust aside <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> through the power of discernment, abiding solely in the form of cognition, with the mere perception of the true nature of <s>puruṣa</s>—this meditation is "what the contemplatives call <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>"—the contemplatives being the <s>yogins</s>.
Having thus explained the nature of the activities, in order to show their cessation, he says: "The power of consciousness..." and so forth. <s>Citi</s> (consciousness) itself is the power (<s>śakti</s>); hence <s>citiśakti</s>. Just as powers such as cooking depend on something possessing that power and do not arise on their own, <s>citi</s>, however, is itself the power—it does not depend on anything else. Hence its eternal abiding. The coordinated predication of the word <s>śakti</s> with the word <s>citi</s>, which denotes mere consciousness, is for the purpose of showing that <s>citi</s>, in its unmodified form, is indeed a cognizer of objects.
Because this is so, it is "non-transforming" (<s>apariṇāminī</s>). Transformation is the disappearance of one property and the appearance of another in an established substance. It is not in her nature to transform, hence she is non-transforming. For this very reason she is "non-transferring" (<s>apratisaṃkramā</s>), since transference is observed only in transforming things like the mind, toward objects and so forth.
For this very reason she is one whose "objects are displayed [to her]" (<s>darśitaviṣayā</s>)—her objects are displayed by the internal organ. Therefore she is "pure" (<s>śuddhā</s>). Therefore she is "infinite" (<s>anantā</s>)—in both space and time. Each preceding [quality] should be seen as the reason for the succeeding one. The counter-example is the mind and the sense-organs. "Whose nature is <s>sattva-guṇa</s>" (<s>sattvaguṇātmikā</s>)—<s>sattva</s> itself is the <s>guṇa</s>; <s>sattva-guṇa</s>; its nature (<s>ātman</s>), its essential form, is manifestation—this means she has manifestation as her essential nature. Or she is called <s>sattvaguṇātmikā</s> because her activity is not different from her nature.
Alternatively, it is connected with <s>khyāti</s>: the discriminative knowledge is <s>sattvaguṇātmikā</s>. Therefore, discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>), being the opposite—i.e., having different characteristics—of <s>citiśakti</s> as described, possesses transformation and the rest.
Because it is inferior, possessing the qualities of transformation and the like, compared to <s>puruṣa</s> who is superior and free from such qualities—therefore, seeing the defect in its own nature, the mind, "detached even from that cognition," restrains it.
"In that state"—the state of cessation (<s>nirodha</s>)—"accompanied only by latent impressions" (<s>saṃskāras</s>)—with only <s>saṃskāras</s> as remainder. When the activities are restrained, only the <s>saṃskāras</s> generated by the activities remain. The <s>samādhi</s> in this ground of cessation is "seedless" (<s>nirbīja</s>)—the seed, namely the seed of <s>kleśas</s> and the rest, has departed; all is eradicated in this state. Therefore he concludes that the <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of defining <s>asaṃprajñāta samādhi</s>: "That <s>yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind." // 2 //

body.text: tadavasthe cetasi viṣayābhāvādbuddhibodhātmā puruṣaḥ kiṁsvabhāva iti –
body.translated_text: When the mind is in that state, since objects are absent, what is the nature of <s>puruṣa</s>, whose essence is the awareness of cognition (<s>buddhi</s>)?

body.text: tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam ॥ 3 ॥
body.translated_text: Then [there is] the seer's abiding in its own nature. // 3 //

body.text: svarūpapratiṣṭhā tadānīṁ citiśaktiryathā kaivalye। vyutthānacitte tu sati tathā'pi bhavantī na tathā ॥ 3 ॥
body.translated_text: The power of consciousness is then established in its own nature, as in <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation). But when the mind is in the state of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>), although it is so, it does not appear so. // 3 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yogaścittavṛttinirodha ityuktaṁ, tatra boddhṛtvenaiva puruṣasadbhāvādhigamaḥ, viṣayabhūtavṛttinirodhe ca viṣayiṇo'pi boddhuḥ puruṣasya nirodhaṁ kaścidāśaṅketāpi, tathā ca sati tatkaivalyaprāptyupāyasyāpi vivekakhyāteranarthakatvaṁ manvīta yogānuśāsanasyāpi tadarthasya niṣphalatvaṁ pratipadyeta, tasmātpuruṣasya vṛttinirodhādanirodhaṁ darśayitukāmaḥ khyāteścāpi phalaṁ sākṣāddarśayannāha-- [tadavasthe cetasītyādi ॥]
[tadavasthe] -nirodhāvasthe । [svaviṣayābhāvāt] -svaviṣayaścittavṛtistadabhā(ve)vāt । [buddhibodhātmā] buddhiṁ vṛttirūpeṇa pariṇatāṁ budhyata iti buddhebauddhā puruṣaḥ । tadbodhanameva hi puruṣasya svaṁ rūpaṁ, nānyo boddhā, nānyadbodhanam । boddhuśca bodhanādanyatve sati vikriyātmakatā syāt । tataśca darśitaviṣayatvaṁ ca na syāt । tathā ca karaṇāntarāpekṣitvaṁ puruṣasya prasajyeta । tasmādbodhane boddhṛtvaṁ copacaritaṁ tadvṛttasārūpyeṇa । tathā ca vakṣyati-‘ [draṣṭā dṛśibhātraḥ’] iti । tasmādāha buddhibodhanamevātmā svarūpaṁ yasya sa buddhibodhātmā puruṣaḥ kiṁsvabhāvaḥ kiṁ naśvarasvabhāvaḥ, sadbhāve vā [kiṁsvabhāvaḥ] , kathaṁ vā sadbhāva iti ? ॥ [tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam ॥] yadā niruddhā vṛttayaḥ, [svarūpapratiṣṭhā tadānīṁ citiśaktiḥ ॥] svarūpapratiṣṭhetyarthaḥ । [yathā kaivalye ॥] tadā sadbhāvaṁ tu ‘ [na tatsvābhāsaṁ dṛśyatvāt’] ityevamādinā vakṣyati । tatra siddhe sadbhāve tata ākṛṣya prāptāśaṅkānivṛttyarthamucyata- [svarūpapratiṣṭhati ॥]
siddhavadvyākhyātaṁ sūtram । tatredaṁ prasaktamitaratra na svarūpapratiṣṭheti । anyathā hi tadeti viśeṣaṇānathaikyaṁ syāt । na cedanyatra svarūpapratiṣṭhā tatrāvasthāntarayogāt pariṇāmitvādidoṣaḥ prāpnotīti tatparihīrṣayāha– [vyutthānacitte tu sati tathāpi bhavantīti ।] [anena] anyatrāpi svarūpapratiṣṭhatvaṁ darśayati ॥
na tathetyanena tadeti viśeṣaṇasyārthavattvaṁ khyāpayati ॥ 3 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
It has been said that <s>yoga</s> is the cessation of the activities of the mind. Since <s>puruṣa</s>'s existence is apprehended only through its role as knower (<s>boddhṛ</s>), and since upon the cessation of the activities that are its objects, someone might suspect the cessation of the knower—<s>puruṣa</s>—as well, and in that case one might consider even discriminative knowledge, the means to attaining <s>kaivalya</s>, to be purposeless, and would conclude that the teaching of <s>yoga</s>, which exists for that purpose, is fruitless—therefore, wishing to show that <s>puruṣa</s> is not destroyed by the cessation of activities, and also directly showing the fruit of discriminative knowledge, he says: "When the mind is in that state..." and so forth.
"In that state"—the state of cessation. "Since its own objects are absent"—the mind's activity is its own object; in the absence of that. "Whose essence is the awareness of cognition" (<s>buddhibodhātmā</s>)—<s>puruṣa</s> cognizes <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) transformed in the form of activities; hence he is the knower of <s>buddhi</s>. That awareness of <s>buddhi</s> is indeed <s>puruṣa</s>'s own nature—there is no other knower, no other knowing. For if the knower were different from the knowing, it would be of the nature of change. And then it would not have its objects displayed to it. And so <s>puruṣa</s> would require another instrument [of cognition]. Therefore, the knower-status attributed to knowing is figurative, through conformity with the form of the activity. Thus it will be said: "The seer is mere seeing" (YS 2.20). Therefore he says: <s>puruṣa</s>, whose essence is the awareness of <s>buddhi</s>—of what nature is he? Is he of perishable nature? Or, given his existence, of what nature? And how does his existence stand?
"Then [there is] the seer's abiding in its own nature." When the activities are restrained—"The power of consciousness is then established in its own nature." That is the meaning. "As in <s>kaivalya</s>." Its existence, however, will be explained by means such as "It is not self-luminous, because it is an object of perception" (YS 4.19) and the rest. Once existence is established there, it is drawn here and stated to remove the apprehended doubt—"established in its own nature."
The <s>sūtra</s> is explained as though [this is] established. And here the implication is that in the other case [i.e., in <s>vyutthāna</s>] it is not established in its own nature. For otherwise the qualifier 'then' (<s>tadā</s>) would be meaningless. And if it were not established in its own nature elsewhere, the fault of being transforming and the rest would follow, since it would be subject to different states. To remove that, he says: "But when the mind is in the state of emergence, although it is so, it does not appear so." By this he shows that even elsewhere, it is established in its own nature.
And by "not so" he makes the qualifier 'then' meaningful. // 3 //

body.text: kathaṁ tarhi, darśitaviṣayatvāt –
body.translated_text: How then [does it appear otherwise]? Because its objects are displayed [to it]—

body.text: vṛttisārupyamitaratra ॥ 4 ॥
body.translated_text: There is conformity with the activities at other times. // 4 //

body.text: vyutthāne yāścittavṛttayastadaviśiṣṭavṛttiḥ puruṣaḥ। tathā ca sūtram – “ekameva darśanaṁ khyātireva darśanam” iti। cittamayaskāntamaṇikalpaṁ saṁnidhimātropakāri dṛśyatvena svaṁ bhavati puruṣasya svāminaḥ। tasmāccittavṛttibodhe puruṣasyānādiḥ saṁbandho hetuḥ ॥ 4 ॥
body.translated_text: In the state of emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>), whatever <s>cittavṛttis</s> (mental modifications) there are — the <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self) has a modification indistinguishable from those. And thus the <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism) [of the earlier teacher]: 'There is only one seeing; <s>khyāti</s> (cognition) alone is seeing.' The <s>citta</s> (mind) is like a lodestone — it assists merely through proximity; by virtue of its visibility (<s>dṛśyatva</s>), it becomes the property of the <s>Puruṣa</s>, its master. Therefore, the beginningless connection (<s>anādi-saṃbandha</s>) of the <s>Puruṣa</s> is the cause of [its] awareness of <s>cittavṛttis</s>. || 4 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
itarastu tathāpi bhavantītyanena cetsvarūpapratiṣṭhatvamucyate, na tatheti ca svarūpapratiṣṭhatvaniṣedhaścedekasya vastunastathābhāvaścātathābhāvaśva virudhyata iti vīkṣāpannaḥ pṛcchati-- [kathaṁ tarhi] iti ॥ itara āha-- [vṛttisārūpyamitaratreti ॥] kasmāt punarvṛttisārūpyam ? [darśitaviṣayatvāt ॥] ubhayatra svarūpapratiṣṭhatvāviśeṣe'pi vṛttisārūpyāsārūpyakṛtī viśeṣa iti, na tathābhāvātathābhāvavirodhaḥ ॥
nanu ca vṛttisārūpyayoge sati avasthāntarayogāt pariṇāmitvādidoṣaḥ prāpnotyeva । na । darśitaviṣayatvena parihṛtatvāt । cittavṛttyadhyāropitaṁ hi tat, na svataḥ, sphaṭikādyupadhānoparāgavat । [vyutthāna] iti ॥ nirodhādanyatra yāścittasya kliṣṭādayo vṛttayaḥ tābhiraviśiṣṭā sadṛśī vṛttiḥ svarūpamasya, cittavṛttivyatirekeṇa svarūpavyatirekeṇa ca puruṣasya vṛtyabhāvāt sadā jñātaviṣayatve pariṇāmānupapatteśca ।
tathā ca pūrvācāryasūtram [ekameva darśanaṁ] -buddhipuruṣayoḥ । kiṁ tadityāha-- [khyātireva darśanam] । buddhivṛttireva darśanam । khyāyate puruṣeṇeti ca khyātiḥ khyāyate'nayā ca buddhipuruṣayoḥ svarūpamiti khyātiḥ । saivārthākāro'nayā (kāratayā) gṛhyata iti karaṇaṁ, svena ca khyātirūpeṇa gṛhyata iti karma ca bhavati । tathā dṛśyata iti darśanaṁ, dṛśyate'neneti ca, [jñāyata iti jñānaṁ,] jñāyate'neneti ca sarvamevamādi draṣṭavyam ॥
yattu khyātikartṛtve cittasya tadeva jñāyate jānāti ceti (jñānāditiceti) jñānāntarakalpanāvaiyarthyaprasaṅga iti, tasya ‘ [na tatsvābhāsaṁ dṛśyatvāt] ' ityatraiva pariharaṁ vakṣyāmaḥ ।
nanu ca yadi cittaparivijṛmbhitamevedaṁ sarvaṁ puruṣaścedudāste kathamasau bhokteti ? na-kārakavaicitryāt । kānicidvyāpriyamāṇāni kārakāṇi, kānicidyāpārādṛte sannidhimātreṇa kartṛtvaṁ pratipadyante ॥
yathā pacatītyadhiśrayaṇādiṣu vyāpriyamāṇaḥ puruṣaḥ kartetyucyate । sthālī sambhavadhāraṇābhyāmavyāpriyamāgaiva pacatītyucyate । tathā sthālīmadhyagatamākāśamavakāśe dadāti, na tasya vyāpāraṁ pratīmaḥ । ।
yathā ca rājā darśanamātreṇaiva kartā । sarvaṇi ca kārakāṇi sveṣu vyāpāreṣu kartṝṇi । na cādityaḥ prakāśayan karaṇāntaramapekṣate, vyāpriyate vā । na hi prakāśanamavidyamānamutpādayati gamanādivat । prakāśātmataiva hi tasya sadbhāvaḥ, tathāpi sannidhimātraṇa ghaṭādīnāṁ prakāśarūpeṇa abhivyakteḥ prakāśayatītyucyate, evamihāpi dṛśimātreṇa puruṣeṇa dṛśyānāṁ cittavṛttīnāṁ cidātmanā vyāpyamānatvātū, draṣṭā puruṣa itīmamarthaṁ darśayati- [cittamayaskāntamaṇikalpamiti ॥]
yasyāpyātmamanassaṁyogāt jñānamutpadyate, tasyāpi jñānena jñeyaṁ vyāpnuvannātmā jñātetyucyate, na vyāpriyamāṇaḥ । jñānama(syā)pi guṇatve sati niṣkriyatvādātmana evārthaṁ darśayati । nāpi kriyānabhyupagamāt jānātītyādi nopapadyate । jñānena hi jñeyaṁ vyāpnuvan jānātītyucyate ॥
kiṁ cānyat–ātmamanassaṁyogādapūrvajñānotpattau satyāmātmanastajjñānaṁ, na manasaḥ । ātmaiva jānāti, na mana iti ko heturbhavet ? athāpi syāt ātmanaḥ samavāyikāraṇatvāditi । naitadevaṁ, asiddhatvāt । yathaiva jñānamātmana iti sādhyaṁ, evamātmana eva samavāyikāraṇatvaṁ na manasa iti sādhyam, anātmasvarūpatve satyubhayasaṁyegajatvābhyupagamāt ॥
athāpi syāt-jñānāhitasaṁskārasyātma[naḥ]smṛtyekakartṛtvena pratisandhānadarśanāditi-na-tasyāpi sādhyatvāt । tatrāpi jñānasaṁskārasmṛtipratisandhānādīnyātmana eva, na manasa iti sādhanīyāni । phalena samānāśrayavādicchādīnāmiti cet-na-tatrapi tulyatvāt । saṁyogajatve satyātmanaḥ phalecchādīni, na manasa iti duḥsādhameva ॥
kiṁ cāsya jñānasyāpi jñeyatvābhyupagamādanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ । na hi jñānamanyena karaṇabhūtena jñānena vijñātuṁ śakyaṁ, tadapyanyena tadapyanyenelyaniṣṭaprasaṅgāt ॥
athānavasthāprasaṅgaparihārāya dūramapi gatvā kiṁcijjñānamādyaṁ vā jñānāntareṇa na gṛhyate svayamātmanaiva gṛhyata iti, tathā jñānavadarthasyāpi svayaṁ grahaṇaprasaṅgaḥ ॥
atha dīpavat svayamavabhāsate cāvabhāsayati ca avabhāsātmakatvāt, arthasyānavabhāsātmakatvādadoṣa iti cet-tathāpi prakāśasvarūpeṣvartheṣu vijñānenāgrahaṇaprasaṅgaḥ ।
atha jñānasyātmasamavetatvābhāsanarūpābhyāṁ svayaṁ grahaṇaṁ, bahiḥprakāśātmakānāṁ tu jñānaviparītadharmatvādadoṣa iti cet-tacca na-yadi cātmasamavetatvaṁ prakāśātmakatvaṁ ca jñānasya svayaṁgrahaṇe hetuḥ syāt sarve sarvajñāḥ prāpnuvanti ॥
atha grāhyākāratvamapi kāraṇaṁ cet---tacca na ; anyasya jñānasyānyākāratayā karaṇatve yathā, tathā jñānasyapi grāhyasyānyākaraṇānyadeva jñāne karaṇaṁ syāt, tathā cānavasthā duṣpariharaiva ॥
kiṁ cānyat---na hi kaścit svayaṁgrāhyagrāhakatvaprasādhanāya dṛṣṭānto vidyate, pradīpasyāpi cakṣurādigrāhyatvāt । na cāpyaṁśadvayamasti jñānasya, niravayavatvāt । satyapi cāṁśadvaye tayoḥ prakāśātmakatvānnānyonyagrāhyagrāhakabhāvaḥ pradīpayoriva dvayoḥ ॥
kiṁ cānyat-jñānasya grāhyagrāhakatvābhyupagame satyātmasadbhāvo'pi dussampāda eva । tasmādarthākārajñānasmṛtipratisandhānaprayatnecchādīnāmanātmadharmatvaṁ grāhyatvāt rūpādīnāmiva । parārthatvācca saṅghātāśrayatvaṁ rūpādinidarśanenaiva । tathā āśrayavattvādanityatvācca prayatnapūrvakatvāccetyevamādibhyo'nātmadharmatvasiddhiḥ ॥
[ayaskāntamaṇikalpam ॥] ayaskāntamaṇiriva । yathā ayaskāntamaṇirayasaḥ svātmavyāptiṁ pratyupakaroti sannidhimātreṇa, tathā cittamapi citsvarūpasyātmanaḥ svātmavyāptiṁ pratyupakaroti dṛśyatvena ॥
nartakīva darśitaviṣayatvādantaḥkaraṇenetyuktam-tatra darśayitṛtvaṁ cittasya, draṣṭṛtvaṁ ca puruṣasya kiṁkṛtam ? svasvāmitvakṛtam । kathaṁ punaḥ svasvāmitvam ? vastusvabhāvatvāt । kathamiti ceduktaṁ- [cittamayaskāntamaṇikalpamiti ॥] atha cittavṛttīnāṁ bodhe ko hetuḥ puruṣasyeti ? ucyate - yasmādevaṁ [sannidhimātropakāri] cittaṁ [dṛśyatvena,] tasmā [ccittavṛttīnāṁ bodhe puruṣasya] ayaṁ [hetuḥ] bhavati, yo'sau [anādisambandhaḥ] ॥ 4 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
If by the [statement] 'the other [i.e., Puruṣa] nevertheless exists thus,' establishment in one's own nature (<s>svarūpa-pratiṣṭhatva</s>) is being stated, and by 'not thus,' establishment in one's own nature is being denied — then for a single entity, being-thus and not-being-thus would be contradictory. Perplexed by this observation, [the student] asks: 'How then [is this possible]?' The other [teacher] says: '[There is] conformity with the mental modifications (<s>vṛtti-sārūpya</s>) in the other [state, i.e., emergence].' Why is there conformity with the modifications? '[Because of] having been shown as an object (<s>darśita-viṣayatva</s>).' Even though there is no difference in establishment in one's own nature in both [states], the distinction is produced by conformity and non-conformity with the modifications — therefore there is no contradiction between being-thus and not-being-thus.
But if there is conformity with the modifications, then since there would be [different] states, the fault of changeability (<s>pariṇāmitva</s>) and the like would certainly follow. No — because it is resolved by [the qualification] 'having been shown as an object.' For that [conformity] is superimposed by the <s>cittavṛtti</s>, not intrinsic [to Puruṣa] — like the coloration of a crystal by a [colored] substrate placed near it. '[In] emergence (<s>vyutthāna</s>)' — in states other than cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), whatever <s>kliṣṭa</s> (afflicted) and other modifications of the <s>citta</s> exist, the <s>Puruṣa</s>'s own nature is a modification indistinguishable from and similar to those — because apart from the <s>cittavṛtti</s> and apart from its own nature, there is no [separate] modification of <s>Puruṣa</s>, and because if it always had known objects [independently], transformation would be inexplicable.
And thus the <s>sūtra</s> of the earlier teacher: '[There is] only one seeing' — of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) and <s>Puruṣa</s>. What is that? He says: '<s>Khyāti</s> (cognition) alone is seeing.' The <s>buddhi-vṛtti</s> (intellectual modification) alone is seeing. '<s>Khyāti</s>' because it is cognized by <s>Puruṣa</s>; and '<s>khyāti</s>' because the own-nature of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> is cognized through it. That very [thing], because the form of the object is grasped by means of it (<s>kāratā</s>), is an instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>); and because it is grasped in its own cognitive form, it also becomes an object (<s>karma</s>). Likewise: 'it is seen' — hence 'seeing' (<s>darśana</s>); 'it is seen by means of this' — and so on. ['It is known' — hence 'knowledge' (<s>jñāna</s>); 'it is known by means of this' — ] all such [expressions] should be understood in this manner.
As for [the objection] that if the <s>citta</s> is the agent of cognition, then [the same thing] 'is known' and 'knows' — leading to the absurdity of postulating another cognition — we shall state the resolution of that at [the sūtra] 'It does not self-illuminate, because of its visibility (<s>dṛśyatva</s>).'
But if all this is merely the display of the <s>citta</s> and the <s>Puruṣa</s> remains inactive, how is he the experiencer (<s>bhoktṛ</s>)? No [problem] — because of the variety of causal factors (<s>kāraka</s>). Some causal factors [are called agents] while actively operating; others assume agency merely through proximity, without [actually] operating.
Just as in 'he cooks' — the person who engages in placing [the pot] on the fire and the like is called the agent. The pot — without operating, merely through its capacities of producing and containing — is [also] said to 'cook.' Similarly, the space within the pot gives room [to the contents], yet we do not perceive any operation of it.
And just as a king is the agent merely by seeing [overseeing]. And all causal factors are agents in their respective operations. And the sun, while illuminating, does not require another instrument, nor does it operate. For illumination does not produce something non-existent, like movement and the like. Its very nature is luminosity; yet because of the manifestation of pots and the like in the form of illumination through mere proximity, it is said to 'illuminate.' So here too — because <s>Puruṣa</s>, through mere seeing (<s>dṛśimātra</s>), pervades the visible <s>cittavṛttis</s> with the nature of consciousness (<s>cidātman</s>), [he is called] the Seer (<s>Draṣṭṛ</s>). To demonstrate this meaning, [the text says]: '[The citta is] like a lodestone.'
Even for one who holds that knowledge arises from the conjunction of <s>Ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> (mind) — even there the <s>Ātman</s>, pervading the knowable through knowledge, is called 'the knower,' without operating. Even for him, since knowledge is a <s>guṇa</s> (quality) [of the Self] and the Self is actionless — this demonstrates the very same point. Nor is it the case that because action is not accepted, [expressions like] 'he knows' are inapplicable — for pervading the knowable through knowledge, one is said to 'know.'
Furthermore — if, from the conjunction of <s>Ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, a previously non-existent knowledge arises, and that knowledge belongs to the <s>Ātman</s>, not to <s>manas</s> — the <s>Ātman</s> alone knows, not <s>manas</s> — what would be the reason [for this]? If one should say: 'Because the <s>Ātman</s> is the inherent cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>)' — this is not so, because it is unestablished. Just as 'knowledge belongs to the Self' is something to be proved, so too 'the inherent causality belongs to the Self alone and not to manas' is something to be proved — since, given that [knowledge] is not of the nature of either [Ātman or manas independently], conjunction-born-ness [from both] is accepted.
If one should say: 'Because memory — bearing the impressions deposited by knowledge — [demonstrates] single agency [of the Self] through the evidence of recognition (<s>pratisandhāna</s>)' — no, because that too is something to be proved. There too, knowledge, impression, memory, recognition, etc. belong to the Self alone and not to manas — [these all] need to be established. [If one argues:] 'Because [their] fruits — desire and the like — reside in the same substrate [as the Self]' — no, because [the difficulty is] equal there too. Given that [they are] born from conjunction, [proving that] the fruits such as desire belong to the Self and not to manas is indeed difficult to establish.
