'Because of non-attainment' is the reason (<s>hetu</s>). 'Like <s>Caitra</s>' is the example, which, like 'like a crow's eye,' applies to both formulations. ['The moon and stars possess motion'] establishes the relation through agreement (<s>sādharmya</s>); ['the <s>Vindhya</s> has not reached'] through difference (<s>vaidharmya</s>). This being so, the observation of both positive and negative concomitance causes no fault.

Alternatively, in this formulation, the absence of fault is demonstrated through the observation of the converse of the negative concomitance. And because the definition is implied by a particular instance of what is defined, there is no fault.

A trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is one motivated by the desire to benefit others, free from faults, and who has perceived or inferred the matter in question. ['The matter perceived or inferred by him'] is communicated to a particular listener ['for the transfer of his own knowledge'] for the transmission of his own understanding ['through speech' (<s>śabda</s>)]—'speech' means a sentence, since the understanding of a specific meaning comes from it. Therefore, from the sentence taught by him, ['the cognitive activity whose object is that']—the cognitive activity whose object is the meaning of the sentence—that, like inference, is predominantly characterized by the ascertainment of the universal.

Thus, preceded by the apprehension of properties such as trustworthiness, ['scripture (<s>āgama</s>) belongs to the listener'], not to the speaker. For the speaker has perceived or inferred the matter; his knowledge is either perceptual or inferential. But the listener's certain cognition, preceded by hearing, is distinct from both inferential and perceptual. That scripture (<s>āgama</s>) is not perception, because it does not have a sense-object as its domain; and it is not inference, because it is independent of the stated relation between mark and marked. For the knowledge connected with the meaning of words about heaven, <s>apūrva</s>, deities, and the like does not arise preceded by the acquisition of the relation between mark and marked. The result, however, is in all cases merely a difference in human cognitive activity.

['Whose speaker'] is the speaker of the scripture, the cause of the cognitive activity called scripture, by uttering words... The result has been demonstrated through the presentation of the prior scripture; the result, however, is as before. Even if there is only one prior scripture, since only the mere existence or non-existence of what is to be established and what establishes it is intended, there is no fault from the observation of reversed negative concomitance—so it is said.

Scripture is qualified as having an untrustworthy speaker. How is that speaker untrustworthy? Hence it is said: ['The matter has been neither perceived nor inferred'] by that speaker. One who teaches contrary to what is well-known to the learned world—such as a <s>Buddha</s>, an <s>Arhat</s>, etc. For one whose inner faculties are not damaged by faults such as passion does not describe what is well-known otherwise. ['That scripture floats']—becomes mere semblance.

Although the showing of semblances of perception and inference was not done explicitly by its own term, nevertheless through the presentation of semblances of scripture, the semblances of perception, inference, etc. should also be understood as being contrary to the stated definitions—this is stated by implication.

['But in the case of the original speaker']—in the case of the first speaker, <s>Īśvara</s> (God)—the scripture arising from him, because of the absence of a cause for its floating, would be unfloating. Like a truthful speaker.

Comparison (<s>upamāna</s>) is preceded by verbal communication. Because it falls within the scope of scripture, it is not a separate means of valid knowledge. For instance, when one is told 'a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is like a cow,' merely from that sentence one has ascertained the similarity. Then upon seeing a <s>gavaya</s> in the forest, there is merely the memory of the similarity presented by the previously heard sentence—nothing more. The similarity has been understood from the sentence itself.

Nor is it a means of valid knowledge merely from the understanding of the relation between name and named, since that too is understood from that very sentence. For one who has not learned the name '<s>gavaya</s>' from the mere word 'cow,' even upon seeing a <s>gavaya</s> in the forest, does not have the understanding of the relation between name and named: 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>.'

Therefore, in that sentence, the word '<s>gavaya</s>' must also be expected in 'a <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow.' This being so, everything is understood from the previously heard sentence alone. Even if one were to say 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>' is not the object of previous cognition—even that, for those who also see the resolution of this objection, appears to be a position maintained in a corner, like that of a squeezed domestic animal.

For thus, many different types of comparison would follow due to differences in proximity and distance of place, time, etc. If one says 'let it be so'—then this has already been established earlier, that either the non-factual nature through previous cognition alone, or the thing with all its particularities internally contained, should be understood as before. For without the specification of place, time, etc., there is no understanding of meaning from the word 'cow' when connected with 'like.'

Furthermore, comparison is not the understanding of the relation between name and named. For that by which comparison is made is comparison—and that is the knowledge of similarity. For nothing is compared merely through the understanding of the relation between names; that comes later. For only after ascertaining similarity does 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>' also follow.

Then it might be a separate means of valid knowledge not preceded by words, as when a villager, from seeing a <s>gavaya</s>, has the cognition 'this is similar to my cow'—but this too is not so, because of the absence of an object of knowledge. For when a means of valid knowledge is accepted as apprehending what exists, it operates only when there is an object of knowledge. But between a cow and a <s>gavaya</s>, there is in reality no single entity called 'similarity' that is both excluded and included.

Objection: But this person certainly has a cognition of similarity; it cannot be without a basis. True. The investigation there is: is that cognition like the cognition of a forest etc.? Or like the cognition of a pot etc.? What follows? If it is like the forest-cognition, then just as trees with a specific configuration are the causes of the forest-cognition without being a single entity separate from themselves, similarly the parts of a cow and a <s>gavaya</s>, merely through the observation and memory of both, would be the cause of the cognition of similarity, which is non-existent as something separate from them—thus its non-substantiality follows.

But if its substantiality and status as a means of valid knowledge are like the cognition of a pot etc., then it would exist.

There we investigate: what kind of entity is it? Is it a single similarity present in both cow and <s>gavaya</s>, different from cowness and <s>gavaya</s>-ness? Or are they themselves mutually qualified? Or are there two separate similarities in the substrates, cow and <s>gavaya</s>, different from those two, mutually independent or dependent? Is it a particular, qualified by one of the universals? Is it a universal, qualified by one or both particulars? Or is it the relation among these, as appropriate to each alternative?—one should elaborate many more alternatives through individual, mutual, qualifier-qualified relations, etc.

If there is a single similarity present in both, then there would be no comparison because of oneness, as in 'a cow is like a cow.' If a particular is compared through it—this too is not so, because it belongs to itself: 'a cow is like cowness.' If one particular is compared to another through what possesses it—this too is not so, for cowness is not the cause of the comparison of the hornless or tonsured. If similarity is said to be the cause of that cognition in dependence on another property—then similarity is destroyed; let that property itself be the cause of that cognition; what use is similarity, that imposed fiction?

Moreover, that property, when considered—is it one, like similarity, present in both, or different?—the same alternatives arise, and the impossibility is as before. If similarity is said to be different—this too is not so, because of the very difference; for one does not say 'a cow is like a horse.' Just as the impossibility arises from oneness, so too from many things being considered together. By this, the previously imagined alternatives of universal, particular, and relation are refuted.

If similarity is posited because the arising of the cognition cannot be explained otherwise—even so, since the experience of forest, cave, north, south, etc. cognitions cannot be explained otherwise, why not posit their substantiality? One might think: 'this is your position—the trees themselves are the causes of that cognition there.' If so, then the cognition 'the cow is similar to the <s>gavaya</s>' is a false cognition, like the forest-cognition. If those parts are excluded from each other—what then is the purpose of comparison? 'A cow is like a horse.' But if those parts, having both excluded and included aspects, are causes of that cognition—even then, the same as the forest-cognition follows.

Therefore, upon examination it does not withstand scrutiny. Those very parts perceived in both, being numerous, are the cause of the similarity-cognition, just as trees are of the forest-cognition. Thus it is established that comparison is not a separate means of valid knowledge.

Nor should one posit a duality of means of valid knowledge from a duality of objects of knowledge. Why? Because the understanding of objects follows from the means of valid knowledge, not the positing of means of knowledge from objects. If means of knowledge were posited from objects, this cannot be done now, because people are not omniscient. The cognition 'heaven results from worshipping a <s>caitya</s> (shrine)'—the cognition that worshipping a shrine is the cause of heaven, since it is not the domain of perception or inference, would be false. Or a separate means of knowledge would have to be posited for it.

If one says that cognition is the result of inference—then the unwanted consequence that the result would arise from something other than the means of valid knowledge. Similarly, the cognition of the meaning of sentences about the three instruments etc. would also follow.

Nor is the purpose here to establish the definition of means of valid knowledge, since the text is concerned with demonstrating the means of cessation of well-known cognitive activities such as means of valid knowledge etc. For this very reason the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras) did not compose a sūtra on this. But the commentator merely relied on some restatement of what is well-known, and following that, something has been said. (6-7)

body.text: viparyayo mithyājñānamatadrūpapratiṣṭham ॥ 8 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Viparyaya</s> (error) is false knowledge not established in the true form [of the object]. // 8 //

body.text: sa kasmānna pramāṇam? yataḥ pramāṇena bādhyate। bhūtārthaviṣayatvātpramāṇasya। tatra pramāṇena bādhanamapramāṇasya dṛṣṭam। tadyathā – dvicandradarśanaṁ sadviṣayeṇaikacandradarśanena bādhyata iti।
body.translated_text: Why is it not a valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>)? Because it is contradicted by valid knowledge. For valid knowledge has a real object as its content. It is observed that what is not valid knowledge is contradicted by valid knowledge. For example, the perception of two moons is contradicted by the single-moon perception whose object is real.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
pramāṇākhyāṁ vṛttiṁ vyākhyāya viparyayābhidhānāṁ vṛttimidānīmupavyācikhyāsamāna āha- [viparyayo mithyājñānamiti] ॥
nanu nirodhasya prakṛtatvāttasya ca hānatvāddhānasya ca heyāpekṣatvāddheyasya cāvidyāmūlatvādavidyā ca viparyaya iti sa eva prādhānyena niroddhavyaḥ । tatprabhavatvāddheyasya । kāraṇanirodhe hi kāryamarthādeva niruddhaṁ syāt । tasmādviparyayaḥ prādhānyāt pramāṇāta pūrvaṁ vyākhyātavyaḥ ॥
satyamevamasyeva prāthamyaṁ viparyayasya nirodhanīyatayā, tathāpi guṇadoṣajñānāpekṣatvānnirodhaṁ prati puruṣapravṛtteḥ । pramāṇameva hi guṇadoṣajñānam । na hyapramāṇena viparyayasya duṣṭatvaṁ gamyate, nirodhatatphalasādhanāni vā jñāyante । tasmāt pramāṇavṛttereva prāthamyaṁ yuktam । jñāyete ca guṇadoṣau pramāṇeneti tadanantaraṁ viparyayābhidhānam । vṛtyantarāpekṣayā tu viparyayasya prāthamyam । tanmūlasvācca vṛttyantarāṇāṁ tannirodhapūrvamevānyanirodhopapatteḥ ॥
[viparyayo mithyājñāna] miti paryāyakathanam । [atadrūpapratiṣṭha] miti lakṣaṇe.oktiḥ ! tasya rūpaṁ tadrūpaṁ na tadrūpamatadrūpaṁ, yadābhāsaṁ vijñānaṁ tasya vijñānasya ca sā pratiṣṭhā ālambanam । agṛhītaviśeṣasya sāmānyamātra-- buddhirupalabdhapūrvānyavastusmṛtyupasaṁhitā niścayākaraṇopasaṁhitā niścayākāreṇīpajāyamānā viparyayaḥ ॥
saṁśayo hyubhayoridaṁ sāmānyamityevaṁ gṛhītasāmānyasya viśeṣameva bubhutsamānasya jāyata iti smṛtāvevāntarbhavati । yathā sthāṇuḥ kiṁ vā puruṣa iti gṛhītapūrvasyaiva viśeṣasya smarataḥ saṁśaye । jāyate, na tathā viparyayaḥ । anyatarasmaraṇamātreṇaivāvasitatvāt । tadyathā---sthāṇau purastādavasthite pariṇāhārohaṇādisāmānyamātropalambhena samupajātapuruṣasmaraṇasya puruṣa evāyamiti niścitā buddhirutpadyate ॥
sā yadyapīndriyamārgeṇopalabhyamānavastusāmānyapradhānā, tathāpi smaryamāṇātadvastupratiṣṭhatvānna pramāṇam ! smṛtyavasānā hi sā, [yataḥ pramāṇena prabādhyate] a(ā) bhūtārtha(rthādi)viṣayatvāt ! (ityataḥ pratiṣṭhatvādityetat) abhūto hi smaryamāṇo'rthastadā ! yadyevaṁ smṛtireva prāpnoti-na-viśiṣṭatvāt । upalabhyamānaṁ vastu nimitīkṛtyānyatra smṛtirjāyate yathānubhūtavastuviṣayā । na viparyayastathā । sannihitasāmānyamātre deśakālādiviśeṣānugate vastuni smaraṇaparyavasānatve satyapyayamiti viśeṣarūpeṇa viparyayapratyayo jāyate । tasmādevaṁ na pramāṇadharmoṁ nāpi smṛtidharma iti vṛtyantaratvam ॥
tatrāpramāṇasya pramāṇena bādhasaṁdarśanārthamudāharaṇaṁ darśayani- [tadyathā dvicandradarśanamiti ।] yathā kācakāmalādyupahatadarśanasyābhūtārthaviṣayatvāddhi dvicandradarśanasya [sadviṣayeṇa] bhūtārthaviṣayeṇa [ekacandradarśanena] dvitīyacandrābhāvopapattijñānasmṛtyanugṛhītena bādhanam ॥
nanu ca dvicandramiti dvipūlī pañcapūlītivat dviguṇasamāsatvāt “dvigurekavacanam' iti pratilabdhe tadbhāvāt ‘akārāntottarapado dviguḥ striyāmiṣṭaḥ’ iti dvigorakārāntāt (iti) dvicandraśabdādīkāraḥ prāpnoti-naiṣa doṣaḥ-pātrādipratiṣedhāt । tatra cādiśabdasya prakāravacanatvāt । prakārasya ca śiṣṭaprayogānusāritvāt samādhipādaḥ prathamaḥ ।
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Having explained the cognitive modification called <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge), now wishing to explain the modification called <s>viparyaya</s> (error), he says: ["<s>Viparyaya</s> is false knowledge..."].
Objection: Since <s>nirodha</s> (cessation) is the subject under discussion, and since it is to be abandoned (<s>hāna</s>), and since what is to be abandoned depends upon what is to be rejected (<s>heya</s>), and since what is to be rejected is rooted in <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), and since <s>avidyā</s> is <s>viparyaya</s>—that very thing should primarily be suppressed, because what is to be rejected originates from it. For when the cause is suppressed, the effect would naturally be suppressed too. Therefore, <s>viparyaya</s>, being primary, should have been explained before <s>pramāṇa</s>.
True, <s>viparyaya</s> does indeed have primacy insofar as it is to be suppressed; nevertheless, because a person's effort toward <s>nirodha</s> depends on the knowledge of merits and faults, and valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) itself is the knowledge of merits and faults—for it is not through invalid knowledge that the faultiness of <s>viparyaya</s> is understood, nor are <s>nirodha</s>, its fruit, and the means [to it] known [thereby]—therefore the primacy of the <s>pramāṇa</s> modification is justified. And since merits and faults are known through <s>pramāṇa</s>, the discussion of <s>viparyaya</s> follows immediately after. But relative to the other modifications, <s>viparyaya</s> has primacy, because the other modifications are rooted in it, and the suppression of the others is possible only after its suppression.
["<s>Viparyaya</s> is false knowledge"]—this is a statement of synonyms. ["Not established in the true form"]—this is the statement of the definition. Its form is 'that-form' (<s>tadrūpa</s>); not that-form is 'not-that-form' (<s>atadrūpa</s>)—that is, a cognition whose appearance [does not correspond to the real object]; and that [not-that-form] is its basis (<s>pratiṣṭhā</s>), its support (<s>ālambana</s>). <s>Viparyaya</s> is a cognition that, when the specific [nature of an object] has not been grasped, being merely a general notion conjoined with the memory of some previously perceived object, arises in the form of a determinate judgment without [actually] producing certainty.
For doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) arises in one who, having grasped the common feature [thinking] 'this is what both share,' wishes to know the specific difference—thus it falls within memory. Just as one who remembers a previously perceived specific [feature] has the doubt 'Is it a post or a person?'—<s>viparyaya</s> does not arise in that way, because it is settled merely by the recollection of one [alternative]. For example: when a post stands before one, through the mere perception of general features such as girth and height, the memory of a person arises, and the determinate cognition 'this is indeed a person' is produced.
Even though this [cognition] is predominantly based on the general features of the object perceived through the sense-channel, nevertheless, because it is established in an unreal object that is [merely] remembered, it is not valid knowledge. For it concludes in memory. ["Because it is contradicted by valid knowledge"]—since its object is not real. For the remembered object is unreal at that time. If so, it would amount to mere memory—no, because it is distinct. Memory arises by taking some perceived object as a cause, having as its content a previously experienced object. <s>Viparyaya</s> is not like that. Though it concludes in recollection regarding an object that merely possesses the general feature present [before one], endowed with specific [characteristics of] place, time, and so forth, the <s>viparyaya</s> cognition arises in the form of a specific [determination] 'this [is that].' Therefore it has neither the character of valid knowledge nor the character of memory—hence it is a distinct kind of modification.
To illustrate the contradiction of what is not valid knowledge by valid knowledge, he presents an example: ["For example, the perception of two moons..."]. Just as the perception of two moons by one whose vision is impaired by a crystal, jaundice, or the like—having an unreal object as its content—is contradicted by the single-moon perception whose object is real, aided by the knowledge and memory that a second moon does not exist.
Now, 'two-moon' (<s>dvicandra</s>)—since this is a <s>dvigu</s> compound like 'two-sheaves' or 'five-sheaves,' and since by the rule 'a <s>dvigu</s> is singular,' and since the compound-final [suffix] would apply, and since by the rule 'a <s>dvigu</s> ending in <s>-a</s> with a following member takes <s>-ī</s> in the feminine'—the <s>ī</s>-suffix would be expected from the word <s>dvicandra</s>. This is not a fault—because of the prohibition in the case of vessels (<s>pātra</s>) and the like. And there the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) denotes kinds. And kinds follow established scholarly usage. First chapter, the chapter on <s>samādhi</s>.

body.text: seyaṁ pañcaparvā bhavatyavidyā, avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśā iti। eta eva svasaṁjñābhistamo moho mahāmohastāmisro'ndhatāmisra iti। ete cittamalaprasaṅgenābhidhāsyante ॥ 8 ॥
body.translated_text: This [<s>viparyaya</s>] constitutes five-branched <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance): <s>avidyā</s>, <s>asmitā</s> (egoism), <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>abhiniveśa</s> (clinging to life)—these are the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). These same, by their own designations, are called <s>tamas</s> (darkness), <s>moha</s> (delusion), <s>mahāmoha</s> (great delusion), <s>tāmisra</s> (gloom), and <s>andhatāmisra</s> (blind darkness). These will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind (<s>cittamala</s>). // 8 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
dvicandro'pi pātrādiṣu draṣṭavyaḥ । dvau candrau yasmin darśana iti bahuvrīhiḥ । ekacandraśabdasya advigutvādeva codhābhāvaḥ । [sā ca pañcaparvā avidyāḥ sā] viparyayavṛtti [ravidyā] pañca parvāṇi asyā iti ॥
kāni punastānītyāha- [avidyāsmitetyādi । eta eva] avidyādayaḥ kleśāḥ [svasaṁjñābhiḥ] svabhiḥ śāstrāntaraprasiddhābhistamaādisaṁjñābhiḥ viśiṣṭāḥ [cittamalaprasaṅgenābhidhāyiṣyante] dvitīyapāde ॥ 8 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
'Two moons' (<s>dvicandra</s>) is also to be understood in the case of vessels (<s>pātra</s>) and the like. 'A perception in which there are two moons'—this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound. The word 'one moon' (<s>ekacandra</s>), being itself a <s>dvigu</s> compound, is free from the objection. ["And this five-branched <s>avidyā</s>"—that] <s>viparyaya</s> modification [which is <s>avidyā</s>] has five branches (<s>parvan</s>).
What then are those? He says: ["<s>Avidyā</s>, <s>asmitā</s>," etc.] These afflictions beginning with <s>avidyā</s>, ["by their own designations"]—that is, distinguished by their own designations well-known in other <s>śāstras</s>, namely the designations <s>tamas</s> and so forth—["will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind"] in the second chapter. // 8 //

body.text: śabdajñānānupātī vastuśūnyo vikalpaḥ ॥ 9 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction) follows verbal knowledge (<s>śabdajñāna</s>) and is devoid of a [corresponding] real object. // 9 //

body.text: sa na pramāṇopārohī। na viparyayopārohī ca। vastuśūnyatve'pi śabdajñānamāhātmyanibandhano vyavahāro dṛśyate। tadyathā – caitanyaṁ puruṣasya svarūpamiti। yadā citireva puruṣastadā kimatra kena vyapadiśyate।
body.translated_text: It does not fall under <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid knowledge), nor does it fall under <s>viparyaya</s> (error). Even though devoid of a real object, a usage grounded in the power of verbal knowledge is observed. For example: 'Consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) is the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>.' When <s>Puruṣa</s> is nothing other than pure awareness (<s>citi</s>), then what is being predicated of what, and by whom?

body.text:
vivaraṇam
idānīṁ vikalpaṁ darśayati- [śabdajñānānupātī vastuśūnyo vikalpaḥ ॥] śabdasya jñānaṁ śabdajñānama, vācyavācakaniyamena sādhvasādhuśabdajñānaṁ, tadanupatituṁ śīlamasyeti śabdajñānānupātī । [vastuśūnya iti ॥] yathāvācyārthaśūnyaḥ, yasya śabdasya jñānamanupatati tasya śabdasya yathābhūtābhidheyena śūnya iti yāvat । yathābhūtārthavyatirekeṇa hi vikalpanaṁ vikalpaḥ ॥
tasya hi śabdajñānānupātitvādāgamāntaḥpātitvaṁ prāptam, ata āha — [sa na pramāṇopārohīti ॥] na pramāṇāntaḥpāti.īṁ vastuśūnyatvāt । na hyāgamasya śabdajñānānupātitve'pi vastuśūnyatā । yataḥ śabdārthaviṣayā vṛttirāgamaḥ, vikalpastu vastuśūnyatvānna pramāṇam ॥
kiñca-vaktṛśrotrośca tulyo vikalpaḥ । dvayorapi śabdāduccaritādvikalpyaiva hi buddhirjāyate । na tathā āgame ॥ śrotureva hyāgama: । vaktā tu dṛṣṭānumitārthaḥ ॥
kiñca-nirvitarkasamāpannasya vikalpo vivartate nāgamaḥ । tasmānnapramāṇopārohī ॥
yadyevaṁ vastuśūnyatvādviparyayānta:pātitvaṁ prāptam, ata āha- [na viparyayopārohīti ॥] kutaḥ ? śabdajñānānupātitvāt । na hi vastuśūnyatve'pi viparyayaḥ śabdajñānamapekṣate । yataḥ ‘‘ [viparyayo mithyājñānamatadrūpapratiṣṭham’] ityuktam । pramāṇaparicchedyapratyayaṁ pratyatiguṇabhūtatvācca vikalpasya । na hi yathā sarveṣāṁ viparyayo virodhādvādhyate, tathā vikalpaḥ । pramāṇapratyayaguṇabhāvādeva ॥
tasmādvastuśūnyatvagrahaṇena śabdajñānānupātitvagrahaṇena ca parasparasaṁbandhena pramāṇaviparyayābhyāṁ pramāṇaviparyayagandhamātrānuliptamapi bhinnaṁ vikalpākhyaṁ vṛtyantaraṁ darśitam । tadvadgandhānulepanādeva tadānantaryeṇa vikalpasyārambhaḥ । nāpi smṛtitvam । smṛte: kevalānubhūtāspadatvāt ॥
atha na tvīdṛśī cittavṛttiḥ prasiddhā । na hi svabhāvaṁ kiṁcidvṛttinimittamiti cedāha- [vastuśūnyatve'pi śabdajñānamāhātmya[mātra]nibandhano vyavahāro dṛśyate] iti । mātragrahaṇa śabdajñānavyatiriktakāraṇābhāvakhyāpanārtham । kva dṛśyata iti cedāha- [tadyathā caitanyaṁ puruṣasya svarūpamiti ।] citiśaktirapariṇāminītyuktatvāccaitanyameva puruṣaḥ, tadeva ca svarūpamiti vyatirekābhāvādvyatirekopanibandhano vyapadeśo na syāt-'puruṣasya caitanyam' iti । tathā cemamevārthamupāśritya śabdavidā vārtikakāreṇottam-‘siddhaṁ tu vyapadeśivadbhāvāt' iti । tathaivehāpi yathā sati vyatireke [caitrasya gauriti] tadvadeva [caitanyaṁ puruṣasyeti ।] na hi yathā goranyaścaitro vyapadeśahetuḥ, tathā citerarthāntaraṁ puruṣo'sti, yena vyapadiśyeta ।
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Now he shows <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptual construction): ["<s>Vikalpa</s> follows verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object."]. The knowledge of a word is <s>śabdajñāna</s> (verbal knowledge); by the fixed relation of signifier and signified, it is the knowledge of correct and incorrect words; that whose nature is to follow it is <s>śabdajñānānupātī</s> (following verbal knowledge). ["Devoid of a real object"]—that is, empty of the meaning as it truly is for the word whose knowledge it follows; in other words, empty of a real referent as it actually exists. For <s>vikalpa</s> is conceptual construction that deviates from the object as it truly is.
Since it follows verbal knowledge, it would seem to fall within <s>āgama</s> (verbal testimony). Therefore he says: ["It does not fall under <s>pramāṇa</s>."]. It does not fall within <s>pramāṇa</s> because it is devoid of a real object. For <s>āgama</s>, even though it follows verbal knowledge, is not devoid of a real object—since <s>āgama</s> is the cognitive activity directed toward the meaning of a word, whereas <s>vikalpa</s>, being devoid of a real object, is not <s>pramāṇa</s>.
Moreover, <s>vikalpa</s> is the same for both speaker and listener. For both, a merely conceptualized cognition arises from an uttered word. <s>Āgama</s> is not like that—for <s>āgama</s> belongs only to the listener; the speaker, however, [speaks of] what has been directly perceived or inferred.
Furthermore, for one who has attained <s>nirvitarka samāpatti</s> (trans-deliberative attainment), <s>vikalpa</s> ceases but not <s>āgama</s>. Therefore it does not fall under <s>pramāṇa</s>.
If so, then since it is devoid of a real object, it would seem to fall within <s>viparyaya</s>. Therefore he says: ["Nor does it fall under <s>viparyaya</s>."]. Why? Because it follows verbal knowledge. For <s>viparyaya</s>, even though devoid of a real object, does not depend on verbal knowledge—since it has been stated that '<s>viparyaya</s> is false knowledge not established in the true form [of the object].' Also because <s>vikalpa</s> has the character of being subordinate to the cognition delimited by <s>pramāṇa</s>. For <s>vikalpa</s> is not contradicted as <s>viparyaya</s> is contradicted for all—precisely because of its subordinate status to the <s>pramāṇa</s> cognition.
Therefore, by means of the terms 'devoid of a real object' and 'following verbal knowledge' in mutual relation, <s>vikalpa</s> is shown to be a distinct kind of modification, different from both <s>pramāṇa</s> and <s>viparyaya</s>, even though tinged with a trace of both. And it is precisely because of that trace that <s>vikalpa</s> is introduced immediately after them. Nor is it memory, since memory is based solely on what has been previously experienced.
But no such cognitive modification is well-known! For nothing by its own nature is a cause of [such a] modification—if this is objected, he says: ["Even though devoid of a real object, a usage grounded solely in the power of verbal knowledge is observed."]. The word 'solely' (<s>mātra</s>) serves to indicate the absence of any cause other than verbal knowledge. Where is it observed? He says: ["For example: 'Consciousness is the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>.'"]. Since it has been said that the power of awareness (<s>citiśakti</s>) does not undergo transformation, <s>Puruṣa</s> is nothing but consciousness, and that itself is [its] essential nature—hence, because there is no real distinction, a predication based on distinction should not be possible—'the consciousness of <s>Puruṣa</s>.' And relying on just this meaning, the learned author of the <s>Vārttikas</s> has said: 'It is established, because of the character of what is to be predicated.' So here too, just as when there is a [real] distinction [one says] '<s>Caitra</s>'s cow,' in the same way [one says] 'the consciousness of <s>Puruṣa</s>.' For <s>Puruṣa</s> is not something other than <s>citi</s> (awareness) in the way that <s>Caitra</s> is other than the cow, by which it could be predicated.

body.text: bhavati ca vyapadeśe vṛttiḥ। yayā caitrasya gauriti। tathā pratiṣiddhavastudharmo niṣkriyaḥ puruṣaḥ, tiṣṭhati bāṇaḥ sthāsyati sthita iti, gatinivṛttau dhātvarthamātraṁ gamyate। tathā'nutpattidharmā puruṣa iti utpattidharmasyābhāvamātramavagamyate na puruṣānvayī dharmaḥ। tasmādvikalpitaḥ sa dharmastena cāsti vyavahāra iti ॥ 9 ॥
body.translated_text: And there is a cognitive activity in predication, by which [one says] '<s>Caitra</s>'s cow.' Similarly, <s>Puruṣa</s>, whose real properties are negated, is actionless (<s>niṣkriya</s>). [In the case of] 'the arrow stands,' 'will stand,' 'stood'—when motion ceases, only the bare meaning of the verbal root is understood. Similarly, [in] '<s>Puruṣa</s> is of the nature of non-origination' (<s>anutpattidharmā</s>)—only the mere absence of the property of origination is understood, not a property connected with <s>Puruṣa</s>. Therefore that property is conceptually constructed (<s>vikalpita</s>), and through it there is [conventional] usage. // 9 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
nāpi citiḥ puruṣādarthāntaraṁ vyapadiśyeta । tathā'pi vyatirekasaṁbandhaviṣaye bhavati ‘‘caitanyaṁ puruṣasya svarūpam” iti [vyapadeśe vṛttiḥ ॥]
[pratiṣiddhavastudharmeti ।] vastuno dharmo vastudharmaḥ । pratiṣiddho vastudharmo'syeti [pratiṣiddhavastudharmā ।] ‘‘dharmādanic kevalāt” iti vacanāt samāsāntaścintyasamādhiḥ । vastuśabdena sattvādiguṇā ucyante, teṣāṁ dharmāḥ pratiṣiddhā asyeti ॥
na hi pratiṣiddhāḥ sattvādidharmāḥ pratiṣiddhatvādevāsya puruṣasya saṁbandhino bhavanti । yena te puruṣeṇa asyeti vyapadiśyeran । tadabhāvamātrameva tu tatrārthaḥ । tathāpi yathā citrā gāvo'syeti vyapadeśe buddhiḥ tathā pratiṣiddhā vastudharmā asyeti vyapadeśe buddhiḥ ॥
nirgatā kriyā asmādityatrāpi nirgatirapāyaḥ । apāyaśca sambandhapūrvaḥ । yathā caitrānirgatā kriyā । na caiva puruṣe kriyāyā asambhavānnirgati: puruṣāt sabhbhavati । tathā'pi [‘niṣkriyaḥ puruṣa'] iti vyapadeśe bhavati vṛttiḥ ॥
[tathā'nutpattidharmā puruṣa] iti । na vidyate utpattidharmo'syeti pūrvavadeva । atra svayamevārthamācaṣṭe bhāṣyakāraḥ--- [utpattidharmasyābhāva(jñāna)mātramava(matra) gamyate ।] yathā nirguṇo nirañjano niṣkala ityevamādīnyapyudāharaṇāni । ātmaviṣayānekodāharaṇapradarśanamātmatattvanirdhāraṇārthatvāt ॥
[tiṣṭhati bāṇa] iti lokaprasiddhodāharaṇapratipādanamaprasiddhayāśaṅkānivṛttyartham । tiṣṭhatīti gatinivṛttirgatyabhāvaḥ । na cābhāvasya kālatrayayogo bhavati । nāpi bāṇasya kriyānirapekṣasya dravyasya । nīpi cābhāvena gatinivṛtyā bāṇasya vastunaḥ saṁbandhaḥ । [tiṣṭhati bāṇaḥ] [ [sthāsyati sthitaḥ] ] ityevaṁ trīṇyudāharaṇāni ॥
[gatinivṛttau dhātvartha iti ॥] nanu gatinivṛttireva dhātvarthaḥ, tatra kathaṁ gatinivṛttāvityādhāraḥ ? ata evodāharaṇāntarametat । asati vyatireke ādhārādheyabhāvasyābhāvāt । asti ca [gatinivṛttau dhātvartha] iti vyapadeśe śabdasāmarthyasamutthāpitā buddhirādhārādheya[bhāva]saṁbandhāvalambinī । tasmāditthaṁjātīyaṁ vikalpa viṣayamanekamudāharaṇaṁ draṣṭavyam ॥ 9 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Nor could awareness (<s>citi</s>) be predicated as something other than <s>Puruṣa</s>. Nevertheless, with regard to the subject of a relation of distinction, there arises the predication: 'Consciousness is the essential nature of <s>Puruṣa</s>'—[this is] a cognitive activity in [mere] predication.
["Whose real properties are negated."] The property of a real thing is <s>vastudharma</s>; one whose <s>vastudharma</s> is negated is '<s>pratiṣiddhavastudharma</s>.' By the grammatical rule '<s>dharmād anic kevalāt</s>,' the compound-final [suffix] is a matter of deliberation. By the word '<s>vastu</s>' (real thing), the <s>guṇas</s> such as <s>sattva</s> and the rest are meant; their properties are negated in him (<s>Puruṣa</s>).
For the negated properties of <s>sattva</s> and the rest, precisely because they are negated, do not become related to this <s>Puruṣa</s>, by which they could be predicated as 'his.' Rather, the meaning there is merely the absence of those [properties]. Nevertheless, just as in the predication 'one who has variegated cows,' there is a cognition, so too in the predication 'one whose real properties are negated,' there is a cognition.
In '<s>niṣkriya</s>' (actionless)—here too, the departure (<s>nirgati</s>) of action from him implies removal (<s>apāya</s>), and removal presupposes a prior connection, as [when one says] 'the action has departed from <s>Caitra</s>.' But since action is impossible in <s>Puruṣa</s>, departure from <s>Puruṣa</s> cannot occur. Nevertheless, there is a cognitive activity in the predication '<s>Puruṣa</s> is actionless.'
Similarly, '<s>Puruṣa</s> is of the nature of non-origination' (<s>anutpattidharmā</s>)—'one for whom the property of origination does not exist'—is just as before. Here the <s>Bhāṣya</s>-author himself states the meaning: ["Only the mere absence of the property of origination is understood."]. Just as 'without qualities' (<s>nirguṇa</s>), 'without taint' (<s>nirañjana</s>), 'without parts' (<s>niṣkala</s>)—such expressions are also examples. The presentation of multiple examples concerning the self (<s>ātman</s>) serves the purpose of determining the nature of the self.
["The arrow stands"]—a well-known worldly example is presented for the purpose of removing the suspicion [that such usage] is unfamiliar. 'Stands' (<s>tiṣṭhati</s>) means the cessation of motion—that is, the absence of motion. But absence does not have connection with the three times [past, present, future]. Nor does the arrow, which is a substance independent of action, [have such connection]. Nor is there a relation between the absence, namely the cessation of motion, and the arrow as a real thing. [Yet] 'the arrow stands,' 'will stand,' 'stood'—thus there are three examples.
["When motion ceases, the verbal root meaning..."] Objection: If the cessation of motion is itself the meaning of the verbal root, then how can 'in the cessation of motion' be a locative [relation]? Therefore this is indeed another example. Because in the absence of [real] distinction, the relation of container and contained does not exist. Yet ["in the cessation of motion, the verbal root meaning"]—in this predication, a cognition arises, produced by the power of the word, dependent on the relation of container and contained. Therefore, examples of this kind regarding the domain of <s>vikalpa</s> should be understood as manifold. // 9 //

body.text: abhāvaprayayālambanā vṛttirnidrā ॥ 10 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Nidrā</s> (sleep) is the cognitive modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) whose supporting object is the cognition of absence (<s>abhāvapratyaya</s>). // 10 //

body.text: sā ca saṁprabodhe pratyavamarśātpratyayaviśeṣaḥ। kathaṁ, sukhamahamasvāpsam। prasannaṁ me manaḥ prajñāṁ me viśāradī karoti। duḥkhamahamasvāpsaṁ styānaṁ me mano bhramatyanavasthitam। gāḍhaṁ mūḍho'hamasvāpsam। gurūṇi me gātrāṇi। klāntaṁ me cittam। alasaṁ muṣitamiva tiṣṭhatīti। sa khalvayaṁ prabuddhasya pratyavamarśo na syādasati pratyayānubhave tadāśritāḥ smṛtayaśca tadviṣayā na syuḥ। tasmātpratyayaviśeṣo nidrā। sā ca samādhāvitarapratyayavanniroddhavyeti ॥ 10 ॥
body.translated_text: And that [sleep] is known to be a particular kind of cognition from the retrospective awareness upon awakening. How? 'I slept happily; my mind is clear; it makes my understanding sharp.' 'I slept badly; my mind is dull, it wanders unsteadily.' 'I slept deeply in a stupor; my limbs are heavy; my mind is tired, lazy, as if it remains robbed [of function].' Surely this retrospective awareness of one who has awakened would not exist if there had been no experience of a cognition, and memories based on it and having it as their object would not exist [either]. Therefore sleep is a particular kind of cognition. And it, like other cognitions, is to be suppressed in <s>samādhi</s>. // 10 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
nidrākhyāṁ vṛttimidānīmācaṣṭe- [abhāvapratyayālambanā vṛtirnidrā ।] jāgradviṣayatvāt prāguktasya vṛttitrayasya_ tadupamardena ca nidrāsamudbhava iti, tadanantaraṁ nidrākhyā vṛttirvyākhyāyate ॥
[abhāva] iti jāgradviṣayābhāvaḥ, na tvatyantābhāva eva । tatra pratyayānupapatteḥ । abhāve pratyayaḥ [abhāvapratyayaḥ ।] sa eva [ālambanaṁ] yasyāḥ sā [vṛttirabhāvapratyayālambanā ।] sā [nidrā] suṣuptāvasthā ॥
nanu ca svapnāvasthā'pi nidraiva--naiṣa doṣaḥ- [“svapnanidrājñānālambanaṁ vā “] iti sūtrakāreṇa bhedenopadiṣṭatvādiha suṣuptāvasthaiva nidrā'bhipretā ॥
kiṁca-abhāvapratyayālambanatvācca suṣuktameva । na hi svapnasyābhāvapratyayālambanatā, smṛtitvāt । smṛteśvānubhūtaviṣayatvāt । tathā bhāṣyakāraḥ’’svapne bhāvitasmartavyā ‘ iti smṛtitvaṁ darśayati ॥
kiñca-svapnasya cittavṛttitā svasaṁvedyeti nāśaṅkaivopapadyate । tathā ca cittavṛttitāmāśaṅkyāha-sā tu[ca saṁ] [prabodhe pratyavamarśādityādi । tasmāt pratyayaviśeṣo nidrā ।] na hāsati pratyayaviśeṣe parāmarśa yuktaḥ ! asti cāyaṁ prabuddhasya pratyavamarśaḥ ‘ [sukhamahamasvāpsam'] ityādiḥ । pratyavamarśo nāma kimapyanvabhūrvāmi.ita pratyayālocanā । nānubhavābhāve sā bhavet । napi tadviṣayāḥ smṛtayo yuktāḥ । nidrāyā apratyayatve- [prajñāṁ viśāradīkaroti manaḥ] , manasaḥ kartṛtvaṁ, [styānaṁ] stimitam akarmaṇyam, [gurugurūṇīti] ‘prakāre 'guṇavacanasya iti dvirvacarne guruprakārāṇi, [alasaṁ muṣitamiva] mallenāpahṛtamiva, etāni pratyayānubhavakāryaṇi na syuḥ । kāścana smṛtayaḥ kānicit kāryāṇi kecana pratyavamaśaḥ । tadetattrayamapi bhāṣyakāropanyastaॆ pratyayaviśeṣatva evopapadyate ॥
kiñca—garbhagṛhādiṣu cādṛṣṭabāhmanimittānāmasati viśeṣa ciramaī suptavān kṣipramiti ca parāmarśo'nyathā na yujyate ॥
nanu ca nātra smṛtayaḥ, smṛtīnām anvabhavamityevaṁviśiṣṭatvāt । na hi suṣuptādutthito viśeṣaṁ smarati--atrocyate--bālasyeha janmanyananubhūtastanyasaṁbandhasya janmānantarameva tasyābhilāṣo dṛśyate । na ca। sa] svābhāvikaḥ । abālānāṁ smṛtipūrvapravṛttidarśanāt । tathehāpi । tasmāt pratyayapūrvakaḥ suṣuptaviṣayaḥ pratyavamarśaḥ, pratyavamarśatvāt jāgradupalabdhaviṣayapratyavamarśavat । tathā suṣuptotthitasya gātragauravādi kāryaṅ duḥkhādyanubhavapūrvaṅ , gātrādiviṣayagauravādikāryatvāt prasiddhaduḥkhānubhavakāryagātragauravavaditi pratyayaviśeṣo nidreti siddham ॥ 10 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
He now describes the modification called sleep— [Sleep is the modification whose support is the cognition of absence.] Since the three modifications previously stated have waking-state objects as their domain, and since sleep arises from the suppression of those, the modification called sleep is explained next.
'Absence' means the absence of waking-state objects, not absolute absence, because a cognition cannot be supported by absolute absence. The cognition of absence is the 'absence-cognition'; that alone is the support of which modification—that is the modification whose support is the absence-cognition. That sleep is the state of deep sleep (<s>suṣupti</s>).
But surely the dream-state too is sleep—this is not a defect, because the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (aphorist) has taught them as distinct in the <s>sūtra</s> 'or that having dream, sleep, or knowledge as its support' (YS 1.38). Here, only the state of deep sleep is intended as <s>nidrā</s>.
Moreover, it is only deep sleep because of having absence-cognition as its support. For dream does not have absence-cognition as its support, because it is a form of <s>smṛti</s> (memory), and because memory has experienced objects as its content. Thus the commentator (<s>bhāṣyakāra</s>) shows its nature as memory by saying 'in dream, that which has a prepared recollectable.'
Moreover, the nature of dream as a mental modification is self-cognized, so there is no need for doubt. And thus, anticipating doubt about its being a mental modification, he says: 'because of reflection upon awakening' etc. Therefore sleep is a particular type of cognition (<s>pratyaya</s>). For if there were no particular cognition, reflection would not be possible. And there is indeed this reflection of one who has awakened: 'I slept happily' etc. Reflection means the reconsideration 'I must have experienced something'—a reviewing of the cognition. That cannot occur in the absence of experience; nor would memories having that as their object be possible.
If sleep were not a cognition—'the mind sharpens wisdom' (the agency of the mind); '<s>styāna</s>' (torpor)—dullness, inactivity; 'very heavy'—by the reduplication of a quality-word to indicate manner, meaning extremely heavy; 'sluggish, as if robbed'—as if carried away by a wrestler—these, which are effects of the experience of a cognition, would not exist. Certain memories, certain effects, certain reflections—all these three, as presented by the commentator, are established only if sleep is a particular type of cognition.
Moreover, in inner chambers and the like, where no external cause has been seen and there is no temporal distinction, the reflections 'I slept for a long time' or 'I slept briefly' would not otherwise be possible.
But surely there are no memories here, because memories are characterized as 'I experienced such and such.' For one risen from deep sleep does not remember any particulars.
To this it is said: An infant, without having experienced the connection with the breast in this life, is seen to have a desire for it immediately after birth. And that desire is not innate, because in non-infants, activity is seen to be preceded by memory. So here too. Therefore the reflection concerning deep sleep is preceded by a cognition, because it is a reflection, like reflection on objects perceived during waking. Likewise, effects such as bodily heaviness in one who has risen from deep sleep are preceded by the experience of suffering etc., because they are effects of heaviness pertaining to the body, like the well-known bodily heaviness that results from the experience of suffering. Thus it is established that sleep is a particular type of cognition.

body.text: anubhūtaviṣayāsaṁpramoṣaḥ smṛtiḥ ॥ 11 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>anubhūtaviṣayāsaṃpramoṣaḥ smṛtiḥ</s> — <s>Smṛti</s> (memory) is the non-loss of experienced objects. (Sūtra 11)

body.text: kiṁ pratyayasya cittaṁ smarati āhosvidviṣayasyeti। grāhyoparaktaḥ pratyayo grāhyagrahaṇobhayākāranirbhāsastajjātīyakaṁ saṁskāramārabhate। sa saṁskāraḥ svavyañjakāñjanastadākārāmeva grāhyagrahaṇobhayātmikāṁ smṛtiṁ janayati।
body.translated_text: Does the mind remember the cognition or the object? The cognition, being colored by the graspable [object], manifesting in the dual form of the graspable and the grasping, gives rise to an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of the same kind. That impression, activated by its own trigger, produces memory that is of the same dual nature—comprising both the graspable and the grasping.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
smṛtimidānīṁ vyācaṣṭe-- [anubhūtāviṣayāsampramoṣaḥ smṛtiḥ ।] smṛteḥ pramāṇādisarvavṛttikāryatvādante niveśaḥ । anubhūtaścāsau viṣayaśca anubhūtaviṣayaḥ । yo'sāvanubhūtaḥ sa eva viṣayaḥ, na punaryo viṣayaḥ sa evānubhūta iti । tathā ca smṛteraśabdāditvāt smṛtiviṣayāyāḥ smṛterasmṛtitvaṁ prāpnotīti । iṣyate ca smṛtiviṣayā'pi smṛtiḥ svasaṁvedyatvāt । anubhūtaviṣayasyāsaṁprameṣo'napaharaṇamatirobhāvaḥ । pārokṣye'pi sādṛśyādinimittāpekṣayā'nubhūtasya viṣayasya dṛśyamānavadavabhāsaḥ smṛtiḥ ॥
tatra pratyayasmaraṇayorviṣayākārāvabhāsāviśeṣāt, kiṅkṛtastayorbheda iti tadvivekaṁ pradarśayitukāma āha-- [kiṁ pratyayasya cittaṁ smaratī] tyādi ॥ yadyapyanubhūtānanubhūyamānaviṣayatvena vivekaḥ, tathāpi sādṛśyanimittāṁ bhrāntiṁ tayoḥ kāryakāraṇatvapradarśanāya nivartayati । etadeva ca vaināśikānāṁ bahirarthānupapatterbuddhikāraṇam । [kiṁ pratyayasya smaratī] ti karmaṇyubhayatra ṣaṣṭhī । [cittaṁ smaratī] ti puruṣakartṛtvaṁ nivārayati smṛtipratyayayorekakartṛtvapradarśanārtham । na hi puruṣasya pratyayakartṛtvaṁ smṛtikartṛtvaṁ । dṛśyatvāt pratyayānām । dṛśyānāṁ ca svātmātiriktadṛśyatvaṁ ghaṭādivaditi vakṣyāmaḥ । ।
kiñcātaḥ ? yadi viṣayasya smarati, pratyayasyāpi viṣayaviṣayatvādanarthāntaraṁ smṛtiḥ pratyayāt । atha pratyayasya smarati, tadā tvidamayuktam [anubhūtaviṣayāsampramoṣa] iti । tadā hyanubhavāsampramoṣa iti syāttatrāha - [grāhyoparaktaḥ] grāhyo viṣaya ālambanam , tenoparaktaḥ lākṣādyuparaktasphaṭikavat । [grāhyagrahaṇo bhayākāranirbhāsaḥ] grāhyasya ca ghaṭādeḥ pṛthubuddhnādyākāreṇa svena cāvabhāsarūpeṇopajāyamānatvādubhayanirbhāsaḥ ॥
sa ca pratyaya utpadya vinivartamānaḥ svāśraye pratyayini saṁskāramādadhāti । sa ca saṁskāraḥ kāraṇānuvidhāyitvādubhayā(pāta)kāra eva । [svavyañjakāñjana iti ।] saṁskārādhāyinaḥ pratyayasya hetubhūtaṁ yat karma dattaphalaṁ tattulyajātīyaṁ yatkarmāntaraṁ phalapradānāyābhimukhībhavati tat svavyañjakam । tathā ca vakṣyati-‘tatastadvipākānuguṇānāmevābhivyaktirvāsanānām' iti । tatkarmapratyupanītaṁ vā sādṛśyapraṇidhānādi । svena vyañjakenābhivyajyata iti svavyañjakāñjanaḥ । [grāhyagrahaṇātmikāṁ smṛtiṁ janayati ।] anyathā tadvayañjakasya karmaṇo vipākānupapattiḥ ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
He now explains memory— [<s>Smṛti</s> (memory) is the non-loss of experienced objects.] Memory is placed last because it is an effect of all modifications such as <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) etc. 'Experienced' and 'object'—what has been experienced is itself the object, not that whatever is an object has necessarily been experienced. And thus, since memory is not of the nature of verbal testimony etc., the memory whose object is memory would cease to be memory. But memory whose object is memory is indeed accepted, because it is self-cognized. The 'non-loss' of an experienced object means its non-disappearance, its non-concealment. Even when remote, through causes such as similarity, the experienced object appears as if present—that is memory.
Since there is no distinction in the manifestation of the object-form between the cognition and the recollection, what causes their difference? Wishing to show this distinction, he says: 'Does the mind remember the cognition?' etc. Although the distinction lies in the object being experienced versus not-currently-being-experienced, still, to dispel the confusion caused by similarity and to show the causal relation between the two, he addresses this. 'Does it remember the cognition'—the sixth case ending (genitive) is used in both instances in the objective sense. 'The mind remembers' eliminates the agency of the <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self), to show that cognition and memory have the same agent. For the <s>Puruṣa</s> is not the agent of cognition or memory, since cognitions are objects of perception. And we shall explain that objects of perception are seen by something other than themselves, like a pot etc.
Furthermore: if it remembers the object, then since the cognition too has the object as its content, memory would be no different from cognition. But if it remembers the cognition, then the [definition] 'non-loss of experienced objects' would be inappropriate—it should then be 'non-loss of experience.' To this he says: [Colored by the graspable]—the graspable is the object, the support; colored by it, like a crystal colored by lac etc. [Manifesting in the dual form of the graspable and the grasping]—because the cognition arises manifesting both in the form of the graspable (such as a pot with its broad base etc.) and in its own form as apprehension, it has a dual manifestation.
That cognition, having arisen and then ceasing, deposits an impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) in its substrate, the mind. And that impression, conforming to its cause, is indeed of dual form. 'Activated by its own trigger'—the <s>karma</s> that was the cause of the impression-depositing cognition, having given its fruit, and another <s>karma</s> of the same kind becoming ready to give fruit—that is the trigger. As will be stated: 'Then there is the manifestation of impressions conforming to that fruition.' Or alternatively, it is similarity, focused attention, etc., brought about by that <s>karma</s>. 'Activated by its own trigger' means manifested by its own activating cause. [It produces memory comprising both the graspable and the grasping.] Otherwise the fruition of the triggering <s>karma</s> would be inexplicable.

body.text: tatra grahaṇākārapūrvā buddhiḥ। grāhyākārapūrvā smṛtiḥ। sā ca dvayī – bhāvitasmartavyā cābhāvitasmartavyā ca। svapne bhāvitasmartavyā। jāgratsamaye tvabhāvitasmartavyeti। sarvāḥ smṛtayaḥ pramāṇaviparyayavikalpanidrāsmṛtīnāmanubhavātprabhavanti। sarvāścaitā vṛttayaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohātmikāḥ। sukhaduḥkhamohāśca kleśeṣu vyākhyeyāḥ। sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ। duḥkhānuśayī dveṣaḥ। mohaḥ punaravidyeti। etāḥ sarvā vṛttayo niroddhavyāḥ। āsāṁ nirodhe saṁprajñāto vā samādhirbhavatyasaṁprajñāto veti ॥ 11 ॥
body.translated_text: Therein, cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is preceded by the grasping-form. Memory (<s>smṛti</s>) is preceded by the graspable-form. And memory is twofold—with a prepared recollectable (<s>bhāvitasmartavyā</s>) and without a prepared recollectable (<s>abhāvitasmartavyā</s>). In dream, it is with a prepared recollectable. In the waking state, however, it is without a prepared recollectable. All memories arise from the experience of the five modifications—<s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), <s>viparyaya</s> (error), <s>vikalpa</s> (conceptualization), <s>nidrā</s> (sleep), and <s>smṛti</s> (memory). And all these modifications are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Pleasure, pain,

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[tatra grahaṇākārapūrvā buddhiḥ ।] grahaṇam [svī]karaṇaṁ[svī]karaṇameva pūrvaṁ prathamamutpadyamānasya pratyayasya । na hi viṣayaviśeṣamapekṣate pūrvamiṣṭāniṣṭagrahaṇāt , nirbhagnavaṭapradīpavinirgataprabhājālavat ॥
[grahyākārapūrvā smṛtiḥ] anubhūtāpekṣatvāt । yadi ca grahaṇapūrvikā smṛtiḥ pratyayavadabhaviṣyat, anubhūtaṁ nāpaikṣiṣyata । apekṣate tu । tasmādgrāhyo viṣayaḥ pūrvo'syā na grahaṇam । tathāpi tūbhayātmikaiva । smṛtisaṁskārayorekarūpatvāt । nāpyanyatarapratyayākhyānena sambhavati । tathā cānubhūtaviṣayāsampramoṣa ityupapadyate । smṛtipratyayayorapi[samāna]viṣayatvāt, grahaṇatvasya ca sarvatra sambhavāt । tasmāt pakṣadvaye'pyabhihitadoṣo na dṛśyata iti ॥
[sā ca dvayī ।] katham? [bhāvitasmartavyā] bhāvitaṁ pariniṣpannaṁ asakṛdbhāvitatvāt । yathā dravyānteraṇāsakṛdbhāvitaṁ tailādi । asakṛdbhāvitatvādeva praṇidhānādiprayatnāntaraṁ nāpekṣate । bhāvitaṁ smartavyaṁ praṇidhānādiyatnāntara[na]pekṣayā yasyāḥ sā svapne bhāvitasmartavyā । jā[gṛ]gratsamaye tvapekṣate praṇidhānādiśyatnāntarāmiti tadviparītā ॥
[sarvāśca pramāṇādi] vṛttipañcatayā [nubhavādu] dbhavati । [sarvāścaitāḥ sukhādyā] (ssatvādyā)tmikāḥ । tadātmakaśca saṁsāraḥ । [sukhaduḥkhamohāśca kleśeṣu vyākhyātāḥ] sūtrakāreṇa । 'sarvaṁ duḥkhaṁ vivekina:' iti hi vakṣyati । taddhānaṁ ceha vivakṣitam ।
tasmāt sukhaduḥkhamohātmakatvāt [niroddhavyā vṛttaya:।] kiñca - [āsāṁ niroghe samprajñāto vā samādhirbhavatyasamprajñāto vā] ॥ 11 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
[Therein, cognition is preceded by the grasping-form.] Grasping means apprehension—apprehension itself is primary in a cognition that first arises. For it does not depend on the particular nature of the object initially, since the grasping of desirable or undesirable [happens after], like the mass of light issuing from a lamp in a broken vase.
[Memory is preceded by the graspable-form]—because it depends on what has been experienced. If memory, like cognition, were preceded by grasping, it would not depend on what has been experienced. But it does depend on it. Therefore the graspable object is primary for memory, not the grasping. Even so, memory is indeed of both natures, because of the identity of form between memory and impression. Nor can it be accounted for by describing only one of the two aspects. And thus 'non-loss of experienced objects' is appropriate. Since memory and cognition share the same object, and since the grasping-nature is possible everywhere, therefore the stated fault does not appear in either position.
[And it is twofold.] How? [With a prepared recollectable]—'prepared' means fully developed, due to repeated cultivation, like oil etc. that has been repeatedly treated with other substances. Because of being repeatedly cultivated, it does not require additional effort such as focused attention. 'Having a prepared recollectable'—that whose recollectable does not require additional effort such as focused attention—such is the memory in dream, with a prepared recollectable. In the waking state, however, it requires additional effort such as focused attention—the opposite [type].
[And all the fivefold modifications] arise from experience. [And all these are of the nature of pleasure etc.]—and of <s>sattva</s> etc. And <s>saṃsāra</s> is of that nature. [Pleasure, pain, and delusion are explained among the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions)] by the <s>sūtrakāra</s>. For he will say: 'For the discriminating one, all is suffering.' And it is the removal of that which is intended here.
Therefore, because they are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, [the modifications are to be ceased.] Moreover— [Upon their cessation, either <s>saṃprajñāta</s> (cognitive) or <s>asaṃprajñāta</s> (non-cognitive) <s>samādhi</s> arises.]

body.text: athā''sāṁ nirodhe ka upāya iti –
body.translated_text: Then—what is the means for their cessation?—

body.text: abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṁ tannirodhaḥ ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṃ tannirodhaḥ</s> — Their cessation is by <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion). (Sūtra 12)

body.text: cittanadī nāmobhayatovāhinī vahati kalyāṇāya vahati pāpāya ca। yā tu kaivalyaprāgbhārā vivekaviṣayanimnā sā kalyāṇavahā। saṁsāraprāgbhārā'vivekaviṣayanimnā pāpavahā। tatra vairāgyeṇa viṣayasrotaḥ khilīkriyate। vivekadarśanābhyāsena vivekasrota uddhāṭyata ityubhayādhīnaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text: The river of the mind flows in two directions—it flows toward the good and it flows toward evil. That which inclines toward <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation), flowing downward toward the domain of discrimination (<s>viveka</s>)—that is the good-flowing [current]. That which inclines toward <s>saṃsāra</s>, flowing downward toward the domain of non-discrimination—that is the evil-flowing [current]. Through <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), the current toward sense-objects is blocked; through the practice of discriminative vision (<s>vivekadarśana</s>), the current of discrimination is opened. Thus the cessation of the modifications of the mind depends on both.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[atha āsāṁ nirodhe ka upāya iti ॥]
upāyaṁ pravedayati- [abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṁ tannirodha iti ॥] abhyāsavairāgye vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇe । tābhyāṁ yathoktalakṣaṇānāṁ [vṛttīnāṁ] nirodhaḥ virodhanāt । nirodha upaśamaḥ । abhyāsavairāgyayorviṣayavivekapradarśanārthametadbhāṣyam - [cittanadītyādi ।] cittena nadyeva saṁsāriṇaḥ satataṁ viṣaye pariṇīyante । [saṁsāraprāgbhārā] saṁsārāvasānā samudrāvasāneva । [khilīkriyate] pratibadhyata iti । [uddhāṭyate] pravartyate । uddhāṭa: kriyata ityuddhāṭyate । anyathā mitvāt ghaṭādayo mitaḥ iti (hatu) [‘‘mitāṁ hṛsvaḥ’’] iti syāt । evaṁ [ubhayādhīnaḥ] ubhayatantra ityarthaḥ ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
[Then, what is the means for their cessation?]
He declares the means— [Their cessation is by <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion).] <s>Abhyāsa</s> and <s>vairāgya</s> have characteristics that will be described. By these two, the cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) of the modifications of the described nature occurs, meaning their opposition and suppression. <s>Nirodha</s> means pacification. This commentary (<s>bhāṣya</s>) is for the purpose of showing the respective domains of practice and dispassion—namely, object and discrimination. [The river of the mind, etc.]—By the mind, as by a river, beings in <s>saṃsāra</s> are constantly carried along toward objects. 'Inclining toward <s>saṃsāra</s>' means terminating in <s>saṃsāra</s>, like a river terminating in the ocean. 'Blocked' means obstructed. 'Opened' means made to flow; an opening is created. Thus [the cessation] depends on both—meaning it is governed by both.

body.text: tatra sthitau yatnā'bhyāsaḥ ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>tatra sthitau yatno 'bhyāsaḥ</s> — Therein, <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) is the effort toward stability. (Sūtra 13)

body.text: cittasyāvṛttikasya praśāntavāhitā sthitiḥ। tadarthaḥ prayatno vīryamutsāhaḥ। tatsaṁpipādayiṣayā tatsādhanānuṣṭhānamabhyāsaḥ ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text: The stability (<s>sthiti</s>) of the mind when it is free from modifications is the state of tranquil flow (<s>praśāntavāhitā</s>). The effort directed toward that [stability] is vigor, exertion. The performance of the means for achieving that—through the wish to accomplish it—is <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tatrābhyāsatvarūpaṁ pratipādayiṣyannāha-- [tatra sthitau yatno'bhyāsaḥ । tatra] tasminnirodhe । sā ca nimittasaptamī । nirodhanimittā cittasya yā [sthitiḥ] yatnasya phalabhūtā tasyā nimitto[kta bhūto]yo [yattraḥ so'bhyāsaḥ ।] tathā cāha- [avṛttikasya] praśāntapaṅkajkara(ṅga)ñjasyevābhbhasaḥ praśāntavāhitā prasannarūpata ya pariṇāmo "niruddhavṛttikasya [cittasya] । [yatno] vīryamabhyutsāha iti paryāyāḥ । sthiti [saṁpipādayiṣayā] yamaniyamādiyogasādhanānuṣṭhānamabhyāsaṁ iti ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
Wishing to establish the nature of practice, he says— [Therein, <s>abhyāsa</s> is the effort toward stability. 'Therein'] means in that cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). And that is a causal locative. The stability (<s>sthiti</s>) of the mind, which is the fruit of effort and which has cessation as its cause—the effort that is the cause of that [stability] is <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice). And thus he says— ['Free from modifications']—like a tranquil pool, the state of tranquil flow is the serene transformation of the mind whose modifications have been suppressed. ['Effort']—vigor, exertion are synonyms. ['Through the wish to accomplish stability']—the performance of the means of <s>yoga</s> such as <s>yama</s> (restraints), <s>niyama</s> (observances), etc.—that is practice.

body.text: sa tu dīrghakālanairantaryasatkārāsevito dṛḍhabhūmiḥ ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>sa tu dīrghakālanairantaryasatkārāsevito dṛḍhabhūmiḥ</s> — But that [practice] becomes firmly grounded when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion. (Sūtra 14)

body.text: dīrghakālāsevito nirantarāsevitaḥ satkārāsevitaḥ। tapasā brahmacaryeṇa vidyayā śraddhayā ca saṁpāditaḥ satkāravāndṛḍhabhūmirbhavati। vyutthānasaṁskāreṇa drāgityevānabhibhūtaviṣaya ityarthaḥ ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text: Cultivated for a long time, cultivated without interruption, cultivated with devotion—acquired through <s>tapas</s> (austerity), <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy), <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), and <s>śraddhā</s> (faith)—such [practice], endowed with devotion, becomes firmly grounded. Its meaning is: it is not quickly overpowered by the impressions of distraction (<s>vyutthānasaṃskāra</s>)—that is the meaning.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
sa tu kathaṁ sthirībhavatītyata āha-- [dīrghakālanairantaryasevitaḥ] dīrghakāla tvavarjito vā [nairantaryavarjito vā na] [dṛḍhabhūmi] rbhavatyabhyāsaḥ । tasmādubhayorapi (viśeṣya)viśeṣaṇatvameva । [saṁskārāsevita] iti tvabhyāsa eva viśeṣyate । [dṛḍhabhūmi] rityasya vyākhyānaṁ [vyutthānasaṁskāreṇeti ।] vyutthānajena saṁskāreṇa [drāgiti] sahasā nābhibhūyate ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
But how does it become stable? To this he says— [Cultivated for a long time, without interruption.] If either long duration is absent or uninterruptedness is absent, practice does not become firmly grounded. Therefore both serve as qualifications of the [same thing]. 'Cultivated with devotion' however qualifies practice itself. The explanation of 'firmly grounded' is: [it is not quickly overpowered by the impressions of distraction]—it is not suddenly overwhelmed by impressions born of distraction (<s>vyutthāna</s>).

body.text: dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayavitṛṣṇasya vaśīkārasaṁjñā vairāgyam ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayavitṛṣṇasya vaśīkārasaṃjñā vairāgyam</s> — <s>Vairāgya</s> (dispassion) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from craving for objects both seen and heard of. (Sūtra 15)

body.text: striyo'nnapānamaiśvaryamiti dṛṣṭaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya svargavaidehyaprakṛtilayatvaprāptāvānuśravikaviṣaye vitṛṣṇasya divyādivyaviṣayasaṁprayoge'pi cittasya viṣayadoṣadarśinaḥ prasaṁkhyānabalādanābhogātmikā heyopādeyaśūnyā vaśīkārasaṁjñā vairāgyam ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text: The mastery-designation (<s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s>) is the state of detachment (<s>vairāgya</s>) of one who is free from craving toward seen objects—such as women, food, drink, and sovereignty—and free from craving toward scriptural objects—such as the attainment of heaven, disembodiment, and absorption in <s>Prakṛti</s>—whose mind, even upon contact with divine and non-divine objects, sees the faults of objects, by the power of discernment (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), is of the nature of non-engagement, and is devoid of what is to be rejected or accepted. // 15 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
vairāgyapratipādanārthamāha- [dṛṣṭānuśravikāvaṣayavitṛṣṇasya vaśīkārasaṁjñāvairāgyam । viṣaya] śabdaḥ pratyekamabhisaṁbadhyate [vitṛṣṇasya] iti ca, dṛṣṭaviṣayavitṛṣṇasya ānuśravikaviṣayavitṛṣṇasya ceti ।
[dṛṣṭaścāsau viṣayaśca tasmin ॥] kaḥ punarasai.au ? [striyo'nnaṁ pānamaiścaryamiti] vyakktyapekṣayā । śabdādīnāmānantye'pi rāgaprabalatvameteṣvatitarāmiti stryādagrahaṇaṁ prādhānyāt । atra hi prabalataro rāgaḥ । sa prayatnatareṇa niṣeddhabyaḥ । evam [ānuśravikaviṣayaḥ ।] ānuśraviko nāma āgamika iha । sa ca svargādiprāptyānubhavanīyaḥ prakṛtilayagatabhogyo vaidehmaprāptau upabhogyaśca ॥
nanu ca vaitṛṣṇyameva vairāgyam , tathā ‘ [rāgastṛṣṇā garddhaḥ'] iti hi vakṣyati । na - avasthāviśeṣasya vivakṣitatvāt । tathā ca yatamānasaṁjñā, vyatikrāntasaṁjñā, ekendriyasaṁjñā, vaśīkārasaṁjñeti catasṛṇāmāsāṁ sāmānyasaṁjñā । vairāgyamiti । evaṁ sati dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayavitṛṣṇasyetyetaduktaṁ bhavati- adhigatapūrvāvasthātrayasya caturthī yā avasthā sā tviha vairāgyaṁmiti vivakṣitam । tasmādiha vaitṛṣṇyādanyavairāgyamābhipretam । tathā ca darśayati-- [viṣayadoṣadarśinaḥ] doṣadarśanasya viṣayanivṛttihetutvāt । tadguṇadarśanaṁ hi rāgakāraṇam । [prasaṁkhyānabalāt] -taddoṣadarśanābhyāsabalāt । [anābhogātmikā] viṣayāvyatikarāmikā । [divyādivyayoḥ] samprayoge'pi [heyopādeyaśūnyā] rañjanāvamuktasyeva sphaṭikasya viṣayarāgavimuktasya cittasyāvasthānam । [vaśīkārasaṁjñā] -vaśīkartuṁ śakyante'syāmavasthāyāṁ sarve gauṇā: padārthā: vaśīkartavyatvena saṁjñāyante, vaśīkṛtani ca tasyāmavasthāyāmindriyāṇi saṁjñāyante, vaśīkaraṇaṁ vā saṁjñāyate'syāmiti ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
In order to explain detachment, he says: "Detachment is the mastery-designation of one who is free from craving toward seen and scriptural objects." The word 'object' is connected with each: 'free from craving toward seen objects' and 'free from craving toward scriptural objects.'
"Seen" and "object"—and therein: what are these [seen objects]? "Women, food, drink, and sovereignty"—with reference to particular instances. Although sense-objects such as sound are infinite, attachment is most powerful with regard to these, hence the mention of women and the rest, by way of predominance. For here attachment is strongest. It must be overcome with the greatest effort. Similarly, the "scriptural object"—'scriptural' (<s>ānuśravika</s>) means 'derived from scripture' (<s>āgamika</s>) here. And that is what is to be experienced through attaining heaven and the like, what is enjoyed when one has reached absorption in <s>Prakṛti</s>, and what is to be enjoyed upon attaining disembodiment.
Objection: Freedom from craving is itself detachment, as will be said: "Attachment is craving, desire." Reply: No—because a specific stage is what is intended. Thus the general designation 'detachment' (<s>vairāgya</s>) covers four stages: the 'striving' designation (<s>yatamāna-saṃjñā</s>), the 'gone-beyond' designation (<s>vyatikrānta-saṃjñā</s>), the 'single-sense' designation (<s>ekendriya-saṃjñā</s>), and the 'mastery' designation (<s>vaśīkāra-saṃjñā</s>). This being so, 'of one free from craving toward seen and scriptural objects' means: of one who has traversed the first three stages, the fourth stage is here intended as detachment. Therefore, the detachment intended here is different from mere freedom from craving. And thus he shows: "who sees the faults of objects"—because seeing faults is the cause of turning away from objects. For seeing their qualities is the cause of attachment. "By the power of discernment"—by the power of habitual practice of seeing faults therein. "Of the nature of non-engagement"—not interacting with objects. "Even upon contact" with "divine and non-divine" objects—"devoid of what is to be rejected or accepted"—like a crystal freed from the coloring that had dyed it, the mind freed from attachment to objects abides [in this state]. "Mastery-designation"—in this state, all secondary entities can be mastered, and they are designated as masterable; and in this state, the sense-organs are designated as mastered; or, mastery is designated in this [state]. // 15 //

body.text: tatparaṁ puruṣakhyāterguṇavetṛṣṇyam ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: The supreme [detachment] is indifference to the <s>guṇas</s>, arising from the knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>. // 16 //

body.text: dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayadoṣadarśī viraktaḥ puruṣadarśanābhyāsāttacchuddhipravivekāpyāyitabuddhirguṇebhyo vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyo virakta iti। tadvayaṁ vairāgyam। tatra yaduttaraṁ tajjñānaprasādamātram। yasyodaye sati yogī pratyuditakhyātirevaṁ manyate – prāptaṁ prāpaṇīyaṁ, kṣīṇāḥ kṣetavyāḥ kleśāḥ, chinnaḥ śliṣṭaparvā bhavasaṁkramaḥ, yasyāvicchedājjanitvā mriyate mṛtvā ca jāyata iti। jñānasyaiva parā kāṣṭhā vairāgyam। etasyaiva hi nāntarīyakaṁ kaivalyamiti ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: One who sees the faults of seen and scriptural objects and is detached, whose intellect is nourished by the purity and discrimination attained through the practice of seeing <s>Puruṣa</s>, is detached from the <s>guṇas</s> themselves—whether in their manifest or unmanifest form. That is the twofold detachment. Of the two, the latter is mere clarity of knowledge. Upon its arising, the <s>yogin</s>, with knowledge fully manifest, thinks thus: 'What was to be attained has been attained; the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) that were to be destroyed have been destroyed; the chain of continuous existence, whose links are closely joined, has been cut—that chain by whose unbroken continuity one dies after being born and is born after dying.' The supreme culmination of knowledge is detachment. For <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) is the inseparable consequence of this alone. // 16 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tacca dvividham - paraṁ cāparaṁ ca viṣayanimittabhedena । aparaṁ vyākhyātam । adhunā paramucyate-- [tatparaṁ puruṣakhyāterguṇavaitṛṣṇyam । tadi] ti vairāgyaṁ parāmṛśyate ।
[paramiti] pūrvoktavairāgyāduttarakālabhāvīti । yadi vā --tasya viṣayanimittābhyāmutkṛṣṭīnimittaviṣayatvāt , kaivalyasya vā pratyāsannataratvāt paramutkṛṣṭam ।
kiṁ nimittamasyetyāha— [puruṣakhyāte] rnimittāt । kiṁviṣayamityāha— [guṇavaitṛṣṇyamiti ।] guṇeṣu sattvādiṣuvaitṛṣṇyam । [dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayadoṣadarśīti ।] pūrvavairāgyanimittaviṣayaparāmarśanamasya viṣayanimittabhedavivekārtham । [puruṣadarśanābhyāsāt] nimittāt । [tacchuddhipravivekāpyāyitabuddhiḥ । taditi] puruṣadarśanaṁ parāmṛśyate । tasya śuddhiḥ [tacchuddhiḥ] nirṇiktakleśādimalatvam । athavā tasya puruṣasya śuddhistacchuddhiḥ । tacchuddhestadālambanadarśanaṁ pravivicyate । [tatpravivekenāpyāyitā] buddhirasya yoginaḥ ॥
guṇebhya iti viṣayapratipādanam । pūrvastu dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayabhyo('pi) viraktaḥ । eṣa tatkāraṇebhyo guṇebhya eva । [vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyaḥ] mahadādisaṁsthitā vyaktadharmakāḥ । pradhānāvasthitā avyaktadharmakāḥ । tebhyo virakta iti । [tat dvayaṁ vairāgyaṁ] pūrvamidaṁ ca । [tatna yaduttaraṁ] puruṣadarśananimittaṁ guṇaviṣayaṁ [tajjñānaprasādaḥ mātram ।] puruṣadarśanasyaiva paraḥ praviveka iti yāvat ॥
puruṣadarśī hi heyopādeyaśūnyacitto bhavati । tadāha--- [’'prasaṁkhyāne'pyakusīdasya sarvathā vivekakhyātedharmarmagheḥ samādhiḥ'] iti ॥
[yasyodaye] yasya vairāgyasyodaye । [pratyuditakhyātiḥ] pratyutpannadarśanaḥ । [evaṁ manyate prāptaṁ prāpaṇīyam] ityādi । [etasya hi nāntarīyakaṁ kevalyaṁ] tataḥ paraṁ sādhanānapekṣatvāt ! vairāgyasya jñānaprasādamātratve jñānavairāgyayorananyatvāt tadviparītayośca rāgājñānayoranarthāntaratvameva siddham । evaṁ sati rāgo'pyavidyāyā evāvasthāntaramiti pañcaparvā avidyetyupapannaṁ bhavati ॥
nanu caivaṁ buddheraṣṭaguṇatvaṁ bādhyeta । ṣaḍguṇatvaṁ hi dhyānāvasthābhedābhyupagamāt । jñānatve'pi vairāgyasya prasannataratvābhyupagamaḥ । rāgo'pyajñānasyāvasthāntaraviśeṣaḥ ।
nanu caivaṁ sati jñānājñānayoranekāvasthābhedādaṣṭaguṇatvaṁ punarapi na prāpnoti । naiṣa doṣaḥ । phalavattvapratyanīka-tvaniyamāt । jñānāvasthācatuṣṭayasya phalavattvena bhedaniyamaḥ । tathā ajñānāvasthācatuṣṭaya pratyanīkatvenādharmadicatuṣṭayaniyama ityaṣṭaguṇatvasiddhiḥ । dharmādipratidvandvina eva hi guṇatvena niyamyate, nājñānabhedāḥ sarva eva ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
And that is twofold—supreme and non-supreme, distinguished by their respective objects and causes. The non-supreme has been explained. Now the supreme is stated: "The supreme is indifference to the <s>guṇas</s>, arising from the knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>." The word 'that' refers back to detachment.
'Supreme' means arising at a time subsequent to the previously described detachment. Alternatively, it is supreme because its object and cause are superior to those of the former, or because it is closer to <s>kaivalya</s>.
What is its cause? He says: arising from "the knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>." What is its object? He says: "indifference to the <s>guṇas</s>"—indifference toward <s>sattva</s> and the other <s>guṇas</s>. "One who sees the faults of seen and scriptural objects"—this reference to the cause and object of the prior detachment is for the purpose of distinguishing them from one another. "Through the practice of seeing <s>Puruṣa</s>"—this is the cause. "Whose intellect is nourished by the purity and discrimination thereof"—'thereof' refers to the seeing of <s>Puruṣa</s>; 'its purity' is the state of being cleansed of the stain of <s>kleśas</s> and the rest. Or: 'the purity of that <s>Puruṣa</s>' is 'its purity'; the perception focused on that purity is discerned as discrimination. "The intellect nourished by that discrimination" belongs to this <s>yogin</s>.
"From the <s>guṇas</s>"—this indicates the object. The former detachment is from seen and scriptural objects; this one is from the <s>guṇas</s> themselves, which are their cause. "Whether in manifest or unmanifest form"—the manifest forms are those established in <s>mahat</s> (cosmic intellect) and the rest; the unmanifest forms are those established in <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial nature). Detached from these. "That is the twofold detachment"—the previous and this one. "Of the two, the latter"—caused by the knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>, with the <s>guṇas</s> as object—"is mere clarity of knowledge." The supreme discrimination of <s>Puruṣa</s>-knowledge is the highest point.
For one who sees <s>Puruṣa</s> becomes devoid of what is to be rejected or accepted. Thus he says: "Even for one who is not complacent in discernment, from discriminative knowledge in all ways, the <s>dharmamegha</s> <s>samādhi</s> [arises]" (YS 4.29).
"Upon whose arising"—upon the arising of that detachment. "With knowledge fully manifest"—with perception present. "He thinks: 'What was to be attained has been attained...'" and so forth. "For <s>kaivalya</s> is the inseparable consequence of this"—because it requires no further means beyond this. Since detachment is mere clarity of knowledge, knowledge and detachment are not different, and their opposites—attachment and ignorance—are also established as not essentially different. This being so, attachment too is but another state of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)—and so the proposition that <s>avidyā</s> has five branches is well-supported.
Objection: In that case, the eightfold nature of <s>buddhi</s> would be contradicted. Reply: Its sixfold nature, given the acceptance of distinctions among meditative states. Even when detachment is essentially knowledge, the acceptance of its being more refined [still holds]. And attachment too is a particular variant state of ignorance.
Objection: In that case, since knowledge and ignorance each have multiple variant states, the eightfold nature would again not be obtained. Reply: This is not a fault—because of the restriction to fruitfulness and opposition. The fourfold states of knowledge are restricted [to four] by their fruitfulness. Similarly, the fourfold states of ignorance are restricted to four by their opposition to <s>dharma</s> and the rest—thus the eightfold nature is established. For only the counterparts of <s>dharma</s> and the rest are restricted as qualities, not all the variants of ignorance. // 16 //

body.text: athopāyadvayena niruddhacittavṛtteḥ kathamucyate saṁprajñātaḥ samādhiriti –
body.translated_text: Then, how is <s>saṃprajñāta samādhi</s> described for one whose mental activities have been restrained by the twofold means?

body.text: vitarkavicārānandāsmitārūpānugamātsaṁprajñātaḥ ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Saṃprajñāta</s> [samādhi] is that which is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation), <s>vicāra</s> (reflection), <s>ānanda</s> (bliss), and <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness). // 17 //

body.text: vitarkaścittasyā''lambane sthūla ābhogaḥ ānando hlādaḥ। sūkṣmo vicāraḥ। ekātmikā saṁvidasmitā। tatra prathamaścatuṣṭayānugataḥ samādhiḥ savitarkaḥ। dvitīyo vitarkavikalaḥ savicāraḥ। tṛtīyo vicāravikalaḥ sānandaḥ। caturthastadvikalo'smitāmātra iti। sarva ete sālambanāḥ samādhayaḥ ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Vitarka</s> is the mind's gross engagement with its object. <s>Ānanda</s> is joy. The subtle [engagement] is <s>vicāra</s>. The unified awareness is <s>asmitā</s>. Of these, the first <s>samādhi</s>, accompanied by all four, is <s>savitarka</s> (with deliberation). The second, devoid of <s>vitarka</s>, is <s>savicāra</s> (with reflection). The third, devoid of <s>vicāra</s>, is <s>sānanda</s> (with bliss). The fourth, devoid of that too, is <s>asmitāmātra</s> (mere I-am-ness). All of these are <s>samādhis</s> with a support (<s>sālambana</s>). // 17 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
uktaṁ purastāt ' [samprajñātaḥ samādhirvitarkādyanugata ityupariṣṭāt pravedayiṣyāmaḥ'] iti । so'vasaraprāpta idānīṁ lakṣyeta । [upāyadvayena niruddhavṛtteḥ] vairāgyadvayaṁ parāparatvena vyākhyātam । abhyāsasyāpi dvitvaṁ sāmarthyādavasīyate । katham ? viśiṣṭamasamprajñātasamādherabhyāsaṁ sūtreṇaiva vakṣyati--’’ [virāmapratyayābhyāsapūrvaḥ’’] iti । tena sālambanaviṣayaḥ pūrvābhyāsa iti niścīyate । vakṣyati ca - [‘tatpratiṣedhārtham ekatatvābhyāsaḥ’] iti ॥
bhāṣyakāro'pyavādīt - ‘vairāgyeṇa viṣayasrota: khilīkriyate । vivekadarśanābhyāsena kalyāṇasrota uddhāṭyate? iti । nāvocata vṛttisvarūpatiraskārameva samprajñātasamādheḥ । vṛttinirodhaprabhavatvamaniṣṭaviṣayapravṛtyuparamottara-kālabhāvitvāpekṣayā, vṛttiviṣayaviśeṣānugata eva hi saḥ ॥
tathā ca dvitīyasūtre samprajñātasya nirodho na lakṣaṇamiti vyākhyātam । ataḥ pūrvoktābhyāsavairāgyopāyadvayena [niruddhavṛtteścittasya kathamucyate] -kathaṁ lakṣaṇamucyata iti yāvat । [vitarkavicārānandāsmitārūpānugamāt samprajñātaḥ ।] anugamaśabdaḥ pratyekaṁ saṁbandhanīyaḥ । vitarkānugamādvicārānugamādānandānugamādasmitārūpānugamāditi । rūpaśabdo mātrārtho vitarkādipūrvadharmatrayavārjatakhakhyāpanārthaḥ ॥
[vitarkaścittasyālambane sthūla ābhogaḥ ।] syūla(pi)miśrībhāvaḥ prathamamālambanākāreṇa pariṇamamānasya cittasya ya ālambanavyatikaraḥ sa vitarkaḥ ॥ [sūkṣmo vicāraḥ] ābhogaḥ sūkṣma iti saṁbandhaḥ । [ānando hlādaḥ] vicāraḥ sūkṣmatara ābhogastṛtīyaḥ । sānandatā viśeṣaḥ । ' [ekarūpātmikā saṁvidasmitā] svasyāṁ prakṛtāvasmitāyāṁ samāpannasya [asmitā] pratyayamātratā ekarūpātmakatvam । tathā codāhariṣyati- tamaṇumātmānamanvavaityāsmītyetāvatsaṁjānīta iti ॥
nanu cāsmitā kleśeṣu paṭhiṣyati 'dṛgdarśanaśaktyorekātmatevāsmitā' iti । tatkathamivāsmitārūpeṇa kleśena samādhiranugamyata iti । satyamevaṁ– prakṛṣṭasvakāraṇākārāvabhāsakatvādanyaviṣayavinivṛttātmakatvāñcāsmitāyā: samādhirūpatve'pyadoṣaḥ ॥
yadi vā asmitārūpasyālambanasyāvidyātve'pi na yogipratyayasyāvidyātvam । na hi khalu paracittavividiṣāyāṁ parasyāvidyātvam । na hi khalu paracittapratyayaṁ gṛhṇan parakīyāvidyāpratyayarūpālambanadoṣeṇa svayamavidyāvān bhavati ॥
athāsamprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ kimupāyaḥ ? kiṁsvabhāvo vā ? iti yaḥ punaḥ kleśaḥ sa viparyeyaviśiṣṭa eva । yathā---ahaṁ gacchāmi kṛśo'hamiti । yogicittasya tannyagbhūte rajastamasī iti na tathā ॥
tatra pūrvaḥ pūrvaḥ svakīyottarottaradharmānugataḥ । paraḥ parastu pūrvapūrvadharmavikalaḥ । yasmāccaitaddharmacatuṣṭayānugata evāyaṁ samprajñātaḥ samādhistasmādetallakṣaṇa iti lakṣaṇārthaṁ sūtram । loke'pi yo yadasādhāraṇadharmānuyātaḥ sa tallakṣaṇaḥ, yathā sāsnādilakṣaṇo gauriti ॥
asmitāmātragrahaṇānnirālambanatāmeṣāṁ samādhīnāṁ mā kaścidāśaṅkiṣṭatyāha- [sarva ete sālambanā iti ।] yaḥ punarmanyate nirvikalpatvamasmiteti--tadasat । asmitāśabdasyāhaṅkāre prasiddhatvāt । tathā cāha--asmibhāvo'smitā ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
It was stated previously: 'We shall explain hereafter that <s>saṃprajñāta samādhi</s> is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s> and the rest.' That occasion has now arrived and should be defined. "For one whose activities have been restrained by the twofold means"—the twofold detachment has been explained as supreme and non-supreme. The twofold nature of practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is also determined by implication. How? The <s>sūtra</s> itself will state the distinguished practice for <s>asaṃprajñāta samādhi</s>: "preceded by the practice of the cessation-cognition" (YS 1.18). From this it is determined that the prior practice has objects with support. And he will say: "For the prevention of that, the practice of one reality" (YS 1.32).
The <s>Bhāṣya</s>-author also said: 'By detachment, the current of objects is dammed up; by the practice of discriminative seeing, the auspicious current is opened.' He did not say that <s>saṃprajñāta samādhi</s> consists merely in the concealment of the nature of activities. Its capacity for producing the cessation of activities is with reference to its arising after the subsiding of activity toward undesired objects—for it is indeed accompanied by specific objects of activity.
Thus it was explained in the second <s>sūtra</s> that cessation is not the definition of <s>saṃprajñāta</s>.
