Just as a lamp enclosed by a covering such as a chamber illuminates externally only through the apertures in that covering; but that same lamp, when the covering is broken, illuminates in all directions without depending on particular aperture-paths.
Likewise, the <s>sattva</s> of <s>Īśvara</s>, due to the absence of connection with obstructions such as <s>kleśas</s>, when there is no cause that obstructs particular objects, simultaneously grasps all objects. And thereby, defects such as transgressing or not transgressing one's own scope are absent.
Because everything is an object of knowledge, the entire world has a single Lord—because of consisting of many particular objects such as places requiring a protector, like a well-known kingdom of this kind.
Likewise, because of possessing many instruments as causes of regulated stability, because of consisting of many regions endowed with formidable strongholds capable of overpowering each other, and because of possessing divisions of bodies with stable arrangement—like a well-known kingdom of this kind.
The practices of the <s>varṇas</s> (social classes), <s>āśramas</s> (life-stages), etc. have been taught by one possessing knowledge of the particular connections between the actions, means, and fruits of many agents and experiencers—because they are performed by those who desire fruit and fear adverse consequences, like the practice of medicine, rejuvenation treatments, etc.
Likewise, the teachings [of the <s>Vedas</s>]—because they are for the benefit of others, because they are teachings, because they are to be trusted by the wise, and because their meaning cannot be understood by humans without teaching—like the teaching of medicine etc.
The body and sense organs have been produced by a single efficient cause who knows all their purposes—because of possessing instruments as causes of regulated activity and stability, like a palace, house, wooden mechanism, etc.
Here it is stated: The arrangement of earth etc. is not, firstly, natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>). For no example exists that establishes that. And the sharpness of thorns etc. is not accepted as natural.
If one says that, like the heat of fire etc., the arrangement of earth is a property of the substance and therefore natural—there would be inconclusive reasoning (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>), since the arrangement of a palace is also a property of a substance.
If one says 'because it is natural'—that is unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), because it is accepted that the arrangement of the world is motivated by the enjoyment of the fruits of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit). The existence of the agent's <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> will be established below.
Therefore the arrangement of earth etc. is not natural—because of being for the enjoyment of living beings, like the arrangement of a palace. The movement of the moon etc. is not natural—because of being movement, like our own movement.
If one says our movement too is natural—no, because then there would be the unwanted consequence of permanence, like the heat of fire. For the heat of fire, being natural and invariable, does not require any cause for its own arising beyond the existence of the substance. But for actions, fruits, arrangements, etc., the requirement of a specific cause for their own arising shows they are not natural.
If one says that requiring a specific cause is also the nature of the arrangement of palaces etc.—let it be so. Even then, the arrangement of earth etc. has the nature of requiring a specific cause, just like a palace. And therefore the disagreement is merely verbal—the thesis remains unrefuted, because dependence on another agent is established.
The [opponent's] arguments are not valid proofs (<s>apramāṇa</s>) because of contradicting reasoning, scripture, and common experience. We state the contradiction with reasoning from [the premises of] surpassability etc.
And we state the contradiction with scripture from [passages such as] 'He who is omniscient, all-knowing,' 'The one controller,' etc.
And also the contradiction with universal common experience: all people, from cowherd to king, constantly engaged in worldly dealings, with minds directed toward names such as <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, etc.—even when contradicted, with their understanding unshaken, disregarding the leaves of objection against it—bow their heads to the supreme Lord and worship with offerings of flower-handfuls and the like. And they pray for fruits from Him alone.
If one were to say that their own arguments establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being contradict our thesis—to this it is said:
These are not valid proofs. How? Firstly, the thesis itself is defective. If the meaning of the word '<s>Īśvara</s>' is that the omniscient one does not exist, and if your intended sense of '<s>Īśvara</s>' is stated, then there would be the defect of proving what is already established.
If it is our intended sense, then for you there would be the defect of an unestablished qualifier.
If it is said that the <s>Īśvara</s>-nature includes non-omniscience, even then what is already established is being proved.
Likewise, there is also contradiction with one's own presuppositions. How? Since sovereignty and the seed of omniscience increase [in degree], their reaching the ultimate limit must be accepted, just as with magnitude. And the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' must be understood as denoting [beings with] sovereignty and omniscience that have reached their ultimate limit. And reaching the limit means being unsurpassable—just as the infinite magnitude of the soul, space, etc. is the endpoint of magnitudes. Thus there would be contradictions with reasoning, one's own presuppositions, and one's own words.
Moreover, if the meaning of the word ['<s>Īśvara</s>'] and the reaching of the ultimate limit of sovereignty are abandoned, there arises the fallacy of abandoning the meaning of words. For a word uttered after abandoning a portion of its denotation [is not properly used].
If one says that even magnitude etc. are not accepted as having an unsurpassable limit—that contradicts the established doctrine. For if the soul, space, etc. did not have all-pervasiveness, there would be the unwanted consequence of defects such as medium magnitude and impermanence. Even if the all-pervasiveness of the soul is [inferred] from the fact that its effects are seen everywhere, even then, by the very inference from general observation, the souls of birds etc. would pervade the space accessible to humans. And here too, who can prevent [the use of] an inference from general observation?
If one says 'it cannot be determined due to contradiction with reasoning'—then, regarding the soul etc. too, the raising of a contradiction with reasoning from [premises such as] measurability, substantiality, etc. is possible, [arguing that they are] like earth etc. Yet that alone does not make it a genuine contradiction with reasoning, because that would lead to the absence of all inference.
If one says 'the absence of inference is accepted'—then there should be no trust even in perception. But if the validity of perception lies in the arising of a definite cognition, then let inference too have validity by virtue of producing definite cognition. If one says 'only inference concerning objects with observed connections, such as smoke, [is valid]'—even there, there would be absence of inference: 'This region, though containing smoke, has no fire—because, when no connection with fire is perceived, it is a region, like a region perceived as devoid of fire.' 
If the validity of inference regarding objects with unobserved connections is established by corroboration from other means of knowledge, then perception too would be a means of knowledge [only] due to corroboration from other means of knowledge—because of being a means of knowledge, just like inference. Or it would be invalid, due to absence of corroboration from other means of knowledge, like inference from general observation. Therefore the validity of inference from general observation, producing definite cognition, cannot be denied.
Moreover: for one who does not accept the validity of inference from general observation, the fear of serpents etc. would be inexplicable, because the connection between one's own body and death has never been previously observed. Treatment through medicine for disease would not be possible, for lack of a cause for the apprehension of death. Likewise, since birth too has not been observed, one might consider one's own body as unborn. And there would be no injunction to avoid or adopt [certain courses of action].
Therefore, from the general observation that magnitude etc. are surpassable, the unsurpassability of <s>Īśvara</s>'s knowledge is established.
Furthermore: since the omniscience of <s>Īśvara</s> is the very thing being denied, its existence is thereby acknowledged, because a non-entity cannot be denied. For 'not' (<s>na</s>) is not used in isolation. It is said '<s>Īśvara</s>, the omniscient, does not exist.' Therein, omniscience is acknowledged as existing somewhere.
Just as [in the statements] 'the hare has no horn,' 'the barren woman has no son,' 'the sky has no flower'—the denial concerns horns, sons, flowers etc., which exist elsewhere, with respect to the hare etc.—so too here.
Moreover: by saying '<s>Īśvara</s> is not omniscient,' by denying the connection of the word-meaning '<s>Īśvara</s>' with omniscience, one acknowledges the omniscience of something other than <s>Īśvara</s>. For a denial of connection cannot be made without accepting both relata.
This proper connection is denied, and an improper one is accepted—that is mere futile effort. Because the well-established meanings of the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' are not denied. For it is not appropriate to deny the well-established infinite magnitude of space by saying 'infinite space does not exist' and then establish that [magnitude] in pots etc. which do not have established infinite magnitude.
If both relata—<s>Īśvara</s> and omniscience themselves—are denied, the thesis would contradict its own statement, because of accepting that <s>Īśvara</s> and omniscience are the meanings of the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient.' One cannot say 'fire is not the meaning of the word fire.'
If the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' have no established meanings—even then the denial of their meanings would be impossible, because an unestablished meaning cannot be reached. For no one can deny an unknown goat-wife on this peak. Moreover, the use of the words would be purposeless, because of having no established meaning.
If the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient,' having established meanings, are said by some to have a connection—like the sky with flowers—with unestablished unsurpassable sovereignty and omniscience, and that connection is what is denied—even then the thesis would contradict its own presupposition, because of denying an accepted meaning. For the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient,' by the inferential sign that they denote universals pervading instances of <s>Īśvara</s> and omniscience of varying degrees, already illuminate the existence of an unsurpassable <s>Īśvara</s> and omniscient being—like the words 'great,' 'many,' 'all,' 'infinite magnitude,' etc.
Just as these words 'great' etc., while denoting universals pervading well-known surpassable instances of greatness etc., serve as inferential signs for the existence of unsurpassable instances of greatness, manyness, totality, and infinite magnitude—because the universals pervading surpassable instances have the power to pervade unsurpassable instances too, and a universal that exists cannot fail to pervade an existing meaning it is capable of pervading. And since there is nothing to be pervaded beyond the unsurpassable, the universal reaches its terminus precisely in the domain of the unsurpassable as its final instance. Therefore, since the meanings of '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' are established by valid means of knowledge, one who tries to establish their non-existence commits the defect of denying an accepted meaning—the thesis is defective.
Nor can one make the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' denote something other than their [established] meaning. Since the power, knowledge, and sovereignty belonging to each person are surpassable and of varying degrees, the primary denotation of the words '<s>Īśvara</s>' and 'omniscient' does not apply to them—just as the words 'great' etc. are non-primary when applied to pots etc. where greatness varies, but are primary for space etc. Similarly here too, unsurpassable sovereignty and omniscience alone, being invariable, constitute the primary meaning of the words. And the denial of the primary meaning cannot succeed as a valid proof.
Moreover, just as the opponent denies the omniscience of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is established by reasoning and scripture, through the classification of properties such as knowability etc., saying 'like a pot'—by the very same properties of knowability etc., the consequence of unconsciousness, like a pot, would follow. Because there is no incompatibility—just as knowability is pervaded by non-omniscience [for the opponent], it could equally be pervaded by unconsciousness.
If one says 'there is contradiction with perception'—then here too, why do you not even glance at the contradiction with reasoning and scripture?
Nor can the properties such as knowability, which are common to all, prove anything in the concordant or discordant instances, because knowability etc. exist everywhere among real objects. The presentation of knowability etc. is not meant to confuse the mind.
If one says 'because of selfhood etc.'—then the consequence of non-omniscience would follow for your lords too, like a liberated soul. If one says 'there is contradiction with perception etc.'—here too, there is contradiction with reasoning etc., just as before.
As for the claim that <s>Īśvara</s> is not perceived in past and future times—since those who perceive presently existing lords are inconclusive, due to properties like 'being a living entity,' etc.—moreover, there are and will be living beings in past and future times too who perceive [<s>Īśvara</s>] through the inferential signs of surpassability etc., skilled in means of knowledge, because of being skilled in means of knowledge, like us. If one says '<s>Īśvara</s> is not omniscient because of being bodiless, like a liberated soul or space'—no, because of being embodied. For all manifest and unmanifest [beings] are both bodiless and embodied. If one says 'because of being embodied, <s>Īśvara</s>'s sovereignty would be impermanent, dependent on <s>dharma</s> etc.'—no, because of being [also] embodied. If one says 'there is contradiction between being embodied and bodiless'—no, because one sees both bodilessness and embodiment in a single soul that is liberated and being liberated. If one says 'there is no contradiction there because of different times'—no, because here too different times are accepted.
Moreover, because of the very nature of <s>Īśvara</s>'s sovereignty, both [embodiment and bodilessness] are simultaneously possible. Being with instruments and being without instruments are both fitting due to <s>Īśvara</s>'s nature. And thus the <s>śrutis</s> (scriptures) declare: 'Bodiless among bodies'; likewise, 'He who abides in all beings'; likewise, 'He who is omniscient, all-knowing,' etc.
If one says the <s>śrutis</s> are not authoritative regarding <s>Īśvara</s>, being arthavāda (eulogistic passages) due to mutual contradiction—no, because they are not subordinate to anything else. For when [the <s>Upaniṣads</s>] are not subordinate to ritual, none of the means of valid knowledge such as <s>śruti</s>, <s>liṅga</s> (indicative sign), etc. [supports the subordination].
If one says they are subordinate to the Vedic recitation injunction, as auxiliaries to the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> etc.—no, because, just as for the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> etc., there is no relationship of principal and subsidiary between separate procedural contexts. Just as the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> etc. are not subsidiaries of each other due to having separate procedures—likewise, being the subject of [injunctions such as] 'He is to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon deeply,' it is not fitting that they are subsidiary to the <s>Agnihotra</s> etc.
If one says 'because of the absence of a fruit [for the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> passages]'—no, because they are enjoined with reference to fruits such as 'He attains all worlds and all desires who knows that Self.'
If one says even so, being subsidiary to the injunction of meditation, they are merely praise (<s>stuti</s>)—praise is not possible with something entirely nonexistent. For [the statement] '<s>Vāyu</s> is the swiftest deity' does not assert that <s>Vāyu</s> is not the swiftest. If one says praise is possible even with something nonexistent—no, because what is established by inference is employed here.
If one says that due to <s>Īśvara</s>'s connection with the production of all effects, he would be connected with the pleasure and suffering of all beings—no, because of the difference in causes. The connection with body etc. for those in <s>saṃsāra</s> is caused by <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit). The connection with suffering etc. is caused by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. <s>Īśvara</s> has no <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>—because his connection with the production of body etc. is caused by unsurpassable sovereignty etc., like [the relationship between] a planet and one possessed by it.
If one says 'because of having sense organs like the eye etc., he does not perceive everything, like us'—no, because there is no obstructing cause for sense organs capable of grasping all objects. For the all-pervading sense organs have their scope contracted by the veiling of <s>adharma</s> etc. But for one who has no veil or obstruction of <s>dharma</s> etc., the sense organs grasp all their objects without remainder, due to the absence of that [veil]—and this is not defective.
Alternatively, <s>Īśvara</s>, through the sense organs of all beings—being a separate Self, even without His own [external] sense organs—experiences everything, like a spirit-possession, through all. And there is no object devoid of living beings—'He who abides in the earth,' 'He who abides in the waters'—from such <s>śruti</s> passages declaring the Inner Controller (<s>Antaryāmin</s>), the abiding of <s>Īśvara</s> in all [beings] is heard.
Or alternatively, <s>sattva</s> (the pure constituent) itself, supreme, endowed with the attributes of power, knowledge, and sovereignty that are unsurpassable, is all-pervading like space and hence connected with all; being of the nature of all objects, it illuminates all objects; and being inseparable from <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, it has unobstructed power. Thus, even on the hypothesis of [<s>Īśvara</s>] having no body or sense organs, the omniscience of <s>Īśvara</s> is established.
If one says the mind's capacity to grasp form etc. depends on the eye etc.—no, because that [objection] has been refuted by the absence of sovereignty and <s>dharma</s> [as obstructions in <s>Īśvara</s>].
Moreover, in the world, we see that even what is graspable by the eye is sometimes not grasped by the eye. All darkness, which is graspable by the eye, is perceived even by those with closed eyes whose inner organ is sound. Yet that very dense darkness is not grasped even by those with wide-open eyes whose minds are elsewhere—just as light in the very space being perceived.
If one were to say that darkness is merely the absence of light, not a real substance—that is not so, because an absence does not have the power to conceal a real thing.
If one were to say that the non-grasping of pots etc. is due to the absence of light, which is the cause of grasping, not because darkness is a concealing substance—no, because the eye, being illuminating, should not require the assistance of [external] light. In the absence of an obstructing substance of a different kind, whatever measure of illuminating capacity the eye has should illuminate objects through that capacity alone. For a lamp does not require a second lamp to illuminate.
Moreover, if the eye required the assistance of external light, then at night too, with the eye assisted by the light of the lord of stars (the moon), there would be the unwanted consequence of grasping form etc. as in daytime—in the absence of any cause of concealment.
Furthermore, if darkness is an absence, then on moonlit nights, since there are luminaries, darkness should not operate even mildly—it should cease entirely, because of the presence of luminaries. But a real substance can have degrees of intensity and weakness, not an absence, which is undifferentiated.
Moreover, the claim that non-perception is due to the absence of the capacity for perception through lack of an auxiliary—this too is contradicted. For even when there is the very intense light of lightning, and the brilliant play of lightning, why does the eye not perceive? For it is not reasonable that grasping fails due to the eye being startled by the lightning's auxiliary, because there is no incompatibility.
Moreover, in the medical treatise (<s>cikitsāśāstra</s>), shade is said to be 'sweet and cool.' But an absence cannot be sweet or cool. And shade has the quality of being wholesome. No one would attribute wholesomeness or unwholesomeness to an absence.
Also from the perception of lamp-shadow: if darkness were an absence, how could there be a lamp's shadow within the lamp's field of light? If one says 'even if it is a substance, it is not possible due to mutual opposition'—no, because of the possibility [of co-existence], as with poison and serpents. Just as poison, though capable of destroying life, is not capable of destroying the serpent's life—so too with a lamp and its shadow.
Therefore darkness is a real substance—because of possessing degrees of intensity and weakness, like light; because of being removable by an opposing substance, like a pot; and because of creating obstruction for the perceiver, like a wall.
From this [it follows that] the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>), even without sense organs, is capable of grasping the objects of the sense organs. For one whose ear-openings are blocked perceives sounds. And one cannot infer a separate organ of hearing for one whose ear-passages are blocked, because even a deaf person with blocked ear-passages does not grasp [sounds].
Moreover, the grasping of form etc. is seen to be independent of the sense organs through the knowledge of resolve (<s>pratijñā</s>).
Furthermore, if the mind could not grasp objects with surpassed capacity independent of the sense organs, memories would be inexplicable. But dream-memories of form etc. are vivid.
If form-grasping were to be accomplished previously only through the inner organ conjoined with the eye etc., then in dream too it would grasp only through the same [organs]. But that is not the case. The independence of the mind in grasping pleasure etc. is universally acknowledged.
Therefore, the sense organs are for the mind what light is for [ordinary perception]—while the mind itself is independent in grasping objects. As stated: 'through the channel of the sense-organ.' And the <s>śruti</s> too says: 'For one sees with the mind, one hears with the mind.'
If one were to say that, just as [ordinary] perception requires the assistance of light, the inner organ too requires the assistance of the sense organs to grasp—that is not so, because of counterexamples. Night-moving creatures grasp form in the day just as by different illumination. Even when light is present, owls etc. do not grasp form during the day.
Moreover, for a being who has accomplished mastery, the knowledge of the measure of gold etc. is seen from mere sight alone, without the instrument of a balance, even though balance etc. are generally required for measurement.
If one were to say 'then the sense organs would be purposeless'—one should reply: just as the balance etc. have a purpose elsewhere. Just as, through the culmination of expertise in the subject matter of the balance, a person can assess the measure of gold etc. by mere sight without the instrument of a balance—likewise the capacity of the inner organ to grasp form etc. even without the assistance of the eye etc. is not negated by the culmination of its expertise.
Nor is an action that can be accomplished by many necessarily unable to be accomplished by one. For we see that stones etc. being lifted by many are lifted by certain individual elephants, persons, etc. without assistance.
Likewise, forms etc., grasped by the inner organs of others with the assistance of the sense organs, are grasped by the <s>citta-sattva</s> (pure mind-substance) of the supreme Lord alone, without the activity of the eye etc.—because the unsurpassable culmination of sovereign expertise is such that it cannot be undermined.
For those in <s>saṃsāra</s>, being inferior to that, with sovereignty, power, knowledge etc. stained by the impurity of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and the like, the inner organ requires the assistance of the sense organs—like those of inferior strength [requiring assistance] in lifting stones.
But as for those who, while still being worldly beings, become sovereign—such as the foremost <s>Buddhas</s> etc.—their having unsurpassable power, knowledge, and sovereignty is not possible, because their [sovereignty] is limited by time. And those who praise their [system] accept that [the sovereignty] of these [<s>Buddhas</s> etc.] is limited by time.
Our <s>Īśvara</s> is not limited by time. He is to be inferred by the <s>Buddhas</s> etc. of that time and all prior times, through the inferential signs of surpassability of sovereignty etc., which they did not fully comprehend. He is not inferred by anyone in any of the three ways—'born at this time, being born, will be born'—for that would contradict unsurpassability.
Therefore, because the <s>Buddhas</s> etc. depend on accomplishment, and because earlier <s>Buddhas</s> have priority in time, it is not contradictory that a later <s>Buddha</s> too lacks unsurpassable power, sovereignty, and knowledge. If one were to say that those with equal power, knowledge, and sovereignty—like kings of equal kingdoms—merely exist at different times, even then, due to the frustration of the desire to pervade the time of other <s>Buddhas</s>, there is absence of unsurpassable sovereignty.
For someone desires to bring another <s>Buddha</s> under control and to pervade his domain—because desire is unrestricted. And if one cannot bring another <s>Buddha</s> under control, one's mastery over all is diminished.
If one says that because another <s>Buddha</s> needs no grace, and because of the absence of attachment etc., there is no desire to pervade his domain—to this it is said: just as the abiding of one who has attained Buddhahood for some time is preceded by desire, so too there must be desire for abiding during the time of another <s>Buddha</s>.
And because other beings who need grace exist, it is fitting that there be desire for abiding in another time-period. And not all living beings will be graced by a future <s>Buddha</s>.
Moreover, even if Buddhahood is of the nature of suffering, since the <s>Buddha</s>'s abiding is for the benefit of living beings, there must be a desire for abiding in another time-period. And since before accomplishment there is the grasp of <s>avidyā</s> etc., and since the Buddhahood's own nature, being devoid of suffering etc., is accepted by them—the unsurpassable power, knowledge, and sovereignty of the foremost <s>Buddhas</s> and other <s>tīrthaṅkaras</s> (founders of other traditions) is not established.
But because our <s>Īśvara</s> is not limited by time, these defects do not apply. And from the inference that power, knowledge, and sovereignty are unsurpassable, the defects of surpassability, instability, etc. are not to be feared any more than for the soul, space, etc.

body.text: sāmānyamātropasaṁhāre ca kṛtopakṣayamanumānaṁ na viśeṣapratipattau samarthamiti। tasya saṁjñādiviśeṣapratipattirāgamataḥ paryanveṣyā। tasyā''tmānugrahābhāve'pi bhūtānugrahaḥ prayojanam। jñānadharmopadeśena kalpapralayamahāpralayeṣu saṁsāriṇaḥ puruṣānuddhariṣyāmīti। tathā coktam – ādividvānnirmāṇacittamadhiṣṭhāya kāruṇyādbhagavānparamarṣirāsuraye jijñāsamānāya tatraṁ provāceti ॥ 25 ॥
body.translated_text: And when the conclusion pertains to the universal alone, inference—having exhausted its utility—is not capable of establishing the specific. The knowledge of specifics such as His name etc. must be sought from scripture (<s>āgama</s>). Even though there is no benefit to Himself, the benefiting of beings is His purpose. 'Through the teaching of the <s>dharma</s> of knowledge, I shall uplift beings wandering in <s>saṃsāra</s> during <s>kalpa-pralayas</s> (periodic dissolutions) and <s>mahā-pralayas</s> (great dissolutions).' And thus it is said: 'The first knower (<s>ādi-vidvān</s>), out of compassion, governing through a mentally created body (<s>nirmāṇa-citta</s>), the Blessed One, the Supreme Seer (<s>parama-ṛṣi</s>), taught the doctrine to <s>Āsuri</s> who wished to know.' (Sūtra 25)

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tathā ca darśayati - [sāmānyamātropasaṁhāre kṛtopakṣayamanumānam iti ।] niratiśayaśaktijñānaiśvaryayuktapuruṣaviśeṣasattvasāmānyamātropasaṁhāre [kṛtopakṣayaṁ] kṛta upakṣayo yasyānumānasya tatkṛtopakṣayaṁ sātiśayatvāditi । taduktamanumāne-yatra prāptistatra gatimātramiti । tasmānneśvarasaṁjñāguṇādiviśeṣāṇāṁ satāmapi pratipādane samartham । sāmānyamātropasaṁhāraparatvāt ॥
tadetaduktaṁ bhavati । yadaivaṁ satāmapi guṇānāṁ sāmānyapratipādanakṛtakṣayatvānna pratipādakamanumānam, kimaṅga punaranyantāsambhāvyamānasannidhīnāmanumeyadharmaviruddhānāmaśaktyajñānadharmādharmānaiśvaryādīnāṁ [na]tatpratyāyakamiti ॥
ata eva ca viruddhapratisādhanānupapattiḥ । sarvajñāstitvānumānavat prathamaṁ tadabhāvapratipādakānumānāpravṛtteḥ । na hyanumānasya paroktyudīkṣādharmatvamasti । na hi dhūmadarśanenāgnyanumāne vaktrantaroktirudīkṣyate ॥
na ca svayameva sarvajñāstitvaṁ nāstitvaṁ vā buddhi(prati)pūrvamāśaṅkayate । ghaṭādivat sarvajñasadbhāvasya svayamanabhyupagamāt । na hyanirdhāritaśaśisvarūpaḥ śaśe viṣāṇamasti nāstīti kaścidāśaṅkate ॥
paravākyāt pratipadyāśaṅkata iti cet-pareṇāpi kathamaprasiddheśvarasadbhāvanāśaṅkitamiti vaktavyam । atha parasya bhrāntiriti cet-na sāmānyānupalambhe bhrāntikāraṇamasti । na hi śuktikāyāṁ pikabhramaḥ kasyacidupajāyate । tasmādāha- [saṁjñādiviśeṣapratipattirāgamataḥ paryanveṣyā] iti । vedetihāsapurāṇayogadharmaśāstrādyāgamataḥ paryanveṣyā ॥
[tasyātmānugrahābhāve'pi] tasyātmārthamavāptavyābhāvāt [bhūtānāṁ] cāvidyāpaṅkanimagnānāṁ saṁsārasāgarottaraṇopāyaplavopadeśyantarasyābhāvāt [tadanugrahaḥ prayojanam । jñānadharmopadeśena] ye'nanyaśaraṇāstasmin sarvātmanā niveditātmānastān [kalpapralayamahāpralayeṣu] īśvarānugṛhītāgamajñānaviśeṣeṣvācāryeṣu pralīneṣu puna:punarjātakāruṇyāmṛtaḥ san [uddhariṣyāmīti] pravartata iti vākyaśeṣaḥ ॥
tathā [coktamādividvāniti] -ādau vidvān [ādividvān] rajastamobhyāmanabhibhūtajñāna ityarthaḥ । jñānadharmadi vā tata ādīyate ityādiḥ, ādiścāsau vidvāṁśca [adividvān nirmāṇacittaṁ] saṁkalpamātranirmitaṁ yogicittam āveśagrahavadupadeśanārtham [adhiṣṭhāya bhagavān paramarṣiḥ] paramadarśana ityarthaḥ । paramatvaṁ cāgamataḥ । darśanārthasya vā gatyarthasya vā dhātoḥ ṛṣergrahaṇam । paramarṣirīśvara eva kapilanārāyaṇādisaṁjña: [āsuraye provāceti ॥]
tasmāt pradhānapuruṣavyatiriktaḥ sarvvaprāṇibhāvakarmaphalaparisphuraṇajñānāttadanugrahakāraṇam īśvaraḥ siddhaḥ । sa prakṛṣṭasattvadhanopādānaṁ īśvaraḥ kathaṁ kartā ? kathaṁ cānugṛhṇāti ? ityevamādi na codayitavyam । [āgamataḥ paryanveṣyā] ityuktatvāt । anumānasya ca tadviṣayasyānupapattiḥ viśeṣasaṁbandhāgrahaṇāditi ॥ 25 ॥
body.translated_text:
Commentary (<s>Vivaraṇa</s>)
And thus he demonstrates: ['When the conclusion pertains to the universal alone, inference has exhausted its utility.'] When the conclusion pertains merely to the universal—the existence of a special being (<s>puruṣa-viśeṣa</s>) endowed with unsurpassed power, knowledge, and sovereignty—inference has its utility exhausted, i.e., that inference whose usefulness has been consumed, because of the possibility of something superior. As was stated regarding inference: 'Where there is attainment, there is only the fact of motion.' Therefore, inference is not capable of establishing the specifics of His name, qualities, etc., even though they exist, because it is limited to establishing the universal alone.

This amounts to saying: When even existing qualities are not established by inference due to its exhaustion in establishing universals, how much less can inference demonstrate properties such as lack of power, ignorance, lack of dharma, and lack of sovereignty—which are utterly impossible, contrary to the inferable property, and whose proximity cannot be conceived?

For this very reason, the objection of counter-proof (<s>viruddha-pratisādhana</s>) is untenable—just as with the inference for the existence of an omniscient being, because the inference establishing His non-existence does not operate in the first place. For inference does not have the property of awaiting someone else's utterance. For when inferring fire from seeing smoke, one does not wait for another speaker's statement.

Nor does one first raise the doubt 'Does an omniscient being exist or not?' by one's own prior cognition, since the existence of an omniscient being is not accepted by oneself, like a pot etc. For no one whose nature of the hare has not been ascertained raises the doubt 'Does the hare have horns or not?'

If one says the doubt arises from another's statement—even that other person must explain how the doubt about the existence of an unestablished <s>Īśvara</s> arose. If one says it is the other's error—there is no cause for error when a universal is not apprehended. For no one has the delusion of a cuckoo in a mother-of-pearl. Therefore he says: ['The knowledge of specifics such as His name must be sought from scripture (<s>āgama</s>)']—it must be sought from scriptures such as the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Itihāsas</s>, <s>Purāṇas</s>, <s>Yoga</s>, <s>Dharmaśāstras</s>, etc.

['Even though there is no benefit to Himself']—because there is nothing to be obtained for Himself. ['Of beings']—of those sunk in the mire of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), because there is no other instructor of the means, the raft for crossing the ocean of <s>saṃsāra</s>—['their benefiting is the purpose. Through the teaching of the dharma of knowledge,'] those who have no other refuge and who have surrendered themselves entirely to Him, ['during kalpa-pralayas and mahā-pralayas,'] when teachers favored by <s>Īśvara</s> with special scriptural knowledge have dissolved, again and again, being immortal with reborn compassion, ['I shall uplift them']—thus He proceeds; this is the completion of the sentence.

Thus ['it is said: the first knower (<s>ādi-vidvān</s>)']—one who was wise at the beginning, the <s>ādi-vidvān</s>; meaning: one whose knowledge is not overwhelmed by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. Or, 'that from which <s>dharma</s> of knowledge etc. is taken is <s>ādi</s>' (the beginning); he is both the beginning and the knower. ['Governing through a nirmāṇa-citta']—a yogic mind created by mere intention, like a possessed medium, for the purpose of teaching. ['The Blessed One, the Supreme Seer (<s>parama-ṛṣi</s>)']—meaning: one of supreme vision. His supremacy is known from scripture. The word <s>ṛṣi</s> is derived from the root meaning 'to see' or 'to go.' The Supreme Seer is <s>Īśvara</s> Himself, known by names such as <s>Kapila</s>, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, etc. ['He taught <s>Āsuri</s>.']

Therefore, <s>Īśvara</s> is established as distinct from <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>puruṣa</s> (individual soul), because His knowledge illuminates the states, <s>karmas</s>, and fruits of all living beings, and because He is the cause of their benefit. One should not raise objections such as: 'How can <s>Īśvara</s>, who takes on pre-eminent <s>sattva</s> as His material basis, be an agent? And how does He benefit beings?'—because it has been stated ['it must be sought from scripture']. And the inapplicability of inference to that domain has been shown, due to the non-apprehension of the relation with specifics. (Sūtra 25)

body.text: sa eṣaḥ –
body.translated_text: He is—

body.text: pūrveṣāmapi guruḥ kālenānavacchedāt ॥ 26 ॥
body.translated_text: the teacher even of the ancients, because He is not limited by time. (Sūtra 26)

body.text: pūrve hi guravaḥ kālenāvacchidyante। yatrāvacchedārthena kālo nopāvartate sa eṣa pūrveṣāmapi guruḥ। yathā'sya sargasyā''dau prakarṣagatyā siddhastathā'tikrāntasargādiṣvapi pratyetavyaḥ ॥ 26 ॥
body.translated_text: For earlier teachers are limited by time. He, where time does not serve the purpose of limitation—He is the teacher even of the ancients. Just as He is established at the beginning of this creation through the argument of excellence, so too He should be understood in past creations as well. (Sūtra 26)

body.text:
vivaraṇam
saḥ yathottarūpaḥ parameśvaraḥ [pūrveṣāmapi] gurūṇām abhyudayaniḥśreyasasarvasādhanasādhyasaṁbandhopadeśināṁ [guruḥ] teṣāmapi jñānopadeśasya kartetyarthaḥ । tadudbhavatvāt sarvajñānānām । yathā jvalanalavaṇajaladhisamudbhavā viṣphuliṅgalavaṇakaṇāḥ ॥
tasya cādividvattāmavocama [kālenānavacchedāditi ।] atītānāgatapratyupādīyamānatvaviśiṣṭena kālenānye guravo'vachidyante । sa tvīśvaraḥ sarvadā mukteśvaratvena tairapyasmābhirivānumeyaḥ ॥
kasmāt punastasya vastutve gurutvasāmānye ca sati nāvacchedakaḥ kāla iti cedāha - [yatrāvacchedārthaḥ kāle nopāvartata iti ।] yasminnīśvare viṣaye [avacchedārthaḥ] prasthādivat paricchedakaraḥ [nopāvartate] na paricchedakatveneśvaraṁ viṣayīkaroti sarvapariṇāmavastvavacchedakaro'pi san ॥
nanu ceśvaraprakṛṣṭasattvasya pradhānakāryatvāt, pradhānakāryasya ca kālāvacchedyatvāt, kasmāttatsattvaṁ nāvacchidyate puruṣasvarūpaṁ hi sarveṣāmeva kālānavacchedya(miti nāśaṅkanīya)mapariṇāmitvāt puruṣasya ॥
atha manyethāḥ-tantrāntaraprasiddheśvaravat sattvanirapekṣa īśvara iti tadayuktam-prakṛṣṭasattvāpādānābhyupagamāt ॥
athāpi manvīthāḥ--īśvarasattvāt pravṛttameva kāryamavacchinatti kāle neśvarasattvamiti-tadapyayuktam-vyaktasya paricchedyatvāt । vyaktaṁ ceśvarasattvam ॥
athāpyabhisandadhīthāḥ-pradhānāvasthameveśvarasattvamiti--tadanupapannam-- jñānānupapateḥ ॥
athāpi pratipadyethāḥ-satkāryābhyupagamādbījaphalavallarīkusumādivajjñānādīnāṁ pradhānāvasthā yatsattvameveti-tacca na sādhu-vyavahārayogyatvāt । sarveṣāṁ ca tathā satyanavacchedyatvaṁ jñānādisattāmātrasambandhaviśeṣāt prāpnuyāt ॥
athāpi bruvīthāḥ-vyaktatve satyapi kāryāṇāṁ kasyacit paricchedyatvaṁ kālīnaṁ kasyacinneti-tacca na-nyāyavirodhāt ॥
athāpi pratyavatiṣṭhethāḥ, īśvarasatvasya kālāparicchedyatvamāgamasiddhamiti - tacca na- avadyotakatvādagamasya ॥
athāpyācakṣīthāḥ-vidyamānasyaiva kālāparicchedyatvasyājñātasyāvadyotaka agama iti-taccāpi na -nirodhādisamanuṣṭhānanimittatvāt kālā(ja)vacchedye vaimalyādanavacchedyo vaimalyādanavacchedyaśceti viruddhaṁ syāt ॥
atrocyate-īśvarasatvavaimatyaprakarṣāpekṣatvāt kālānavacchedyatvasyādoṣaḥ ॥
yathā anyeṣāṁ gurūṇāṁ yogadharmādisamanuṣṭhānanimittatvāt kālānavacchedyo vaimatyaprakarṣaḥ, tathā na bhagavataḥ । katham? sarvadā'tyantatirobhūtarajastamastvādanapekṣitadharmādinimitte sakalārthāvadyotakaraṁ kālānavacchedyaṁ sattvasvarūpavadbhagavatsattve jñānam ॥
tathā tatkāryamapyutkarṣa: kālena nāvacchidyate । yathā cāgneruṣṇaprakāśāvagnau kālānavacchedyau, tathā bhagavatsatvasya vaimatyajñānaprakarṣāstatsattve kālānavacchedyatāmupayāntītyetadapekṣayābhihitaṁ [yatnāvacchedārtha: kālo nopāvartata] iti । na tvakāryāpekṣayā hyucyate ॥
gurutvaṁ hi nāvadhimat । tadevāha- [yathā'sya sargasyādau] jñānavaimalpa [prakarṣagatyā siddhaḥ] sargādijanmanāmanumeyatayā siddhaḥ āgamataścājñāyi, [tathā'tikrāntasargādiṣvapi] tatkālajanmanāṁ tataḥ prāktanānāmapi siddhaḥ । tathā bhaviṣyakāle'pyanumānāgamābhyāmavagamyate ॥
asya ca sūtrasyedaṁ prayojanam - yathā dṛṣṭā guravo jñānadharmādyupadeśitvādananyaśaraṇairanavaratamupāsyante, tathā bhagavānayamapi sarvagurūṇāmapi gurutvāttato'pi viśeṣeṇa nārāyaṇādināmā(dīnāma)nanyacetobhiḥ svahṛdayenāniśaṁ dhārayitavya iti ॥
yathā dṛṣṭagurava upāsanenābhimukhīkṛtāstadupāsanaparānanugṛhṇanti, tathā'yaṁ paramagururapyābhidhyānamātreṇānugrahaṁ karoti । tathā ca śrutiḥ-
[“yasya deve parā bhaktiryathā deve tathā gurau ।]
[tasyaite kathitā hyarthāḥ prakāśante mahātmanaḥ ॥ ”] iti ।
smṛtirapi -
[“matkarmakṛnmatparamo madbhaktaḥ saṅgavarjitaḥ ।]
[nirvairaḥ sarvabhūteṣu yaḥ sa māmeti pāṇḍava ॥ “] iti ॥ 26 ॥
body.translated_text:
Commentary (<s>Vivaraṇa</s>)
He, of the nature described, the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>), is ['the teacher even of'] earlier ['teachers']—those who instruct in the means and ends related to worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) and supreme liberation (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>)—['their teacher'] as well; meaning: He is the source of knowledge-instruction even for them. Because all knowledge originates from Him. Just as sparks and salt-grains originate from fire and the salt-ocean.

And we have stated His being the first knower. ['Because He is not limited by time.'] Other teachers are limited by time characterized by past, future, and present. But <s>Īśvara</s>, being always a liberated lord, is to be inferred even by them, just as by us.

If asked: since He exists as a real entity and shares the commonality of being a teacher, why does time not limit Him?—he answers: ['Where time does not serve the purpose of limitation.'] In the case of <s>Īśvara</s>, ['the limiting purpose'] like a measuring vessel, ['does not operate']—does not take <s>Īśvara</s> as its object for the purpose of measurement, even though it limits all things subject to transformation.

Objection: Since <s>Īśvara</s>'s pre-eminent <s>sattva</s> (purity) is an effect of <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), and since effects of <s>pradhāna</s> are subject to temporal limitation, why is that <s>sattva</s> not limited? The nature of <s>puruṣa</s> (soul) is indeed not limited by time for all—this should not be doubted—because <s>puruṣa</s> is beyond transformation.

If you think: '<s>Īśvara</s> is independent of <s>sattva</s>, like the <s>Īśvara</s> well-known in other systems'—that is incorrect, because the acceptance of pre-eminent <s>sattva</s> as His material basis has been upheld.

If you also think: 'Time limits only the effect produced from <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s>, not <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s> itself'—that too is incorrect, because what is manifest is subject to limitation, and <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s> is manifest.

If you intend: '<s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s> is in the state of <s>pradhāna</s> (unmanifest)'—that is untenable, because knowledge would then be impossible.

If you accept: 'Due to the doctrine of <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existence of effect in cause), the <s>sattva</s> that is knowledge etc. exists in the <s>pradhāna</s> state like seed-fruit-vine-flower'—that too is not proper, because it must be fit for conventional usage. And if all things were so, non-limitability would follow for everything, due to the mere relation with the existence of knowledge etc.

If you also say: 'Even when manifest, some effects are limited by time and some are not'—that too is not correct, because it contradicts logic.

If you maintain: 'The non-limitability of <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s> by time is established by scripture (<s>āgama</s>)'—that too is not correct, because scripture merely reveals.

If you also say: 'Scripture reveals the non-limitability by time of something already existing but unknown'—that too is not correct, because [otherwise] since the temporal limitability is caused by the practice of cessation etc., it would be contradictory to say 'limited by time due to purity' and also 'not limited by time due to purity.'

To this we reply: There is no fault, because the non-limitability by time depends on the excellence of <s>Īśvara</s>'s <s>sattva</s>-purity. Just as for other teachers, the excellence of purity is not limited by time because it is caused by the practice of <s>yoga</s>, <s>dharma</s>, etc.—so too, but not for the Blessed One. How so? Because <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> are always and completely vanished, the knowledge in the <s>sattva</s> of the Blessed One, which illuminates all objects, is not limited by time, independent of causes such as <s>dharma</s>—just like the very nature of <s>sattva</s> itself.

Likewise, its effect—the excellence—is also not limited by time. Just as heat and light, being properties of fire, are not limited by time in fire, so the excellences of purity, knowledge, etc. of the Blessed One's <s>sattva</s> attain non-limitability by time in His <s>sattva</s>. It is with reference to this that it is said ['where time does not serve the purpose of limitation'], not with reference to being without effect.

His status as teacher is without boundary. He states: ['Just as He is established at the beginning of this creation'] through the excellence of knowledge and purity, ['established'] as provable through inference by those born at the beginning of creation, and also known through scripture, ['so too in past creations'] He is established for those born at that time and for those even more ancient. Likewise, in future time too, He is known through inference and scripture.

The purpose of this <s>sūtra</s> is this: Just as visible teachers, being instructors of the <s>dharma</s> of knowledge etc., are constantly worshipped by those who have no other refuge—so too this Blessed One, being the teacher of all teachers, should be held in one's heart unceasingly with even greater devotion, by those whose minds are set on none other, through names such as <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> etc.

Just as visible teachers, when propitiated through worship, bestow grace upon those devoted to worshipping them—so too this Supreme Teacher bestows grace merely through meditation. And thus the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) says:

'He who has supreme devotion to God, and to the teacher as to God—to that great soul these teachings become illuminated.'

And the <s>smṛti</s> (tradition) also says:

'He who performs actions for Me, who regards Me as supreme, who is My devotee, free from attachment, without enmity toward all beings—he comes to Me, O son of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>.' (Sūtra 26)

body.text: tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ ॥ 27 ॥
body.translated_text: His designator is <s>praṇava</s> (Oṃ). (Sūtra 27)

body.text: vācya īśvaraḥ praṇavasya। kimasya saṁketakṛtaṁ vācyavācakatvamatha pradīpaprakāśavadavasthitamiti।
body.translated_text: <s>Īśvara</s> is the denoted meaning of <s>praṇava</s>. Is the word-meaning relationship of this based on convention, or is it established like a lamp and its light?

body.text:
vivaraṇam
īśvarapraṇidhānādityuktaṁ, sa kathaṁ praṇidhātavyaḥ ? kiṁ ca tatpraṇidhānasādhanam ? yena praṇidhātā praṇidhatta iti tatpraṇidhānasādhanapratipādanārthamāha - [tasya vācakaḥ praṇava] iti । [tasya] īśvarasya yathoktalakṣaṇasya [vācakaḥ] abhidhāyakaḥ [praṇavaḥ] sāsnādimata iva gośabdaḥ ॥
prakarṣeṇa nūyate stūyate aneneti praṇavaḥ । yadi vā, praṇauti stautīśvaramiti praṇava oṅkāraḥ । praṇidhīyate cānena bhagavān praṇidhātṛbhiriti, praṇamanti vā । aneneti, praṇidhate vā tena bhagavantaṁ cetasīti, dhāño vakāropajanaṁ kṛtvā । śabdena hi parokṣāṇāmarthānāṁ manasi praṇidhānaṁ merurindra iti yathā ॥
tasya coṅkārasya vācyaḥ [īśvaraḥ ।] anvarthaṁ khalvapi nirvacanam । avateḥ rakṣaṇādyarthānmaniṣṭilopaśceti । praṇidhātṝn saṁsārādavatīti, gamayati vā । saṁsāriṇaṁ nirvāṇamiti, niratiśayaṁ vā prīṇayati, samādhyādyanugraheṇāvagamayati vā paramārthamityevamādyarthānugatam sarvathā tu nediṣṭhaṁ priyaṁ nāma bhagavataḥ ॥
tena hi manasi satataṁ praṇidhāyamānaḥ prasīdati । tathā cānekaśaḥ śrutayaḥ- [‘oṁ khaṁ brahma’ ‘omiti brahma’] ityādayaḥ । smṛtayaśca [‘oṁ tatsat’] iti । [‘oṁ viśvaṁ viṣṇuḥ'] ityādayaḥ । oṁśabdasya kṛdantaṁ yanmāntamityavyayatvādvibhaktinivṛttiḥ ।
[kimasya saṅketakṛtaṁ vācyavācakatvaṁ? atha pradīpaprakāśavadavasthitamiti ।] kiṁ cātaḥ ? । yadi tena bhagavatā anyairvā saṁvyavahārārthamasya nābhedamastviti saṁketitam, tato'sya prāgoṁśabdāvācyatvādoṁśabdena vā praṇidhātāraḥ prāṇyadhiṣata, anyena vā nāmāntareṇādhītavantastathedānīmapyastu, kimoṅkārāvaśeṣavacanena । athāpi [pradīpaprakāśavadavasthitaṁ,] tathā'pi prathamaśravaṇe'pīśvara upalabhyeta yathā prakāśena savitā ॥
kiṁ ca-saṅketo'pyanarthakaḥ sthitasambandhatvāt । athāpūrvaṁ saṅketyeta, pūrvoktadoṣaprasaṅga iti manyate ॥
body.translated_text:
Commentary (<s>Vivaraṇa</s>)
It has been said '<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s> (devotion to Īśvara)'—how is He to be meditated upon? And what is the means of that meditation, by which the meditator meditates? To explain the means of that meditation, he says: ['His designator is praṇava.'] ['His']—of <s>Īśvara</s> as previously defined. ['Designator']—that which denotes. ['Praṇava']—just as the word 'cow' denotes what possesses a dewlap etc.

<s>Praṇava</s> means: that by which He is praised (<s>nūyate</s>) eminently (<s>prakarṣeṇa</s>). Or, <s>praṇava</s> is the syllable <s>Oṃ</s>, meaning: it praises <s>Īśvara</s>. The Blessed One is meditated upon (<s>praṇidhīyate</s>) through it by meditators; or they bow (<s>praṇamanti</s>) through it; or the meditator places (<s>praṇidhatte</s>) the Blessed One in his mind through it—applying the suffix to the root meaning 'to place.' For through words, objects that are beyond perception are placed in the mind—as with '<s>Meru</s>' or '<s>Indra</s>.'

And the denoted meaning of <s>Oṃkāra</s> is [<s>Īśvara</s>.] The etymological meaning is also fitting. From the root <s>av</s> meaning 'to protect' etc., with the elision of <s>m</s> and <s>aniṣṭi</s>. He who protects (<s>avati</s>) the meditators from <s>saṃsāra</s>, or who leads them to <s>nirvāṇa</s>, or who gives unsurpassed delight, or who makes them understand the ultimate reality through the grace of <s>samādhi</s> etc.—following such meanings, in every way, <s>Oṃ</s> is the dearest and most intimate name of the Blessed One.

For when He is constantly placed in the mind through it, He becomes gracious. And thus numerous <s>śrutis</s> (scriptures): '<s>Oṃ</s> is space, is <s>Brahman</s>,' '<s>Oṃ</s> is <s>Brahman</s>,' etc. And <s>smṛtis</s> (traditions): '<s>Oṃ tat sat</s>,' '<s>Oṃ</s>, the universe is <s>Viṣṇu</s>,' etc. The word <s>Oṃ</s>, since it ends in a <s>kṛt</s> suffix ending in <s>m</s>, being indeclinable, has no case-endings.

['Is the word-meaning relationship based on convention? Or is it established like a lamp and its light?'] What follows from this? If the Blessed One or others established the convention 'let there be no difference between this' for the purpose of practical usage, then prior to this, <s>Oṃ</s> did not denote <s>Īśvara</s>, and meditators meditated upon Him either through <s>Oṃ</s> or through some other name—then let it be so now too; what is the point of the exclusive statement about <s>Oṃkāra</s>? But if ['it is established like a lamp and its light,'] then even upon first hearing, <s>Īśvara</s> would be apprehended, just as the sun is apprehended through its light.

Furthermore, convention would be purposeless, since the relation is already established. Or if an unprecedented convention were made, the previously stated faults would follow—so he thinks.

body.text: sthito'sya vācyasya vācakena saha saṁbandhaḥ। saṁketastvīśvarasya sthitamevārthamabhinayati। yathā'vasthitaḥ pitāputrayoḥ saṁbandhaḥ saṁketenāvadyotyate, ayamasya pitā, ayamasya putra iti। sargāntareṣvapi vācyavācakaśaktyapekṣastathaiva saṁketaḥ kriyate। saṁpratipattinityatayā nityaḥ śabdārthasaṁbandha ityāgaminaḥ pratijānate ॥ 27 ॥
body.translated_text: The relation between this denoted meaning and the denoting word is established. Convention merely demonstrates the already-established meaning of <s>Īśvara</s>. Just as the relation between father and son is already established, and convention merely reveals it: 'this is his father, this is his son.' In other creations too, convention is made in accordance with the same word-meaning capacity. The followers of the <s>Āgama</s> (scriptural tradition) declare: 'The relation between word and meaning is eternal, because of the eternity of the conventional agreement.' (Sūtra 27)

body.text:
vivaraṇam
atrocyate- [sthito'sya vācyasya vācakena] sambandho yadi nityaḥ śabdo yadi vā anityaḥ, saṅketastu tameva sthitaṁ sambandhamavajvalayati ॥
nanu coktaṁ-sthitaścet prathamaśravaṇe'pi taṁ pratīyuriti । ucyate-na hi pratyāyyapratyāyakasambandhaḥ śabdārthayoḥ sthito'pi sannindriyeṇa gṛhyate । yathendriyārthayoḥ । apratyakṣe hi vācyavācakaśaktī ॥
tataśca yenocyate śabdādartho'numeya iti-tadasat । sambandhāgrahaṇāt । paraprayegavyaṅgyatvācca sambandhasya । na hyanumānaṁ paraprayogamapekṣate ॥
atha brūyādanumitāt saṁbandhādarthānumānamiti । sa vaktavyaḥ kathamanumitaḥ śabdārthasambandhaḥ? iti ॥
sa cet brūyāt-kāryadarśanādarthaṁ hi pratītya paścādanuminoti tatsaṁbandham । yathā cakṣuṣā rūpamupalabhya cakṣussaṁbandhamiti । sa prativaktavyaḥ-siddhaṁ tarhi vinā'numānena śabdādeva pratipattiriti ॥
yo hi grāṣṭrapākenaiva kṛtārtha: kiṁ tasya kilośipākena । athāsakṛt prayogadarśanādgṛhyate sambandhaḥ, yathā'gnidhūmayoriti cet- na tu brūmaḥ na hi sahasreṣvapi prayogeṣu pratyakṣeṇa śavdārthayoḥ saṁbandho gṛhyate yathā'gnidhūmayorādāvapi saṁbandho gṛhyate । vākye'pyayameva ॥ tasmādavasthitameva vācyasyeśvarasya vācakena praṇavena sambandhamavadyotayati saṅketo yathā sthitaṁ pitāputrasaṁbandham । saṅketopāyāpekṣatvāt prathamaśrutānnārthaḥ pratīyate । yathā cakṣuṣa ālokābhāve ॥
nanu ca śabdānityatvapakṣe kathamanitye saṁbandhini nityaḥ saṁbandha iti । na hyanityayo rajjughaṭayoḥ saṁvandho nityaḥ syāt । ucyate-yathā pramāṇaprameyayorindriyaviṣayayośca kriyākārakāṇāṁ saṁbandhaḥ sthita evānityeṣvapi saṁbandhiṣu, tadvadatrāpi sthita evāvyabhicāreṇa saṁbandhaḥ [sargādiṣvapi vācyavācakaśaktyapekṣaḥ saṅketaḥ ।] ।
yathaiva rūpacakṣuṣorgrāhyagrāhakaśaktyapekṣayaiva sargādau sargastathehāpi [vācyavācakaśaktyapekṣayaiva saṅketaḥ kriyate ॥]
sampratipattinityatayā vṛddhaparamparayaiva gamyagamakabhāvena śabdārthayoḥ saṁpratipatirnityā nānyatheti [āgaminī] vedavādina: [pratijānate ।] sampratipattiśca śabdārthasaṁbandhasya hetustadeṣām ॥
tadetaduktaṁ bhavati-yadyāgamipakṣaḥ syādathānyapakṣaḥ, sarvathā sthita eva saṁbandhaḥ pitāputrayoriva saṅketenābhivyajyata iti ॥
vācyavācakayorasthitasaṁbandhatve tu praṇavarūpeṇābhimukhībhavatīśvara iti nāvakalpate । na hi pācyapācakasaṁbandhe na ca sthite pācakāgnyupādānaṁ pākārthaṁ kalpate । sthite tu vācyavācakasaṁbandhe bhagavadārādhanasādhanasya praṇavasyopādānamavakalpata iti tatpratipādanārthaṁ sarvaṁ bhāṣyam ॥ 27 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Here it is stated—["The relation of this signified with its signifier is established"]—whether the word is eternal or non-eternal, convention merely illuminates that already established relation.
Objection: If it is established, then even upon first hearing one should comprehend it. Reply: The relation between signified and signifier, even though established between word and meaning, is not grasped by the senses, just as [the relation] between sense organ and object [is not directly perceived]. For the powers of signified and signifier are imperceptible.
Therefore, whoever says that meaning is to be inferred from the word—that is wrong. Because the relation is not grasped [independently]. And because the relation is revealed only through the usage of others. For inference does not depend on the instruction of others.
If one were to say that the inference of meaning proceeds from the inferred relation—he must be asked: How is the relation between word and meaning inferred?
If he replies: From observing the effect—for having first understood the meaning, one subsequently infers that relation, just as having perceived form through the eye, one [infers] the eye's connection—he should be answered: Then it is established that comprehension comes from the word itself, without inference.
For one who has accomplished his purpose with a village cooking pot—what need has he of a refined vessel? If it be objected that the relation is grasped from observing repeated usage, just as with fire and smoke—we say: No, for even in thousands of usages, the relation between word and meaning is not perceptible to direct perception, whereas the relation between fire and smoke is grasped even at first. The same applies to sentences.
Therefore, convention merely illuminates the already established relation between <s>Īśvara</s> as the signified and <s>Praṇava</s> as the signifier, just as [convention illuminates] the established relation between father and son. Because the means of convention is required, the meaning is not comprehended from what is heard for the first time—just as [one cannot see] with the eye in the absence of light.
Objection: On the view that words are non-eternal, how can the relation be eternal when the relata are non-eternal? For the relation between a non-eternal rope and pot cannot be eternal. Reply: Just as the relation between means of valid knowledge and objects of knowledge, between sense organs and their objects, and between actions and their factors, is established even when the relata are non-eternal, so too here the relation is established without deviation. [Even in successive creations, convention depends on the powers of signified and signifier.]
Just as in each creation the relation between form and the eye depends on the power of apprehensible and apprehender, so too here [convention is made depending on the powers of signified and signifier].
By the eternality of mutual understanding, through the tradition of elders alone, the mutual understanding of word and meaning in the relation of what is to be conveyed and what conveys is eternal and not otherwise—thus the proponents of the [Vedic] tradition [maintain]. And mutual understanding is the ground of the relation between word and meaning—that is their [position].
Thus it has been said: Whether one holds the traditional view or any other view, in every case the relation is established—just as between father and son—and is manifested by convention.
But if the relation between signified and signifier were not established, then the notion that <s>Īśvara</s> is approached through the form of <s>Praṇava</s> would not be tenable. For when the relation of what is to be cooked and the cooker is not established, the use of fire for cooking is not tenable. But when the relation of signified and signifier is established, the adoption of <s>Praṇava</s> as the means of worshipping the <s>Bhagavān</s> (Lord) becomes tenable—to demonstrate this is the purpose of the entire <s>Bhāṣya</s>. // 27 //

body.text: vijñātavācyavācakatvasya yoginaḥ –
body.translated_text: For the <s>yogin</s> who has understood the relation of signified and signifier—

body.text: tajjapastadarthabhāvanam ॥ 28 ॥
body.translated_text: Its repetition (<s>japa</s>) and contemplation of its meaning. // 28 //

body.text: praṇavasya japaḥ praṇavābhidheyasya ceśvarasya bhāvanam। tadasya yoginaḥ praṇavaṁ japataḥ praṇavārthaṁ ca bhāvayataścittamekāgraṁ saṁpadyate। tathā coktam –
body.translated_text: The repetition (<s>japa</s>) of <s>Praṇava</s> and the contemplation (<s>bhāvana</s>) of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is denoted by <s>Praṇava</s>. For this <s>yogin</s> who repeats <s>Praṇava</s> and contemplates the meaning of <s>Praṇava</s>, the mind becomes one-pointed (<s>ekāgra</s>). And thus it has been said—

body.text: svādhyāyādyogamāsīta yogātsvādhyāyamāmanet।
body.translated_text: Through <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study) one should practice <s>yoga</s>; through <s>yoga</s> one should pursue <s>svādhyāya</s>.

body.text: svādhyāyayogasaṁpattyā paramātmā prakāśate ॥ iti ॥ 28 ॥
body.translated_text: By the perfection of <s>svādhyāya</s> (self-study) and <s>yoga</s>, the Supreme Self (<s>Paramātmā</s>) is revealed. // 28 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
evamavagatavācyavācakasaṁbandhasya yoginaḥ parameśvaraprasādanaṁ kathaṁ kriyata iti tadarthamāha- [tajjapastadarthabhāvanam] tasyeśvaravācakasya praṇavasyārdhacaturmātrasya trimātrasya vā japaḥ manasopāṁśu vā āvartanaṁ japaḥ, tadarthasya ceśvarasya praṇavena vācakena samarpitasya buddhau samāropitasya bhāvanamabhidhyānaṁ [tadarthabhāvanam ।] kartavyamiti vākyaśeṣaḥ ॥
tadevamubhayaṁ kurvato yoginaḥ cittamekāgraṁ sampadyate । ekāgrasampattiṁ ca tadārādhanaphalaṁ darśayati- [tathā coktam-svādhyāyādyogamā(tiṣṭhet)sīta svādhyāyāt] praṇavajapādīśvaraṁ pratyavanatacittaḥ san [yogamāsīta ।] tadarthamīśvaraṁ dhyāyet । (rasyayat)tadarthadhyānāccāpracalitamanāḥ [svādhyāyaṁ praṇavamāmanet] manasā'bhijapet । mānaso'bhijapaḥ praśasyate dhyānasyāsannataratvāt । mā viṣayapravaṇacitto bhūditi । evaṁ [svādhyāyayogasampatyā] tadvirodhinā pratyayāntareṇānabhighātaḥ [svādhyāyayogasampattiḥ ।] tayā ca praṇavajapaparameśvaradhyānasampatyā [para ātmā] parameṣṭhī [prakāśate] yogina iti ॥ 28 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
For the <s>yogin</s> who has thus understood the relation of signified and signifier—how is the propitiation of <s>Parameśvara</s> (the Supreme Lord) to be performed? To answer this he says: ["Its repetition and contemplation of its meaning."]. The <s>japa</s> (repetition) of <s>Praṇava</s>, which is the signifier of <s>Īśvara</s>, consisting of three-and-a-half <s>mātrās</s> or three <s>mātrās</s>—<s>japa</s> is the mental or whispered recitation. And the <s>bhāvana</s> (contemplation) of <s>Īśvara</s>, who is the meaning of that [<s>Praṇava</s>], presented through the signifier <s>Praṇava</s> and established in the intellect—["contemplation of its meaning"]—is to be performed; this is the completion of the sentence.
Thus for the <s>yogin</s> who performs both, the mind becomes one-pointed. And he shows that the fruit of one-pointedness results from that worship: ["And thus it has been said: 'Through <s>svādhyāya</s> one should practice <s>yoga</s>'"]. Through the repetition of <s>Praṇava</s>, with the mind inclined toward <s>Īśvara</s>, ["one should practice <s>yoga</s>"]—one should meditate on <s>Īśvara</s> for that purpose. And with the mind steady from meditating on that meaning, ["one should pursue <s>svādhyāya</s>, the <s>Praṇava</s>"]—one should repeat it mentally. Mental repetition is praised because it is closer to meditation—lest the mind become inclined toward sense objects. Thus ["by the perfection of <s>svādhyāya</s> and <s>yoga</s>"]—the non-obstruction by any other thought contrary to it is the perfection of <s>svādhyāya</s> and <s>yoga</s>. And by that perfection of <s>Praṇava</s> repetition and meditation on <s>Parameśvara</s>, ["the supreme Self"], <s>Parameṣṭhin</s> (the Highest), ["is revealed"] to the <s>yogin</s>. // 28 //

body.text: kiṁ cāsya bhavati –
body.translated_text: Moreover, what accrues to him—

body.text: tataḥ pratyaktcetanādhigamo'pyantarāyābhāvaśca ॥ 29 ॥
body.translated_text: From that, the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles. // 29 //

body.text: ye tāvadantarāyā vyādhiprabhṛtayaste tāvadīśvarapraṇidhānānna bhavanti। svarūpadarśanamapyasya bhavati। yathaiveśvaraḥ puruṣaḥ śuddhaḥ prasannaḥ kevalo'nupasargastathā'yamapi buddhe pratisaṁvedī yaḥ puruṣastamadhigacchati ॥ 29 ॥
body.translated_text: The obstacles beginning with disease—by devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s>), these do not arise. And the vision of one's own true nature also occurs for him. Just as <s>Īśvara</s> is a <s>Puruṣa</s> who is pure, luminous, absolute, and free from afflictions, so too does he realize that <s>Puruṣa</s> who is the witness of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>). // 29 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[kiścāsya bhavati ?] pūrvasūtre cittamekāgraṁ sampadyata ityuktamekaṁ phalam , tadepakṣayā kiñceti cakāraḥ । kiñcānyadapyasti phalam ? āhosviccittaikāgratvameveti, tatrāha [-tataḥ pratyakcetanādhigamo'pyantarāyābhāvaśca । tataḥ] tasmādīśvarapraṇidhānāt [pratyakcetanādhigamaḥ pratyak] svabuddhiṁ [cetayata] iti [pratyakcetana] ātmā, tasya [adhigamo] yathāvatsvarūpasaṁvedanam ॥
nanu cādhigata eva pratyātmaṁ puruṣo'haṁ sukhī duḥkhī cāhamiti । evaṁ prasiddhaṁ, tataḥ kiṁ viśeṣeṇocyate iti । satyamevam-kiṁ tvaviśiṣṭo'so pratyayaścittasya vṛtyā । kiñca-sukhī duḥkhī cāhamiti sukhiduḥkhisāmānādhikaraṇyādihāhaṁpratyayasya cittavṛttiviṣayatvādavidyāpratyaya eva prasiddhiḥ ॥
kathaṁ tarhyasyādhigama ityāha- [yathaiveśvaraḥ puruṣaḥ śuddhaḥ] kleśādimalavarjitastata eva [prasannaḥ] svacchastata eva [kevalo] nistriguṇastata eva [nirupasargastā] patrayavarjitaḥ prakṛṣṭasattvapratisaṁvedī [ca tathā'yamapi] madīyaḥ puruṣaḥ śuddhaḥ prasannaḥ kevalo nirupasargo [buddheḥ pratisaṁvedītyavagacchati ॥]
yathā tatheti ca dṛṣṭāntadārṣṭāntikanirdeśādīśvarakṣetrajñayorbheda ukto bhavati । baddhamuktopapatteśca । pradhānasya pārāthyopapatteḥ । kṣetrajñānāṁ cāta eva parasparabhedaḥ ॥
kiñcāsya bhavati ? [ye tāvadantarāyā vyādhiprabhṛtayo] vakṣyamāṇāste'pi cāsye [śvarapraṇidhānānna bhavanti ॥ 29 ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
["Moreover, what accrues to him?"] In the previous <s>sūtra</s>, one result was stated—that the mind becomes one-pointed. In relation to that, the word 'moreover' [indicates]: is there yet another result? Or is it only one-pointedness of mind? To this he says: ["From that, the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles. From that"]—from devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>. ["Attainment of inward consciousness"]—["inward"] means one's own intellect; ["the one who is conscious"] of it is the ["inward conscious one"], the <s>Ātman</s>; its ["attainment"] is the realization of its true nature as it really is.
Objection: But <s>Puruṣa</s> is already known to each individual self—'I am happy,' 'I am suffering.' This is commonly known; what then is specially stated? True—but that cognition is not distinguished from a modification of the mind. Moreover, because in 'I am happy' and 'I am suffering' the 'I'-notion shares a common grammatical substrate with happiness and suffering, and because the 'I'-notion is an object of a mental modification, this common knowledge is merely a product of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).
How then is the attainment [of self-knowledge]? He says: ["Just as <s>Īśvara</s> is a <s>Puruṣa</s> who is pure"]—free from the impurities of <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and the rest; therefore ["luminous"]—transparent; therefore ["absolute"] (<s>kevala</s>)—beyond the three <s>guṇas</s>; therefore ["free from afflictions"]—devoid of calamities, the witness of supreme <s>sattva</s>—["so too does he realize that this <s>Puruṣa</s> of mine"] is pure, luminous, absolute, free from afflictions, ["and the witness of <s>buddhi</s>"].
By the words 'just as' and 'so too,' which indicate an example and its application, the difference between <s>Īśvara</s> and the individual soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>) is stated. And from the logical possibility of both bondage and liberation. And from the fact that <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) serves another's purpose. And from this very reason, the mutual difference among individual souls [is also established].
Moreover, what accrues to him? ["The obstacles beginning with disease"] that will be enumerated—these too, by devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>, ["do not arise."] // 29 //

body.text: atha ke'ntarāyā ye cittasya vikṣepāḥ। ke punaste kiyanto veti –
body.translated_text: Now, what are the obstacles that are distractions of the mind? And what and how many are they?

body.text: vyādhistyāna​saṁśayapramādālasyā​viratibhrāntidarśanālabdha​bhūmikatvānavasthitatvāni citavikṣepāste'ntarāyāḥ ॥ 30 ॥
body.translated_text: Disease, dullness, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, non-abstention, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles. // 30 //

body.text: navāntarāyāścittasya vikṣepāḥ। sahaite cittavṛttibhirbhavanti। eteṣāmabhāve na bhavanti pūrvoktāścittavṛttayaḥ। vyādhirdhāturasakaraṇavaiṣamyam। styānamakarmaṇyatā cittasya। saṁśaya ubhayakoṭispṛgvijñānaṁ syādidamevaṁ naivaṁ syāditi। pramādaḥ samādhisādhanānāmabhāvanam। ālasyaṁ kāyasya cittasya ca gurutvādapravṛttiḥ। aviratiścittasya viṣayasaṁprayogātmā gardhaḥ। bhrāntidarśanaṁ viparyajñānam। alabdhabhūmikatvaṁ samādhibhūmeralābhaḥ। anavasthitatvaṁ yallabdhāyāṁ bhūmau cittasyāpratiṣṭhā। samādhipratilambhe hi sati tadavasthitaṁ syāditi। ete cittavikṣepā nava yogamalā yogapratipakṣā yogāntarāyā ityabhidhīyante ॥ 30 ॥
body.translated_text: The nine obstacles are distractions of the mind. They arise together with the mental modifications. In their absence, the previously mentioned mental modifications do not arise. Disease (<s>vyādhi</s>) is the imbalance of the bodily constituents (<s>dhātus</s>), humors, and sense faculties. Dullness (<s>styāna</s>) is the incapacity of the mind for action. Doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) is a cognition that touches both alternatives—'Perhaps it is thus, perhaps it is not thus.' Heedlessness (<s>pramāda</s>) is the non-cultivation of the means of <s>samādhi</s>. Laziness (<s>ālasya</s>) is non-exertion due to heaviness of body and mind. Non-abstention (<s>avirati</s>) is craving (<s>gardha</s>), which is of the nature of the mind's contact with sense objects. Erroneous perception (<s>bhrāntidarśana</s>) is false knowledge. Failure to attain a stage (<s>alabdhabhūmikatva</s>) is the non-attainment of a level of <s>samādhi</s>. Instability (<s>anavasthitatva</s>) is the mind's failure to remain established in a level once attained—for if <s>samādhi</s> were attained, then the mind would be established in it. These nine distractions of the mind are called impurities of <s>yoga</s>, adversaries of <s>yoga</s>, and obstacles to <s>yoga</s>. // 30 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tatra [ke te'ntarāyāḥ ? kiyanto ve] tyāha- [vyādhistyānetyādi ।] saṁkhyayā tāva [nnavāntarāyāḥ ।] svarūpeṇa ca vyādhyādayaḥ । [vyādhirdhāturasakaraṇavaiṣamyam ।] dhātavo vātapittaśleṣmāṇasteṣāṁ viṣamabhāvo vaiṣamyaṁ, tacca vātapittaśleṣmabhūyiṣṭhadravyopayogādibhyo jāyate । svayonyāgame hi dhātūnāṁ vṛddhimācakṣate ॥
rasa upayuktāhārasya pariṇāmaviśeṣaḥ । [sa] ca saptadhā, rasakāryavādrasa ityucyate rasalohitamedomāṁsāsthimajjāśuklākhyaḥ । tasya vaiṣamyaṁ vṛddhikṣayau । karaṇavaiṣamyamandhabadhiratvādi ॥
[styānamakarmaṇyatā cittasya] stimitam । [saṁśayaḥ] sthāṇurvā puruṣo veti viruddhobhayakoṭispṛkū pratyaya: ॥
[pramādaḥ samādhisādhanānāmabhāvana] maśīlanam । [ālasyaṁ kāyasya cittasya ca gurutvādapravartanam । aviratiścittasya viṣayasamprayoga] svabhāvo viṣayasamprayoganimitto vā [garddhaḥ] abhikāṅkā tṛṣṇā ॥
[bhrāntidarśanaṁ viparyayajñānaṁ] yogasādhaneṣu tanmārge vā viparītavṛttiḥ । [alabdhabhūmikatvaṁ] samādhibhūmeralābha: । bhūmayo vitarkādayaścittasya dharmaviśeṣā uktā vakṣyamāṇāśca । anavasthitāyāmapi samādhibhūmau tataḥ kathamapi pracalitasya cittasya punastatrāvasthitatvameva syāttadalābhastva [navasthitatva] mucyate ॥
[tadete navāntarāyāḥ ।] antaraṁ vivaraṁ vicchedaṁ kurvanta ayāntītyantarāyāḥ [vikṣepāḥ, pratipakṣāḥ] yogaprāpterupasargāḥ । [ete] ca [saha cittavṛttibhirbhavanti ।] cittaṁ vikṣipanti viṣayeṣviti [cittavikṣepāḥ ।] kṣipraṁ te [kṣipanti] [sahaite vṛttibhiḥ] pañcatayībhiranyonyaprayojyaprayojakabhāvena [bhavanti ।] athai [ṣāmabhāve] vyādhiprabhṛtīnāmabhāve sahāyabalābhāvā [nna bhavanti pūrvoktāḥ] pramāṇādaya [ścittavṛttayaḥ ।] tadbhāvabhāvitvātutyapratyanīkā vṛttivikṣepā ityuktaṁ bhavati ॥ 30 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Therein, ["What are those obstacles? And how many?"]—he says: ["Disease, dullness, etc."]. In number, ["there are nine obstacles."]. And in their essential nature, they are disease and the rest. ["Disease is the imbalance of the bodily constituents, humors, and sense faculties."]. The <s>dhātus</s> (bodily constituents) are <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm); their unequal condition is imbalance, and this arises from the intake of substances predominantly of the nature of wind, bile, or phlegm, and so forth. For the increase of the <s>dhātus</s> is described as occurring when they return to their own source.
The <s>rasa</s> (vital fluid) is a specific transformation of the ingested food. It is sevenfold—called <s>rasa</s> because of its being the effect of <s>rasa</s>: namely, <s>rasa</s> (chyle), <s>lohita</s> (blood), <s>medas</s> (fat), <s>māṃsa</s> (flesh), <s>asthi</s> (bone), <s>majjā</s> (marrow), and <s>śukla</s> (semen). Its imbalance consists of increase and decrease. The imbalance of the sense faculties (<s>karaṇa</s>) is blindness, deafness, and the like.
["Dullness is the incapacity of the mind for action"]—a state of torpor. ["Doubt"]—a cognition touching both contradictory alternatives, such as 'Is it a post or a person?'
["Heedlessness is the non-cultivation"]—the non-practice—["of the means of <s>samādhi</s>."]. ["Laziness is non-exertion of body and mind due to heaviness."]. ["Non-abstention is craving"]—desire, thirst—["which is of the nature of the mind's contact with sense objects,"] or which is occasioned by contact with sense objects.
["Erroneous perception is false knowledge"]—a perverted cognition regarding the means of <s>yoga</s> or its path. ["Failure to attain a stage"] is the non-attainment of a level of <s>samādhi</s>. The stages are specific properties of the mind such as <s>vitarka</s> (reasoning) and the rest, already mentioned and to be mentioned. ["Instability"]—even when a level of <s>samādhi</s> is attained, if the mind has somehow been dislodged from it, its mere re-establishment there would [be expected], but the non-attainment of that is called ["instability."].
["These are the nine obstacles."]. They are called <s>antarāyas</s> (obstacles) because they make an opening, a gap, an interruption; they are ["distractions, adversaries,"] calamities to the attainment of <s>yoga</s>. ["And they"] ["arise together with the mental modifications."]. They distract the mind toward sense objects—hence ["distractions of the mind."]. They quickly ["scatter."] ["Together with the modifications"]—the fivefold [modifications], in a relation of mutual cause and effect—["they arise."]. When ["there is an absence"] of disease and the rest, then due to the absence of supporting forces, ["the previously mentioned"] <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition) and other ["mental modifications do not arise."]. Because they exist only when those [obstacles] exist—thus it is said that the modifications and distractions are co-occurring. // 30 //

body.text: duḥkhadaurmanasyāṅgamejayatvaśvāsapraśvāsā vikṣepasahabhuvaḥ ॥ 31 ॥
body.translated_text: Suffering, depression, trembling of the body, [disturbed] inhalation and exhalation—these are the accompaniments of distraction. // 31 //

body.text: duḥkhamādhyātmikamādhibhautikamādhidaivikaṁ ca। yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinastadapaghātāya prayatante tadduḥkham। daurmanasyamicchāvighātāccetasaḥ kṣobhaḥ। yadaṅgānyejayati kampayati tadaṅgamejayatvam। prāṇo yadbāhyaṁ vāyumācāmati sa śvāsaḥ। yatkauṣṭhyaṁ vāyuṁ niḥsārayati sa praśvāsaḥ। ete vikṣepasahabhuvo vikṣiptacittasyaite bhavanti। samāhitacittasyaive na bhavanti ॥ 31 ॥
body.translated_text: Suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>) is of three kinds: <s>ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self), <s>ādhibhautika</s> (pertaining to other beings), and <s>ādhidaivika</s> (pertaining to divine forces). That by which living beings are afflicted and on account of which they strive for its removal—that is suffering. Depression (<s>daurmanasya</s>) is the agitation of the mind due to the frustration of desire. That which causes the limbs to tremble and shake is trembling of the body (<s>aṅgamejayatva</s>). <s>Prāṇa</s>—when it draws in external air, that is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>). When it expels the air in the abdomen, that is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>). These are the accompaniments of distraction—they occur in one whose mind is distracted. They do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated (<s>samāhita</s>). // 31 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[duḥkhaṁ yenābhihatāḥ prāṇinastadapaghātāya prayatante] ceṣṭante । tacca trividham । [ādhyātmikam,] adhi ātmanītyadhyātmam, tatra bhavamādhyātmikam । tacca śārīraṁ mānasaṁ ca । śārīraṁ dhātuvaiṣamyādinimittam । mānasamiṣṭavighātādihetukam । [ādhibhautikam] adhi bhūteṣvityadhibhūtam , tatra bhavamādhibhautikam । tacca paśumṛgādyupanipatitam । [adhidaivikamiti] adhi deveṣvityādhidevam, tatra bhavamādhidaivikam । ['adhyātmādibhyaṣṭhak'] ityupasaṁkhyānāt ṭhak । anuśatikāditvādubhayapadavṛddhiḥ । taccāpi vātavarṣādinimittam । tadekameva sannimittabhedena rajorūpaṁ bhidyate ॥
[daurmanasyamicchāvighātāccetasaḥ kṣobhaḥ] ākulībhāvaḥ sañcalanam । [yadaṅgānyejayati kampayati tadaṅgamejayatvam ।] (n tacca prāṇāyāmādyathābhyāsaprabhavaścāsārvāpi tathā samudbhavaḥ) yadbā [hyaṁ vāyumācāmati] bāhyavāyorākarṣaṇabāhulaka[vyam] niṣkramaṇamandatā ca [śvāsaḥ ।] tadviparītavyāpāraḥ [praśvāsaḥ] - [yatkauṣṭhyaṁ vāyuṁ nissārayati । ete vikṣepasahabhuva:] vikṣepai: sahaite [vikṣiptacittasyaiva bhavantī] ti vikṣepasahabhuvaḥ । [samāhitacittasyaite na bhavantī] ti yāvat । yāvadyāvaccetaḥ samādhīyate tāvattāvanna bhavantīti । [tābhyāmevābhyāsavairāgyābhyā] mupaśamayitavyāḥ । nānyaṁ pratipakṣamapekṣante ॥
abhyāsavairāgye muktvā na hi parameśvarapraṇidhāyinyaḥ[bhyaḥ]prabhāvo bhavatīti gamyate । ' [antarāyābhāvaśca'] ityukyā prāktanādapīśvarapraṇidhānādantarāyā nirudhyante ॥ 31 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
["Suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>) — beings afflicted by it strive for its removal"] — they exert themselves. And that is threefold. ["<s>Ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self)"] — 'relating to the self' (<s>adhi ātmani</s>) is <s>adhyātma</s>; what exists therein is <s>ādhyātmika</s>. And that is both bodily and mental. The bodily arises from causes such as imbalance of the bodily constituents (<s>dhātu-vaiṣamya</s>). The mental arises from causes such as the obstruction of desires. ["<s>Ādhibhautika</s> (pertaining to material beings)"] — 'relating to beings' (<s>adhi bhūteṣu</s>) is <s>adhibhūta</s>; what exists therein is <s>ādhibhautika</s>. And that is caused by animals, wild beasts, and the like. ["<s>Adhidaivika</s> (pertaining to divine forces)"] — 'relating to the gods' (<s>adhi deveṣu</s>) is <s>ādhideva</s>; what exists therein is <s>ādhidaivika</s>. By the grammatical rule '<s>adhyātmādibhyaṣ ṭhak</s>,' the suffix <s>ṭhak</s> is applied by supplementary enumeration. Due to belonging to the <s>anuśatikādi</s> class, both padas undergo <s>vṛddhi</s>. And that too is caused by wind, rain, and the like. That single [suffering], though one, is differentiated by difference of its efficient causes into the form of <s>rajas</s>.
["<s>Daurmanasya</s> (mental distress) is the agitation of the mind due to frustration of desire"] — confusion, trembling. ["That which causes the limbs to tremble and shake is <s>aṅgamejayatva</s> (trembling of limbs)."] (And this, arising from incorrect practice of <s>prāṇāyāma</s> and the like, is also thus produced.) Or alternatively, ["that which draws in external air"] — the predominance of drawing in external air and the slowness of its outgoing ["is <s>śvāsa</s> (inhalation)."] The opposite operation ["is <s>praśvāsa</s> (exhalation)"] — ["which expels the air from the abdomen. These are concomitants of distraction"] — they accompany the distractions; ["they occur only in one whose mind is distracted"] — thus they are concomitants of distraction. ["They do not occur in one whose mind is concentrated"] — this is the import. To the extent that the mind becomes concentrated, to that extent they do not arise.
