["They are to be subdued by those very two — <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion)."] They require no other counteracting means.
Except for <s>abhyāsa</s> and <s>vairāgya</s>, even devotion to the Supreme Lord (<s>parameśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) does not have the power [to remove them] — this is understood. By the statement '[and also the absence of obstacles],' even obstacles are restrained by devotion to <s>Īśvara</s> from a previous [life]. ॥ 31 ॥

body.text: athaite vikṣepāḥ samādhipratipakṣāstābhyāmevābhyāsavairāgyābhyāṁ niroddhavyāḥ। tatrābhyāsasya viṣayamupasaṁharannidamāha –
body.translated_text: Now, these distractions, which are opposed to <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), are to be restrained by those very two — <s>abhyāsa</s> (practice) and <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion). Therein, summarizing the subject matter of <s>abhyāsa</s>, he states —

body.text: tatpratiṣedhārthamekatattvābhyāsaḥ ॥ 32 ॥
body.translated_text: For the prevention of those [distractions], practice on a single principle (<s>ekatattvābhyāsa</s>). ॥ 32 ॥

body.text: vikṣepapratiṣedhārthamekatattvāvalambanaṁ cittamabhyaset। yasya tu pratyarthaniyataṁ pratyayamātraṁ kṣaṇikaṁ ca cittaṁ tasya sarvameva cittamekāgraṁ nāstyeva vikṣiptam। yadi punaridaṁ sarvataḥ pratyāhṛtyaikasminnarthe samādhīyate tadā bhavatyekāgramityato na pratyarthaniyatam।
body.translated_text: One should practice the mind with a single reality (<s>ekatattva</s>) as its support, for the purpose of preventing the distractions. But for one whose mind is determined by each object, is merely a cognition, and is momentary, all mind whatsoever is one-pointed — there is simply no distracted mind. If, however, this [mind], withdrawn from all [objects], is concentrated on a single object, then it becomes one-pointed — therefore it is not determined by each object.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
abhyāsavairāgyābhyāṁ tannirodha ityuktam । tatra vairāgyaviṣayaḥ pratipāditaḥ । idānīmabhyāsasya viṣayamupasaṁharannāha- [tatpratiṣedhārthamekatattvābhyāsa] iti । teṣāṁ vikṣepāṇāṁ pratiṣedhāya [tatpratiṣedhārtham ।] ekaṁ tattva [mekatattvam ।] taccaikaṁ tattvaṁ vastutvānnābhyasituṁ śakyam । na hyātmādivastūnāṁ śīlanaṁ vaktuṁ śakyate । svamāhābhāgyāvasthitāni hi tāni na cittamātrāṇi । vastūnāṁ tu cittatantratāṁ pratiṣedhayiṣyati- [‘na caikacittatantraṁ vastu’] ityādinā । tasmādetadāśaṅkamāno bhāṣyakāra āha- [ekatattvālambanaṁ cittamabhyasediti ।] sūtre'pyekatattvābhyāsa iti samāsādayamartha upātta eva ॥
nanu naikaṁ cittamavasthitamasti, yasyaikatattvāvalambanaḥ pratyaya āpadyeta । pratyayā eva cittam, te ca pratyarthaṁ niyatāḥ kṣaṇapraṇāśinaśca । pratyātmasaṁvedyaṁ ca pratyayānāmanavasthitatvam । nāpi pratyayavyatirekeṇāvasthitaṁ pratyayi cittaṁ nāmopalabhyate । yo'pyahamevāhamiti pratyayaḥ so'pi samānasantatipatitattvātsādṛśyanibandhanaḥ । yathā sa eva pradīpaḥ ta eva keśā iti ॥
tadapyāha-pratyahaṁ[prati]pratyayaṁ pratyayo bhinnaḥ, pratyayebhyo'tyantaparasparabhinnebhyo'nanyatvāt । ekaikapratyayasvarūpasadvartamānāhaṁpratyayaviṣayaḥ pratyayī bhūtabhaviṣyatkālāhaṁpratyayaviṣayāt pratyayino bhinnaḥ, bhinnapratyayaviṣayatvāt , ghaṭāt (gha) paṭa iva । yadi vā-bhinnakālatvāt, vinaṣṭabhaviṣyadghaṭābhyāṁ vartamāno ghaṭaḥ [iva] । ahaṁpratyayā vā sarve bhinnālambanāḥ, pratyayatvāt, ghaṭapaṭadiviṣayapratyayavaditi ॥
atrābhidhīyate-svaśāstravirodho'pi syādevaṁ bruvata ityāha- [kṣaṇikaṁ ca । yasya cittaṁ tasya sarvameva cittam ekāgram] vikṣepābhāvādeva [nāstyeva vikṣiptami] ti sarvacitaikāgratvādvikṣepaprāpyabhāvādvikṣepapratiṣedhāya śāsropadeśo'narthakaḥ syāt । asti ca cittaparikarmārthaṁ maitryādyupadeśaḥ । sa ca virudhyeta itthaṁdharma cittamabhyupagacchataḥ ॥
nanu ca tavāpi vṛttivṛttimatorabhedādanupapanno vikṣepa iti tatpratiṣedhopadeśānarthakyam--naiṣa doṣaḥ-vṛttavṛttimatvābhyupagamāt ॥
yadi vṛttaya eva parasparabhinnāḥ svatantrā vṛttimato'tyantabhinnā jāyeran pratyarthaniyatāśca, tata eṣa doṣaḥ syāt । na caivamabhyupeyate ॥
kathaṁ tarhi ? vṛttimadrūpeṇaikamanekārthaṁ ca tadvṛttīnāṁ viṣayabhedādavasthitaṁ ca sadasatorviparyayānabhyupagamādityevamātmapakṣe samañjasatāṁ darśayati - [yadi punaridaṁ] cittaṁ vṛttibhedenānekadhā (mmilāvayavaddhi) prasṛtaṁ sāṅkhyayogavādina iva tavāpi [sarvataḥ] sarvaibhyaḥ viṣayebhyaḥ [pratyāhṛtya] pratyānīyai [kasminnā] tmā [dyarthe samādhīyeta] sthāpyeta [tadā bhavatye] kāgraṁ puruṣaprayāsabhāvyatvārhamityarthaḥ ॥
tato yuktastatparikarmaṇe śāstropadeśaḥ । (ato na pratyakṣam) ato'smāt kāraṇāt tatparikarmaviṣayaśāstropadeśāt sāṁkhyayogavādivat kṣaṇikavādino'pi ekamanekārthamavasthitaṁ ca cittaṁ [na pratyarthaniyataṁ] (vā) paścādabhyupagamanīyam । anyathā śāsravirodhaḥ syāt ।
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
'Their cessation is by <s>abhyāsa</s> and <s>vairāgya</s>' — this was stated. Therein, the subject of <s>vairāgya</s> has been explained. Now, summarizing the subject of <s>abhyāsa</s>, he says — ["for the prevention of those, practice on a single principle"] — for the prevention of those distractions ["for their prevention."] One principle is a single reality (<s>ekatattva</s>). But that single reality, being a real entity, cannot be practiced. For one cannot speak of 'cultivating' real entities such as the <s>Ātman</s>. They are established in their own inherent nature and are not mere mental constructs. The dependence of real entities on the mind will be refuted by [the sūtra] 'nor is an object dependent on a single mind.' Therefore, anticipating this objection, the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s> says — ["one should practice the mind with a single reality as its support."] Even in the <s>sūtra</s>, by the compound '<s>ekatattvābhyāsa</s>,' this very meaning is conveyed.
But — there is no single enduring mind that could have a cognition supported by a single reality. Cognitions alone constitute the mind, and they are determined by each object and are momentarily perishable. The impermanence of cognitions is self-evident to each person's own experience. Nor is there any perceivable enduring mind-substance apart from cognitions. Even the cognition 'I am the very same I' is based on similarity, since it occurs within the same continuum — just as one says 'that very same lamp' or 'those very same hairs.'
This too he states — each cognition is different from every other, since they are utterly distinct from one another, and [the mind] is not different from the cognitions. The subject of self-awareness (<s>ahaṁ-pratyaya</s>) present in the form of a single momentary cognition is different from the subject of self-awareness pertaining to past and future cognitions, because they have different objects of cognition — just as a pot is different from a cloth. Or alternatively — because they belong to different times, just as a present pot is [different] from a destroyed or future pot. Or, all self-cognitions have different supports, because they are cognitions — like cognitions whose objects are pots, cloths, and the like.
To this he replies — by speaking thus, there would also be a contradiction with your own doctrine — he says: ["And it is momentary. For one whose mind is such, all mind whatsoever is one-pointed"] — due to the absence of distraction, ["there is simply no distracted mind."] Since all mind would be one-pointed, and since there would be no possibility of distraction, scriptural instruction for the prevention of distraction would be pointless. And there is instruction on <s>maitrī</s> (friendliness) and the like for the purpose of purifying the mind. That too would be contradicted if one holds the mind to have such a nature.
But for you as well, since there is no difference between the mental modification (<s>vṛtti</s>) and the mind that undergoes modification, distraction would be untenable, and thus instruction for its prevention would be pointless — this is not a fault, because we accept that the mind undergoes modifications.
If the modifications, being mutually distinct, independent, and utterly different from the mind that undergoes modification, were to arise determined by each object, then this fault would apply. But this is not what we hold.
How then? Showing the consistency of one's own position — ["if, however, this"] mind, spread out in manifold ways through the diversity of modifications — just as for the proponents of <s>Sāṅkhya-Yoga</s>, so for you too — ["withdrawn from all"] objects ["and concentrated on a single"] object such as the <s>Ātman</s> ["it becomes one-pointed"] — meaning it becomes amenable to being cultivated through human effort.
Therefore, scriptural instruction for its purification is appropriate. Therefore, for this very reason — from the fact that there is scriptural instruction concerning its purification — even the proponent of momentariness must ultimately accept, like the proponents of <s>Sāṅkhya-Yoga</s>, that the mind is one, has multiple objects, and is enduring, ["not determined by each object."] Otherwise there would be a contradiction with scripture.

body.text: yo'pi sadṛśapratyayapravāhena cittamekāgraṁ manyate tasyaikāgratā yadi pravāhacittasya dharmastadaikaṁ nāsti pravāhacittaṁ kṣaṇikatvāt। atha pravāhāṁśasyaiva pratyayasya dharmaḥ, sa sarvaḥ sadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā visadṛśapratyayapravāhī vā pratyarthaniyatatvādekāgra eveti vikṣiptacittānupapattiḥ। tasmādekamanekārthamavasthitaṁ cittamiti।
body.translated_text: Even one who considers the mind to be one-pointed through a stream of similar cognitions — if his one-pointedness is a property of the stream-mind, then there is no single stream-mind, because of its momentariness. If, on the other hand, it is a property of the individual cognition that is a part of the stream, then every such [cognition], whether flowing with similar or dissimilar cognitions, would be one-pointed simply because of being determined by its own object — and thus the impossibility of a distracted mind [follows]. Therefore, the mind is one, has multiple objects, and is enduring.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yo'pi sadṛśapratyayapravāhaṁ cittamekāgraṁ manyate] sadṛśaḥ samānaḥ pratyayapravāho yasyaikasyāṁ santatau taccittamekāgram । tadviparītam asamānapratyayapravāhaṁ vikṣiptam । tathā caikāgratā vikṣepapratiṣedhenopapadyate, tadarthopadeśaśceti kutaḥ śāstravirodha iti ॥
itara aha-na-pravāhacittasyaikasya dharmiṇo'nabhyupagamāt । [na hi pravāhacittaṁ nāmaika] matītavartamānabhaviṣyatpratyayānāṁ dharmiṇamabhyupagacchati । yadi hyabhyupagacchet parityaktaḥ svapakṣaḥ । kasmāt ? pravāhacittasyākṣaṇikatvāttadevaikaṁ nāsti, yasyaikāgratā dharmaḥ । pratyayāneva hyanyonyasaṁhatān pipīlikāpaṅktikalpānasāvabhyupagacchati ॥
athaivaṁ manyate, yadyayekaṁ nāsti tathāpi sarveṣāmeva pratyayānāṁ sadṛśapravāhāṇāmekāgratā dharmaḥ pradīpārciṣāmiva prakāśa iti-tatrāha-nāyugapatkālotpattivināśānāṁ samāhāraḥ sambhavati । dṛṣṭāntasya ca sādhyavikalatvāt । na hi bahvīnāmarciṣāmekaḥ prakāśaḥ । pratyarciṣamasya bhedāt । na cāpi prakāśasyārciṣāṁ caiko dharmo nā[mā]sti ॥
[athāpi manyate pravāhāṁśasyaiva pratyayasya] kasyacidekāgratā [dharmaḥ,] yathaikasyāṁ pipīlikāsantatāvekāpi pipīlikā lohiteti-tacca na-pūrvadoṣānuṣakteḥ । [sarvaḥ] pratyayaḥ pravāhāṁśaḥ [sadṛśavāhī visadṛśavāhī vā] pūrvavat [pratyarthaniyatatvādekāgra eveti vikṣiptacittānavalṛptiḥ । tasmādekamanekārthamavasthitaṁ ca cittama] bhyupagantavyam । yadi śāsreṇa cittaparikarmopadekṣyate ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
["Even one who considers the mind to be one-pointed through a stream of similar cognitions"] — a stream of similar, that is, homogeneous cognitions within a single continuum — that mind is one-pointed. The opposite — a stream of dissimilar cognitions — is distracted. Thus, one-pointedness is established through the prevention of distraction, and instruction to that end [makes sense] — so where is the contradiction with scripture?
The other [i.e., the Bhāṣyakāra] replies — no — because there is no acceptance of a single stream-mind as a property-bearer. ["For there is no single entity called 'stream-mind'"] — the Buddhist does not accept a property-bearer for past, present, and future cognitions. For if he did accept one, his own position would be abandoned. Why? Because a stream-mind would be non-momentary, and thus that very single [mind] whose property one-pointedness would be does not exist. For he accepts only the cognitions themselves, mutually conjoined like a row of ants.
Even if one thinks thus — even though there is no single entity, nevertheless one-pointedness is a property of all cognitions in a stream of similar ones, just as illumination is [a property] of lamp flames — to this he replies: there cannot be a collection of things that arise and perish at non-simultaneous times. And the example is deficient with respect to what is to be proved. For there is no single illumination belonging to many flames — because it differs for each flame. Nor is there any single common property of illumination and the flames.
["If, on the other hand, one-pointedness is a property of the individual cognition"] that is some part of the stream — that too is not [tenable], because the previous fault still attaches. ["Every"] cognition that is a part of a stream, ["whether flowing with similar or dissimilar cognitions,"] as before, ["would be one-pointed simply because of being determined by its own object — and thus the impossibility of a distracted mind."] ["Therefore, the mind is one, has multiple objects, and is enduring"] — this must be accepted, if scriptural instruction for the purification of the mind is to be undertaken.

body.text: yadi ca cittenaikenānanvitāḥ svabhāvabhinnāḥ pratyayā jāyerannatha kathamanyapratyayadṛṣṭasyānyaḥ smartā bhavet। anyapratyayopacitasya ca karmāśayasyānyaḥ pratyaya upabhoktā bhavet। kathaṁcitsamādhīyamānamapyetadgomayapāyasīyanyāyamākṣipati।
body.translated_text: And if cognitions, not connected by a single mind, were to arise as intrinsically distinct from one another, then how could one person be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition? And how could one cognition be the experiencer of the fruit of <s>karmāśaya</s> (latent karmic impressions) accumulated by another cognition? Even if this is somehow reconciled, it invites the objection of the <s>gomaya-pāyasīya-nyāya</s> (the maxim of cow-dung and milk-pudding — that unrelated things cannot produce results for each other).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kiṁ ca- [yadi cittenaikenānanvitāḥ] karaṇena [svabhāvabhinnāḥ pratyayā jāyeraṁ] stadā brūhi [kathamanyapratyayadṛṣṭasyānyaḥ pratyayaḥ smartā] bhaveddevadattadṛṣṭasyeva yajñadattaḥ । [anyapratyayopacitasya vā karmāśayasyānyaḥ pratyaya] upabhoktā ॥
na hi bhaviṣyatputraḥ pitrā racitakarmāśayaphalaṁ svargadi pratyupabhuñjīta । atha brūyāt -viśiṣṭabhaviṣyatputravijñānārthaṁ vinaśyatpravṛttivijñānamālayavijñānasaṁskāra kañcanādhatte iti – naitadevam -ālayapravṛttivijñānayoratyantabhedādavastutvācca ॥
yadyālayavijñānānna tatpravṛttivijñānaṁ, tadā tadeva taditi nāmamātrabhedaḥ, tathā ca saṁskārādhānayuktatvāt smṛtyanupaklṛptiḥ । athāpyanyat-evamapyanyatpravṛttavijñānamālayavijñāne saṁskāre nādadhīta, bhinnatvāt । yathā santatyantarālayavijñāne ॥
kiṁca—yadyapi saṁskāramādhattām, tathāpi pravṛttivijñānāpāditasaṁskāramālayavijñānaṁ deśakālāntarākṣamam । tasyāpi kṣaṇikatvābhyupagamādvinaśyacca tāvatyeva nottaravijñānopakārāya paryāpnoti । deśakālāntaravyavahitaṁ cedupakurvīta, tadā bhinnasantānāntarajanmanāpyupakartavyam ॥
atha kālāntarāvasthāyi, tadā kṣaṇikatvahāniḥ । kṣaṇāntaraṁ cedavatiṣṭheta, dīrghakālāvasthāyitve kasya syādakṣamā ॥
athāpi pravṛttivijñānasaṁskāraviśiṣṭasyāntarālabhāvina ātmasadṛśasya bhaviṣyata ālayavijñānasya saṁskāramādhāya pūrvamālayavijñānaṁ vinaṅkṣyatīti
tacca na-saṁskārāntarābhāvāt । asti cedanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ । atha nāstyādhāra:, tatra kiṁ pravṛttivijñānasyālayavijñānakalpanayā saṁskarādhānāya । yathā ālayavijñānamutpitsiṣyamāṇasya tatkālamasataḥ ālayavijñānasya saṁskāramādhatte, tathā pravṛttivijñānamapi utpitsiṣyamāṇasya tatkālamasataḥ pravṛttivijñānasyaiva saṁskāramādhattāmanapekṣyālayavijñānam ॥
na ca vinaśyat anyasya bhāvinastatkālamavidyamānasya saṁskāramādhatte ityasya dṛṣṭānto dṛśyate । nāpi bhāvinyeva saṁskāraṁ kurvīta । pūrvaṇa bhaviṣyatsaṁskriyate, bhaviṣyati ceti viruddham । tatkālaṁ cedasadbhaviṣyatsaṁkriyate, kiṁ tulyātutyasantatikalpanena ? asaṁbandhāviśeṣāt sarvaṁ sarveṇa saṁskriyeta ॥
nāpi bhaviṣyadvinaśyatoryugapadutpattivināśāvakṣaṇikatvaprasaṅgāt । atha tulāntayoriva natyunnatī yugapatpūrvavināśottarasamutpatī syātām (na) vastuneriti cet-na-abhyupagamavirodhāt । na hi vaināśikenotpattivināśakriyāvyatirekeṇa kārakamanyadiṣyate । abhyupagame ca siddhāntāvirodhaḥ ॥
kiṁca-anyatve ca kriyākārakayoryāvatkriyotpatti karakeṇāvasthātavyaṁ, tataśca kṣaṇikatvahāniḥ । a[na]vasthāne ca kriyārthaṁ tataḥ[tasya]upādānamanarthakam ॥
kiṁ cānyat-kriyāyā eva kārakatve kārakasyāpi kriyātve kriyākārakaśabdau paryāyau syātām । tataścāṅkuro jāyate, devadatto jāyata ityaṅkuradevadattayoḥ paryāyatvaṁ syāt । tayorjanikriyāmātratvāt ॥
atha anyajanikrayā devadattaviśiṣṭā anyā cāṅkuraviśiṣṭeti cet - abhyupetaṁ tarhi viśeṣaṇaṁ kārakaṁ, na hi svarūpeṇa kiṁcidviśiṣṭaṁ syāt ॥
athocyeta, svarūpeṇaivotpattikriyā utpattikriyāntarādviśiṣṭā yathā svalakṣaṇāni rūpādīni iti -tacca na-bhāvābhāvayerekatvaprasaṅgāt । ihāṅkuro jāyate naśyatyaṅkura iti ca ya eva jāyate sa eva naśyati tatrāṅkurajananamaṅkuravināśanamiti jananaṁ vināśa ityuktaṁ bhavati । aṅkuro hi kriyaiva kārakamiti vocyeta । (citaḥ) ॥
athāpi syāt-anyai(nyasyai)vāṅkurajananakriyāyā aṅkuravināśakriyeti--tathā'pyaṅkurajananasya nityatvaprasaṅgaḥ । vināśasyānyatvādeva ॥
athāpi nāśajananavadvastu śabalamiti, tathā'pyabhāvasya śabalatvaṁ prasajyeta । katham ? kriyāvyatiriktasya kārakasyābhāve'pi nāśa eva jananavināśavān jananameva jananavināśavaditi । na hyabhāvasya śabalatvādiviśeṣo nirviśeṣatvādbhāvābhāvayoścāvirodhāt pratyakṣānumānānupapattiḥ ॥
yadapyucyate-tulāntayornāmonnāmāviti-tatra yuktā tulāntayorekakālayorvidyamānatvādanyatarasya vastvantaragauravanimittā ānatiranyatarasya cennatiḥ । iha punarbhavadbhaviṣyatkālayorvijñānayornāśotpattī tulānāmahetuvattṛtīyasya nimittāntarasyābhāvādekakālaṁ nopapadyate । vinaśyadeva vijñānamātmasadṛśaṁ janayatīti na śakyaṁ vaktum । na hi devadatto mriyamāṇa evātmasamānaṁ putraṁ janayati vināśenākṣaṇatvāt ॥
atha mṛtpiṇḍo yathā ghaṭamutpādayan vinaśyati, tadvaditi cet-tacca na-mṛdavayavānāmeva ghaṭākareṇa pariṇatatvāt । ekaiva hi mṛtpiṇḍaghaṭādibahudharmayoginī । yaścāpi bījeṣu dravyāntaravāsiteṣu vāsakadravyānuvidhāyitvaṁ vāsyadravyasyeti - tadapyakāraṇam vāsyavāsakayoravasthitatvāt । avasthitānyeva hi bījeṣvaṅkurādīni vāsyante bījavāsanena । tadanyatvāt vāsakadravyasyāpyavayavānanupraviṣṭāḥ sūkṣmā vidyanta eva । tasmādvidyamānānyevāṅkurādīni bījavāsanayā vāsyanta iti yuktam । asatāṁ śaviṣāṇādīnāmutpattyabhāvāt । asatāṁ cedutpattiḥ syādvāsyavāsakayorvinaṣṭatvādavidyamānatvāviśeṣe bāsakadravyānanuvidhāyi notpadyeta । anyadvā hastādi ॥
yadi vā, atyantāsadeva śaśaviṣāṇādyutpadyeta । ato viśiṣṭaṁ hi trayāṇāmasatvaṁ vāsite bīje । tasmādavasthitaṁ kārakaṁ bhūtabhaviṣyatkālānekavṛttiyogi cābhyupagantavyam । anyathā pratyayamātraṁ kṣaṇikaṁ cittamiti samarthyamānasya [samādhīyamānamapi] (samarthyamānamapi) [gomayapāyasīyanyāyamākṣipati ॥]
yathaiva bahubhirapi govikāratvādihetubhiḥ samīhamāne kṛtāṭopenāpi gomayaṁ pāyasīkartuṁ na śakyam, tathā kṣaṇikena cittena smaraṇādi samarthayitum ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
Moreover—[if cognitions, not connected to a single] instrument [mind, arise as] inherently distinct, then tell me: [how could another cognition remember what was seen by one cognition]—as if <s>Yajñadatta</s> could [remember what was] seen by <s>Devadatta</s>? [Or how could another cognition] experience [the karmic store accumulated by one cognition]?
For a future son would not enjoy the fruit—such as heaven—of the karmic store fashioned by the father. Now, if one were to say: 'The perishing active consciousness (<s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>), for the sake of a specific future consciousness, deposits a certain impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) in the storehouse consciousness (<s>ālayavijñāna</s>)'—this is not so, because of the absolute difference between and the unreality of <s>ālayavijñāna</s> and <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>.
If the <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s> is not different from the <s>ālayavijñāna</s>, then the two are identical and differ only in name; and since depositing impressions would then be possible, the impossibility of memory would not follow. But if it is indeed different—even so, the <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s> could not deposit an impression in the <s>ālayavijñāna</s>, because they are distinct—just as in the case of a storehouse consciousness belonging to another continuum.
Moreover—even if it does deposit an impression, the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> endowed with the impression produced by the <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s> would be incapable of lasting across different times and places. For since its momentariness is accepted, being destroyed at that very instant, it cannot serve the purpose of a subsequent consciousness. And if it could assist [a consciousness] separated by different times and places, then one born in a different continuum too should be able to assist [another].
If [the <s>ālayavijñāna</s>] persists across different times, then momentariness is abandoned. And if it persists for even one additional moment, what would be the obstacle to its persisting for a long time?
And if [one says that] the prior <s>ālayavijñāna</s> will perish after depositing an impression in a future <s>ālayavijñāna</s> similar to itself that exists in the interval—that too is not valid, because of the absence of a further impression [to explain the transfer]. And if there is [such a further impression], an infinite regress follows. And if there is none, then what is the need of postulating an <s>ālayavijñāna</s> for the depositing of impressions by the <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s>? Just as the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> deposits an impression in a future <s>ālayavijñāna</s> that is non-existent at that time, so too the <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s> could deposit an impression directly in a future <s>pravṛttivijñāna</s> non-existent at that time, without depending on the <s>ālayavijñāna</s>.
And no example is seen of a perishing entity depositing an impression in another entity that is future and non-existent at that time. Nor could the future entity itself produce the impression. If it is conditioned by the prior, and it itself is future—that is contradictory. And if the future, being non-existent at that time, is conditioned, what is the use of postulating similar and dissimilar continua? Because there is no difference in the absence of connection, everything would be conditioned by everything.
Nor can the perishing and the arising occur simultaneously—that leads to non-momentariness, since production and destruction would occur at the same instant. And if, like the two ends of a balance, the lowering and raising are simultaneous—the prior destruction and subsequent production occurring together—that does not work, because it contradicts one's own accepted position. For the <s>Vaināśika</s> (proponent of destruction) does not accept any agent (<s>kāraka</s>) apart from the acts of production and destruction. And if accepted, it would contradict the established doctrine.
Moreover—if action and agent are different, the agent must persist as long as the action arises—and that contradicts momentariness. And if the agent does not persist, then assuming it for the purpose of action is pointless.
Furthermore—if the action itself is the agent and the agent too is the action, then the words 'action' and 'agent' would be synonyms. In that case, 'a sprout arises' and '<s>Devadatta</s> arises'—the sprout and <s>Devadatta</s> would be synonymous, since both are nothing but the action of arising.
If one says that one arising-action is qualified by <s>Devadatta</s> and another by the sprout—then it is admitted that the qualifier is the agent, for nothing can be qualified by its own nature alone.
If one says that the arising-action is distinguished from other arising-actions by its own nature, just as color and the like are self-characterized (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>)—that too is not valid, because of the absurdity of identity between being and non-being. Here, in 'the sprout arises' and 'the sprout perishes,' the very same thing that arises also perishes; the arising of the sprout is the destruction of the sprout—so 'arising' would mean 'destruction.' For the sprout would be said to be both the action and the agent.
Even if one says that the arising-action of the sprout is different from its destruction-action—even so, the arising of the sprout would be permanent, since destruction is something other than it.
And if one says that a thing is a mixture (<s>śabala</s>) of arising and destruction—even so, non-existence would have to be a mixture. How? Because in the absence of an agent distinct from action, destruction itself would possess both arising and destruction, and arising itself would possess both arising and destruction. And non-existence cannot have such distinctions as mixture, being without distinctions; and since being and non-being would not be contradictory [on this view], perception and inference would be invalidated.
As for the analogy of the two ends of a balance—there, the lowering and raising of the balance-pans is justified because both exist at the same time, with the heaviness of some other object being the cause of one pan's lowering and the other's rising. But here, with cognitions belonging to the present and future, destruction and production cannot occur at the same time due to the absence of a third causal factor, and the balance analogy lacks a reason. It cannot be said that the very perishing consciousness generates one similar to itself. For <s>Devadatta</s> does not beget a son identical to himself at the very moment of dying—because destruction does not admit of non-momentariness.
If one says that just as a lump of clay perishes while producing a pot, so too with consciousness—that too is not valid, because it is the very parts of the clay that have transformed into the form of the pot. For one and the same entity—the clay-lump—participates in many properties such as the pot-form. And as for the argument about the scenting-substance conforming to the substance scented in seeds impregnated with another substance—that too is no reason, because both the scented and the scenting persist. For it is the sprouts and such that already exist in the seeds that are scented by the seed-scenting. And because the scenting substance is different from those, its subtle particles indeed exist, having entered the seeds. Therefore, it is proper that the sprouts and such, already existing, are scented by the seed-scenting—because non-existent things like a hare's horn do not arise. And if non-existent things could arise, then since both the scented and the scenting have perished and there is no difference in their non-existence, what arises would not conform to the scenting substance—or else anything, such as a hand, etc., could arise instead.
Or rather, the completely non-existent—like a hare's horn—would arise. Therefore, the threefold non-existence in the impregnated seed is distinguished [i.e., it is not absolute non-existence]. Therefore, one must accept an agent (<s>kāraka</s>) that is enduring and participates in multiple states across past and future times. Otherwise, for one who maintains that consciousness is merely momentary cognitions, the argument, [even when being established], invites the cowdung-milk analogy (<s>gomayapāyasīya-nyāya</s>).
Just as, even with many reasons such as being a modification of a cow, however much one strives, one cannot make milk from cowdung—so too, with a momentary consciousness, one cannot establish memory and the like.

body.text: kiṁ ca svātmānubhavāpahnavaścittasyānyatve prāpnoti। kathaṁ, yadahamadrākṣaṁ tatspṛśāmi yaccāsprākṣaṁ tatpaśyāmītyahamiti pratyayaḥ sarvasya pratyayasya bhede sati pratyayinyabhedenopasthitaḥ। ekapratyayaviṣayo'yamabhedātmā'hamiti pratyayaḥ kathamatyantabhinneṣu citteṣu vartamānaḥ sāmānyamekaṁ pratyayinamāśrayet। svānubhavagrāhyaścāyamabhedātmā'hamiti pratyayaḥ। na ca pratyakṣasya māhātmyaṁ pramāṇāntareṇābhibhūyate। pramāṇāntaraṁ ca pratyakṣabalenaiva vyavahāraṁ labhate। tasmādekamanekārthamavasthitaṁ ca cittam ॥ 32 ॥
body.translated_text: Moreover, the denial of one's own experience follows if the mind is different [at each moment]. How? The cognition 'I'—as in 'what I saw, that I touch' and 'what I touched, that I see'—is present, with the unchanging subject (<s>pratyayin</s>), despite the difference in all cognitions. How could this cognition 'I,' which is of the nature of non-difference and has a single object, occurring among absolutely different minds, refer to a single, common subject? And this cognition 'I,' of the nature of non-difference, is grasped by one's own experience. And the authority of direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) is not overridden by another means of knowledge. And the other means of knowledge gain their validity only by the strength of direct perception. Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is enduring. // 32 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[kiñca-svātmānubhavāpahnavaḥ cittasyānyatve] pratyayamātratve ’nānyadṛṣṭamanusmaratīti svātmanānubhūtamapahnuvīna ॥
kiṁ tvamadrākṣīrityukto dṛṣṭavānapi nāhamadrākṣamiti buvīta । anyena hi tatpakṣe tat dṛṣṭaṁ dṛśyate । tadapahnave cānubhūtasya pratipattiḥ katham ? ‘ [yadahamadrākṣaṁ tat] ahameva [spṛśāmi’ ‘yadahamasprākṣaṁ tat] ahameva [smarāmi’] iti । saiṣā pratyayasmaraṇayorekakartṛtve sati ghaṭanāmupaḍhaukate pratipattiḥ । anyathā matsadṛśe । yadadrākṣīttatsadṛśo'haṁ taṁ spṛśāmīti smarāmīti ca syāt । [sarvasya puruṣasyāhamiti pratyayaḥ] smṛtipratyayayorekasmin kartari vartamānaḥ [pratyayabhede] paśyāmi spṛśāmi smarāmītyādipratyayabhede sati teṣāṁ ca pratyayānāmekasmin kartari [pratyayinyabhinne copasthitaḥ] pratyakṣaśca ॥
nanvekapratyayaviṣaya evānyaḥ smṛterekatve'pi karturahaṁ pratyemi smarāmyahamiti ca na bhavitavyaṁ, pratyetā smarteti śabdabhedādbheda eva । tatrāha-na-pratyakṣatvāt । tadeva darśayati-- [svānubhavagrāhyaścāyamabhedātmā ahamiti pratyayaḥ ॥]
atha pratyetā smarteti śabdabhedāt pratyayabhedāccāhampratyayasya bhinnaviṣayatvamanumāyiṣyata iti cedata aha-- [na hi pratyakṣasya māhātmyaṁ] prāmāṇyaṁ cakṣuṣo rūpa ivānumānā [dabhibhūyate] bādhyate ॥
kiṁ ca- -pratyakṣaṁ pramāṇamayamahaṁpratyayo na tat smṛtipratyayānāmekasmin kartari sāmānyena vartamānaḥ । sa cet pratyakṣapramāṇabhūto'numānenābhibhūyeta, tadānīmanumānasyāpi pramāṇatvaṁ hīyeta । tanmūlatvādanumānasya । tadetadāha- [pramāṇāntaraṁ ca pratyakṣabalenaiva prāmāṇyavyavahāraṁ labhata] iti । tena pratyakṣavirodhena anumānavirodhena ca prativādi(pādita)pramāṇapratijñādoṣo vyākhyata: ॥
atītānāgatapratyayasaṁskārādhārādananyaḥ idānīntanapratyayasaṁskārādhāraḥ, ekasantānasaṁbandhitve sati bodhātmakatvāt, ātmasvarūpādyathā ॥
bhūtabhaviṣyatpratyayasaṁskārāśrayaḥ vartamānapratyayasaṁskārāśrayādananyaḥ, ekasantānasaṁbandhe sati bodhātmakatvāt, ātmana iva svarūpāt ॥
vartamānāhaṁpratyayī bhūtabhaviṣyatpratyayibhyāmabhinnaḥ, ekasantānayoge sati pratyayitvāt, yathā svarūpāt ॥
bhūtabhaviṣyatpratyayibhyāmananyo vartamānaḥ pratyayaḥ, ekasantānasaṁbandhe sati bodhātmakatvāt, ātmarāgasvarūpādibhya iva ॥
bhūtabhaviṣyatpratyayibhyo nānyo vartamānaḥ pratyayī, ekasantānasaṁbandhitve sati bodhātmakatvāt , ātmano yathā svarūpāt ॥
bhinnasantatiṣu parasparasmṛtipratisandhānādyanupalambhādekasantāneṣu ca smṛtyādidarśanādeva siddhamekakartṛtvam । tathā sarvapramāṇebhyo garīyasā pratyakṣeṇa pramāṇena । tatra na kiṁcidanumānena sādhyam । na hi kaścit karatalalāñchanadidṛkṣayā darpaṇamādatte । tathā'pi vaināśikoparacitānumānāpaśadamasahamānāḥ kecit pratyanumānāni peśalāni darśayanti । tathā cāha-- [tasmādekamanekārthamavasthitaṁ ca cittam । yasyedaṁ śāstreṇa parikarma nirdiśyata] iti-śāsropadeśasambandhitvaṁ cittasyāvasthitatve hetumupadiśati । na hi viśīryamāṇasya ghaṭasya prakṣālanaparivartanādisaṁskāraḥ kriyate ॥ 32 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
[Moreover—the denial of one's own experience follows if the mind is different]—if it is merely cognition, 'another does not remember what was seen'—this would be a denial of what was experienced by oneself.
If asked 'Did you see it?', even one who saw would say 'I did not see'—for on that [Buddhist] view, it was another who saw, and it is another who sees. And if one denies that, how can there be recognition of what was experienced? '[What I saw, that] very I [touch'; 'what I touched, that] very I [remember']—this recognition presents itself as having a single agent for both cognition and memory. Otherwise, one would say: 'someone similar to me—what he saw, I, similar to him, touch' or 'I remember.' [The cognition 'I' of every person], occurring with the identical agent as subject despite difference among cognitions such as 'I see,' 'I touch,' 'I remember,' and among these cognitions [with] the subject being non-different—and directly perceived.
Objection: The cognition 'I,' being the object of a single cognition—even if the agent is one, 'I cognize' and 'I remember' would not need to be said, since from the verbal difference between 'cognizer' and 'rememberer,' there is difference indeed. To this he says: No—because of direct perception. He shows this: [And this cognition 'I,' of the nature of non-difference, is grasped by one's own experience.]
Now, if one says that from the verbal difference between 'cognizer' and 'rememberer' and from the difference of cognitions, the I-cognition can be inferred to have different objects—to this he says: [The authority of direct perception]—the validity [is not] defeated [by another means of knowledge] such as inference, just as the authority of the eye regarding color [is not overridden by inference].
Moreover—this I-cognition is a valid means of knowledge based on direct perception, occurring with a single common agent across memory and cognition. If this, being a valid means based on direct perception, were overridden by inference, then even the validity of inference would be undermined—since inference is rooted in direct perception. This is what he says: [And the other means of knowledge gain their validity-practice only by the strength of direct perception.] Therefore, by showing the contradiction with direct perception and the contradiction with inference, the defect in the opponent's proof and thesis is explained.
[Formal inferences:]
The substratum of past and future cognitions and impressions is not different from the substratum of present cognitions and impressions, because, being of the nature of consciousness, it belongs to a single continuum—like the self from its own nature.
The substratum of past and future cognitions and impressions is not different from the substratum of present cognitions and impressions, because, being of the nature of consciousness, it belongs to a single continuum—like the self from its own nature.
The present subject of the 'I'-cognition is not different from the subjects of past and future cognitions, because it is a subject (<s>pratyayin</s>) while being in a single continuum—like the self from its own nature.
Not different from the subjects of past and future cognitions is the present cognition, because, being of the nature of consciousness, it belongs to a single continuum—like the self, its own nature, etc.
Not different from the subjects of past and future cognitions is the present subject—because, being of the nature of consciousness, it belongs to a single continuum—like the self from its own nature.
Since in different continua there is no observation of mutual memory-connection and the like, and since in a single continuum memory and the like are observed, single agentship is thereby established. And likewise by direct perception, which is the most authoritative among all means of knowledge. Therein nothing needs to be proved by inference. For no one takes up a mirror desiring to see the mark on the palm of his hand. Nevertheless, certain thinkers, unable to withstand the reproach of the inference constructed by the <s>Vaināśika</s>, display skillful counter-inferences. And thus he says: [Therefore, the mind is one, has many objects, and is enduring. For which this scriptural discipline is prescribed]—he indicates the endurance of the mind as the reason for the applicability of scriptural instruction. For one does not undertake the refinement—washing, turning, and the like—of a pot that is crumbling. // 32 //

body.text: yasya cittasyāvasthitasyedaṁ śāstreṇa parikarma nirdiśyate tatkatham –
body.translated_text: For which established mind is this refinement prescribed by the scripture—that is as follows:

body.text: maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāṇāṁ sukhaduḥkhapuṇyāpuṇyaviṣayāṇāṁ bhāvanātaścitaprasādanam ॥ 33 ॥
body.translated_text: Through the cultivation of friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>), compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), joy (<s>muditā</s>), and equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) toward objects of happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit, [there arises] the clarification of the mind (<s>cittaprasādana</s>). // 33 //

body.text: tatra sarvaprāṇiṣu sukhasaṁbhogāpanneṣu maitrīṁ bhāvayet। duḥkhiteṣu karuṇām। puṇyātmakeṣu muditām। apuṇyaśīleṣūpekṣām। evamasya bhāvayataḥ śuklo dharma upajāyate। tataśca cittaṁ prasīdati। prasannamekāgraṁ sthitipadaṁ labhate ॥ 33 ॥
body.translated_text: Therein, one should cultivate friendliness toward all beings who have attained the enjoyment of happiness; compassion toward those who are suffering; joy toward those of meritorious nature; equanimity toward those of sinful disposition. For one who cultivates thus, bright <s>dharma</s> arises. And from that, the mind becomes clear. The clear mind, being one-pointed, attains a stable ground. // 33 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kathaṁ cittaparikarma nirdiśyate ? tathaikatatvābhyāsa iti coktam , kiṁ ca tadekaṁ tattvam? yadviṣaye'bhyāsa iti । tata āha—
[maitrīkaruṇāmuditopekṣāṇāṁ sukhaḥdukhapuṇyāpuṇyaviṣayāṇāṁ bhāvanātaścittaprasādanamiti । maitrī] mitraviṣayā bhāvanā । tādṛśī sukhateṣu sukhamanumodayantīmasūyādivarjitām । tathā duḥkhiteṣu [karuṇāṁ] kṛpām anujānatī duḥkham । [puṇyātmakeṣu muditāṁ] puṇyaśīlatāmanujānatīm । [apuṇyaśīleṣu copekṣām] apuṇyaśīlavyāpāreṣūdāsīnatāṁ ca bhāvayedityanuṣajyate ॥
sarvatraiva [masya bhāvayataḥ, śukla] iti viśuddhaḥ prāṇyupaghātādivarjanācchuklo [dharmaḥ । tataḥ] sa dharma iva jāta [ścittaṁ] prasādayati । tena [prasannaṁ cittamekāgraṁ sthitipadaṁ labhate ।] ekāgratayā samādhīyata ityarthaḥ taduktam- ‘prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate’ iti ॥
tatropekṣāyā akriyārūpatvāddhamīhetutve sati kimarthamihopādānam ? ucyate-upekṣānupādāne cāpuṇyaśīleṣvapi cittaṁ vyāpāraṁ yāyāt । tataśca tadvyāpāropadhānakāluṣyānmaitryādibhāvanāyā na yogyaṁ bhavati । apuṇyaśīlanimittanaimittikākāravyāpārādadharmoṁ vā mā saṁjaniṣṭeti cittasthitirevopekṣeti tasyā upādānam । cittasthitiśceha samīhitā ॥
tasmāditthaṁ samāhitacittasya maitrīkaruṇādyekatattvālambanaṁ cittaṁ śīlayataḥ prāgabhihitā antarāyā na janiṣyante ॥ 33 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
How is the purification of the mind (<s>cittaparikarma</s>) being taught? It was stated "by the practice of one reality (<s>ekatatvābhyāsa</s>)"—but what is that one reality upon which practice is directed? To this he says:
["Through the cultivation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) of friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>), compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), joy (<s>muditā</s>), and equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) toward those who are happy, suffering, virtuous, and sinful respectively, there comes clarity of mind (<s>cittaprasādana</s>)." <s>Maitrī</s> (friendliness)] is the cultivation directed toward friends. Such cultivation, free from envy and the like, rejoices in the happiness of those who are happy. Likewise, [<s>karuṇā</s> (compassion)] toward the suffering—sympathizing with their pain. [Toward those of virtuous nature, <s>muditā</s> (joy)]—approving of their virtuous disposition. [And <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity) toward those of sinful conduct]—indifference toward the activities of the sinful—this is what is to be cultivated, as connected with the preceding.
In all cases, [when one cultivates thus, a "white" (<s>śukla</s>)]—that is, pure—[<s>dharma</s> arises, due to abstaining from harm to living beings and the like. From that] <s>dharma</s>, as though newly arisen, [he brings clarity to the mind. The mind thus made clear (<s>prasanna</s>) attains the state of one-pointedness (<s>ekāgratā</s>).]—meaning, through one-pointedness it becomes absorbed in <s>samādhi</s>. As it is said: "For one whose mind is serene, wisdom quickly becomes established."
Regarding this—since <s>upekṣā</s> (equanimity) is of the nature of non-action, what is the purpose of including it here as a cause of <s>dharma</s>? It is said: without the inclusion of <s>upekṣā</s>, the mind would engage even with the sinful. Consequently, due to the impurity arising from engagement with such, it would not be fit for the cultivation of friendliness and the rest. Or, lest <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness) arise from mental activity taking the form of reaction to sinful beings, equanimity is itself the steadiness of mind—hence its inclusion. And steadiness of mind is what is sought here.
Therefore, for one whose mind is thus composed, cultivating the mind with friendliness, compassion, and the rest as the single object of focus (<s>ekatatvālambana</s>), the previously mentioned obstacles will not arise. // 33 //

body.text: pracchardanavidhāraṇābhyāṁ vā prāṇasya ॥ 34 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>Pracchardana</s> (expulsion) and <s>vidhāraṇa</s> (retention) of <s>prāṇa</s> (breath)—or [by these means]. // 34 //

body.text: kauṣṭhyasya vāyornāsikāpuṭābhyāṁ prayatnaviśeṣādvamanaṁ pracchardanaṁ, vidhāraṇaṁ prāṇāyāmastābhyāṁ vā manasaḥ sthitiṁ saṁpādayet ॥ 34 ॥
body.translated_text: The expulsion (<s>pracchardana</s>) is the deliberate ejection of the abdominal breath through the two nostrils by a special effort; <s>vidhāraṇa</s> (retention) is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control). By means of these two, one should bring about steadiness of mind (<s>manasaḥ sthiti</s>). // 34 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[pracchardanavidhāraṇābhyāṁ vā prāṇasya । vā] śabdo maitryādibhāvanopāyāntaravikalpārthaḥ । maitryādibhāvanādyupāyānāmanyatamena yena kenacit cittasthitiḥ sampādanīyeti prakaraṇārthaḥ । anekopāyapradarśanaṁ kasyacit kvacit sukaratābhiprāyeṇa । pracchardanavidhāraṇābhyāṁ vyastābhyāṁ samastābhyāṁ vā । pracchardanam [kauṣṭhyasya vāyo] rātamitorudvamanaṁ [nāsikābhyām,] na mukhena । [vidhāraṇaṁ prāṇāyāma] ātamitoreva । yadyapi pracchardanenāpi prāṇaḥ āyamyate, tathāpi bahirvṛttirna nirudhyata iti vidhāraṇaṁ prāṇāyāma iti viśeṣyate ॥ 34 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["By expulsion and retention of <s>prāṇa</s>—or."] The word "or" (<s>vā</s>) indicates an alternative to the means of cultivating friendliness and the rest. The purport of the section is that steadiness of mind is to be accomplished by any one of the means—be it the cultivation of friendliness and the rest, or any other. The presentation of multiple means is with the understanding that different methods may be easier for different practitioners. By expulsion and retention—either separately or together. <s>Pracchardana</s> (expulsion) is the ejection of the [abdominal breath] in measured manner [through the nostrils,] not through the mouth. [<s>Vidhāraṇa</s> (retention) is <s>prāṇāyāma</s>]—also in measured manner. Although through expulsion too the <s>prāṇa</s> is regulated, nevertheless since the outward movement is not restrained thereby, retention is specifically designated as <s>prāṇāyāma</s>. // 34 //

body.text: viṣayavatī vā pravṛttirutpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanī ॥ 35 ॥
body.translated_text: Or, a supernormal perceptual activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), when arisen, serves to anchor the steadiness of mind. // 35 //

body.text: nāsikāgre dhārayato'sya yā divyagandhasaṁvitsā gandhapravṛttiḥ। jihvāgre rasasaṁvit। tāluni rūpasaṁvit। jihvāmadhye sparśasaṁvit। jihvāmūle śabdasaṁvidityetā vṛttaya utpannāścittaṁ sthitau nibadhnanti, saṁśayaṁ vidhamanti, samādhiprajñāyāṁ ca dvārī bhavantīti। etena candrādityagrahamaṇipradīparaśmyādiṣu pravṛttirutpannā viṣayavatyeva veditavyā। yadyapi hi tattacchāstrānumānācāryopadeśairavagatamarthatattvaṁ sadbhūtameva bhavati, eteṣāṁ yathābhūtārthapratipādanasāmarthyāt tathā'pi yāvadekadeśo'pi kaścinna svakaraṇasaṁvedyo bhavati tāvatsarvaṁ parokṣamivāpavargādiṣu sūkṣmeṣvartheṣu na dṛḍhāṁ buddhimutpādayati। tasmācchāstrānumānācāryopadeśopodbalanārthamevāvaśyaṁ kaścidarthaviśeṣaḥ pratyakṣīkartavyaḥ। tatra tadupadiṣṭārthaikadeśapratyakṣatve sati sarvaṁ sūkṣmaviṣayamapi ā'pavargācchraddhīyate। etadarthamevedaṁ cittaparikarma nirdiśyate। aniyatāsu vṛttiṣu tadviṣayāyāṁ vaśīkārasaṁjñāyāmupajātāyāṁ samarthaṁ syāttasya tasyārthasya pratyakṣīkaraṇāyeti। tathā ca sati śraddhāvīryasmṛtisamādhayo'syāpratibandhena bhaviṣyantīti ॥ 35 ॥
body.translated_text: For one who concentrates on the tip of the nose, there arises a perception of divine fragrance—this is the olfactory <s>pravṛtti</s> (perceptual activity). At the tip of the tongue, perception of taste; at the palate, perception of form; at the middle of the tongue, perception of touch; at the root of the tongue, perception of sound—these activities, when arisen, anchor the mind in steadiness, dispel doubt, and become the gateway to the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>. By this, it should be understood that perceptual activity arising with regard to the rays of the moon, sun, planets, gems, and lamps is likewise "possessing an object" (<s>viṣayavatī</s>). Although the reality of things ascertained through scripture, inference, and the teacher's instruction is indeed as it truly is—owing to their capacity to communicate things as they are—nevertheless, so long as not even a single aspect becomes perceptible through one's own faculties, everything remains as though remote, and does not produce firm conviction regarding subtle matters such as <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) and the like. Therefore, to corroborate scripture, inference, and the teacher's instruction, some particular object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. When even a portion of what has been taught becomes directly perceived, then everything, even the subtlest objects, is believed in all the way up to <s>apavarga</s>. It is for this very purpose that the purification of mind (<s>cittaparikarma</s>) is taught. When, among the unsteady mental activities, the mastery-state (<s>vaśīkārasaṁjñā</s>) pertaining to that object arises, one becomes capable of directly perceiving that particular reality. And when this occurs, faith, vigor, mindfulness, and <s>samādhi</s> will proceed without obstruction. // 35 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[viṣayavatī vā pravṛttirutpannā sthitinibandhinī ।] citasyeti vākyaśeṣaḥ । viṣayā gandhādayo yasyā yogapravṛttergandhādisaṁvedanalakṣaṇāyā ālambanībhūtāḥ, sa viṣayavatītyucyute ॥
[pravṛtti] rnāma yogino yogamabhyasyataḥ abhimukhībhāvaṁ pratipadyamānasya yogasya yaḥ prathamo'bhimukhībhāvaḥ pratyayakaraṇo yogānuṣṭhānaṁ pratyutsāhajanano nirmathyamānasyāgneriva dhūmasamudbhavaḥ, sā pravṛttiḥ । sā ca tādṛśī [pravṛttirutpannā] pratyayakaraṇāt praharṣayantī yogina [ścittaṁ sthitau nibadhnāti ॥]
[nāsikāgre cittaṁ dhārayato gandhasaṁvit] prahvādanakarasurabhigandhasaṁvedanaṁ nirantaratayā sammatasaṁyogamivācakṣāṇā jāyate । [sā gandhapravṛttiḥ ।] tathā । jihvādiṣu । dhārayata iti sambadhyate । [tā etāḥ pravṛttayaḥ sthitau cittaṁ nibadhnanti । saṁśayaṁ vidhamanti samādhiprajñāyāśca dvārībhavanti ॥]
[etena raśmicandrādityagrahapradīpādiṣu cittaṁ] dhārayato hṛdayapuṇḍarīke vā dhārayato vaiṣamyādraśmicandrādyākārā [pravṛttirutpannā viṣayavatītyeva veditavyā ॥]
[yadyapi śāstrānumānācāryebhyo'vagatamarthatattvaṁ tathābhūtameva] avyabhicārisvarūpameva । teṣāmanyathābhūtāpratipādakatvāt । [tathā'pi yāvadekadeśo'pi svakaraṇasaṁvedyo na bhavati] pratyakṣo na bhavati śāstrādyupadiṣṭasyārthasyaikadeśo'pi, [tāvat sarvaṁ parokṣamivāpavargādiṣu sūkṣmeṣvartheṣu na dṛḍhāṁ buddhimutpādayati । tasmācchāstrānumānācāryopodvalanārthamavaśyaṁ kaścidviśeṣa: pratyakṣīkartavyaḥ ॥]
[tatra] śāstrādyu [padiṣṭārthakadeśapratyakṣatve sati sarvaṁ sūkṣmaviṣayamapi ā apavargācchraddhīyate । etadarthamevedaṁ cittaparikarma] yadetat [‘maitrīkaruṇā’] ityādinā [‘paramāṇuparamamahattvānto'sya vaśīkāraḥ’] ityevamantena prakaraṇena yamaniyamāsanaviśiṣṭasya cittaparikarmopadiśyate ॥
tadetaduktaṁ bhavati-etatprakaraṇopadiṣṭānāmupāyānāmanyatamānuṣṭhānāt pratyakṣīkṛtaikadeśatayā vidhūta(pidhmāta)saṁśayaṁ tu ā apavargāt dṛḍhāvasthitaśraddhānādi praśāntabahirvṛtti upasthitavaśīkārasaṁjñāvairāgyaṁ [tasya tasya] tṛtīyapādopadiṣṭapariṇāmatrayāde [rarthasya pratyakṣīkaraṇāya samarthaṁ syāt] jñānavibhūtyādiprāpyarthamiti । tataścaivamarthaṁ cittaparikarmopadiśyata iti prakaraṇārthaḥ । tathā ca bhāṣyakāraḥ pradarśitavān- [‘etadarthamevedaṁ cittaparikarma’] ityevamādinā ॥ 35 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["A supernormal perceptual activity possessing an object (<s>viṣayavatī</s>), when arisen, anchors the steadiness"]—of the mind, is the completion of the sentence. The objects—fragrance and the rest—which serve as the supports (<s>ālambana</s>) of this yogic activity characterized by the perception of fragrance and so forth, make it "possessing objects" (<s>viṣayavatī</s>).
[<s>Pravṛtti</s> (activity)] is the name for the first turning toward [the goal] that occurs for the yogin who is practicing <s>yoga</s> and approaching it face to face—producing conviction, generating enthusiasm for yogic practice—like the appearance of smoke from fire being kindled. This is <s>pravṛtti</s>. And such [activity, when arisen,] by producing conviction, delights the yogin and [anchors the mind in steadiness.]
[For one concentrating on the tip of the nose, there arises a perception of fragrance]—a perception of pleasing, delightful fragrance, as though declaring an unbroken connection, continuously. [This is the olfactory <s>pravṛtti</s>.] Similarly for the tongue and the rest—"concentrating" is to be connected with each. [These activities anchor the mind in steadiness, dispel doubt, and become the gateway to the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.]
[By this, when one concentrates on the rays of the moon, sun, planets, lamps, and the like,] or concentrates on the heart-lotus, [the activity that arises, due to its extraordinary character, taking the form of the rays of the moon, sun, and so forth, should be understood as "possessing an object" (<s>viṣayavatī</s>).]
[Although the reality of things ascertained from scripture, inference, and the teacher is indeed as it truly is]—of unerring nature—because they do not communicate what is otherwise than the truth. [Nevertheless, so long as not even a single aspect becomes perceptible through one's own faculties,] so long as not even a portion of the meaning taught by scripture and the rest becomes directly perceived, [everything remains as though remote and does not produce firm conviction regarding subtle matters such as <s>apavarga</s>. Therefore, to corroborate scripture, inference, and the teacher, some particular [object] must necessarily be made directly perceptible.]
[When] even a portion of the meaning taught by scripture and the rest [becomes directly perceived, then everything, even the subtlest objects, is believed in all the way up to <s>apavarga</s>. It is for this very purpose that this purification of mind (<s>cittaparikarma</s>)]—which is taught in this entire section beginning with ["friendliness, compassion"] and ending with ["his mastery extends from the minutest atom to the greatest magnitude"]—is taught for one who is qualified by <s>yama</s> (restraints), <s>niyama</s> (observances), and <s>āsana</s> (posture).
Thus what is stated amounts to this: through the practice of any one of the means taught in this section, having made even a portion directly perceptible, with doubt dispelled, with faith and the rest firmly established all the way to <s>apavarga</s>, with external activities pacified, and with the mastery-state of <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion) at hand, [one becomes capable of directly perceiving] the transformation-triad and other [matters] taught in the third <s>pāda</s>—that is, capable of attaining knowledge, supernatural powers (<s>vibhūti</s>), and so forth. And thus it is for this purpose that the purification of mind is taught—this is the purport of the section. As the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator <s>Vyāsa</s>) has shown with the words ["It is for this very purpose that this purification of mind..."] and so forth. // 35 //

body.text: viśokā vā jyotiṣmatī ॥ 36 ॥
body.translated_text: Or, the luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>) and sorrowless (<s>viśokā</s>) [activity]. // 36 //

body.text: pravṛttirutpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhanītyanuvartate। hṛdayapuṇḍarīke dhārayato yā buddhisaṁvit buddhisattvaṁ hi bhāsvaramākāśakalpaṁ, tatra sthitivaiśāradyātpravṛttiḥ sūryendugrahamaṇiprabhārūpākāreṇa vikalpate। tathā'smitāyāṁ samāpannaṁ cittaṁ nistaraṅgamahodadhikalpaṁ śāntamanantamasmitāmātraṁ bhavati। yatredamuktam – “tamaṇumātramātmānamanuvidyāsmītyevaṁ tāvatsaṁprajānīte” iti। eṣā dvayī viśokā viṣayavatī, asmitāmātrā ca pravṛttirjyotiṣmatītyucyate। yayā yoginaścittaṁ sthitipadaṁ labhata iti ॥ 36 ॥
body.translated_text: "A [perceptual] activity, when arisen, anchors the steadiness of mind"—this carries over from the preceding. For one who concentrates on the heart-lotus, there arises a cognition of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect)—for the <s>sattva</s> (essence) of <s>buddhi</s> is luminous and space-like. Through proficiency in steadiness there, the activity manifests in the form of the radiance of the sun, moon, planets, and gems. Likewise, the mind absorbed in <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness) becomes like a waveless great ocean—peaceful, infinite, consisting of mere <s>asmitā</s>. As it has been said: "Having found this self, minute in measure, one knows thus: 'I am'—to that extent." This twofold [activity]—the sorrowless (<s>viśokā</s>) one that possesses objects (<s>viṣayavatī</s>), and the one consisting of mere <s>asmitā</s>—is called <s>jyotiṣmatī</s> (luminous). By this the yogin's mind attains the state of steadiness. // 36 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[viśokā vā jyotiṣmatī pravṛttirutpannā manasaḥ sthitinibandhinīti] prakṛtamabhisaṁbadhyate । jyotiryasyāṁ vidyate pravṛttau sā [jyotiṣmatī ।] sā ca śokaṁ vyapagamayatīti [viśokā nāma ॥]
sā ca kathamupajāyata ityāha- [hṛdayapuṇḍarīke dhārayato buddhisaṁvidbhavati] svarūpasaṁvedanam । buddhisatvaṁ hi kiṁrūpamityāha- [buddhisatvaṁ hi prabhāsvaraṁ] prabhāsanaśīla [mākāśakalpaṁ] vyāpi । [yatra] yasmin buddhisattve ॥
[sthitivaiṣamyāditi ।] buddhisattvātmatāsāmyānāpattariti । hṛdayapuṇḍarīka eva dhārayata: pravṛttijyotiṣmatī [sūryendumaṇiprabhārūpākāreṇa vikalpate । tathā cāsmitāyām] ahaṅkāre [samāpannaṁ] syāt buddhisatvaṁ svarūpeṇa sāmyāpatte [rnistaraṅgamahodadhikalpaṁ śāntamanantamasmitāmātraṁ bhavati ॥]
[yatredamuktaṁ yatrā] smitāsamāpattau । taṁ etaṁ prakṛtamasmitātmānamahaṅkāram aṇu sūkṣmam [ātmānamanuvidya] prāpya [asmītvevaṁtāvatsaṁjānīta] iti । yādṛśamālambanasvarūpaṁ tāvanmātraṁ sañjānīte । ahaṅkārasvarūpeṇaiva tadānurūpyādavacchidyate, sphaṭikamaṇirivopadhānarūpeṇa । evaṁ [dvayī viśokā] pravṛtti [rviṣayavatī cāsmitāmātrā ca ।] tatra gandhasaṁvidādirāsmitāmātrāntā sarvā viśokaiva । jyetiṣmatī punargandhasaṁvidādipravṛttipañcatayādanyatra । viṣayavatī tvasmitāmātrāt prāgevetyevaṁ viṣayavibhāgaḥ । [yayā] viśokayā jyotiṣmatyā [yoginaścittaṁ sthitipadaṁ labhate ॥ 36 ॥]
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["The sorrowless (<s>viśokā</s>) and luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>) activity, when arisen, anchors the steadiness of mind"]—this is connected with the topic under discussion. That yogic activity in which light (<s>jyotis</s>) is present is [<s>jyotiṣmatī</s> (luminous).] And since it dispels sorrow, it is [called <s>viśokā</s> (sorrowless).]
How does it arise? He explains: [For one concentrating on the heart-lotus, there arises a cognition of <s>buddhi</s>]—a perception of its own nature. What is the nature of the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>? He says: [The <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> is self-luminous (<s>prabhāsvara</s>)]—having the nature of illumination—[and space-like (<s>ākāśakalpa</s>)]—all-pervading. [Where]—in that <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>,
["due to proficiency in steadiness"]—because identity with the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> has not yet been achieved. For one concentrating on the heart-lotus itself, the luminous activity [takes the form of the radiance of the sun, moon, gems, and the like. Likewise, when absorbed in <s>asmitā</s>]—in the ego-sense—the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> would, through attaining identity with its own nature, [become like a waveless great ocean—peaceful, infinite, consisting of mere <s>asmitā</s>.]
[As it has been said, "where"]—in the absorption into <s>asmitā</s>. [Having found] this <s>asmitā</s>-self, the ego-sense, which is the subject under discussion, [as minute]—subtle—[as a self, one knows thus: "I am"—to that extent.] One cognizes only to the extent of the nature of the support (<s>ālambana</s>). It is delimited by the very nature of the ego-sense, conforming to it, just as a crystal gem [takes on the form] of the object placed near it. Thus [this twofold <s>viśokā</s> (sorrowless) activity is both the <s>viṣayavatī</s> (object-possessing) and the <s>asmitā</s>-mātра (pure I-am-ness).] Of these, all activities from the perception of fragrance up to mere <s>asmitā</s> are indeed <s>viśokā</s> (sorrowless). But <s>jyotiṣmatī</s> (luminous) applies to those other than the fivefold activities of fragrance-perception and the like. And <s>viṣayavatī</s> (object-possessing) applies only to those prior to mere <s>asmitā</s>—thus is the distinction of domains. [By this] sorrowless and luminous [activity, the yogin's mind attains the state of steadiness.] // 36 //

body.text: vītarāgaviṣayaṁ vā cittam ॥ 37 ॥
body.translated_text: Or, the mind directed toward one who is free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>). // 37 //

body.text: vītarāgacittālambanoparaktaṁ vā yoginaścittaṁ sthitipadaṁ labhata iti ॥ 37 ॥
body.translated_text: The mind of the yogin, colored by taking as its support the mind of one free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>), attains the state of steadiness. // 37 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[vītarāgaviṣayaṁ vā cittaṁ] vīto rāgo yasmāta pratyayāt sa vītarāgaḥ rāgaśūnya ityarthaḥ । sa eṣa viṣaya ālambanaṁ yasya cittasya tadvītarāgaviṣayam । vītarāgaśca pratyayaḥ prasiddho loke । rāgiṇo'pi hi puruṣasya rāgakāraṇe'pi viṣaye, yaḥ strīṣu mātrādiṣu । sa eva pratyayaḥ [tameva pratyayaṁ] vītarāgaḥ [gaṁ] alambanatve nābhyasyet ; na tu tasya yo viṣayaḥ ālambanam । viṣayāṇāṁ khalatvāt । tat [vītarāgapralayālambanoparaktaṁ cittaṁ] tadvadeva vītarāgaṁ prasannataraṁ [sthitipadaṁ labhate ।] rāgādikhalīkṛtaṁ hi kṛtakhalīnamiva turaṅgamānanaṁ pracalati ॥ 37 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["Or, the mind directed toward one free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>)."]
<s>Vītarāga</s> means one from whom passion has departed—that is, one devoid of passion. That mental state (<s>pratyaya</s>) which is the object and support of the mind is called "having a passion-free object" (<s>vītarāgaviṣaya</s>). And such a passion-free mental state is well-known in the world. Even for a person who has passion, regarding objects that cause passion—such as women, mothers, and the like—[that same mental state], that very passion-free [mental state, should be] practiced as an object of meditation; not the external object that is its content, since external objects have a coarsening effect. [The mind] thus colored by taking as support [the mental state of] one free from passion, [itself becomes] similarly free from passion, exceedingly clear, [and attains the state of steadiness.] For a mind roughened by passion and the like wavers, just as the face of a horse made restive. // 37 //

body.text: svapnanidrājñānālambanaṁ vā ॥ 38 ॥
body.translated_text: Or, [the mind] supported by the knowledge arising from dream and sleep. // 38 //

body.text: svapnajñānālambanaṁ vā nidrājñānālambanaṁ vā tadākāraṁ yoginaścittaṁ sthitipadaṁ labhata iti ॥ 38 ॥
body.translated_text: The mind of the yogin, supported by the knowledge of dream, or supported by the knowledge of sleep, taking on that form, attains the state of steadiness. // 38 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[svapnanidrājñānālambanaṁ vā । svapnajñānālambanaṁ vā nidrājñānālambanaṁ vā cittaṁ tadākārameva] bhavati । evaṁsvabhāvaṁ hi cittaṁ yadālambate [tadākāraṁ bhavati ।] svapne ca śabdādiviṣayaśūnyaṁ jñānam । jñānasyāpi svabhāvo'vabhāsakatā । tatrāpi jñānasvarūpamevālambate । na tu smaryamāṇaviṣayasvarūpam । smaryamāṇenāpi viṣayeṇa khalīkāro dṛśyate । nidrājñānaṁ tu viśeṣāgrahaṇātmakamabhāvapratyayālambanaṁ śāntamanantamanubhūyamānācalanadharmakam । tataśca tadālambanaṁ saccittaṁ [sthitipadaṁ labhata iti] yuktam ॥ 38 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["Or, supported by the knowledge arising from dream and sleep. The mind, supported by dream-knowledge or by sleep-knowledge,] takes on that very form." For the mind is of such a nature that [whatever it takes as its support, it assumes that form.] In dream, knowledge is devoid of external objects such as sound and the rest. Yet the nature of knowledge is illumination. Even there, it takes as its support only the nature of knowledge itself, not the nature of the objects being remembered. For even through remembered objects, a coarsening effect is observed. Sleep-knowledge, however—being of the nature of non-apprehension of particulars, having the absence [of content] as its object of cognition, peaceful, infinite, experienced as having the quality of motionlessness—when the mind takes this as its support, [it attains the state of steadiness]—this is fitting. // 38 //

body.text: yathābhimatadhyānādvā ॥ 39 ॥
body.translated_text: Or, by meditation on any desired [object]. // 39 //

body.text: yadevābhimataṁ tadeva dhyāyet। tatra labdhasthitikamanyatrāpi sthitipadaṁ labhata iti ॥ 39 ॥
body.translated_text: Whatever is desired, let one meditate on that very thing. Having gained steadiness there, one attains the state of steadiness elsewhere as well. // 39 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yathābhimatadhyānādvā । yadevābhimatamiti] cittasthityapekṣayā । cittasthiteḥ prakṛtatvāt । na tu sukhādyapekṣayā । pratiṣiddhatvācca- [“na tveva viṣayān prāpya dhārayeta kathaṁcana”] iti । [tatra labdhasthitikaṁ] karmaṇyaṁ sat [anyatra] śāstrīyeṣu [api sthitipadaṁ labhate ॥ 39 ॥]
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa (Elucidation)]
["Or, by meditation on any desired object."] ["Whatever is desired"]—this is with reference to steadiness of mind, since steadiness of mind is the topic under discussion—not with reference to pleasure and the like, since it is prohibited: ["One should never, having obtained sense objects, hold onto them."] [Having gained steadiness there,] the mind, having become fit for work, [attains the state of steadiness in other,] scriptural [objects as well.] // 39 //

body.text: paramāṇuparamamahattvānto'sya vaśīkāraḥ ॥ 40 ॥
body.translated_text: His mastery extends from the minutest atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) to the greatest magnitude (<s>paramamahattva</s>). // 40 //

body.text: sūkṣme niviśamānasya paramāṇvantaṁ sthitipadaṁ labhata iti। sthūle niviśamānasya paramamahattvāntaṁ sthitipadaṁ cittasya। evaṁ tāmubhayīṁ koṭimanudhāvato yo'syāpratīghātaḥ sa paro vaśīkāraḥ। tadvaśīkārātparipūrṇaṁ yoginaścittaṁ na punarabhyāsakṛtaṁ parikarmāpekṣata iti ॥ 40 ॥
body.translated_text: For one who concentrates upon the subtle, the stable ground extends to the limit of the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>). For one who concentrates upon the gross, the stable ground of the mind extends to the limit of the greatest magnitude (<s>paramamahattva</s>). Thus, for one who pursues both these limits, the unobstructed [mastery] that is his—that is the supreme mastery (<s>vaśīkāra</s>). Through that mastery, the <s>yogin</s>'s mind, being fully perfected, no longer requires the refinement produced by practice. // 40 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[paramāṇuparamamahattvānto'sya vaśīkāraḥ ।] antaśabdaḥ pratyekaṁ saṁbadhyate । [sūkṣme niviśamānasya] parimāṇe niviśamānasya yoginā saṁkṣipyamāṇasya । abhyāsakāle svalpamalpataraṁ ca krameṇālecayatparamāṇvantaṁ saṁkṣipyate । sa ca paramāṇuścittasya saṁkṣepakoṭiḥ । tena [tadantaṁ sthitipadam ॥]
[itthamubhayakoṭimanudhāvataścittasya] saṁkṣepaṁ vistāraṁ cānubhavato [yaḥ] tadvirodhinā pratyayāntareṇa [apratighātaḥ sa paro vaśīkāraḥ ।] pūrve'pi pare eva । tathā'pyasyāyaṁ viśeṣaḥ । [tadvaśīkārāt paripūrṇam] anavakhaṇḍitaṁ labdhasthitikaṁ [na punarabhyāsakṛtaṁ parikarmāpekṣata iti ।] pūrvaṁ tu kiyadapi parikamantaramapekṣante ॥
tatra saṁkṣiptā viśālā vikaraṇī ceti trayī dhāraṇā । tatrebhayakoṭisparśinī vikaraṇī । paramamahatvāntaspṛgviśālā । paramāṇvantaspṛkū saṁkṣiptā । sā ca trayyapāha sūtropāttā ॥ 40 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
[His mastery extends to the limit of the atom and the greatest magnitude.] The word 'limit' (<s>anta</s>) is connected with each separately. [For one who concentrates upon the subtle]—for one who concentrates upon dimension, whose [mind] is being contracted by the <s>yogin</s>. During the time of practice, [the mind] is contracted progressively to something smaller and yet smaller, until it reaches the limit of the atom. And that atom is the limit of the mind's contraction. Hence [it is said that] the stable ground has that as its limit.
[Thus, for one who pursues both limits of the mind]—for one who experiences both contraction and expansion—[the] unobstructedness by any contrary cognition [is] the supreme mastery. The earlier [stages of mastery] too are supreme indeed; yet here is the specific distinction: [through that mastery] the mind is fully perfected (<s>paripūrṇa</s>), uninterrupted, having attained stability, and [it no longer requires the refinement produced by practice.] Previously, however, some further refinement was still required.
Therein, the threefold <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration) is: contracted (<s>saṃkṣiptā</s>), expanded (<s>viśālā</s>), and modified (<s>vikaraṇī</s>). Of these, the one touching both limits is the modified. The one reaching the limit of the greatest magnitude is the expanded. The one reaching the limit of the atom is the contracted. And this threefold [dhāraṇā], he says, is taken up by the <s>sūtra</s>. // 40 //

body.text: atha labdhasthitikasya cetasaḥ kiṁsvarūpā kiṁviṣayā vā samāpattiriti, taducyate –
body.translated_text: Now, for one whose mind has attained stability, what is the nature and what is the object of <s>samāpatti</s> (cognitive absorption)? That is stated:

body.text: kṣīṇavṛtterabhijātasyeva maṇergrahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ ॥ 41 ॥
body.translated_text: Like a flawless jewel, [the mind] whose activities have dwindled, taking on the coloring and conforming to the grasper (<s>grahītṛ</s>), the grasping (<s>grahaṇa</s>), and the grasped (<s>grāhya</s>)—that is <s>samāpatti</s>. // 41 //

body.text: kṣīṇavṛtteriti pratyastamitapratyayasyetyarthaḥ। abhijātasyeva maṇeriti dṛṣṭāntopādānam। yathā sphaṭika upāśrayabhedāttattadrūpoparakta upāśrayarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate tathā grāhyālambanoparaktaṁ cittaṁ grāhyasamāpannaṁ grāhyasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate। bhūtasūkṣmoparaktaṁ bhūtasūkṣmasamāpannaṁ bhūtasūkṣmasvarūpābhāsaṁ bhavati। tathā sthūlālambanoparaktaṁ sthūlarūpasamāpannaṁ sthūlarūpābhāsaṁ bhavati। tathā viśvabhedoparaktaṁ viśvabhedasamāpannaṁ viśvarūpābhāsaṁ bhavati।
body.translated_text: 'Whose activities have dwindled' means one whose [external] cognitions have subsided—that is the meaning. 'Like a flawless jewel' is the introduction of an illustration. Just as a crystal, colored by different substrates, appears in the form of the substrate—so too the mind, colored by a grasped object (<s>grāhya</s>), having attained [absorption in] the grasped, appears in the form of the grasped object. Colored by subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>), having attained [absorption in] the subtle elements, it becomes an appearance of the form of the subtle elements. Likewise, colored by a gross object (<s>sthūlālambana</s>), having attained [absorption in] the gross form, it becomes an appearance of the gross form. Likewise, colored by the universal differentiation (<s>viśvabheda</s>), having attained [absorption in] the universal differentiation, it becomes an appearance of the universal form.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[atha labdhasthitikasya cetasaḥ] atha uktānāmanyatamenopāyena labdhasthitikasya [kiṁsvarūpā । kiṁviṣayā vā samāpattiriti] tannididarśayiṣayedaṁ sūtraṁ pravavṛte- [kṣīṇavṛtterabhijātasyeva maṇergrahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu tatsthatadañjanatā samāpattiḥ ॥]
nanu ca samāpatterviṣayaṁ vakṣyati tṛtīyapāde ‘ [parārthāt svārthasaṁyamāt puruṣajñānam’] ityādinā । samāpattisvarūpaṁ ca saṁyamasvarūpaṁ tatkāryanirvartanenaiva setsyati । tataścānarthakamidaṁ sūtram-naiṣa doṣaḥ-pūrvoktopāyavaśīkāraṇārthavatvapradarśanārthatvāt । evaṁ hyeṣa cittavaśīkāro'rthavān, yena grahītrādyarthasamāpannaṁ cittaṁ tadābhāsaṁ bhavatīti ॥
kiñca-‘vitakadyanugamāt saṁprajñātaḥ’ ityuktam vitarkādisvarūpaṁ ceha darśayitavyam । anuktāyāṁ samāpattau vitarkādisvarūpaṁ na śakyaṁ darśayituṁ samāpattidharmā(di)vitarkādaya iti । [kṣīṇavṛtteriti pratyasta] mitabāhyapramāṇādi [pratyayasye] tyarthaḥ ॥
nanu sarva eva pratyayāḥ pratyastamitāḥ । sarvapratyastamaye hi avasitādhikāraṁ na sthūlasūkṣmādikamālambate ॥
[abhijātasyeva maṇeriti dṛṣṭāntopādānam । yathā sphaṭika upāśrayabhedāttattadrūpoparakta upāśrayākareṇa nirbhāsate । tathā grāhyālambanoparaktaṁ cittaṁ grāhyasamāpannaṁ grāhyasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate ॥]
[tathā bhūtasūkṣmoparaktaṁ] tanmātroparaktaṁ [bhūtasūkṣmasamāpannaṁ bhūtasūkṣmasvarūpāvabhāsam] avabhāsate ॥
[[tathā sthūlālambanoparaktaṁ sthūlarūpasamāpannaṁ sthūlarūpāmāsaṁ bhavati । tathā viśvabhedoparaktaṁ viśvabhedasamāpannaṁ viśvarūpābhāsaṁ bhavati ॥]
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
[Now, for one whose mind has attained stability], by whichever of the aforementioned means the mind has attained stability—[what is its nature and what is its object—that is, of <s>samāpatti</s>]—wishing to demonstrate that, this <s>sūtra</s> was composed: [Like a flawless jewel, the mind whose activities have dwindled, taking on the coloring and conforming to the grasper, grasping, and grasped—that is <s>samāpatti</s>.]
Objection: He will state the object of <s>samāpatti</s> in the third <s>pāda</s>: '[Through <s>saṃyama</s>] directed toward another's purpose, from <s>saṃyama</s> directed toward one's own purpose, knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>' (YS 3.36) and so forth. And the nature of <s>samāpatti</s> will be established through the nature of <s>saṃyama</s> and its effects. Therefore this <s>sūtra</s> is purposeless. Reply: This is not a fault—because it serves to demonstrate that the mastery described earlier is meaningful. For this mastery of the mind is meaningful in that the mind, having attained absorption in the grasper and the rest, becomes an appearance of that.
Moreover—it was said: '<s>saṃprajñāta</s> [is defined] by the accompaniment of <s>vitarka</s> and the rest.' And the nature of <s>vitarka</s> and the rest must be shown here. Without stating <s>samāpatti</s>, the nature of <s>vitarka</s> and the rest cannot be shown, since <s>vitarka</s> and the rest are properties of <s>samāpatti</s>. ['Whose activities have dwindled' means one whose] external valid cognition and other [cognitions have] subsided—that is the meaning.
Objection: All cognitions whatsoever have subsided—for when all [cognitions] have subsided, the mind whose task is finished would not take on a gross, subtle, or other object. Reply: [Like a flawless jewel—this is the introduction of an illustration. Just as a crystal, colored by different substrates, appears in the form of the substrate. So too the mind, colored by the grasped object, having attained absorption in the grasped, appears in the form of the grasped object.]
[Likewise, colored by subtle elements]—colored by <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements), [having attained absorption in the subtle elements, it appears as] an appearance of the form of the subtle elements.
[Likewise, colored by a gross object, having attained absorption in the gross form, it becomes an appearance of the gross form. Likewise, colored by the universal differentiation, having attained absorption in the universal differentiation, it becomes an appearance of the universal form.]

body.text: tathā grahaṇeṣvapīndriyeṣvapi draṣṭavyam। grahaṇālambanoparaktaṁ grahaṇasamāpannaṁ grahaṇasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate। tathā grahītṛpuruṣālambanoparaktaṁ grahītṛpuruṣasamāpannaṁ grahītṛpuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate। tathā muktapuruṣālambanoparaktaṁ muktapuruṣasamāpannaṁ muktapuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsata iti। tadevamabhijātamaṇikalpasya cetaso grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu puruṣendriyabhūteṣu yā tatsthatadañjanatā teṣu sthitasya tadākārāpattiḥ sā samāpattirityucyate ॥ 41 ॥
body.translated_text: Likewise, regarding the grasping—the sense-organs too—it should be understood similarly. Colored by the grasping as object, having attained [absorption in] the grasping, [the mind] appears in the form of the grasping. Likewise, colored by the grasper-<s>Puruṣa</s> as object, having attained [absorption in] the grasper-<s>Puruṣa</s>, it appears in the form of the grasper-<s>Puruṣa</s>. Likewise, colored by the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s> as object, having attained [absorption in] the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s>, it appears in the form of the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s>. Thus, for the mind that is like a flawless jewel, that coloring and conformity to the grasper, grasping, and grasped—<s>Puruṣa</s>, sense-organs, and elements—that resting-in-them and taking-on-their-form is called <s>samāpatti</s>. // 41 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[tathā grahaṇeṣvapīndriyeṣvapi draṣṭavyam । grahaṇālambanoparaktaṁ grahaṇasamāpannaṁ grahaṇasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate ॥] yujyate । saṁbandhaviśeṣācca yathā svapuruṣo grahītṛsvarūpaśca muktaśca cittavṛttiviśeṣasaṁbandhāt gṛhyate tadvat । na tu sarvātmanaiva mahadahaṅkārayorapi grahaṇaṁ mahattvāt ॥
tayorapi [tāvapi] yadi sarvātmanā gṛhyeyātām , cittasattvamātrātmānau jāyeyātām , tathā ca sati tadviṣayagrahaṇameva na syāt । pradhānapuruṣayostu tatsaṁbandhasya cātyantamavyaktasvarūpatvānna svarūpagrahaṇam । nanu ceśvarasyāsarvajñatā, [yataḥ] pradhānapuruṣatatsaṁbandhā na pratyakṣā iti । ucyate-pradhānapuruṣasaṁvandhebhyo'nyatsarvaṁ pratyakṣamityatra tāvat avipratipattiḥ, niravadhikapratyakṣajñānābhyupagamāt । (yatra tvanumānāgocaraḥ) [yattu asmākamagocaraḥ tat] sa eveśvaro jñātumarhati । jñeyaṁ cedasti tatsarvamasau yathā vā tathā vā jānātīti niścayaḥ । ajñātṛkasya jñeyatvānupapatteḥ ॥
kiñca-yadi prakṛtipuruṣau svarūpeṇa jñeyatvamā(nā)padyeyātāṁ tadā buddhivadbhogyatāprasaṅgaḥ । tataśca parārtho'pi syāt paraścānyaḥ kalpyaḥ syāt ॥
nanu puruṣāṇāmanyonyabhogyateti na paro bhoktā kalpyaḥ-naitadevamsamatvāt puruṣāṇāṁ viṣayaviṣayitvānupapatteḥ । na hi pradīpāvanyonyamupakurutaḥ । kiñca - bhogyatve sukhadirūpatāprasaṅgaśca puruṣasya । tathā ca sati pradhānasya nirhetukatvaprasaṅgaścetyevamādayo bhūyāṁso doṣāḥ ॥
nanu ca [‘parārthāt svārtasaṁyamāt puruṣajñānam'] iti puruṣapratyakṣatāṁ vakṣyati-satyaṁ yuktamuktam । ata evocyate puruṣo na svarūpeṇa viṣayībhavatīti । yenaivaṁ tatroktam ["na ca puruṣapratyayena buddhisatvātmanā puruṣo dṛśyate । puruṣa eva taṁ pratyayaṁ svālambanaṁ paśyatīti । tathā hyuktam ‘vijñātāramare kena vijānayāt"] itīti ॥
nanu puruṣālambanoparakta cittaṁ puruṣasya viṣayaḥ । tathā ca sati pratyakṣa eva puruṣaḥ । yathā ghaṭālambanoparakte pratyaye puruṣeṇopalabhyamāne ghaṭaḥ pratyakṣa ucyate-naiṣa doṣaḥ-ghaṭavatpuruṣasya cittenāvyāpyatvāt । ghaṭādistu bāhyaścittena vyāpyate, na puruṣaḥ, ānantyāt ॥
paricchinnaṁ hi cittaṁ viṣayīkurvanna puruṣaṁ viṣayiṇamanantaṁ vyāptumutsahate । yadi puruṣaṁ vyāpnoti pradhānamapi vyāpnuyāt ॥
tasmādyathā darpaṇe mukhaṁ chāyārūpeṇa gṛhyate, tathā puruṣacchāyākāreṇa pariṇataḥ pratyayo gṛhyate puruṣeṇa । tathā ca vyāsaḥ [‘yathā''darśatalaprakhye paśyatyātmānamātmani' ॥] iti ।
na tu muktānyapuruṣākāreṇa pariṇatau dvāramasti । yadi tadākareṇa pariṇameta, muktasyāpi tatsvameveti dṛśyaṁ syāt । na hi cittasya pariṇāmādanyatvaṁ nāmasti । svākoraṇa hi pariṇataṁ puruṣe na tu cittaṁ na paśyati । svapuruṣe svatvātsati saṁbandhe pariṇatidvāramasti ॥
kathaṁ tarhi svapuruṣādanyasya svatvāsaṁbandhino grahaṇam-ucyate-yathā paradarpaṇadvāreṇa paramukhadarśanaṁ, tathā darpaṇasthānīyaparasatvākārapariṇataṁ svasatvaṁ puruṣaḥ paśyan paramapi puruṣaṁ jānāti ॥
tasyāyamātmā mamāyamityanyatvantvanumānādeva pratipadyate svakīyādanyadīyasatvagataviśeṣaliṅgena । satvānāṁ ca triguṇatvādavaśyaṁ viśeṣāḥ santi । puruṣāṇāṁ tu nirviśeṣatvātsvarūpeṇa bhedī duravabodha eva ॥
[tasmādevamabhijātamaṇikalpasya cetaso grahītṛgrahaṇagrāhyeṣu puruṣendriyabhūteṣu tatsthatadañjanatā ।] teṣu grahītrādiṣu tiṣṭhatīti tatsthaṁ tatsthatāviśiṣṭā yā grahītrādyañjanatā, tadevāha- [teṣu sthitasya tadākārāpattiḥ samāpatirityucyate ॥]
samyagāpattiḥ samāpattiḥ sā ca tādṛśī pratyastamitabahirvṛttereva bhavati । yadyapi vyutthitacittasyāpi samāpattirasti । tathā'pi sā na samīcīnatarā, rajastamobhyāṁ cittasatvasyātyantābhibhūtatvāditi ॥ 41 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
[Likewise, regarding the grasping—the sense-organs too—it should be understood similarly. Colored by the grasping as object, having attained absorption in the grasping, it appears in the form of the grasping.] This is justified. And due to a specific connection, just as one's own <s>Puruṣa</s> in the form of the grasper and the liberated [<s>Puruṣa</s>] are grasped through a specific connection with mental modifications—so too [with the sense-organs]. But <s>mahat</s> (cosmic intellect) and <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle) cannot be grasped in their entirety, because of their vastness.
If even those two were grasped in their entirety, they would become identical with the <s>sattva</s> of the mind alone; and in that case, the grasping of an object pertaining to them would not be possible. But as for <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> and their mutual connection—because their nature is utterly unmanifest, there is no grasping of their own form. Objection: Then <s>Īśvara</s> would not be omniscient, since <s>pradhāna</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s>, and their connection would not be directly perceived [by Him]. Reply: As for everything other than <s>pradhāna</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s>, and their connection being directly perceived—there is no dispute about that, given the acceptance of unlimited perceptual knowledge. [As for that which is beyond our reach], only <s>Īśvara</s> Himself is capable of knowing it. And if there is something knowable, He knows all of it in one way or another—this is certain, because the knowability of something that has no knower is impossible.
Moreover—if <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> were to become objects of knowledge in their own form, then, like <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), the absurdity of their being objects of enjoyment would follow. And then [<s>Puruṣa</s>] too would be 'for another's purpose,' and yet another [entity] would have to be postulated.
Objection: Since <s>Puruṣas</s> are mutually enjoyable, no further enjoyer need be postulated. Reply: This is not so—because of the equality of <s>Puruṣas</s>, the relation of object and subject is impossible. For lamps do not illuminate each other. Moreover—if <s>Puruṣa</s> were an object of enjoyment, the absurdity of it having the nature of pleasure and the like would follow. And in that case, the absurdity of <s>pradhāna</s> being without a cause would follow—and many other such defects.
Objection: But he will state in '[Through <s>saṃyama</s>] directed toward another's purpose, from <s>saṃyama</s> directed toward one's own purpose, knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s>' (YS 3.36) that <s>Puruṣa</s> is directly perceivable.
