Reply: True, what was said is proper. Precisely for this reason it is said that <s>Puruṣa</s> does not become an object in its own form. That is why it was stated there: ['<s>Puruṣa</s> is not seen by a cognition that has the nature of the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>. Rather, <s>Puruṣa</s> itself sees that cognition as its own object. As it has been said: "The knower, O dear one, by what would you know it?"']
Objection: The mind colored by <s>Puruṣa</s> as object is <s>Puruṣa</s>'s object. And in that case, <s>Puruṣa</s> is indeed directly perceived. Just as when a cognition colored by a pot as object is apprehended by <s>Puruṣa</s>, the pot is called 'directly perceived.' Reply: This is not a fault—because, unlike a pot, <s>Puruṣa</s> is not encompassed by the mind. A pot and other external objects are encompassed by the mind, but <s>Puruṣa</s> is not, because of its infinitude.
For the mind, being finite, while objectifying, is unable to encompass <s>Puruṣa</s>, who is infinite as an object. If it could encompass <s>Puruṣa</s>, it could encompass <s>pradhāna</s> too.
Therefore, just as a face is grasped in a mirror in the form of a reflection, so a cognition transformed into the form of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s reflection is grasped by <s>Puruṣa</s>. And thus <s>Vyāsa</s> [says]: ['As in a mirror's surface, one sees the Self by the Self.'] But for a liberated or another <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is no doorway through transformation into their form. If [the mind] were to transform into their form, then even the liberated one's [nature] would be 'his own,' and thus would be something seen. For the mind has no nature other than its transformation. Having transformed into one's own form, <s>Puruṣa</s> indeed sees—it is not that the mind does not see. For one's own <s>Puruṣa</s>, because of the relation of ownership, there is a doorway through transformation.
How then is another [<s>Puruṣa</s>], with whom there is no relation of ownership, grasped? Reply: Just as through another's mirror one sees another's face, so too <s>Puruṣa</s>, seeing his own <s>sattva</s> transformed into the form of another's <s>sattva</s>, knows the other <s>Puruṣa</s> as well.
The distinction 'this self belongs to him, this to me'—the otherness is known only through inference, by means of distinguishing marks found in another's <s>sattva</s> as different from one's own. And since <s>sattvas</s> are constituted of the three <s>guṇas</s>, there are necessarily distinctions. But since <s>Puruṣas</s> are without distinctions, the difference in their own form is indeed difficult to comprehend.
[Thus, for the mind that is like a flawless jewel, the coloring and conformity to the grasper, grasping, and grasped—<s>Puruṣa</s>, sense-organs, and elements.] It abides in them—the grasper and the rest—hence 'resting-in-them'; qualified by that resting-in-them is the conformity to the grasper and the rest—this is what he says: [For one abiding in them, the taking-on-of-their-form is called <s>samāpatti</s>.]
<s>Samāpatti</s> is proper attainment (<s>samyag āpattiḥ</s>), and such [proper attainment] occurs only for one whose external activities have subsided. Although even the mind in the ordinary state (<s>vyutthita</s>) has <s>samāpatti</s>, still that is not entirely proper, because the <s>sattva</s> of the mind is thoroughly overwhelmed by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>. // 41 //

body.text: tatra śabdārthajñānavikalpaiḥ saṁkīrṇā savitarkā samāpattiḥ ॥ 42 ॥
body.translated_text: Therein, the <s>savitarkā samāpatti</s> (absorption with deliberation) is that which is intermixed with conceptual constructs of word, meaning, and knowledge. // 42 //

body.text: tadyathā gauritiśabdo gaurityartho gauriti jñānamityavibhāgena vibhaktānāmapi grahaṇaṁ dṛṣṭam। vibhajyamānāścānye śabdadharmā anye'rthadharmā anye vijñānadharmā ityeteṣāṁ vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ। tatra samāpannasya yogino yo gavādyarthaḥ samādhiprajñāyāṁ samārūḍhaḥ sa cecchabdārthajñānavikalpānuviddha upāvartate sā saṁkīrṇā samāpattiḥ savitarketyucyate ।
body.translated_text: For example, [the words] 'cow'—the word, 'cow'—the object, 'cow'—the knowledge: the grasping of these, though they are distinct, is seen as undifferentiated. But when analyzed, the properties of the word are one thing, the properties of the object another, and the properties of cognition yet another—their paths are distinct. Therein, for the <s>yogin</s> in <s>samāpatti</s>, when the object such as a cow, having risen in the <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom, appears pervaded by the conceptual constructs of word, meaning, and knowledge—that mixed absorption is called <s>savitarkā</s> (with deliberation).

body.text: yadā punaḥ śabdasaṁketasmṛtipariśuddhau śrutānumānajñānavikalpaśūnyāyāṁ samādhiprajñāyāṁ svarūpamātreṇāvasthito'rthastatsvarūpākāramātratayaivāvacchidyate। sā ca nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ। tatparaṁ pratyakṣam। tacca śrutānumānayorbījam। tataḥ śrutānumāne prabhavataḥ। na ca śrutānumānajñānasahabhūtaṁ taddarśanam। tasmādasaṁkīrṇaṁ pramāṇāntareṇa yogino nirvitarkasamādhijaṁ darśanamiti ॥ 42 ॥
body.translated_text: But when, with the purification of memory from verbal conventions, the <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom, empty of the conceptual constructs of scriptural and inferential knowledge, rests upon the object in its own form alone—[the mind] is delimited solely by the form of that object's own nature. And that is the <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (absorption without deliberation). That is the supreme direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). And that is the seed of scriptural and inferential knowledge. From it, scriptural and inferential knowledge arise. And the vision born of that [<s>nirvitarka samādhi</s>] does not coexist with scriptural and inferential knowledge. Therefore, the <s>yogin</s>'s vision born of <s>nirvitarka samādhi</s> is unmixed with any other means of knowledge. // 42 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
saiṣā samāpattiścatuṣṭayī । tatra prathamāṁ samāpattiṁ vyācaṣṭe - [śabdārthajñānavikalpaiḥ saṅkīrṇā savitarkā samāpattiḥ ।] śabdaścārthaśca jñānaṁ ca śabdārthajñānāni teṣāṁ vikalpāḥ śabdārthajñānavikalpāḥ । dhyātavyālambanaviṣayairvikalpaiḥ saṁkīrṇā vimiśrā itaretarapratyayānuviddhā sā saṁkīrṇasamāpatiḥ ॥
nanu ca śabdārthapratyayā itaretaravyāvṛttasvarūpāḥ, yogī caikaṁ vastu dhyeyatvenālambate śabdamarthaṁ pratyayaṁ vā, tatra kaḥ śabdārthajñānavikalpasaṅkaraḥ ? ॥
evamevaitat । tathā'pi ayameva saṁvyavahāro loke, yadutāvibhāgena grahaṇam । [tadyathā gauriti śabdo gaurityartho gauriti jñānami] tyavibhāgena loke [grahaṇaṁ dṛṣṭam ।] evaṁ hi lokaḥ trayamapi gaurityeva vyapadiśati । tathā'nyataragrahaṇe'vaśiṣṭayorapi smṛtiḥ ॥
nanu ca tathābhūtametadvastu-naivaṁ-śabdārthasaṅketagrahaṇottarakālabhāvitvāt । nanu saṅketādapi prāk sāmānyaśabdaṁ yaṁ kañcidadhyavasyatyeva-na-viviktānāmapi grahaṇadarśanāt । [vivicyamānāścānye śabdadharmā] gakārādivarṇodāttasvaritadrutamadhya- vilambitaśrotragrahaṇādayaḥ । te nārthajñānayoḥ । tathā [nye'rthadharmāḥ] sāsnālāṅgūlakakudakhuraviṣāṇadarśanasparśanādayaḥ । tathā (ca) [anye pratyayadharmāḥ] puruṣagrāhyātmakatvāvabhāsātmakatvasaṁskārādhāyitvādayaḥ, na te śabdārthayoḥ । na [tena]paramārthato'nyonyadharmasaṅkaragandho'pyasti । tena [viviktaḥ panthāsteṣām ॥]
tatra yatra kvacana [samāpannasya yo hyevārthaḥ samādhiprajñāmupārūḍhaḥ sa cecchabdārthajñānavikalpānuviddhaḥ] śabdārthasaddhetakṛto ya itaretarasmṛtyanuvyādhastadviśiṣṭathedartha [upāvartate sā saṅkīrṇā samāpattiḥ savitarketyucyate ॥]
anekajanmāntaraśabdārthasaddhetujñānasaṁskāraviśiṣṭatvādyogino'pi prathamatarāsamāpatirlokapratyayāviśiṣṭā । eṣa tu viśeṣo yat labdhasthitipadatvādyogicittasya samānapratyayapravāhateti ॥ 42 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
This <s>samāpatti</s> (attainment) is fourfold. Of these, he explains the first attainment: ["<s>Savitarkā samāpatti</s> is that which is mixed with conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpa</s>) of word, object, and knowledge."]. Word, object, and knowledge—these are <s>śabdārthajñāna</s>; their conceptual constructions (<s>vikalpas</s>) are <s>��abdārthajñānavikalpas</s>. Mixed (<s>saṅk��rṇā</s>)—that is, blended, pervaded by mutual cognitions—with conceptual constructions whose content is the object of meditation: that is the mixed attainment.
Objection: But word, object, and cognition have mutually distinct natures, and the <s>yogin</s> takes as his meditative support a single thing—either the word, the object, or the cognition. So what is this mingling of word, object, and knowledge?
This is just so. Nevertheless, this is the very convention in the world—namely, apprehension without distinction. ["For example, the word 'cow,' the object 'cow,' the knowledge 'cow'"]—in the world, these are apprehended without distinction. For the world designates all three simply as 'cow.' And when any one [of the three] is apprehended, the memory of the remaining two [also arises].
Objection: But the thing is of such nature [i.e., they are really mixed]—no, because [the mingling] arises only subsequent to the apprehension of the convention connecting word and meaning. But even before the convention, one determines some general word or other—no, because distinct apprehension is also observed. ["When discriminated, the properties of the word are different"]—the letters beginning with 'g,' the accents <s>udātta</s>, <s>svarita</s>, the tempos rapid, medium, slow, auditory apprehension, and so forth. These do not belong to the object or to knowledge. Similarly, ["the properties of the object are different"]—dewlap, tail, hump, hoof, horn, visual perception, tactile perception, and so forth. Similarly, ["the properties of cognition are different"]—being apprehensible by <s>Puruṣa</s>, being of the nature of illumination, being a depositor of impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>), and so forth—these do not belong to word or object. ["Therefore,"] in the ultimate sense, there is not even a trace of mingling of one another's properties. Therefore, ["their paths are distinct."]
Therein, ["for one who has attained [<s>samāpatti</s>] in any [object] whatsoever, the very object that has risen to the level of <s>samādhi</s> wisdom, if it is pervaded by conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge"]—if it is distinguished by the mutual superimposition of memories caused by the association of word and meaning, [that object "presents itself—that is the mixed attainment, called <s>savitarkā</s>."]
Because even the <s>yogin</s> possesses impressions from knowledge of word-meaning associations across many lifetimes, his very first attainment is not different from ordinary cognition. But the distinguishing feature is that, because the <s>yogin</s>'s mind has attained stability, there is a continuous flow of homogeneous cognition. // 42 //

body.text: nirvitarkāyāḥ samāpatterasyāḥ sūtreṇa lakṣaṇaṁ dyotyate –
body.translated_text: The definition of this <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (trans-deliberative attainment) is indicated by the <s>sūtra</s>—

body.text: smṛtipariśuddhau svarūpaśūnyevārthamātranirbhāsā nirvitarkā ॥ 43 ॥
body.translated_text: When memory is purified, [the mind], as if empty of its own form, shining forth as the object alone—that is <s>nirvitarkā</s> (trans-deliberative). // 43 //

body.text: yā śabdasaṁketaśrutānumānajñānavikalpasmṛtipariśuddhau grāhyasvarūpoparaktā prajñā svamiva prajñāsvarūpaṁ grahaṇātmakaṁ tyaktvā padārthamātrasvarūpā grāhyasvarūpāpanneva bhavati sā tadā nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ।
body.translated_text: When [the mind] is purified of the memory of conceptual constructions arising from verbal convention, received tradition (<s>śruta</s>), and inferential knowledge—the wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), colored by the nature of the apprehensible object, as if abandoning its own nature as wisdom whose essence is apprehension, becoming of the nature of the mere object, as if having assumed the very form of the apprehensible—that is then the <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (trans-deliberative attainment).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
idānīṁ nirvitarkā samāpattirucyate । [yadā punaḥ śabdasaṅketasmṛtipariśuddhau ।] śabdasaṅketo'syāyaṁ vācakaḥ ayamasya vācya iti samayapratipattiḥ । tajjanitasmṛtiḥ śabdasaṅketasmṛtiḥ । tasyāḥ pariśuddhirmithyātvādvinivṛttiḥ । sā rajastamasornyagbhāvāt ॥
[śrutajñānaṁ] āgamikam , [anumānajñānaṁ] laiṅgikaṁ, te ca sāmānyaviṣaya evānumānāgamajñāne, tayorvikalpo hi viśeṣādhyāropaḥ tenādhyāsena [śūnyāyāṁ] yoginaḥ [samādhiprajñāyāṁ] vyāvṛtalaiṅgikasāṅketikajñānādhyāsāyāṁ [svarūpamātreṇa] mātragrahaṇaṁ digdeśakālānubhāvādibhyo'pi vyāvṛtta ityevamarthaṁ, svaireva dharmairmahīyamānaḥ [tatsvarūpamātratayaiva] tasyārthasya svarūpamātratayaiva yoginaḥ prajñā [avacchidyate ।] na tasmādarthādbahirdeśakālādi kiṁcidālocayatītyarthaḥ ।
svamapi grahaṇātmakaṁ rūpaṁ tatprajñā nālocayati, nirmalataratvāt । grāhyamātraiva sā vibhāvyate । [sā ca] tādṛśī [nirvitarkā samāpatiḥ ।] nirgato vitarko'syāḥ nirvitarkaḥ vitarko'dhyāropaḥ । so'syāṁ nāsti ॥
[tat] etat [paraṁ] utkṛṣṭaṁ [śuddhaṁ pratyakṣaṁ] aparaṁ pratyakṣaṁ sarvasādhāraṇaṁ purastādvṛttimadhye paṭhitamidaṁ yogina eveti । [tacchrutānumānayorbījam ।] yadyapi pūrvoktamapi śrutānumānayorbījameva, tathā'pi tatkārye śrutānumānena vyabhicarato'pi, na punarnirvatarkasamādhijapratyakṣaprabhave vyabhicarata ityata āha- [tataḥ śrutānumāne prabhavata iti ॥]
[na ca (nanu) śrutānumānajñānasahabhūtaṁ taddarśanam,] śrutānumānajñānābhyāmasamānaviṣayamityetat । viśeṣaviṣayaṁ hi taddarśanaṁ, sāmānyaviṣaye śrutānumānajñāne । [tasmādasaṅkīrṇaṁ pramāṇāntareṇa yogino nirvitarkajaṁ darśanamiti (tannirvitarkāyāḥ] taditi tasmāditi) [samāpatterasyāḥ sūtreṇa lakṣaṇaṁ dyotyate- smṛtipariśuddhau svarūpaśūnyavārthamātranirbhāsānnirvitarkā ॥]
[śabdasaṅketaśrutānumānajñānavikalpasmṛtipariśuddhau] śabdasaṅketavikalpaḥ śrutajñānavikalpaḥ anumānajñānavikalpaśca, sa eva smṛtiḥ । smaraṇena hyanyasyānyadharmo'dhyāropyate । na hi vastu svarūpeṇa vastvantare'dhyāropayituṁ śakyam ।
nanu ca kathaṁ śrutānumite pratyakṣe'dhyāropyate । nanu ca prasiddho'dhyāropaḥ, tathā cedaṁ mayā śrutamidaṁ mayā'numitamidamiti ca paśyati ॥
nanu tadeva tat dṛśyamānamapi yadanumitaṁ śrutaṁ ca-na-sāmānyaviśeṣabhedāt । sāmānyaṁ śrutamanumitaṁ ca । viśeṣastu pratyakṣasya viṣayaḥ । tasmiṁśca tatsāmānyādhyāsaḥ prasiddha eva ॥
[grāhyoparaktā] yoginaḥ [prajñā svaṁ prajñārūpaṁ grahaṇātmakaṁ tyaktvā padārthamātrasvabhāvā grāhyasvarūpāpanneva bhavati ।] ivaśabdena grahaṇātmakatāṁ na jahātīti । na hi sphaṭika upādhyāśrayatāyāṁ svāṁ svaccharūpatāṁ hāsyati । kiñca-grahaṇavyatiriktaṁ ca grāhyaṁ vastvantaramastīti coktaṁ bhavati ॥
[sā nirvitarkā samāpatiḥ ।]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Now the <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (trans-deliberative attainment) is described. ["When the memory of verbal convention is purified."] Verbal convention (<s>śabdasaṅketa</s>) is the conventional understanding that 'this is the signifier of this, this is the signified of this.' The memory born from that is the memory of verbal convention. Its purification means its cessation due to its being erroneous. That [purification occurs] from the subordination of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>.
["<s>Śruta</s>-knowledge"] means knowledge from scripture (<s>āgama</s>); ["inferential knowledge"] means knowledge from logical marks (<s>liṅga</s>). Both inferential and scriptural knowledge have universals alone as their objects; their conceptual construction is the superimposition of particulars. When the <s>yogin</s>'s <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom is ["empty"] of the superimposition of inferential and conventional knowledge—that is, when the superimposition is removed—[shining] by its own nature alone, where the word 'alone' (<s>mātra</s>) means freed even from place, direction, time, power, and the like; being magnified by its own properties alone, [the wisdom] is ["delimited"] by the mere essential nature of that object alone—meaning it does not contemplate anything external to that object, such as place, time, and so forth.
Nor does that wisdom contemplate its own form as apprehension, because of its extreme purity. It is perceived as nothing but the apprehensible. ["That"] such ["is the <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>."]. '<s>Nirvitarka</s>' means 'from which deliberation has departed'—deliberation being superimposition. That does not exist in it.
["That"] is ["the supreme"]—that is, the most excellent—["direct perception."] The other, ordinary direct perception, common to all, was listed earlier among the [five] modifications. This belongs to the <s>yogin</s> alone. ["And that is the seed of scriptural and inferential [knowledge]."]. Although the previously mentioned [ordinary perception] is also indeed a seed of scriptural and inferential knowledge, nevertheless, whereas scriptural and inferential knowledge may deviate from that [ordinary perception's] effect, they do not deviate from [knowledge] born of the direct perception arising from <s>nirvitarka samādhi</s>. Therefore he says: ["From that, scriptural and inferential knowledge arise."]
["And that perception is not concomitant with scriptural and inferential knowledge"]—meaning its object is not the same as that of scriptural and inferential knowledge. For that perception has particulars as its object, whereas scriptural and inferential knowledge have universals as their objects. ["Therefore, the <s>yogin</s>'s perception born of <s>nirvitarka</s> is unmixed with any other means of knowledge."] ["Of that <s>nirvitarkā</s>] accordingly" ["the definition of this attainment is indicated by the <s>sūtra</s>: 'When memory is purified, as if empty of its own form, shining forth as the object alone—that is <s>nirvitarkā</s>.'"]
["Purified of the memory of conceptual constructions of verbal convention, received tradition, and inferential knowledge"]—the conceptual construction of verbal convention, the conceptual construction of received knowledge, and the conceptual construction of inferential knowledge—that itself is memory. For it is through recollection that one property of a thing is superimposed on another. For a thing cannot be superimposed on another thing by its own essential nature.
Objection: How is what is heard or inferred superimposed upon what is directly perceived? But surely superimposition is well known—thus one perceives: 'this was heard by me,' 'this was inferred by me,' 'this I see.'
Objection: What is seen is the very same thing that was inferred or heard—no, because of the distinction between universal and particular. The universal is what is heard and inferred; the particular is the object of direct perception. And the superimposition of the universal upon it [the particular] is indeed well known.
["The wisdom"] of the <s>yogin</s>, ["colored by the apprehensible, abandoning its own wisdom-nature whose essence is apprehension, becoming of the nature of the mere object, as if having assumed the very form of the apprehensible."] The word 'as if' (<s>iva</s>) indicates that it does not [actually] abandon its nature as apprehension. For a crystal, even when assuming the color of an adjacent object, does not abandon its own transparent nature. Moreover, it is thereby also stated that the apprehensible is a real thing distinct from apprehension.
["That is the <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>."]

body.text: tathā ca vyākhyātam – tasyā ekabuddhyupakramo hyarthātmā'ṇupracayaviśeṣātmā gavādirghaṭādirvā lokaḥ।
body.translated_text: And thus it has been explained: the object of that [attainment]—which is apprehended by a single cognition, whose nature is objective reality, whose nature is a specific configuration of atoms—is the world of cows and the like, or pots and the like.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[tathā ca vyākhyātam । tasyā hyekabuddhyupakramo'rthātmā ।] upakramyate ekayā buddhayā yaḥ sa ekabuddhyupakramaḥ ekabudviparicchedya iti । [arthātmā] bodhyātmetyetat ॥
gavādirghaṭādirvā viṣayaḥ na tu bodha eva gavādyākāro viṣayaḥ । [aṇupracayaviśeṣātmā] aṇūnāṁ tanmātrāvayavānāṁ pracayaviśeṣa ātmā yasya sa [gavādidhaṭādirvā] ālambanaṁ buddheḥ [sa ca] viṣayaḥ [saṁsthānaviśeṣaḥ] tathā saṁsthitāni hi tāni bhūtasūkṣmāṇi ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
["And thus it has been explained. Of that [attainment], the object is apprehended by a single cognition."]. That which is approached by a single cognition is 'apprehended by a single cognition' (<s>ekabuddhyupakrama</s>)—that is, delimited by a single cognition. ["Whose nature is objective reality (<s>arthātmā</s>)"]—meaning whose nature is to be known.
The object is a cow or a pot and the like—but it is not that the mere cow-shaped form of cognition is the object. ["Whose nature is a specific configuration of atoms"]—one whose essence is a specific accumulation of atoms, that is, of <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element) parts—that [is the cow or pot and the like,] the support of cognition. ["And that"] object ["is a specific configuration"]—for those subtle elements are so configured.

body.text: sa ca saṁsthānaviśeṣo bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṁ sādhāraṇo dharma ātmabhūtaḥ phalena vyaktenānumitaḥ svavyañjakāñjanaḥ prādarbhavati। dharmāntarasya kapālāderudaye ca tiro bhavati। sa eṣa dhairmo'vayavītyucyate। yo'sāvekaśca mahāṁścāṇīyāṁśca sparśavāṁśca kriyādharmakaścānityaśca tenāvayavinā vyavahārāḥ kriyante।
body.translated_text: And that specific configuration is a common property of the subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>), being their essential nature, inferred from its manifest effect, appearing through its own manifesting agent. And when another property, such as a potsherd, arises, it [the previous configuration] disappears. This property is called the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>). That which is one, large, minute, tangible, possessing the property of action, and impermanent—with that composite whole, [conventional] usages are carried out.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
etaduktaṁ bhavāti- [bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṁ sādhāraṇo dharma iti ātmabhūto] na vyatiriktaḥ । yathā sarpasya ābhogakuṇḍalanādi ॥
yeṣāṁ punaratyantavyatiriktamanyadeva kāraṇāt kāryaṁ, teṣāṁ kāraṇatantratvaṁ kāryasya na prāpnoti । aṁśutantro hi tantuḥ tantutantraśva paṭa: । na cātyantānyatve'nyatantratvaṁ dṛṣṭamanyasya । yathā mṛtpiṇḍatantratā na paṭasya, tantūnāṁ vā ॥
kiñca-tadvināśānuvināśitvaṁ ca na śakyaṁ, na hi kapālavināśamanuvinaśyati paṭa: ॥
athocyeta, sambandhaḥ kāraṇamiti । paṭasya hi tantavastantūnāñcāṁśava iti sambandhastatra hetuḥ kāraṇaṁ tattantratvatadanuvināśayoriti ॥
atrocyata-caitrakṣetrādisambandhe'pi prasaṅgaḥ syāt । caitrasyāpi kṣetrāditantratā tadanuvināśitvaṁ ca sambandhaviśeṣāt prasajyeta ॥
athāpi syāt-samavāyalakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ kāraṇamiti – na - tasyāpi saṁbandhatvāviśeṣādahetutvaṁ, yathānyasaṁbandhaḥ saṁbandhinoranyataratantratvādyahetuḥ evaṁ samavāyalakṣaṇasyāpi saṁbandhavādanyataratantravādāvahetutvam ॥
api ca-na dravyavyatirekeṇa karmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyāḥ santi । dravyatantratvādyupapattereva । tatrāpi sambandhasyāpyahetutvameva ॥
kiñcānyat-saṁbandhasya ca saṁbandhinorevānyataratantratvādihetutve samavāyasyāpi samavāyāntaraṁ tasyāpyanya ityanavasthā prasajyeta । yathā guṇādīnāṁ samavāyalakṣaṇāt saṁbandhāt dravyatantratvaṁ, tathā samavāyasyāpi dravyavyatiriktatve dravyatantratvārthaṁ samavāyāntaraṁ kalpyeta, tasyāpyanyattasyāpyanyadityanavasthā syāt ॥
prāgutpatterabhāvāt kāryasya kāraṇena saṁbandhānupapattiḥ, aviśiṣṭaṁ cāsatvaṁ śaśaviṣāṇasya ghaṭasya ca । tatra ghaṭenaiva kāraṇasya saṁbandho na śaśaviṣāṇmādibhiriti heturvaditavyaḥ ॥
prāk asannotpadyeta śaśaviṣāṇavat । yastu tantubhyo'nyaḥ sa tantubhyo notpadyate, tantubhyo'nyatvāt । yathā tantubhyo ghaṭaḥ ॥
itara āha-prāk sannapi notpadyeta, satvāt, vidyamānaghaṭavaditi । yo yasmādananyaḥ so'pi tasmānnotpadyate, vidyamānatvāt, svarūpavaditi ॥
apara āha-yadi sannotpadyata iti sata uttpatyabhāva ucyeta, siddhasādhyatā syāt । athābhivyaktyabhāvaḥ, tadā dṛṣṭāntābhāvaḥ ॥
yadapyucyate yo yasmādananya iti, tatrāpi siddhasādhyatā dṛṣṭāntābhāvaśca । svarūpādeva hyabhivyajyate, nāsatyabhivyaṅgyasvarūpe'bhivyaktirabhivyañjakasahasreṇāpi śakyate kartum ॥
kiñcānyat-sarvavyavahāralopaśca । kathaṁ ? yadā devadattasya gairaśvo vā prātarvidyamānakarṇalāṅgūla: punaraṭavīṁ gataḥ kenacillūnakarṇo lūnalāṅgūle vā syāt, tadā pūrvāvayavavibhāgādvinaṣṭaḥ, anyastu navaḥ pralūnakarṇalāṅgūlo'svāmikaḥ sañjāta iti yena kenacidupādīyeta, tathā cāvayavavibhāgaḥ sarvatra sambhavatīti svasvāmisambandhādiniyamābhāvādaśeṣavyavahāralopaḥ syāt ॥
atha brūyāt-pūrvopārjitāvayavairevāvayavī navaḥ pralūnakarṇalāṅgūla ārabdha iti-naivam-na hi mātāpitrādivyatirekeṇedānīntanalūnakarṇalāṅgūlāvayavyantarapratyārambhiṇo dṛśyante ॥
kiṁca-yasya ca kṣetre lūnakarṇalāṅglo jātastasyaivāsau syāt, na pūrvāvayavikasya, tatkṣetrajātatṛṇapalāśādivat ॥
yathā cānyakṣetragatāni bījāni salilaughenānyakṣetramupanītāni cetaktadbījaniṣpannasasyaṁ kṣetravāneva gṛhṇāti, na tu pūrvabījavān (taḥ) । na cāsyāsau pratibadhnāti vidvānapi madīyabījapariniṣpannaṁ sasyamahamupādīyeti ॥
tathā lūnakarṇalāṅgūlamapi kṣetravāneva gṛhṇīta । na tatra pratibandha(rūpa) nīyammadīyāvayavairārabdho'yamavayavīti ॥
yeṣāmapyekasmingṛhīte tasminnaśve lūnakarṇalāṅgūlake jāte svakṣetre ca dṛṣṭe sa evāśvadātā anyoyaṁ (vitisanyoyaṁ) mahattamādaśvānmayā datto mahattama iti hareta । haratāmiti cetsarvavyavahāralopaprasaṅgaḥ śāstrake.opaśca । tasmāda[nanyo']vayavebhyaḥ kāraṇebhya eko'vayavī kāryamiti siddham ॥
yadapyucyata-śabdapratyayadharmādibhedādanya iti, tadapyayuktam । dṛśyate hi śabdādibhede'pyananyatvam । yathā hastaḥ karaḥ pāṇiriti śabdabheda ekasya, pitṛtvaṁ putratvaṁ ca, pratyayabheda ekasyaiva baddhaḥ punarmuktaḥ sthito gataśceti kālabhedāt । dāhakatvaṁ pācakatvamityādayo dharmabhedā iti । digdeśādibhedāstvasiddhā eva । tasmādāha-ātmabhūtā iti ॥
sa ca [svaphalena vyaktenānumitaḥ । phalena] udakāharaṇadhāraṇasambhavanādinā । yasya hi phalaṁ kāryaṁ vyaktamupalabhyate so'stīti niścayaḥ । [anumita] iti vipratipannāpekṣayā, sādhāraṇaśabdena śaktirūpeṇa vocyate । sa tu pratyakṣa eva avyaktena daṇḍasūtrakulālādikārakavyāpārābhivyaktena [phalena] kāryeṇa ghaṭākhyena prāgapi mṛdādyavasthāyāmāstitvena anumitaḥ sa eva daṇḍādikārakaiḥ [svavyañjakairābhivyajyamānaḥ prādurbhavati dharmāntarodaye ca tirobhavati sa eṣa] bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṁ [dharmo'vayavītyucyate ॥]
etaduktaṁ bhavati--aṇūnāmapratyakṣatvānnāvirbhāvatirobhāvo yuktau । (tata) staśca to । tasmādya āvirbhavati, dharmāntarodaye virodhāttirobhavati ca, āvirbhave ca yo vyañjakādyapekṣate [so'vayavītyucyate ।] yaścaivaṁdharmaḥ so'ṇubhyo'nya iti ॥
kiñca-amī apyanye hetavo'vayavisadbhāve- [yo'sāvekaśca mahāṁ ścāṇīyāṁśca kriyādharmakaścānityaśca ।] pratyekamete hetavaḥ ॥
api ca-eko ghaṭa iti ghaṭaśabdavācyasyaikatvena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt । asti cedaṁ sāmānādhikaraṇyaṁ yo'sāveka iti । na hi bahūnāmaṇūnāmekatvena sāmānādhikaraṇyamupakalpate ॥
tathā mahatvena । na cāṇūnāṁ amahatāṁ mahatvena sāmānādhikaraṇyaṁ yujyate । tathā'ṇīyastvena । na hyaṇūnāmaṇvantarāpekṣayā aṇīyastvaṁ ghaṭate । sarva eva hi te'ṇīyāṁsaḥ । nāpi cāṇūnāmaṇutvaṁ gṛhyate'ṇubhyaḥ । aṇutve vastvantarasyāṇīyastvamupapatsyate ॥
kiñca-kriyādharmakaśca । kriyā dharmo yasya sa kriyādharmakaḥ । phalavadvayāpāranirvṛttikaratvadityuktaṁ bhavati । na hyaṇūnāṁ phalavadvyāpāranirmuktikaratvaṁ yuktam । aśakyaprayojyatvādasmadādibhiḥ । kiñca-anityatvāt । na hyaṇūnāmānityatvaṁ gṛhyate ॥
kiṁca-dṛśyatvāt । na hyaṇavo dṛśyante । tathā spṛśyatvācca hānāccopādānācca dhāraṇāccetyevamādayaḥ । [tenāvayavinā vyavahārāḥ kriyante nāṇubhiriti ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
This is what has been stated: ["A common property of the subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>)," meaning "being their essential nature"]—not distinct [from them]. Just as the coiling and spiral forms of a serpent [are not distinct from the serpent].
But for those who hold that the effect is something absolutely distinct from the cause, the dependence of the effect upon the cause cannot be established. For the thread depends on fibers, and the cloth depends on threads. But when there is absolute otherness, the dependence of one upon another is not observed—just as the cloth does not depend on a lump of clay, nor [do] threads.
Moreover, the destruction of one causing the destruction of the other would be impossible, for a cloth is not destroyed when a potsherd is destroyed.
If it be said that the relation is the cause—namely, threads belong to cloth and fibers belong to threads, and this relation is the cause of the dependence and co-destruction—
To this we reply: the same absurd consequence would follow in the case of the relation between <s>Caitra</s> and his field. For <s>Caitra</s> too would depend on his field and be destroyed along with it, because of a particular relation.
If one were to say that the relation characterized as inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) is the cause—no, because inherence too, being undifferentiated from other relations, would likewise not be a cause. Just as any other relation is not a cause of one relatum's dependence on the other, so too the relation characterized as inherence would not be such a cause.
Furthermore, apart from substance, action, universal, particular, and inherence do not exist independently—since the dependence [of these categories] on substance can itself be accounted for. And there too, the relation itself would not be a cause.
Moreover, if the relation were the cause of one relatum's dependence on the other, then inherence too would require another inherence, and that yet another—resulting in an infinite regress. Just as the dependence of qualities and the rest on substance is [said to be] due to the relation characterized as inherence, so too, if inherence itself were distinct from substance, another inherence would have to be postulated for it to depend on substance, and for that yet another—there would be an infinite regress.
Since the effect does not exist before its origination, the relation of the effect with the cause cannot be established. And the non-existence of a hare's horn and of a pot [before origination] would be indistinguishable. A reason must therefore be stated as to why the cause is related to the pot alone and not to hare's horns and the like.
[If the effect were] non-existent before, it could not originate, like a hare's horn. And that which is other than the threads could not originate from the threads, because of its being other than the threads—just as a pot [does not originate] from threads.
The other [school] says: even if existing [in the cause] before, it would not originate, because it [already] exists—like an already-existing pot. And that which is non-different from something also does not originate from it, because of [already] existing—like its own nature.
Another says: if it is said that what exists does not originate, and if this means the absence of origination [of an existent thing], then this would be proving what is already established. If it means the absence of manifestation, then there is no supporting example.
As for the statement 'that which is non-different [from something does not originate from it]'—there too, [one encounters] the fallacy of proving what is already established and the absence of a supporting example. For it is manifested from its own essential nature alone, and where the essential nature of the thing to be manifested does not exist, manifestation cannot be produced even by a thousand manifesting agents.
Furthermore, there would be the loss of all conventional usage. How? Suppose <s>Devadatta</s>'s horse, whose ears and tail were present in the morning, goes to the forest and someone cuts off its ears and tail. Then [according to you], [the original horse] has perished due to the dissolution of its former parts, and a new horse, shorn of ears and tail, ownerless, has come into being—and could be taken by anyone. And since the dissolution of parts occurs everywhere, there would be no fixed relation of ownership and the like, resulting in the loss of all conventional usage.
If one were to say that the new composite, shorn of ears and tail, is produced by the very same previously acquired parts—this is not so, for apart from parents and the like, no other factors producing a new earless-tailless composite are seen.
Moreover, the horse born earless and tailless in someone's field would belong to that field-owner, not to the owner of the original composite—like grass and leaves born in that field.
Just as seeds carried by a flood from one field to another [produce crops that belong to] the field-owner, not the original seed-owner—and even a wise man does not contest this, saying 'the crop was produced from my seeds, so I should take it'—
So too the earless-tailless [horse] would be claimed by the field-owner. No one would contest, saying 'this composite was produced from my parts.'
Even for those who hold that once [the horse] is taken, and when that earless-tailless horse is born in one's own field and is seen there—the very horse-giver could claim 'this is a different one from the great horse I gave'—if he takes it, then the absurd consequence of the loss of all conventional usage and the disruption of <s>śāstra</s> (authoritative texts) would follow. Therefore it is established that the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>), being non-different from the parts (causes), is one, and is the effect.
As for the statement that [the composite] is other [than its parts] because of the difference of word, cognition, properties, and so forth—this too is unjustified. For even when words and the like differ, non-difference is observed. For example: 'hand' (<s>hasta</s>), 'hand' (<s>kara</s>), 'hand' (<s>pāṇi</s>)—different words for one thing. Fatherhood and sonhood—different cognitions of one and the same person. 'Bound,' 'then freed,' 'standing,' 'gone'—[different states of the same thing] due to temporal difference. The properties of burning and cooking—different properties [of the same fire]. But differences of direction, place, and the like are unestablished. Therefore he says: 'being their essential nature.'
["And that"] composite ["is inferred from its manifest effect." "From the effect"]—such as the capacity for carrying water, holding, and so forth. For when a manifest effect or product is perceived, there is the certainty that [its cause] exists. ["Inferred"] is said with reference to those who are in doubt, or it may be expressed in the common term of 'capacity.' But it is in fact directly perceived. [The composite is] inferred by [its] unmanifest [state to be existing] even before, in the state of clay and so forth, [and then] by [its manifest] effect, namely the product called a pot, manifested by the activity of the agents—stick, string, potter, and the like—["appearing through its own manifesting agents, and disappearing when another property arises. This property of the subtle elements is called the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>)."]
This is what has been stated: Since atoms are imperceptible, their appearance and disappearance are not possible. Therefore, that which appears, which disappears through opposition when another property arises, and which depends on manifesting agents for its appearance—["that is called the composite whole."]. And that which has such properties is other than the atoms.
Moreover, these are additional reasons for the existence of the composite whole: ["That which is one, large, minute, possessing the property of action, and impermanent."] Each of these is a separate reason.
Furthermore, 'one pot'—because the word 'pot' is used in co-reference with 'one.' This co-reference exists: 'that which is one.' But co-reference with oneness cannot be applied to many atoms.
Likewise with largeness. Co-reference with largeness is not possible for atoms, which are not large. Likewise with minuteness. For the relative minuteness of atoms compared to other atoms is not possible—for they are all equally minute. Nor is the atomicity of atoms grasped [by perception] from [other] atoms. If [one thing has] atomicity, the relative minuteness of another thing would be established.
Moreover, [the composite] possesses the property of action. 'Possessing the property of action' means that which has action as its property—meaning it can accomplish productive, purposeful activity. For the capacity of atoms to accomplish productive, purposeful activity is not possible, since they cannot be employed by us and others. Moreover, because of impermanence—for the impermanence of atoms is not perceived.
Furthermore, because of being visible. For atoms are not visible. Likewise because of being tangible, because of being abandonable, takeable, holdable, and so forth. ["With that composite whole, conventional usages are carried out, not with atoms."]

body.text: yasya punaravastukaḥ sa pracayaviśeṣaḥ sūkṣmaṁ ca kāraṇamanupalabhyamavikalpasya tasyāvayavyabhāvādatadrūpapratiṣṭhaṁ mithyājñānamiti prāyeṇa sarvameva prāptaṁ mithyājñānamiti।
body.translated_text: But for one who holds that the specific configuration is unreal, and the subtle cause is imperceptible—since the composite whole does not exist for him, [all knowledge would be] false knowledge not established in the true form [of the object]. Thus, practically all [knowledge] would amount to false knowledge.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yasya punaḥ] itthaṁ pramāṇasuprasiddhasattāko'pi [avastu[kaḥ]] avayavī, [sa pracayaviśeṣaḥ sūkṣmaṁ ca kāraṇamanupalabhyaṁ] aṇvādi, [tasyāvayavyabhāvādatadrūpapratiṣṭhaṁ mithyājñānamiti prāyeṇa sarvameva] viṣayajñānaṁ [prāptaṁ mithyājñānam ॥]
tataḥ sarvameva jñānaṁ śabdādyākāreṇa sukhādyākāreṇa tadjñānākāreṇa copajāyate । śabdādayaśca jñānākārakarāvayavitvābhimatā nābhyupagamyanta । sukhādayo'pi viṣayatvādavayavipakṣā eva । tathā tajjñānameva jñānākārakaratvātsvarūpamapi mithyeti prāptaṁ sarvameva mithyājñānam ॥
tataśca pratyakṣānumānayorapyābhāsatvameva tenābhyupetaṁ tayorapi śabdādiviṣayatvāt ।
yadapi sarvajñajñānamanityaduḥkhaśūnyānātmakatvādiviṣayaṁ tasyāpi viṣayābhāvāttadapi mithyājñānaṁ prāptamiti, svatantrasya tīrthakarasya cāprāmāṇyaṁ, tatra tīrthakarasahadharmābhāvaścābhyupagato bhavati । śabdādivatpramāṇaviṣayatvāviśeṣāt ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
["But for one who"] thus [holds that] the composite whole, even though its existence is well-established through valid means of knowledge, ["is unreal"], ["that specific configuration and the subtle cause are imperceptible"]—namely atoms and the like—["since the composite whole does not exist for him, 'false knowledge not established in the true form' — practically all"] knowledge of objects ["would amount to false knowledge."]
Consequently, all knowledge arises in the form of words and the like, in the form of pleasure and the like, and in the form of the knowledge thereof. But words and the like, being accepted as composites that produce the cognitive form, are not [by him] acknowledged. Pleasures and the like, being objects, fall on the side of the composite [and would also be false]. And the knowledge of these, because it produces the cognitive form, would also be false even in its own nature—thus all knowledge would be false.
Consequently, even direct perception and inference would be mere appearances, since they too have words and the like as their objects.
Even the omniscient one's knowledge, having as its objects impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the like—because of the non-existence of those objects, that too would amount to false knowledge. And thus the unreliability of the independent founder (<s>tīrthakara</s>) would also follow, and the absence of properties common to the founder would also be entailed—because there is no distinction from the case of words and the like being objects of valid knowledge.

body.text: tadā ca samyagjñānamapi kiṁ syādviṣayābhāvāt। yadyadupalabhyate tattadavayavitvenā''mnātam। tasmādastyavayavī yo mahattvādivyavahārāpannaḥ samāpatternirvitarkāyā viṣayī bhavati ॥ 43 ॥
body.translated_text: And then, would there even be right knowledge, given the non-existence of [its] objects? For whatever is apprehended is acknowledged as a composite whole. Therefore, the composite whole exists—it is that which enters into conventional usage through [properties] such as largeness, and which becomes the object of <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s> (trans-deliberative attainment). // 43 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tadetatpratipādayati- [samyagjñānamapi kiṁ syādviṣayābhāvāt । yadyadupalabhyate tattadavayavitvenāghrātamiti,] jñānasya svākārasamarpakavāviśeṣāt । tacca svākārasamarpakaṁ kiñcana nābhyupeyata iti sarvasyātmīyasya jñānasya tena mithyātvamāpāditam ।
tathā ca samyagjñānamapi kiṁ syāt, yadapekṣayā mithyājñānamabhisandhīyate ॥
yadā cāvayavinaṁ sarvapramāṇasamyaksarvajñānasiddhamapahnute tadā na samyagjñānasya viṣayaḥ sampādayituṁ pāryate ॥
yadā ca na pārayati, tadā kathamabhisandadhīta sarvaṁ mithyeti । samyagjñānamapekṣya mithyājñānaṁ mithyābhāvamāsīdati āpekṣikatvātsamyaṅmithyājñānayoḥ ॥
yaścāpi manyate-nirviṣayaṁ jñānaṁ samyagiti, tasyāpi svarūpāgrahaṇāt tadastitvānupapattiḥ । gṛhyate cedviṣayatvādavayavimithyātvaṁ, tanmithyātvācca tajjñānamithyātvaṁ, tathā tajjñānamapīti sarvamithyātvamuktaṁ pūrvameva ॥
api ca-nirviṣayajñānasamyaktve sarvajñānasya viṣayānabhyupagamānnirviṣayatvamiti, samyaktvameva prāpnuyāt । tathāpi tu sarvajñānasamyaktvānmithyājñānaṁ kiṁsyāditi vaktavyam ॥
athāpi brūyāt-yatsaviṣayamivābhāti tanmithyājñānaṁ, yadatyantanirviṣayaṁ tatsamyagiti । tathā'pi tasyāstatve pramāṇābhāva ityukta eva doṣaḥ । tasmādavayavī samyagjñānasya viṣayo'vaśyābhyupagantavyaḥ ityāha- [tasmādastyavayavī yo mahatvādvyavahārāpannaḥ samāpaternirvitarkayā viṣayībhavatīti ॥ 43 ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
He demonstrates this very point: ["Would there even be right knowledge, given the non-existence of [its] objects? For whatever is apprehended is acknowledged as a composite whole"]—because knowledge does not differ in its capacity to convey its own form. And [the opponent] does not acknowledge anything that conveys its own form to knowledge, so the falsity of all his own knowledge has been brought about by him.
And thus, would there even be right knowledge—right knowledge with reference to which false knowledge is designated as false?
When [the opponent] denies the composite whole, which is well-established through all valid means of knowledge and through correct omniscient knowledge, then no object of right knowledge can be produced.
And when [the object] cannot be produced, how can he assert 'everything is false'? It is with reference to right knowledge that false knowledge is established as false—because the rightness and falsity of knowledge are relative.
And even one who thinks 'knowledge without an object is right'—for him too, since his own nature is not apprehended, the existence of that [knowledge] is impossible. If it is apprehended, then because it has an object, it would be false in the same way as composites; and from the falsity of that knowledge, the knowledge of it too would be false—and thus universal falsity follows, as already stated.
Moreover, if knowledge without an object were right, then since all knowledge [according to him] has no acknowledged objects, all knowledge would be objectless—and therefore right. But then, given the rightness of all knowledge, what would false knowledge be? This must be explained.
If one were to say: that which appears as if having an object is false knowledge, and that which is entirely without an object is right—even so, there is no valid means for establishing the existence of such [objectless right knowledge]. This is the very fault already stated. Therefore, the composite whole must necessarily be acknowledged as the object of right knowledge. Thus he says: ["Therefore, the composite whole exists, which enters into conventional usage through largeness and the like, and which becomes the object of <s>nirvitarkā samāpatti</s>." // 43 //]

body.text: etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā ॥ 44 ॥
body.translated_text: By this very [explanation], the <s>savicārā</s> (reflective) and <s>nirvicārā</s> (trans-reflective) [attainments], which have subtle objects, have [also] been explained. // 44 //

body.text: tatra bhūtasūkṣmakeṣvabhivyaktadharmakeṣu deśakālanimittānubhavāvacchinneṣu yā samāpattiḥ sā savicāretyucyate। tatrāpyekabuddhinirgrāhyamevoditadharmaviśiṣṭaṁ bhūtasūkṣmamālambanībhūtaṁ samādhiprajñāyāmupatiṣṭhate।
body.translated_text: Therein, the attainment that takes as its object the subtle elements (<s>bhūtasūkṣma</s>) with manifest properties, delimited by place, time, cause, and experience—that is called <s>savicārā</s> (reflective). And there too, the subtle element with its arisen properties, apprehensible by a single cognition, presents itself as the support of <s>samādhi</s> wisdom.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[etayaiva savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣmaviṣayā vyākhyātā । tatra bhūtasūkṣmeṣvabhivyaktadharmakeṣu] tanmātreṣveva [deśakālanimittānubhavāvacchinneṣu] deśāvacchinneṣu kālāvacchinneṣu nimittāvacchinneṣvanubhavāvacchinneṣviti pratyeyakamavacchinnaśabdaḥ । sarvaṁ hi vastu deśādibhiravacchidyamānaṁ viṣayiṇā jñātrā saṁbadhyamānaṁ vyavahārāya kalpate । teṣvevaṁbhūteṣvevaṁbhūtaiva deśādivikalpābhisaṁhitaiva [yā samāpattiḥ sā savicāretyucyate ।] tataśca savicārāyāḥ savitarkāviśeṣatvaṁ siddham ॥
katham ? ihāpyadhyāsaviśeṣāt । ayantu viśeṣaḥ śabdasaṅketārthajñānadeśādisarvādhyāsāḥ savitarkāyām ॥
iha punastanmātrasūkṣmadharmeṣu śabdasaṅketasyāprasiddhatvādviśiṣṭanāmasaṅketajñānānadhyāsaḥ deśādyadhyāsaśca sūkṣmaviṣayatvañceti savitarkāviśeṣatvasiddhiḥ ॥
[tatrāpyekabuddhinigrāhyamevoditadharmaviśiṣṭaṁ] uktadeśādidharmaviśiṣṭamudbhūtadharmaviśiṣṭaṁ vā [bhūtasūkṣmamālambanībhūtaṁ] na tu nirviṣayaṁ jñānameva [samādhiprajñāyāmupatiṣṭhate ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[By this very method, <s>savicārā</s> (reflective) and <s>nirvicārā</s> (non-reflective) <s>samāpatti</s> having subtle objects has been explained. There, among the subtle elements of the <s>bhūtas</s>,] the word 'delimited' applies separately to each — delimited by place, delimited by time, delimited by cause, and delimited by experience — with respect to the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) [whose properties are manifest, which are delimited by place, time, cause, and experience]. For every object, being delimited by place and so forth and being connected with a knowing subject, becomes fit for practical transaction. When the <s>tanmātras</s> are of this nature, [the <s>samāpatti</s> that is] precisely of this nature — accompanied by conceptual distinctions of place and so forth — [is called <s>savicārā</s>.] Thus the non-difference of <s>savicārā</s> from <s>savitarkā</s> is established.
How? Because here too there is a specific superimposition. But this is the distinction: in <s>savitarkā</s>, there are superimpositions of all kinds — word-convention, meaning-cognition, place, and so forth.
Here, however, since word-conventions are not well-established with respect to the subtle properties of the <s>tanmātras</s>, there is no superimposition of specific name-convention cognition, but there is superimposition of place and so forth, and the object is subtle — thus the establishment of non-difference from <s>savitarkā</s> is achieved.
[There too, what is grasped by a single cognition is the subtle element] qualified by the stated properties of place and so forth, or qualified by manifest properties, [which serves as the object-support] — but not cognition devoid of an object — [that presents itself to the cognitive insight of <s>samādhi</s>.]

body.text: yā punaḥ sarvathā sarvataḥ śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmānavacchinneṣu sarvadharmānupātiṣu sarvadharmātmakeṣu samāpattiḥ sā nirvicāretyucyate। evaṁ svarūpaṁ hi tadbhūtasūkṣmametenaiva svarūpeṇā''lambanībhūtameva samādhiprajñāsvarūpamuparañjayati।
body.translated_text: But the <s>samāpatti</s> that relates to [subtle elements] undelimited in every way and from every direction by properties that are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable — [subtle elements] that pervade all properties and whose nature encompasses all properties — that is called <s>nirvicārā</s>. For the subtle element, being of such a nature, serving as the object-support in precisely this form, colors the essential nature of the cognitive insight of <s>samādhi</s>.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yadā punaḥ sarvathā] sarvaprakāreṇa [sarvataḥ] sarvatra [śāntāścoditāścābyapadeśyāśca] ye [dharmā] ste [śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmāḥ] taiḥ [anavacchinneṣu ।] śānta iti yo vyāpāraṁ kṛtvoparato dharmaḥ । udita iti yo vyāpāramārūḍha़: । avyapadeśya iti na śānto nāpyuditaḥ nāpyudbhāvayaddṛśyamānanimittaḥ । tadyathā- suvarṇasyādṛṣṭānekāśrutākāropajanaśaktayastā avyapadeśyā dharmāḥ । [tairanavacchinneṣu] bhūtasūkṣmeṣu [sarvadharmānupātiṣu] sarvandharmānanupatanti tāni sūkṣmāṇi sarvaviśeṣārambhakatvāt । [sarvātmakeṣu] sarvebhyo viṣayebhyo'nanyatvāttanmātrāṇām । [tatra yā samāpattiḥ sā nirvicāre] ti । nirvitarkāyā yallakṣaṇaṁ tatsarvamiha nivicārāyāṁ draṣṭavyam ॥
taddarśayati-- [evaṁsvarūpaṁ hi tadbhūtasūkṣmamanenaiva svarūpeṇa] deśakālanimittānubhavādiviśeṣavirahitena sarvātmakena sarvadharmānupātinā [ālambanībhūtameva samādhiprajñāmuparañjayati ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[When, however, 'in every way'] — in every manner — ['from every direction'] — everywhere — [the properties that are quiescent, arisen, and indeterminable] — these are [the 'quiescent-arisen-indeterminable properties'] — by these [the subtle elements are] undelimited. 'Quiescent' means a property that has ceased after performing its function. 'Arisen' means one that has entered into activity. 'Indeterminable' means neither quiescent nor arisen, nor manifesting with a visible cause — for example, the powers of gold to produce unseen and unheard-of forms are indeterminable properties. [By these, the subtle elements are] undelimited, [pervading all properties] — all properties pervade those subtle elements, because they are the originators of all particulars. [Whose nature encompasses all] — because the <s>tanmātras</s> are non-different from all objects. [The <s>samāpatti</s> that occurs there is <s>nirvicārā</s>.] Whatever is the characteristic of <s>nirvitarkā</s>, all of that should be understood here with respect to <s>nirvicārā</s>.
He shows this — [The subtle element, being of such a nature, in precisely this form] — devoid of the particularities of place, time, cause, experience and so forth, encompassing all, pervading all properties — [serving as the object-support, colors the cognitive insight of <s>samādhi</s>.]

body.text: prajñā ca svarūpaśūnyevārthamātrā yadā bhavati tadā nirvicāretyucyate। tatra mahadvastuviṣayā savitarkā nirvitarkā ca, sūkṣmavastuviṣayā savicārā nirvicārā ca। evamubhayoretayaiva nirvitarkayā vikalpahānirvyākhyāteti ॥ 44 ॥
body.translated_text: And when the cognitive insight becomes as if empty of its own form, being nothing but the object alone, then it is called <s>nirvicārā</s>. In this regard, <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā</s> have gross objects, while <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> have subtle objects. Thus, by this very [explanation of] <s>nirvitarkā</s>, the abandonment of conceptual construction in both [pairs] has been explained. || 44 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[prajñā ca svarūpaśūnyevārthamātrā yadā bhavati tadā nirvicārā ।] tasmannirvitarkāviśeṣā nirvicārā । tatsvayameva darśayati- [mahadvastuviṣayā ।] mahataḥ vastu mahadvāstviti samāsaḥ rāhuśira iti yathā । tadviṣayo yasyāḥ sā [mahadvastuviṣayā savitarkā nirvitarkā ca sūkṣmavastuviṣayā savicārā nirvicārā] ceti ॥
etayaiva savitarkanirvitarkākhyayā dvayyā samāpatyā savicārā nirvicārā ca samāpattirdvayī vyākhyātā । [ubhayoriti] savitarkanirvitarkayormadhye [etayaiva nirvitarkayā vitarkahānirvyākhyātā] nirvicārā vyākhyāteti । savicārā cārthātsavitarkayā vyākhyātā lakṣaṇasyebhayatra samānatvāt ॥ uktaśca viśeṣaḥ ॥ 44 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[And when the cognitive insight becomes as if empty of its own form, being nothing but the object alone, then it is <s>nirvicārā</s>.] Therefore <s>nirvicārā</s> is non-different from <s>nirvitarkā</s>. He himself shows this — ['having gross objects.'] The compound 'gross object' (<s>mahad-vastu</s>) is formed like '<s>Rāhu</s>'s head' (<s>rāhu-śiras</s>). That whose object is this is [called] <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā</s> having gross objects, and <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> having subtle objects.
By this very pair of <s>samāpattis</s> called <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā</s>, the pair of <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> <s>samāpatti</s> has been explained. ['Of both'] means that among <s>savitarkā</s> and <s>nirvitarkā</s>, [by this very <s>nirvitarkā</s>, the abandonment of <s>vitarka</s> has been explained] — that is, <s>nirvicārā</s> has been explained. And <s>savicārā</s> is explained by implication through <s>savitarkā</s>, since the defining characteristics are the same in both. And the distinction has been stated. || 44 ||

body.text: sūkṣmaviṣayatvaṁ cāliṅgaparyavasānam ॥ 45 ॥
body.translated_text: And the range of subtle objects extends up to <s>aliṅga</s> (the unmanifest). || 45 ||

body.text: pārthivasyāṇorgandhatanmātraṁ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ। āpyasya rasatanmātram। taijasasya rūpatanmātram। vāyavīyasya sparśatanmātram। ākāśasya śabdatanmātramiti। teṣāmahaṁkāraḥ। asyāpi liṅgamātraṁ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ। liṅgamātrasyāpyaliṅgaṁ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ। na cāliṅgātparaṁ sūkṣmamasti। nanvasti puruṣaḥ sūkṣma iti। satyam। yathā liṅgātparamaliṅgasya saukṣmyaṁ na caivaṁ puruṣasya। kiṁtu, liṅgasyānvayikāraṇaṁ puruṣo na bhavati, hetustu bhavatīti। ataḥ pradhāne saukṣmyaṁ niratiśayaṁ vyākhyātam ॥ 45 ॥
body.translated_text: The subtle object of the earth-atom is the <s>gandha-tanmātra</s> (smell-potential). Of the water-atom, the <s>rasa-tanmātra</s> (taste-potential). Of the fire-atom, the <s>rūpa-tanmātra</s> (form-potential). Of the air-atom, the <s>sparśa-tanmātra</s> (touch-potential). Of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), the <s>śabda-tanmātra</s> (sound-potential). Of these [<s>tanmātras</s>], <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-principle) [is the subtle object]. And of that too, <s>liṅga-mātra</s> (the mere manifest, i.e., <s>mahat</s>) is the subtle object. And of <s>liṅga-mātra</s>, <s>aliṅga</s> (the unmanifest, i.e., <s>pradhāna</s>) is the subtle object. And there is nothing subtler than <s>aliṅga</s>. But is not <s>Puruṣa</s> subtle? True. Just as <s>aliṅga</s> is subtler than <s>liṅga</s>, the subtlety of <s>Puruṣa</s> is not of that kind. Rather, <s>Puruṣa</s> is not the material cause of <s>liṅga</s>, but is its efficient cause. Therefore the unsurpassed subtlety of <s>pradhāna</s> has been explained. || 45 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
savicārā nirvicārā ca samāpattiḥ sūkṣmaviṣayetyuktam । tatprasaṅgenedaṁ cintyate-ki(masamānaṁ)mavasānaṁ sūkṣmaviṣayatvamiti ॥ [sūkṣmaviṣayatvañcāliṅgaparyavasānam । pārthivasyāṇorgandha] mātrasvarūpamātrateti pṛthivīsamīkṣayā [sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ ॥]
gandhamātrasvarūpamātrasyāpi [liṅgamātraṁ] mahattatvaṁ [sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ ।] tato liṅgamātrānmahate nirvṛttāni sahāhaṅkāreṇa tanmātrāṇi layaṁ gacchantīti liṅgaṁ, layādvā pradhānālliṅgātpratyāgacchantīti liṅgaṁ, tadviparīta [maliṅgaṁ] pradhānaṁ na layaṁ gacchati, nāpyanyataḥ kutaścit layādāgacchati । [liṅgamātrasyāliṅgaṁ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ ॥]
[na cāliṅgātparaṁ sūkṣmamasti ।] sūkṣmaṁ nāma sthūlakāryāpekṣayā kāraṇaṁ, taccāliṅgāvasānam । [na cāliṅgāt] pradhānā(lliṅgā) [danyatsūkṣmaṁ kāraṇamasti ॥]
[nanu puruṣa iti ।] nanu tatra puruṣasyānāśaṅkaiva, kāryakāraṇasūkṣmatayā prakramāt-naiṣa doṣaḥ-puruṣasyāpi kaiścitkāraṇatvasyābhyupagamāt । tadāśaṅkayaiva hyetaducyate [nanu puruṣa iti ।] satyamaliṅgātmaka[tva]maliṅgasya saukṣmyam । kutaḥ? yataḥ kāraṇamaliṅgaṁ liṅgasya । yadyasyānvayikāraṇaṁ tattadapekṣayā sūkṣmamiti prakṛtam । nanu puruṣo'pyaliṅgātmaka eva । bāḍhaṁ, na tu liṅgāpekṣayā puruṣaḥ sūkṣmaḥ । kutaḥ ? yatastu liṅgasyānvayikāraṇaṁ puruṣo na bhavati satyapyaliṅgātmakatve । kāryasya caitanyenānanvitatvāt ॥
kiñca-puruṣasyāpi bhogyatvaprasaṅgaḥ । tathā ca pārārthyaṁ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakatvaṁ ca, nirhetukatvaṁ ca pradhānasya (puruṣasya) । tacca sarvapramāṇa(prāṇa) viprakupitamityata āha-- [hetustu bhavatīti ।] pradhānapravṛttau bhoktṛtvena nimittaṁ bhavatītyarthaḥ । [ataḥ pradhānasya saukṣmyaṁ niratiśayaṁ vyākhyātam ॥ 45 ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
It has been said that <s>savicārā</s> and <s>nirvicārā</s> <s>samāpatti</s> have subtle objects. In that connection, this is considered — what is the ultimate limit of subtle objecthood? [The range of subtle objects extends up to <s>aliṅga</s>. Of the earth-atom, the smell-]potential, having the essential nature of mere form — this is [the subtle object] from the standpoint of earth.
Of the smell-potential having the nature of mere form too, [<s>liṅga-mātra</s>,] the <s>mahat-tattva</s> (great principle), [is the subtle object.] From <s>liṅga-mātra</s>, i.e., <s>mahat</s>, the <s>tanmātras</s> together with <s>ahaṃkāra</s> undergo dissolution — hence it is called <s>liṅga</s> (the manifest); or because they return from dissolution in <s>pradhāna</s> — hence <s>liṅga</s>. The opposite of that is [<s>aliṅga</s>] — <s>pradhāna</s> does not undergo dissolution, nor does it come from dissolution in anything else. [Of <s>liṅga-mātra</s>, <s>aliṅga</s> is the subtle object.]
[And there is nothing subtler than <s>aliṅga</s>.] 'Subtle' means the cause relative to its gross effect, and that terminates in <s>aliṅga</s>. [There is no] cause subtler [than <s>aliṅga</s>,] i.e., than <s>pradhāna</s>.
[But <s>Puruṣa</s>!] — Now, there should be no such doubt regarding <s>Puruṣa</s>, given the context of subtlety as the cause-effect relation — [yet] this is not a fault, since some do accept <s>Puruṣa</s>'s causal status. It is precisely with this doubt in mind that it is said [But <s>Puruṣa</s>!]. True, <s>aliṅga</s> has the nature of the unmanifest, and that is the subtlety of <s>aliṅga</s>. Why? Because <s>aliṅga</s> is the cause of <s>liṅga</s>. Whatever is the material cause of something is subtle relative to it — this is what has been established. But is not <s>Puruṣa</s> too of the nature of the unmanifest? Indeed, but <s>Puruṣa</s> is not subtle relative to <s>liṅga</s>. Why? Because <s>Puruṣa</s> is not the material cause of <s>liṅga</s>, even though it shares the nature of the unmanifest — for effects are not pervaded by consciousness.
Moreover, there would be the unwanted consequence that <s>Puruṣa</s> too would be an object of experience. And then there would follow subservience [to another], the nature of pleasure-pain-delusion, and causelessness of <s>pradhāna</s> [would apply to <s>Puruṣa</s>]. And that would contradict all means of valid knowledge — therefore he says [but it is the efficient cause]. The meaning is that [<s>Puruṣa</s>] serves as the occasion, in the capacity of experiencer, for the activity of <s>pradhāna</s>. [Therefore the unsurpassed subtlety of <s>pradhāna</s> has been explained. || 45 ||]

body.text: tā eva sabījaḥ samādhiḥ ॥ 46 ॥
body.translated_text: These very [<s>samāpattis</s>] constitute <s>sabīja samādhi</s> (seeded meditation). || 46 ||

body.text: tāścatasraḥ samāpattayo bahirvastubījā iti samādhirapi sabījaḥ। tatra sthūle'rthe savitarko nirvitarkaḥ, sūkṣme'rthe savicāro nirvicāra iti caturdhopasaṁkhyātaḥ samādhiriti ॥ 46 ॥
body.translated_text: These four <s>samāpattis</s>, having external objects as their seeds, make the <s>samādhi</s> too <s>sabīja</s> (seeded). In this regard, with respect to a gross object there is <s>savitarka</s> and <s>nirvitarka</s>; with respect to a subtle object there is <s>savicāra</s> and <s>nirvicāra</s> — thus <s>samādhi</s> is reckoned as fourfold. || 46 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[tā eva sabījaḥ samādhiḥ । catasraḥ samāpattayo bahirvastuviṣayā iti] bahirvastuviṣayatvaṁ hetuḥ sabījatve । [samādhirapi sabījaḥ] samprajñāto [‘vitarkavicārānandāsmitārūpānugamātsamprajñātaḥ'] ityupavyākhyātaḥ । [sthūle'rthe savitarko nirvitarkaḥ, sūkṣme'rthe savicāro nirvicāra iti copavyākhyātaḥ] vitarkādilakṣaṇasūtreṇa ॥ 46 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[These very constitute <s>sabīja samādhi</s>. The four <s>samāpattis</s>, having external objects as their domain] — having external objects as their domain is the reason for being <s>sabīja</s> (seeded). [The <s>samādhi</s> too is <s>sabīja</s>] — the <s>samprajñāta</s> (cognitive) [<s>samādhi</s>] has been explained [in the sūtra] '<s>samprajñāta</s> is that which is accompanied by <s>vitarka</s>, <s>vicāra</s>, <s>ānanda</s>, and <s>asmitā</s>.' [With respect to a gross object there is <s>savitarka</s> and <s>nirvitarka</s>, with respect to a subtle object there is <s>savicāra</s> and <s>nirvicāra</s> — and this has been explained] by the sūtra defining the characteristics of <s>vitarka</s> and the rest. || 46 ||

body.text: nirvicāravaiśāradye'dhyātmaprasādaḥ ॥ 47 ॥
body.translated_text: Upon the clarity of <s>nirvicāra</s> [<s>samādhi</s>], there is <s>adhyātma-prasāda</s> (inner luminosity). || 47 ||

body.text: aśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpetasya prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya rajastamobhyāmanabhibhūtaḥ svacchaḥ sthitipravāho vaiśāradyam। yadā nirvicārasya samādhervaiśāradyamidaṁ jāyate tadā yogino bhavatyadhyātmaprasādo bhūtārthaviṣayaḥ kramānanurodhī sphuṭaḥ prajñālokaḥ। tathā coktam –
body.translated_text: When the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), whose nature is luminosity, is freed from the impurity that is its covering and defilement, and is not overpowered by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> — the limpid, steady flow [of cognition] is <s>vaiśāradya</s> (clarity). When this clarity of <s>nirvicāra samādhi</s> arises, then there comes to the <s>yogin</s> <s>adhyātma-prasāda</s> (inner luminosity) — a light of wisdom that has real entities as its objects, that follows a sequential order, and that is vivid. As it has been said —

body.text: prajñāprasādamāruhya aśocyaḥ śocato janān।
body.translated_text: Having ascended the terrace of wisdom, free from sorrow, [the wise one looks upon] sorrowing people;

body.text: bhūmiṣṭhāniva śailasthaḥ sarvānprājño'nupaśyati ॥ 47 ॥
body.translated_text: Like one standing on a mountain [looking upon] those on the ground, the wise one sees all. || 47 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[nirvicāravaiśāradye'dhyātmaprasādaḥ । aśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpetasya] aśuddhirevāvaraṇaṁ tadeva malaṁ kleśādikaṁ tasmādapetasya [prakāśātmano buddhisatvasya rajastamobhyāmanabhibhūtaḥ svacchaḥ sthitipravāho vaiśāradyam । yadā nirvicārasya samādhervaiśāradyamidaṁ jāyate, tadā yogino bhavatyadhyātmaprasādaḥ] ātmādijñānavivekaḥ । asyaiva vyākhyānaṁ [bhūtārthaviṣayaḥ kramānurodhī] paripāṭikayā yāvatkleśakṣayamanuruddhayata iti kramānurodhī [sphuṭaṁ] viviktataraṁ śuddhatarātmaka: [prajñālokaḥ] prajñaivālokaḥ tayā hi yathāvastu jānāti ॥
[tathā coktam “prajñāprāsādamāruhya aśocyaḥ śocato janān । bhūmiṣṭhāniva śailasthaḥ sarvānprājño'nupaśyati ॥ ” iti ॥ 47 ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[Upon the clarity of <s>nirvicāra</s>, there is <s>adhyātma-prasāda</s>. 'Freed from the impurity that is the covering and defilement'] — impurity itself is the covering, that itself is the defilement, namely the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) and so forth; freed from that. [The <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>, whose nature is luminosity, not overpowered by <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, the limpid, steady flow is <s>vaiśāradya</s>. When this clarity of <s>nirvicāra samādhi</s> arises, then there comes to the <s>yogin</s> <s>adhyātma-prasāda</s>] — the discriminative knowledge of the self and so forth. The explanation of this is: ['having real entities as its objects, following a sequential order'] — following in due succession until the destruction of the <s>kleśas</s>, thus 'following a sequential order'; ['vivid'] means increasingly distinct, of an increasingly pure nature; ['the light of wisdom'] — wisdom itself is the light, for by it one knows things as they truly are.
[As it has been said: 'Having ascended the terrace of wisdom, free from sorrow, [looking upon] sorrowing people; like one standing on a mountain, the wise one sees all.' || 47 ||]

body.text: ṛtaṁbharā tatra prajñā ॥ 48 ॥
body.translated_text: There, the wisdom is <s>ṛtambharā</s> (truth-bearing). || 48 ||

body.text: tasminsamāhitacittasya yā prajñā jāyate tasyā ṛtaṁbhareti saṁjñā bhavati। anvarthā ca sā, satyameva bibharti na ca tatra viparyāsajñānagandho'pyastīti। tathā coktam –
body.translated_text: The wisdom that arises in one whose mind is thus composed receives the designation <s>ṛtambharā</s>. And it is apt in meaning, for it bears only truth, and there is not even a trace of erroneous knowledge in it. As it has been said —

body.text: āgamenānumānena dhyānābhyāsarasena ca।
body.translated_text: Through scripture, through inference, and through the savor of meditative practice,

body.text: tridhā prakalpayanprajñā labhata yogamuttamam ॥ iti ॥ 48 ॥
body.translated_text: cultivating wisdom in these three ways, one attains the highest <s>Yoga</s>. || 48 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[ṛtaṁbharā] tatra [prajñā । tasmin] prajñāloke'dhyātmaprasāde [samāhitasya yā prajñā jāyate] vivekajanmā, [tasyā] vivekajanmanaḥ [ṛtambhareti saṁjñā bhavati । anvarthaiva sā satyameva bibharti na tatra viparyāsajñānagandho'pyasti ।] prakṣīṇasakalaviparyāsakalmaṣasya hi jāyate । jāyamānā ca viṣayakaळṅgamapanudati ॥
[tathā coktam -]
[‘āgamenānumānena dhyānābhyāsarasena ca । tridhā prakalpayanprajñāṁ labhate yogamuttamam ॥ ' iti ।]
yogāṅgaprajñāṁ tridhā vibhajate । tatraiko bhāgaḥ śāsrācāryopadiṣṭārthānusārī । dvitīyastasyaiva yuktyā'numānena vicāryāgamārthavirodhinirākaraṇapūrvakaṁ tatsamyagupapādanaparaḥ । tṛtīyastu sadāgamānumānasamyagupapakṣārthīlambanasya pratyayasyānuśīlanaṁ rasopayegī । taditthaṁ tridhā prakalpayanyogī yogaṁ labhate ॥ 48 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[<s>Ṛtambharā</s>] — there — [wisdom. In that] light of wisdom, that <s>adhyātma-prasāda</s>, [the wisdom that arises in one whose mind is composed] — born of discrimination — [receives the designation <s>ṛtambharā</s>. It is apt in meaning; it bears only truth; there is not even a trace of erroneous knowledge in it.] For it arises in one whose entire defilement of error has been extinguished. And as it arises, it dispels the taint [clinging to] its object.
[As it has been said —]
['Through scripture, through inference, and through the savor of meditative practice, cultivating wisdom in these three ways, one attains the highest <s>Yoga</s>.']
He divides the wisdom pertaining to the limbs of <s>Yoga</s> into three parts. The first part follows the meaning taught by scripture and the teacher. The second is devoted to properly establishing that same [meaning] through reasoning and inference, preceded by the refutation of what contradicts the meaning of scripture. The third is the cultivation of the mental state whose object-support is the meaning well-established by valid scripture and inference — this is conducive to [direct] experience. Thus, cultivating [wisdom] in these three ways, the <s>yogin</s> attains <s>Yoga</s>. || 48 ||

body.text: sā punaḥ –
body.translated_text: That [wisdom], moreover —

body.text: śrutānumānaprajñābhyāmanyaviṣayā viśeṣārthatvāt ॥ 49 ॥
body.translated_text: has a different domain from the wisdom born of scripture and inference, because its object is the particular. || 49 ||

body.text: śrutamāgamavijñānaṁ tatsāmānyaviṣayam। na hyāgamena śakyo viśeṣo'bhidhātuṁ, kasmāt, na hi viśeṣeṇa kṛtasaṁketaḥ śabda iti। tathā'numānaṁ sāmānyaviṣayameva। yatra prāptistatra gatiryatrāprāptistatra na bhavati gatirityuktam। anumānena ca sāmānyenopasaṁhāraḥ। tasmācchrutānumānaviṣayo na viśeṣaḥ kaścidastīti।
body.translated_text: Scriptural knowledge is <s>āgama</s>-knowledge (knowledge from tradition); its domain is the general. For a particular cannot be conveyed by scripture. Why? Because words are conventionally linked only with universals. Likewise, inference has only the general as its domain. It has been said: 'Where there is reach, there is movement; where there is no reach, there is no movement.' And through inference, one subsumes only under the general. Therefore, there is no particular that is the domain of scriptural and inferential knowledge.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[sā punaḥ] ṛtambharā prajñā sāmānyapuruṣapratyayaviṣayādanyaviṣayetyāha-- [śrutānumānaprajñābhyāmanyaviṣayā । viśeṣaḥ] viśeṣāṇāmānanyānna saṅketayitu śakyate । sāmānyena hi kṛtasaṅketaḥ śabdaḥ । tataścāgṛhītaviśeṣasaṅketo na viśeṣamabhidhātuṁ jñāpayituṁ vā śanketi ॥
[tathānumānaṁ sāmānyaviṣayameva ।] tadapyuktameva ['sāmānyāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ'] iti । tathe.odāharaṇena ca pratipāditam * [yatra prāptistatra gatiḥ । yatrāprāptistatra na bhavati gatiḥ' iti । anumānena sāmānyopasaṁhāraḥ ।] sā mānyamātramanumānenopasaṁhriyate । [tasmācchutānumānavijñānaviṣayo na viśeṣaḥ kaścidasti] ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Commentary):
[That, moreover,] the <s>ṛtambharā</s> wisdom has a domain different from that of ordinary cognitive states — he says: [its domain is different from the wisdom born of scripture and inference.] [A particular,] owing to the inexhaustibility of particulars, cannot be conventionally designated. For words are conventionally linked with universals. Therefore, one whose grasp of particular-conventions is unacquired cannot express or make known a particular.
[Likewise, inference has only the general as its domain.] This too has already been stated — ['the mental operation is principally the ascertainment of universals.'] And this has been demonstrated with an example: ['Where there is reach, there is movement; where there is no reach, there is no movement.' Through inference, there is subsumption under the general.] Only the mere universal is subsumed through inference. [Therefore, there is no particular that is the domain of scriptural and inferential knowledge.]

body.text: na cāsya sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭasya vastuno lokapratyakṣeṇa grahaṇamasti। na cāsya viśeṣasyāpramāṇakasyābhāvo'stīti samādhiprajñānirgrāhya eva sa viśeṣo bhavati bhūtasṛ'kṣmagato vā puruṣagato vā। tasmācchratānumānaprajñābhyāmanyaviṣayā sā prajñā viśeṣārthatvāditi ॥ 49 ॥
body.translated_text: Nor can this object — subtle, concealed, or remote — be grasped by ordinary perception. Nor is this particular nonexistent merely because it lacks a [conventional] means of knowledge — rather, it is grasped only by the cognitive insight of <s>samādhi</s>, whether it pertains to the subtle elements or to <s>Puruṣa</s>. Therefore, that wisdom has a different domain from the wisdom born of scripture and inference, because its object is the particular. || 49 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yadyevaṁ na lokapratyakṣeṇāpareṇa bhūtasūkṣmagataḥ puruṣagato vā viśeṣa: prajñāyeta । nānyacca pramāṇatrayavyatiriktaṁ pramāṇamasti, yena tadviśeṣaṁ sañjānīmahe iti cedāi-- [na cāsya sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭasya vastuno lokapratyakṣeṇa grahaṇam । na cāsya viśeṣasyāpramāṇikasyābhāvo'stīti ।] pramāṇāvagamyamānarūpo hi bhāvo'sti rājavīthīmadhirohati । tasmāt [samādhiprajñānigrahma eva viśeṣo bhavati bhūtasūkṣmagataḥ puruṣagato vā ॥]
nanu ca te sūkṣmagatā viśeṣāḥ pratyakṣeṇāvagamyante iti kimīśvarājñāpitam ? vastutvādavagamyanta iti cet---āgamānumānābhyāṁ santītyavagamyanta eva । na ca niyāmaka kiṁcidasti pratyakṣeṇaiva nirgrahyā iti । na hi viśeṣā hastatalagatā api sarve gṛhyante-na-anyavastugataviśeṣāṇāṁ pratyakṣagrāhyatvasyānumeyatvāt ॥
katham ? evaṁ manyate-bhūtasūkṣmādigatā viśeṣāḥ pratyakṣagrāhyāḥ kasya cit, kāryavastuviśeṣatvāt, gṛhyamāṇasvapāṇigatāviśeṣavaditi । [tasmācchrutānumānaprajñābhyāmanyaviṣayā sā prajñā, viśeṣārthatvāditi ।] viśeṣārthā hi sā ॥ 49 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
If this is so, then the particular distinction residing in the subtle elements or in <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self) cannot be known by ordinary perception. And there is no means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) other than the three [perception, inference, scripture] by which we could know that distinction—if one were to say this: [Nor can this object—subtle, obscured, or remote—be grasped by ordinary perception. Nor is this distinction non-existent merely because it is not reached by [ordinary] means of knowledge.] For a reality whose nature is ascertained by [valid] means of knowledge exists and is as evident as the royal highway. Therefore, [the distinction, whether residing in the subtle elements or in <s>Puruṣa</s>, is grasped only by the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>.]
But that those subtle distinctions are known by perception—is this proclaimed by <s>Īśvara</s>'s command? If one says 'they are known because they are real'—their existence is indeed known through scripture (<s>āgama</s>) and inference. And there is no determining factor that they must be grasped by perception alone. For not all distinctions, even those in one's own palm, are grasped—no, because the perceptibility of distinctions in other objects is itself to be inferred.
How? The reasoning is thus: the distinctions residing in subtle elements etc. are perceptible to someone, because they are particular real effects, like the distinctions in one's own hand that are being grasped. [Therefore, that wisdom has a different object than the wisdom born of scripture and inference, because it has the particular distinctions as its object.] For it has the particular distinctions as its object.

body.text: samādhiprajñāpratilambhe yoginaḥ prajñākṛtaḥ saṁskāro navo navo jāyate –
body.translated_text: Upon the attainment of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) produced by the <s>yogin</s>'s wisdom arises ever anew—

body.text: tajjaḥ saṁskāro'nyasaṁskārapratibandhī ॥ 50 ॥
body.translated_text: <s>tajjaḥ saṃskāro 'nyasaṃskārapratibandhī</s> — The impression born of that [wisdom] obstructs other impressions. (Sūtra 50)

body.text: samādhiprajñāprabhavaḥ saṁskāro vyutthānasaṁskārāśayaṁ bādhate। vyutthānasaṁskārābhibhavāttatprabhavāḥ pratyayā na bhavanti। pratyayanirodhe samādhirupatiṣṭhate। tataḥ samādhijā prajñā, tataḥ prajñākṛtāḥ saṁskārā iti navo navaḥ saṁskārāśayo jāyate। tataśca prajñā, tataśca saṁskārā iti। kathamasau saṁskārātiśayaścittaṁ sādhikāraṁ na kariṣyatīti। na te prajñākṛtāḥ saṁskārāḥ kleśakṣayahetutvāccittamadhikāraviśiṣṭaṁ kurvanti। cittaṁ hi te svakāryādavasādayanti। khyātiparyavasānaṁ hi cittaceṣṭitamiti ॥ 50 ॥
body.translated_text: The impression born of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> suppresses the repository of impressions of distraction (<s>vyutthāna</s>). Due to the suppression of the impressions of distraction, the cognitions born from them do not arise. When cognitions are suppressed, <s>samādhi</s> becomes established. From that arises the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, from that arise impressions produced by wisdom—thus an ever-new repository of impressions is born. From that again, wisdom; from that again, impressions. 'How will this excess of impressions not render the mind capable of further activity?' Those impressions produced by wisdom do not render the mind disposed to further activity, because they are the cause of the destruction of the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions). Rather, they bring the mind to rest from its own function. For the activity of the mind culminates in discriminative knowledge (<s>khyāti</s>).

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[samādhiprajñāpratilambhe yoginaḥ prajñākṛtaḥ saṁskāro navo jāyate ।] prajñā hi saṁskārārāmbhaṇīti siddham । prajñābhinavatvāttatsaṁskāraḥ pratyagrataro jāyate iti viśeṣaḥ । prajñānavatvaṁ tu tasyā (sāmānya) anyaviṣayatvāt । tajja [ssaṁskāro'nyasaṁskārapratibandhī] ṛtambhara [prajñāprabhavasaṁskāro vyutthānasaṁskārāśayaṁ anyaṁ bādhate] viśiṣṭayathārthaviṣayaprabhavatvātpratibadhnāti । āmokṣāccheta iti [saṁskārāśayaḥ ॥]
[vyutthānasaṁskārābhibhavāt] vyutthānasaṁskārāśayasya samādhiprajñāsaṁskāreṇābhibhavāt [tatprabhavāḥ] vyutthānasaṁskāraprabhavāḥ [pratyayā na bhavanti । pratyayanirodhe] vyutthānapratyayanirodhe [samādhiḥ] samprajñāta iva [upatiṣṭhate । tataḥ samadhijā prajñā, tataḥ prajñākṛtāḥ saṁskārā iti,] evaṁ [navaḥ saṁskārāśayo] vardhate । [tataśca prajñā tataśca saṁskārā] iti ॥
atrāha-samādhiprajñābhavaḥ saṁskārāśayaścittasyādhikārapravṛttihetuḥ, pratyayaprabhavatvāt, vyutthānaprabhavasaṁskārāśayavaditi, tathā cittasaṁskāratvācceti । tadetaddarśayati- [kathamasau saṁskārāśayaḥ cittaṁ sādhikāraṁ] saṁskāropetaṁ na kariṣyatīti ? ॥
naiṣa doṣaḥ-tadvirodhitvāt । kathaṁ ? [te saṁskārāḥ kleśakṣayahetutvāccittamadhikāraviśiṣṭaṁ na kurvanti ।] vyutthānapratyayaprabhavānāṁ hi saṁskārāṇāmavidyādikleśahetutvacittasaṁskārābhimukhabhāvakāraṇatā । tadvirodhipratyayaprabhavatvāttu na samādhijapratyayajanmanāṁ saṁskārāṇāmadhikārābhimukhyanimittatā ॥
kiñca- [cittañca te svakāryāt] saṁskārābhimukhavṛttibhye' [vasādayanti] viramayanti । [khyātipayarvasānaṁ hi cittaviceṣṭitam ।] puruṣakhyātiśca jātā saṁskāraśva bhavatīti viruddham ॥
yo hi vigatatṛṣṇāsamudāyo, nāsau pānīyaṁ pipāsati । etāvadeva cittena puruṣasya karaṇīyam । na hi kaśvit kṛtaṁ karaṇīyaṁ cikīrṣati ॥ 50 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
[Upon the attainment of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s>, the impression produced by the <s>yogin</s>'s wisdom arises anew.] For it is established that wisdom initiates impressions. The distinction is that, due to the freshness of the wisdom, its impression arises ever more recent. But the 'newness' of that [impression] is due to its different object. [The impression born of that obstructs other impressions.] The impression born of <s>ṛtambharā prajñā</s> (truth-bearing wisdom) [suppresses the repository of other impressions of distraction]—because it is born of a [cognition] whose object is the correct reality of a distinguished [truth], it obstructs [the others]. Until liberation it cuts off—thus [it is called] the 'repository of impressions.'
[Due to the suppression of the impressions of distraction]—by the impression of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> suppressing the repository of distraction-impressions, [the cognitions born of those]—born of distraction-impressions—[do not arise. When cognitions cease]—when distraction-cognitions cease—[<s>samādhi</s>] like <s>saṃprajñāta</s> [becomes established. From that, the wisdom born of <s>samādhi</s>; from that, impressions produced by wisdom]—thus [the new repository of impressions] grows. [From that, wisdom; from that, impressions.]
Here an objection is raised: the repository of impressions born of the wisdom of <s>samādhi</s> should be a cause of the mind's continued activity, because it is born of a cognition, like the repository of impressions born of distraction; and also because it is an impression of the mind. This he shows: [How will this repository of impressions not render the mind disposed to further activity?]
This is not a defect—because it is opposed to that. How? [Those impressions, being the cause of the destruction of the <s>kleśas</s>, do not render the mind disposed to further activity.] For the impressions born of distraction-cognitions have the nature of being causes of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and other <s>kleśas</s>, and thus cause the mind to face toward [further] impressions. But because the impressions born of <s>samādhi</s>-cognitions are born of cognitions that oppose those, they are not causes directing [the mind] toward further activity.
Moreover, [they bring the mind to rest from its own function]—they cause it to cease from the modifications directed toward impressions. [For the activity of the mind culminates in discriminative knowledge.] And when the knowledge of <s>Puruṣa</s> has arisen and its impression exists—that is contradictory [to further activity].
For one in whom the assemblage of craving has ceased does not thirst for water. This alone is all that the mind needs to accomplish for <s>Puruṣa</s>. For no one desires to do what has already been done.

body.text: kiṁ cāsya bhavati –
body.translated_text: What further happens to it—

body.text: tasyāpi nirodhe sarvanirodhānnirbījaḥ samādhiḥ ॥ 51 ॥
