body.text: yā bhogeṣvindriyāṇāṁ tṛpterupaśāntistatsukham। yā laulyādanupaśāntistadduḥkham। na cendriyāṇāṁ bhogābhyāsena vaitṛṣṇyaṁ kartuṁ śakyam। kasmāt, yato bhogābhyāsamanu vivardhante rāgāḥ kauśalāni cendriyāṇāmiti। tasmādanupāyaḥ sukhasya bhogābhyāsa iti। sa khalvayaṁ vṛścikaviṣabhīta ivā''śīviṣeṇa daṣṭo yaḥ sukhārthī viṣayānuvāsito mahati duḥkhapaṅke nimagna iti। eṣā pariṇāmaduḥkhatā nāma pratikūlā sukhāvasthāyāmapi yoginameva kliśnāti।
body.translated_text: The happiness that arises from the quiescence of the senses' craving in enjoyments — that is pleasure. The restlessness that arises from their greed and lack of quiescence — that is pain. And it is not possible to produce dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) in the senses through repeated enjoyment. Why? Because following repeated enjoyment, the attachments of the senses increase, as do their skills. Therefore, repeated enjoyment is not the means to happiness; rather, cessation from repeated enjoyment is happiness. Indeed, one who, seeking happiness, has attached himself to sense objects is like a person who, afraid of a scorpion, is bitten by a cobra — he is plunged into a great swamp of suffering. This is what is called transformation-suffering (<s>pariṇāma-duḥkhatā</s>), which is adverse [to well-being] and afflicts the <s>yogin</s> even during the state of pleasure.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
viṣayasukhaṁ cāvidyetyasyaivārthasya prakāśanārtha tantrasiddhamudāharaṇaṁ darśayati-- [yā bhogoṣvindriyāṇāṁ] bhujyanta iti bhogāḥ śabdādayaḥ teṣu nimitteṣu yā tṛptiḥ tata indriyāṇām [upaśāntiḥ] upaśamaḥ kimanarthāyāsahetukayā vṛttyeti nirākulatayāvasthānaṁ tat [sukham ॥]
yā tu lailyādīpsayā tṛṇāta: sakāśaldanupaśāntaḥ anuparatiḥ tadduḥkham । taduktam -
[“nāsti tṛṣṇāsamaṁ duḥkhaṁ nāstyatṛṣṇāsamaṁ sukham” iti ॥]
nanu copabhogenaiva vaitṛṣṇye bhavati upabhogānte । upabhogaśva sukheṁ bhaviṣyati । tata āha-- [na cendriyāṇāṁ bhogābhyāsena śakyaṁ vaitṛṣṇyaṁ kartum । kasmāt ?] ata āha-- [yato bhogābhyāsamanu vivardhante indriyāṇāṁ rāgāḥ ।] tathā cetam –
[“ na jātu kāmaḥ kāmānāmupabhogena śāmyati ।]
[haviṣā kṛṣṇavartmeva bhūya evābhivardhate ॥ '] iti ॥
[kauśalāni] naipuṇāni ca bhogābhyāseṣvandriyāṇāmanu vivardhante । yadyapi mana:kauśalapūrvakamindriyāṇāṁ kauśalaṁ, tathā'pi dṛśyata eva bhikṣā[kṣvā]dīnāmindriyasyāpi kauśalam । [tasmādanupāyaḥ sukhasya bhogābhyāsa iti] bhogābhyāsānnivṛttireva sukham ॥
[sa khalvayaṁ vṛścikabhīta ivāśīviṣeṇa daṣṭo yaḥ sukhārthī viṣayānanvavasitaḥ] anvavabaddhaḥ anupravṛtto'nuvyavasito vā, yathā mandaviṣādvṛścikādupajātabhīti: paṭutareṇāśīviṣeṇa prasto mahattaraṁ du:khamabhiprapadyate,
tathā'yamapraduḥkhābhāsāyāḥ pariṇāmamahāsukhāyā nivṛtto duḥkhabuddhyā bhītaḥ sannapāre [mahati duḥkhapaṅke magna iyeṣā pariṇāmadu:khatā] sukhasya [pratikūlā sukhāvasthāyāmapi yoginaḥ ।] sa he yogī pravṛttavepathunaiva hṛdayena pratiniyatavedanīyasya kurmaṇo balīyasvādanubhuṅkte sukham । tasmāt sarvaṁ duḥkhaṁ vivekinaḥ ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
To illuminate the very meaning of 'sensory pleasure is <s>avidyā</s>,' he presents an illustration established in the tradition — ['That which, among enjoyments,'] — things enjoyed are <s>bhogas</s>, i.e., sound and so forth; among those serving as causes, ['the quiescence'] — the calming — of the senses, that is, their abiding in a state free from purposeless agitation through activity — that is ['pleasure.']
But the restlessness arising from craving (<s>laulya</s>), the non-cessation [of desire arising] from <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (thirst) — that is suffering. Thus it has been said:
['There is no suffering equal to craving, and no happiness equal to freedom from craving.']
Now, if one objects that dispassion arises through enjoyment itself, at the end of enjoyment, and that enjoyment will be pleasurable — to this he says: ['It is not possible to produce dispassion in the senses through repeated enjoyment. Why?'] To this he replies: ['Because following repeated enjoyment, the attachments of the senses increase.'] And thus it is said:
['Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desires;']
['Like fire fed with clarified butter, it only grows more.']
['Skills'] — proficiencies — of the senses in the practice of enjoyment also increase. Although the skill of the senses is preceded by the skill of the mind, nevertheless, the skill of the senses themselves is also observed, as in beggars and others. ['Therefore, repeated enjoyment is not the means to happiness'] — cessation from repeated enjoyment alone is happiness.
['Indeed, one who, seeking happiness, has attached himself to'] — bound to, engaged with, or devoted to — ['sense objects, is like one afraid of a scorpion who is bitten by a cobra'] — plunged into a great swamp [of suffering]. Just as one who, frightened of a scorpion whose poison is mild, is struck by a more potent cobra and undergoes even greater suffering,
so too this person, having turned away from the apparent non-suffering of the great pleasure of transformation out of the conviction that it is suffering, being frightened, is submerged in the unfathomable ['great swamp of suffering. This is transformation-suffering,'] which is ['adverse'] to pleasure, [and afflicts] ['the <s>yogin</s> even during the state of pleasure.'] For the <s>yogin</s>, with a heart already trembling at the very onset of activity, experiences even pleasure as belonging to <s>karma</s> whose fruition is definitely determined — and that more powerful [<s>karma</s>] prevails. Therefore, all is suffering for the discerning one.

body.text: atha kā tāpaduḥkhatā, sarvasya dveṣānuviddhaścetanācetanasādhanādhīnastāpānubhava iti tatrāsti dveṣajaḥ karmāśayaḥ। sukhasādhanāni ca prārthayamānaḥ kāyena vācā manasā ca parispandate tataḥ paramanugṛhṇātyupahanti ceti parānugrahapīḍābhyāṁ dharmādharmāvupacinoti। sa karmāśayo lobhānmohācca bhavatītyeṣā tāpaduḥkhatocyate। kā punaḥ saṁskāraduḥkhatā, sukhānubhavātsukhasaṁskārāśayo duḥkhānubhavādapi duḥkhasaṁskārāśaya iti। evaṁ karmabhyo vipāke'nubhūyamāne sukhe duḥkhe vā punaḥ karmāśayapracaya iti।
body.translated_text: Now, what is burning-suffering (<s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>)? Everyone's experience of torment is pervaded by <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) and dependent on sentient and insentient means — therefore there exists a store of <s>karma</s> born of aversion. And one who desires the means of happiness exerts oneself through body, speech, and mind; thereby one either benefits or harms others. Through these acts of benefiting and harming others, one accumulates <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> (merit and demerit). That <s>karmāśaya</s> arises from greed and delusion — this is called burning-suffering. And what is <s>saṁskāra</s>-suffering (impression-suffering)? From the experience of pleasure arises a residual impression (<s>saṁskāra</s>) of pleasure; from the experience of pain arises a residual impression of pain. Thus, when the fruition of <s>karmas</s> is being experienced — whether pleasure or pain — there is again an accumulation of the store of <s>karma</s>.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
atha tāpaduḥkhatā vyākhyāyate – sukhepabhogastu pariṇamamānaḥ sannanubandhe vijñāte viṣadigdhasvādudadhyodanopabhogavaddduḥkhībhavati, svarūpataḥ punaravidyārūpo'nukūlavedanāgandho'pi । iha punaḥ svarūpata eva duḥkhatā tāpasya pratikūlātmakatvāt ॥
katham ? [sarvasya dveṣānuviddhaḥ] dveṣānugataḥ [cetanācetanasādhanādhīnaḥ] śatrukaṇṭakādisāṁdhanayaṁttaḥ tāpānubhavaḥ pūrvavardevadharmaphalaṁmanu bhavati apūrvaścopacīyamānaḥ [tatrāsti dveṣajaḥ karmāśayaḥ ॥]
tena ca duḥkhena paritapyamānaḥ sukhasādhanāni candanādīni [prārthayamānaḥ kāyena vācā manasā ca parispandate] ceṣṭate । tacca paripandanaṁ parānugrahāya parapīḍanāya vā bhavati । tataḥ [parānugrahapīḍābhyāṁ dharmādharmāvupacinoti । sa ca] parānugrahapīḍākṛto dharmādharmākhyaḥ [karmāśayo lobhānmohācca prabhavatītyeṣā] tāvat [tāpaduḥkhatā] dradhīyasī viprasṛtā । evaṁ paśyato vivekinaḥ sarvamevāśrayaviṣayanimittairduḥkhabhiti ॥
adhunā hlādaparitāpānubhavajanitasaṁskāraduḥkhamucyate--- [kāḥ punaḥ saṁskāradu:khatā? sukhānubhavāt sukhasaṁskārāśaya, dukhānubhavādapi । duḥkhasaṁskārāśayaḥ ।] sukhaduḥkhayo rāgaṁdveṣānuviddhatvātatsaṁskārāśayāvapi rāgadveṣānuviddhau । [evaṁ karmaṇo vipāke] jātyāyurbhogākhye' [nubhūyamāne sukhaduḥkhe] bhavataḥ ॥
tato'pi sukhadu:khānubhavasaṁskārāśaya: yathā nairantaryeṇa sukhadu:khānubhavastathaiva tadanubhavasaṁskārāvapi rāgadveṣānuviddhau nirantaratayā bhavataḥ । tau ca saiskārāśayau kriyāyā upabhogasya cāṅgībhavataḥ । evaṁ saṁskārāśayaṁsya duḥkhahetutvam । saṁskārahetukaṁ saṁskāradu:khaṁ, tathā ca tatsaṁskāraduḥkhatā । na hmasmarannupabhogmaya kriyāyai vā sādhanamupādatte । smṛteśca saṁskāranimittatvamupapāditam ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
Now the painfulness of <s>tāpa</s> (burning affliction) is explained — The enjoyment of pleasure, while undergoing transformation, when its subsequent consequence is known, becomes painful — like the enjoyment of sweet rice mixed with poison. And in its essential nature too, being of the form of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), even though it bears a trace of agreeable sensation. Here, however, <s>tāpa</s> is painful in its very essence, because it is of a disagreeable nature.
How? ['Everything is tinged with <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion)'] — tinged with aversion,

body.text: evamidamanādi duḥkhasroto viprasṛtaṁ yoginameva pratikūlātmakatvādudvejayati। kasmāt, akṣipātrakalpo hi vidvāniti। yathorṇātanturakṣipātre nyastaḥ sparśena duḥkhayati na cānyeṣu gātrāvayaveṣu, evametāni duḥkhānyakṣipātrakalpaṁ yoginameva kliśnanti netaraṁ pratipattāram। itaraṁ tu svakarmopahṛtaṁ duḥkhamupāttamupāttaṁ tyajantaṁ tyaktaṁ tyaktamupādadānamanādivāsanāvicitrayā cittavṛttyā samantato'nuviddhamivāvidyayā hātavya evāhaṁkāramamakārānupātinaṁ jātaṁ jātaṁ bāhyādhyātmakobhayanimittāstriparvāṇastāpā anuplavante। tadevamanādinā duḥkhasrotasā vyuhyamānamātmānaṁ bhūtagrāmaṁ ca dṛṣṭvā yogī sarvaduḥkhakṣayakāraṇaṁ samyagdarśanaṁ śaraṇaṁ prapadyata iti।
body.translated_text: Thus this beginningless stream of suffering, flowing forth, agitates only the <s>yogin</s>, because of its disagreeable nature. Why? Because the wise one is like the surface of the eye. Just as a thread of wool placed on the surface of the eye causes pain by its touch, but not on other parts of the body — so too these sufferings torment only the <s>yogin</s>, who is like the surface of the eye, and not the ordinary person. The ordinary person, however, brought by his own <s>karma</s> to suffering,

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yadyapi saṁskārasya svarūpato duḥkhatā nāsti, tathāpi saṁskārasya da:khahetutāṁ jānato vivekina: sattāmātreṇa du:khatvaṁ, bhakṣitamātraviṣavat । itthametaiḥ pariṇāmatāpasaṁskārahetubhiḥ sarvemevaṁ duḥkhamitya [nādiduḥkhasroto yoginameva pratikūlātmakatvādudvejayati ॥]
nanu cetarasyāpi pratikūlātmakameva, kasmānna tamudvejayati । nātyantakleśādikāluṣyāvivekakiṇīkṛtacetastvāditaramudrejayati । na pratikūlātmakatā prabhāvyate । yo hi dayitāmuṣṭighātaṁ mudgarābhighātadeśīyamapi mastakena pratīcchati । putrasya vā mūtrapurīṣamurasā dhārayati । asāvānandamahodanvattaraṅgāyamāṇaḥ [ṇaṁ] svātmanyapi na vātitarām [svātmānamapi na veti tarām] । na hi tasya tatpratikūlātmakam । rāgameva hi taditarasya pratipattṛtvādabhivardhayati tarām ॥
nanu ca yogino'pi tatsamānaṁ nimittaṁ, kasmāttamudvejayatīti । udvejatyeva tam । [kasmāt ? akṣipātrakalpo hi saḥ ।] prasannatvādviraktatvādityarthaḥ । tasmānna samānaṁ nimittaṁ tasya, yato'sau [vidvāniti । na hi viduṣaḥ kleśādi] kāluṣyāvivekakiṇīkṛtacetastvam । na ca tatkirṇākṛtacetasvatiraskārādṛte vidvattā । tasmādakṣipātrakalpatvādvidvāṁsamevodvaijayati, netaram ॥
tatra dṛṣṭāntābhyāṁ vidvadaviduṣorantaramācaṣṭe-- [yathorṇātanturatimṛdusparśī'pyakṣipātre nyastaḥ sparśena duḥkhayati] svacchataratvadakṣipātrasya, tathā yoginaṁ viviktataraprajñānamakaluṣahṛdayamudvejayati duḥkham । sa evorṇātanturanyeṣu gātreṣu kṣiptaḥ kharatarasaṁsparśenāpi na duḥkhayati, tathā [netaraṁ pratipattāraṁ] duḥkhaṁ pīḍayati, kleśādikiṇīkṛtacetasvāt kaṭhinataretaragātrāvayavakalpo hi saḥ ॥
tadidamāha-- [evametāni du:khāni akṣipātrakalpaṁ yoginameva kliśnanti netaraṁ pratipattāram ।] itarasya tu pratipatturitaragātrāvayavasvabhāvatāṁ darśayannāha-- [itaraṁ tviti । tāpā anuplavanta] ityevamantena vākyasamaptiḥ ॥
[svakāraṇopahṛtaṁ] duḥkhaprāptinimittaiścetanācetanādibhirupahṛtamupanītaṁ buddhivṛttidvoraṇa puruṣasya karmatāmāpāditaṁ, [duḥkhamupāttaṁ tyajantaṁ] śarīratyāgena, anyatra ca [tyaktaṁ] punaranyaṁ śarīrādilakṣaṇameva du:khasamudāyamu [pādadānamanādivāsanācitrayā] avidyayā [cittavṛtyā sarvato'nuviddhamiva ॥]
[itaraṁ] pratipattāraṁ kiṁviśiṣṭam ? [hātavyāhaṅkāramamakārānupātinam ।] kāryakaraṇeṣu taddharmaṣu ca kriyāguṇaphaleṣu viparyayeṇa pratipattirahaṅkāraḥ । mamakārastu teṣu bāhyeṣu ca cetanācetaneṣu mameti pratyayaḥ । tau ca viparyayatvāt samastakleśakarma vipākabījatvāca hātavyau । na hi tāvantareṇa rāgādayaḥ karmavipākā vā samudācaranti । tasmāddhātavyau tau tāvanupatituṁ śīlamasyeti hātavyāhaṅgāramamakārānupātī, tamū ॥
[jātaṁ jātam] anyagātrāvayavakalpaṁ [bāhyādhyātmikobhayanimittāḥ] bāhyaṁ devatā bhūtāni ca, adhyātmikaṁ kāryaṁ kāraṇaṁ ca, bāhyādhyātmikāni cobhayāni ca nimittaṁ yeṣāṁ te bāhyādhyātmikobhayanimittāḥ ॥
[triparvāṇaḥ] bāhyādinimittameva triparvatvam । bhūtabhaviṣyadvartamānatvaṁ vā triparvatvam । vakṣyati ca [“heyaṁ duḥkhamanāgatam' iti ।] yadvā, kleśakarmavipākātmakatvam । yadvā, pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraduḥkhatvam । ataste triparvāṇa [stāpā anuplāvante] anuṣajyanti ॥
[ta(me)devaṁ] aviveka pratipattāram [anādidu:khasrotasohyamānamātmānaṁ ca] duḥkhasrotasi magnaṁ tathā [bhūtagrāmaṁ ca dṛṣṭvā yogī sarvadu:khakṣayakaraṁ samyagdarśana śaraṇaṁ prapadyata iti ॥]
nanu ca yogitvādeva samyagdarśanaṁ pratipannaḥ । ucyate – yogāṅgānuṣṭhānādeva yogitvam, ṛte'pi samyagdarśanāt । tasmāt samyagdarśanasādhanatvaṁ yogasya darśayati । yogaṁ yogaphalaṁ ca sarvameva duḥkhaṁ paśyan samyagdarśanaikaśaraṇaṁ pratipadyate । tathā ca vakṣyati – [“tadvairāgyādapi doṣabījakṣaye kaivalyam?] iti ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
Although <s>saṁskāra</s> (latent impression) is not painful in its own nature, nevertheless for the discerning one (<s>vivekin</s>) who knows <s>saṁskāra</s> to be a cause of suffering, its mere existence constitutes painfulness — like poison that has merely been eaten. In this way, through these causes — transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>), burning (<s>tāpa</s>), and <s>saṁskāra</s> — everything is indeed painful. [This beginningless stream of suffering agitates only the <s>yogin</s>, because of its disagreeable nature.]
But surely the ordinary person too is affected by the disagreeable nature,

body.text: guṇavṛttivirodhācca duḥravameva sarvaṁ vivekinaḥ। prakhyāpravṛttisthitirūpā buddhiguṇāḥ parasparānugrahatantrī bhūtvā śāntaṁ ghoraṁ mūḍhaṁ vā pratyayaṁ triguṇamevā''rabhante। calaṁ ca guṇavṛttamiti kṣiprapariṇāmi cittamuktam। rūpātiśayā vṛttyatiśayāśca paraspareṇa virudhyante, sāmānyāni tvatiśayaiḥ saha pravartante। evamete guṇā itaretarāśrayeṇopārjitasukhaduḥkhamohapratyayāḥ sarve sarvarūpā bhavantīti, guṇapradhānabhāvakṛtastveṣāṁ viśeṣa iti। tasmādduḥkhameva sarvaṁ vivekina iti।
body.translated_text: And because of the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s> (fundamental qualities), everything is indeed painful for the discerning one. The qualities of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) — having the forms of <s>prakhyā</s> (illumination), <s>pravṛtti</s> (activity), and <s>sthiti</s> (inertia) — being dependent on mutual support, always produce a cognition that is <s>śānta</s> (tranquil), <s>ghora</s> (violent), or <s>mūḍha</s> (deluded), and thus consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s> alone. And because the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is restless, the <s>citta</s> (mind) has been called 'of rapidly changing transformation.' The excesses of form and the excesses of activity mutually conflict with one another, while the general aspects are not conflicted by the excesses,

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[itaśva sarvaṁ duḥrkhaṁ vivekinaḥ ।] kutaśva ? [guṇavṛttivirodhāccāpi ।] nanu ca kimarthaṁ sūtre pṛthagvibhaktikriyā? yāvatā pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraguṇavṛttivirodhairiyeva kartavyam । naiṣa doṣaḥ sukhaduḥkhānubhavatadvāsanāḥ sarvajanaprasiddhā iti pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraduḥkhairiti nirdiṣṭāḥ । tatkāraṇavibhāgajñānaviśāradasyaiva vivekaprakarṣavato guṇavṛttivirodhā vijñeyā iti pṛthakkaraṇam । sarvaduḥkhahetutvasāmānyātvekasūtravinyāsaḥ ॥
guṇāḥ sattvādayaḥ, teṣāṁ vṛttayo guṇavṛttayaḥ, tāsāṁ virodhādguṇavṛttivirodhāt । te ca guṇā antaḥkaraṇadyākārasanniviṣṭāḥ । teṣāṁ guṇapradhānabhāvenābhinnapariṇāmatvācca viruddhavṛttitvaṁ bhavati । anyatamavṛttirudbhavantyā'nyatamavṛttyā'bhibhūyate ॥
evaṁ trayāṇāmapi pratikṣaṇa(pakṣa)manyenyavṛttitiraskāra itaretaravṛttyudbhāvitvaṁ ca । na sukhaduḥkhamohātmakānāṁ guṇānāmanyatamavṛttilābho'nyatamānanusaṁhitaḥ । tata etatsiddhaṁ bhavati – yadā duḥkhātmikaṁ raja udbhavati, tadā duḥkhatvādeva tadvṛtterna duḥkhamiti vaktavyam । sattvatamase.ārīpa rajo'nugatirastyeveti tayerapi duḥkhatvameva । satvatamaḥpravṛttinivṛtyorapi rajovyāpārānujavādduḥkhatvameva sarvasyeti ॥
etadupabyācaṣṭe – [prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlābhirvṛttibhirguṇāḥ parasparānugrahatantrāḥ] parasparaviruddhā api parasparopakāryopakārakabhāvena tailavartyagnivat [śāntaṁ] sāttvikaṁ [ghoraṁ] rājasaṁ [mūḍha़ṁ] tāmasaṁ [pratyayaṁ triguṇamevārabhante ।] i(tare)tarayoraṅgabhāvenānugatatvādyadā sāttvikaḥ śāntaḥ pratyaya udbhūtaḥ so'nantaramevodbubhūṣatā tamo'nusaṁhitena ghoreṇa rājasena pralyayena hanyate ॥
yadā ca rājaso ghoraḥ pratyaya itaraguṇānugata udbhūto bhavati so'nantaramevodbubhūṣatā tāmasena pratyayena mūḍhena sattvānugatena sāttvikena vā tamo'nugatena hanyate । tathā tāmaso'pītarapratyayāmyāṁ paryāyeṇa । tathā sāttvikena itarāvityanyonyodayābhibhavapravṛttayā guṇāḥ ॥
kasmāt ? yataḥ [calaṁ guṇavṛttaṁ] guṇasvabhāvatvaṁ cittākāreṇa guṇāḥ sanniviṣṭā iti [kṣiprapariṇāmaṁ cittamuktam ।] kva ? tantre ॥
kasmāt punarguṇā virudhyanta iti । anekātiśayānāmekatrāsambhavāt । yathā apavarake tamaḥprakāśayoratiśayavatoḥ, evamantaḥkaraṇākārasanniveśināṁ sukhaduḥkhamoharūpāṇāṁ prakāśapravṛttiniyamavṛttīnāṁ guṇānāṁ rūpeṇa vā sukhādinā vṛttyā vā jñānādilakṣaṇayā yugapadatiśayo na sambhavati ॥
sāmānyānāṁ tvavirodhādavyaktarūpāṇāmatiśayarvyaktaiḥ saha vṛttiryuktā । tena [‘rūpātiśayā vṛttyatiśayāśca virudhyante । sāmānyāni tvatiśayaiḥ saha vartante’] ityucyate । yadā sukharūpātiśayastadā na duḥkharūpātiśayo moharūpātiśayo vā । ’ tathā itarātiśaye netarātiśayaḥ । tathā, jñānavṛttyatiśaye na lobhapratatyavṛttyatiśayaḥ । tathā, anyatamavṛttyatiśaye nānyatamavṛttyatiśayaḥ ॥
[evamete guṇā itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitasukhaduḥkhamohapratyayāḥ ।] sukhena rajastasaupāśrayeṇopārjitaḥ sukhapratyayaḥ । rajasāpi sattvatamaupāśrayeṇopārjito duḥkhapratyayaḥ । tasamāpi sattvarajaupāśrayeṇopārjito mohapratyayaḥ । tataḥ [sarve sarvakāryā bhavanti ॥]
yadyevamayaṁ pratyayaḥ sāttvikaḥ, tāmaso'yaṁ, rājasaścāyamiti viśeṣaḥ ka ityāha – [guṇapradhānabhāvakṛtastveṣāṁ viśeṣa] iti । pradhānopasarjanatayā saṁjñālābhālābhau । yathā pāñcabhautiktave'pi pārthivaṁ taijasamāpyamiti ॥
yata evaṁ guṇavṛttivirodhaḥ, [tasmāt sarvameva duḥkhaṁ vivekina iti ।] guṇavṛttivirodhādityetatparavairāgyārtham । kathaṁ ? pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraduḥkhairiti dṛṣṭānuśravikraviṣayāvatṛṣṇasyaiva sarvasya du:khapratipādanārtha pṛthagvibhaktikaṁ kṛtam । na hi tatra duḥkhatvamapaśyato vairāgyamupakalppata iti ॥
etattu guṇavṛttivirodhāceti guṇānāṁ parasparavirodhivṛttitvena duḥkhatvapratipādanāttebhyo vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyaḥ paraṁ vairāgyamupakalpyata ityevamartham । tathā cātrāpi pradhānopasarjanabhāvena sarve sarvarūpā bhavantīti vyaktāvyaktadharmatvaṁ pratipāditam । evaṁ ca kṛtvā sūtre'pi guṇavṛttivirodhācceti pṛthak paṭhitam ॥
body.translated_text:
Commentary (<s>Vivaraṇa</s>)
['And furthermore, everything is suffering for the discriminating person.'] Why? ['Because of the conflict of the activities of the <s>guṇas</s>.'] But why is there a separate statement in the <s>sūtra</s>? Since 'by transformation-suffering, anguish-suffering, and <s>saṃskāra</s>-suffering' would suffice. There is no fault—because the experience of pleasure and pain and their impressions are well-known to all people, they are indicated by 'transformation-suffering, anguish-suffering, and <s>saṃskāra</s>-suffering.' But the conflicts of the <s>guṇa</s>-activities are to be known only by one who is accomplished in the knowledge of the classification of their causes and who has the highest degree of discrimination—hence the separate statement. The inclusion in one <s>sūtra</s> is because of the commonality of being a cause of all suffering.

The <s>guṇas</s> are <s>sattva</s> and the rest; their activities are the <s>guṇa</s>-activities; from the conflict of these is the conflict of <s>guṇa</s>-activities. And those <s>guṇas</s> are situated in the form of the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). Because their transformations are undifferentiated through the relation of being predominant and subordinate, they have conflicting activities. When one activity arises, it is overcome by another activity.

Thus, for all three, at every moment there is the suppression of one another's activities and the arising of one another's activities. The attainment of one particular activity among the <s>guṇas</s> whose nature is pleasure, pain, and delusion is never unaccompanied by another. Hence this is established: when <s>rajas</s>, whose nature is pain, arises, it need not be said that its activity is painful because it is intrinsically pain. The accompaniment of <s>rajas</s> with <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s> is always present, so they too are essentially painful. And since the arising and cessation of <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s> activities also follow from the operation of <s>rajas</s>, everything is indeed suffering.

He explains this: ['The <s>guṇas</s>, with their activities characterized by luminosity, activity, and stability, are mutually dependent on each other's support'—though mutually opposed, through the relationship of being benefactor and beneficiary, like oil, wick, and fire—'they produce a <s>pratyaya</s> (cognition) that is always threefold: <s>śānta</s> (tranquil)']—<s>sāttvika</s>—['<s>ghora</s> (fierce)']—<s>rājasa</s>—['<s>mūḍha</s> (deluded)']—<s>tāmasa</s>. Because the other two are always present as subsidiary components, when a <s>sāttvika</s> tranquil cognition has arisen, it is immediately destroyed by a fierce <s>rājasa</s> cognition accompanied by <s>tamas</s>, which desires to arise.

And when a <s>rājasa</s> fierce cognition accompanied by the other <s>guṇas</s> has arisen, it is immediately destroyed either by a <s>tāmasa</s> deluded cognition accompanied by <s>sattva</s>, or by a <s>sāttvika</s> cognition accompanied by <s>tamas</s>, which desires to arise. Similarly, the <s>tāmasa</s> cognition too is destroyed by the other cognitions in turn. Likewise, the <s>sāttvika</s> destroys the other two—thus the <s>guṇas</s> function through mutual arising and suppression.

Why? Because ['the activity of the <s>guṇas</s> is restless']—the <s>guṇas</s> being situated in the form of the mind (<s>citta</s>), which is of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>—['the mind is said to be of rapid transformation.'] Where? In the <s>Tantra</s> (i.e., the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> system).

Why then do the <s>guṇas</s> conflict? Because many excellences cannot coexist in one place simultaneously. Just as in a room, darkness and light in their fullness cannot coexist, so too the <s>guṇas</s>—whose natures are pleasure, pain, and delusion, and whose activities are illumination, activity, and restraint—being situated in the form of the inner organ, cannot simultaneously reach excellence either in their form (pleasure etc.) or in their activity (knowledge etc.).

However, since universals do not conflict, the co-operation of unmanifest forms with the manifest excellences is appropriate. Hence it is said: ['Excellences of form and excellences of activity conflict; but the universals co-exist with the excellences.'] When there is excellence of the form of pleasure, there is no excellence of the form of pain or of delusion. Likewise, when there is excellence of another, there is no excellence of the others. Similarly, when there is excellence of the activity of knowledge, there is no excellence of the activity of greed. Thus, when there is excellence of one activity, there is no excellence of another activity.

['Thus, these <s>guṇas</s>, through mutual dependence, produce cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion.'] Through dependence on <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>, <s>sattva</s> produces the cognition of pleasure. Through dependence on <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>, <s>rajas</s> too produces the cognition of pain. Through dependence on <s>sattva</s> and <s>rajas</s>, <s>tamas</s> too produces the cognition of delusion. Hence ['all become the causes of all effects.']

If so, what is the distinction—'this cognition is <s>sāttvika</s>, this is <s>tāmasa</s>, this is <s>rājasa</s>'?—he says: ['The distinction among them is made by the predominance of one <s>guṇa</s>'] over the others. The designation is gained or not gained according to being predominant or subordinate. Just as in the case of something made of all five elements, it is called earthy, fiery, or watery.

Since the conflict of <s>guṇa</s>-activities is thus, ['therefore everything is suffering for the discriminating person.'] 'Because of the conflict of <s>guṇa</s>-activities'—this is for the purpose of supreme dispassion (<s>para-vairāgya</s>). How? 'By transformation-suffering, anguish-suffering, and <s>saṃskāra</s>-suffering'—this separate statement was made for demonstrating that everything is suffering for one who has already attained freedom from desire toward objects seen and heard of. For without seeing suffering in them, dispassion does not arise.

But this—'because of the conflict of <s>guṇa</s>-activities'—by demonstrating the painful nature of the <s>guṇas</s> through their mutually conflicting activities, supreme dispassion toward them, both manifest and unmanifest in nature, is brought about—this is the purpose. And thus here too it has been demonstrated that all things are of all forms through the relation of predominance and subordination—this is the nature of being manifest and unmanifest. And having done so, in the <s>sūtra</s> too 'because of the conflict of <s>guṇa</s>-activities' is read separately.

body.text: tadasya mahato duḥkhasamudāyasya prabhavabījamavidyā। tasyāśca samyagdarśanamabhāvahetuḥ। yathā cikitsāśāstraṁ caturvyūham – rogo rogaheturārogyaṁ bhaiṣajyamiti, evamidamapi śāstraṁ caturvyūhameva। tadyathā – saṁsāraḥ saṁsāraheturmokṣo mokṣopāya iti। tatra duḥkhabahulaḥ saṁsāro heyaḥ। pradhānapuruṣayoḥ saṁyogo heyahetuḥ। saṁyogasyā''tyantikī nivṛttirhānam। hānopāyaḥ samyagdarśanam।
body.translated_text: Of this great mass of suffering, the source-seed is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). And right vision (<s>samyag-darśana</s>) is the cause of its destruction. Just as the science of medicine (<s>cikitsā-śāstra</s>) has a four-fold structure—disease, cause of disease, health, and remedy—so too this teaching has a four-fold structure: <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation), and the means of <s>mokṣa</s>. Of these, <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is full of suffering, is what is to be abandoned (<s>heya</s>). The conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (the self) is the cause of what is to be abandoned. The absolute cessation of that conjunction is the abandonment (<s>hāna</s>). The means of abandonment is right vision.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
pariṇāmatāpasaṁskāraduḥkhadharmatvāt [tasyaitasya mahato] guṇagauṇalakṣaṇasya [duḥkhasamudāyasya prabhavabījamavidyā । tasyāśva samyagdarśanamabhāvahetuḥ] pratipakṣatvāt । bhūtārthāśrayatvādvidyāyā abhūtārthāśrayatvāccāvidyāyā vidyaivābhāvahetuḥ । yathā sadviṣayeṇaikacandradarśanenasidviṣayasyānekacandradarśanasya bādhanam ॥
saha duḥkhanidānana kleśakarmavipākalakṣaṇena sarva duḥkhamityupapāditam । anena duḥkhena yo duḥkhī vivekī sa etasya samyagdarśanaśāstrasya viṣayaḥ adhikṛto, netaro du:khasyaiva pratipattṛtvādityetaddṛṣṭāntena pratipipādayeṣanāha – [yathā cikitsāśāsraṁ caturvyūham – rogo rogaheturārogyaṁ bhaiṣajyamiti ।] rogarogohatumāṁstannivivartayiṣurbhaiṣajyasya śāstrasyārogyasya prayojanasya viṣayaḥ ॥
[evamidamapi śāsraṁ caturyūhameva । yathā—saṁsāraḥ saṁsaheturmīkṣo mokṣahetuḥ । tatra duḥkhabahulaḥ saṁsāro] heyaḥ । [pradhānapuruṣasaṁyogo heyahetuḥ । saṁyogusyāntitikī nivṛttirhānam । hānopāyaḥ samyagdarśanami] tyete catvāro vyūhāḥ ॥
yathā cikitsāśāstraṁ roge rogahatau cārogye ca tatprayojanake bhaiṣajaye ca catuṣṭaye svarūpapratipādanāya vyūhitaṁ, tata eva ca rogādayo'sya catvāro vyūhā iti caturvyūhaṁ, tathā asya śāstrasya । duḥkhabahulaḥ saṁsāraḥ [heyaḥ], avidyāhetukaśca pradhānapuruṣasaṁyogo hetuḥ, sanimittasya saṁsārasya hānaṁ samyagdarśanaśāstrasya prayojanaṁ, tathā samyagdarśarna ceti catvāra ete vyūhā asyāpi iti caturvyūhaṁ śāstram । eṣu vā'rtheṣu caturdhā vyūho'syeti catuvryūham ॥
body.translated_text:
Commentary (<s>Vivaraṇa</s>)
Because of having the nature of transformation-suffering, anguish-suffering, and <s>saṃskāra</s>-suffering, ['of this great'] mass of suffering characterized by the principal and secondary aspects of the <s>guṇas</s>, ['the source-seed is <s>avidyā</s>. And right vision is the cause of its destruction']—because it is the counteragent. Because <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge) has real being as its object, and <s>avidyā</s> has unreal being as its object, <s>vidyā</s> alone is the cause of the destruction of <s>avidyā</s>. Just as the perception of a single moon, which has a real object, annuls the perception of multiple moons, which has an unreal object.

Together with the cause of suffering characterized by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s>, and <s>vipāka</s> (fruition), everything has been demonstrated to be suffering. The person who, possessing discrimination, is afflicted by this suffering, is the qualified subject (<s>adhikṛta</s>) of this teaching of right vision—not another, since only such a person truly apprehends suffering. He illustrates this with an analogy: ['Just as the science of medicine has a four-fold structure—disease, cause of disease, health, and remedy.'] One who has disease and the cause of disease, and who wishes to eliminate them, is the qualified subject of the teaching (remedy) and its fruit (health).

['So too this teaching has a four-fold structure: <s>saṃsāra</s>, the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>, <s>mokṣa</s>, and the means of <s>mokṣa</s>. Of these, <s>saṃsāra</s>, full of suffering,'] is what is to be abandoned. ['The conjunction of <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> is the cause of what is to be abandoned. The absolute cessation of that conjunction is the abandonment. The means of abandonment is right vision.'] These are the four divisions.

Just as the science of medicine is structured in four divisions for the purpose of establishing the true nature of disease, the cause of disease, health, and the remedy that has health as its fruit—and from these very things disease and the rest are its four divisions, hence it is 'four-fold'—so too for this teaching. <s>Saṃsāra</s>, full of suffering, is what is to be abandoned; the conjunction of <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, caused by <s>avidyā</s>, is the cause; the cessation of <s>saṃsāra</s>, which has a cause, is the fruit of the teaching of right vision; and right vision itself—these are the four divisions of this teaching too, hence it is a 'four-fold teaching.' Or, the fourfold arrangement (<s>vyūha</s>) of this teaching concerning these four topics makes it 'four-fold.'

body.text: tatra hātuḥ svarūpamupādeyaṁ vā heyaṁ vā na bhavitumarhatīti hāne tasyocchedavādaprasaṅga upādāne ca hetuvādaḥ। ubhayapratyākhyāne śāśvatavāda ityetatsamyagdarśanam ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text: Therein, the essential nature of the one who is to be abandoned is neither fit to be taken up nor fit to be abandoned. If it were abandoned, there would be the absurd consequence of the annihilationist doctrine (<s>ucchedavāda</s>); if taken up, there would be the eternalist doctrine (<s>hetuvāda</s>). If both are rejected, there would be the doctrine of permanence (<s>śāśvatavāda</s>)—this is what constitutes right vision. (Sūtra 15)

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[tatra hātuḥ svarūpamiti । nanu ‘draṣṭā dṛśimātra'] iti hātṛlakṣaṇasūtra etadvaditavyam । naiṣa doṣaḥ । śāstrārambhaprayojanapratipipādayiṣuṇā kleśādikaḥ samasto duḥkhāvasānaḥ saṁsāro nirvarṇitaḥ । saṁsārī ca yaḥ saṁsāraduḥkhena nirviṇṇo vivekī so'sya śāstrasya viṣaya upapāditaḥ । tasya vivekinaḥ śāstramata: paramārabhyate । etacca prathamasūtre pradarśitam । ābhyamāṇasya śāsrasya samyagdarśanameva prayojanam । tacca saṁsāraduḥkhanirvarṇanānantaramavasaraprāptaṁ pratipādayitavyamityetaducyate – [tatra hātuḥ svarūpamiti ॥]
hātā puruṣaḥ, tasya [svarūpamupādeyaṁ vā heyaṁ vā na bhavati ।] kuta etadevam ? heyopādeyavyatirekeṇa vastvadarśanāt । yathā loke sukhaṁ tatkāraṇaṁ copādeyaṁ, duḥkhaṁ tatkāraṇaṁ ca heyam , evamayamapi puruṣo vastutvādanyataradharmī bhavitumarhatītyabhiprāyaḥ । kimato yadyevam ? ata etadbhavati, [hāne tvasyocchedavādaprasaṅga] iti ॥
yadyasau heyatvadharmā, tata eṣa hātavyaḥ । hāne tvasya kiṁ syāt ? ā.ātmocchedavādaprasaṅgaḥ syāt । ataḥ ko doṣaḥ syāt ? doṣaṁ kaivalyapāde pratipādayiṣyāmaḥ ॥
kiñcānyat – asya hātrantarasya(kiñcānyatarasya)abhāvāddhānānupapattitvam । svayamevātmana ātmā hāteti cet – na – svātmani kriyāvirodhādbhedābhāvācca । heyādātmana ātmā hātā cedanyastadā'navasthāsaṅgaḥ । yo yo hātā । tasyāpi heyatvāt । na ca yugapaddvayorhatroḥ saṁbhavo'sti । bhinnakālabhāvinostu heyahātṛtvānupapattiḥ ॥
hātuśca heyatvābhyupagame tasyānavasthitatvāddheyasambandhānupapattiḥ । hāturanavasthitatve ca svayameva heyatvapratipatterhāturhānāyodyamānarthakyaprasaṅgaḥ । hānaphalānupapātiśva । na hi baddhasya svarūpanāśa eva phalam । mokṣo hi tasya phalam । nāpi mriyamāṇo'pi jñātakṣaṇāntaramaraṇaḥ svarūpavināśamicchati । vināśasyārthaprāptatvādevamanavasthitaśveddhātā na svarūpahānamicchet, arthaprāserhānasya ॥
yathā ca hāturnitya vaṁ tathā [draṣṭṛsūtre] kaivalyapade ca vyākhyāsyāmahe । tasmānna heyatvadharmaṁ puruṣaḥ । saṁsārastu mahadādivyaktiḥ duḥkhabalo heyaḥ । tattulyadharmakaḥ puruṣo na bhavatītyarthaḥ । tattulyadharbhakatve [tasyocchedavādaprasaṅga] iti ॥
astu tarhyapādeyaḥ, yathā sukhārthaṁ sukhakāraṇaṁ dravyam । naitadevam । kasmāt ? [upādāne] tvasya [hetuvāda] grasaṅgāt । yasya dravyādyupādānaphalena sambandhaḥ [sa] cedupādīyeta, tannirhetumasyopādanaṁ syāt । anyasyopādāturabhāvāt । na hi paṭaḥ paṭenaivopādīyate । anyasya hyanyadupādeyam । upādātrantarasambhave hi tadanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ, so'pyanyenepādīyate so'pi cānyeneti ॥
kiṁ ca – pārārthryaprasaṅgaśca । anyasya hi hetoranyadupādīyate, satvādilakṣaṇasya pradhānasyopādāne puruṣo heturabhyupeyate, yathā ghaṭāya mṛtpiṇḍopādāne kulālo hetuḥ । sa cetpuruṣaḥ pradhānopādanahetuḥ pradhānavadupādīyeta, tasyapi sattvādidharmatvaṁ syāt, upādeyatvānmṛtpiṇḍavat । tate.o'sya pradhānasya nirhetukaṁ kāryārthamupādānaṁ prāpnoti ॥
atheśvarārthamupādeyaḥ, puruṣāṇāṁ vā parasparārthamiti cet, bhogyatvācetanatvapariṇāmitvādidoṣasāmagrī prasajyeta, tasmānnāpi pradhānadharmakaḥ puruṣa [ityupādāne ca hetuvādaprasaṅga] ityucyate ॥
taduktam – [hetustvapuruṣo bhavatīti ।] tasya copādane ahetu: pradhānavṛttirnirhetukī syāt । na ca svayaṁ svārthaṁ śakyaṁ vijñātum । prakāśādiṣu svārthatvādarśanātū ॥
[ubhayapratyākhyāne] heyatvopādeyatvapratyākhyāne । [śāśvatavādaprasaṅgaḥ] ātmanityatvavādaprasaṅgaḥ । yadyapi pradhānasyopādeyasyāpi śāśvatatvaṁ, tathā'pi vikārātmanā tadaśāśvatameva । anekātmakatvamaśucitvamavidyātvaṁ parārthatvamityevamādayo doṣāḥ pradhāna । puruṣāṇāmapi tathātve satyanirmokṣaprasaṅgaḥ । bandhamokṣayostaddhetvośca vidyāvidyayoḥ svarūpāvyatirekādbandhamuktayośva nirviśeṣatvaprasaṅgāt । tasmāddheyopādeyatvapratyākhyānena śāśvatavāda [ityetadeva samyagdarśanam ॥ 15 ॥]
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
["The nature of the abandoner (<s>hātṛ</s>)..."] Objection: Should this not be stated in the <s>sūtra</s> defining the abandoner, '<s>Draṣṭā dṛśimātraḥ</s>' (The seer is mere seeing)? This is not a fault. The one wishing to establish the purpose of undertaking the <s>śāstra</s> has described the totality of <s>saṃsāra</s>—<s>kleśas</s> and the rest—culminating in suffering. And the <s>saṃsārin</s> who, being disgusted by the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, is the discerning one (<s>vivekin</s>)—he has been established as the subject of this <s>śāstra</s>. From here onward, the <s>śāstra</s> begins for that discerning one. This was indicated in the first <s>sūtra</s>. The purpose of the <s>śāstra</s> being studied is right vision (<s>samyagdarśana</s>) alone. And that, following immediately after the description of the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, is now to be taught at the appropriate time—thus it is said: ["The nature of the abandoner."]
The abandoner is <s>Puruṣa</s>. ["His essential nature is neither to be adopted (<s>upādeya</s>) nor to be rejected (<s>heya</s>)."]. Why is this so? Because apart from the rejectable and the adoptable, no [third kind of] entity is observed. Just as in the world, pleasure and its cause are to be adopted, and suffering and its cause are to be rejected—so too this <s>Puruṣa</s>, being an entity, should be characterized by one or the other. What follows if this is so? From this follows: ["But in its rejection, the absurd consequence of the doctrine of annihilation would arise."]
If <s>Puruṣa</s> had the property of being rejectable, then it would have to be rejected. But what would happen upon its rejection? The absurd consequence of the doctrine of self-annihilation (<s>ucchedavāda</s>) would arise. And what fault would that be? We shall demonstrate the fault in the <s>Kaivalya</s> chapter.
Moreover: since there is no other abandoner for this [<s>Puruṣa</s>], its rejection is impossible. If [one says] the self itself is the abandoner of itself—no, because of the contradiction of an action upon oneself, and because of the absence of duality. If the self, being other than what is to be rejected, is the abandoner, then an infinite regress follows—whoever is the abandoner, he too would be rejectable. And two [simultaneous] abandonments are not possible. And for those occurring at different times, the relation of 'to-be-rejected' and 'abandoner' cannot be established.
If the rejectability of the abandoner is accepted, then because of its instability, the relation with what is to be rejected cannot be established. And if the abandoner is unstable, then the effort of the abandoner—who has already realized his own rejectability—toward abandonment would become purposeless. And the fruit of abandonment would be impossible. For the fruit of the bound one is not the destruction of its own nature—rather, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) is its fruit. Not even one who is dying, [though] knowing that death [will come] the next moment, desires the destruction of his own nature. Since destruction comes of its own accord, such an unstable abandoner would not desire the rejection of his own nature, since rejection would come of its own accord.
The eternality of the abandoner will be explained ["in the <s>sūtra</s> on the seer"] and in the <s>Kaivalya</s> chapter. Therefore <s>Puruṣa</s> does not have the property of being rejectable. <s>Saṃsāra</s>, however—the manifest [world] of <s>mahat</s> (the great) and the rest, whose nature is suffering—is to be rejected. <s>Puruṣa</s> does not have properties equal to those—this is the meaning. If it had such equal properties, ["the absurd consequence of the doctrine of annihilation"] would arise.
Let it then be adoptable, as a substance is adopted for the sake of pleasure. This is not so either. Why? ["If adopted, the absurd consequence of the doctrine of [a separate] cause"] would arise. If that which has a connection with the fruit of adopting substances and the like ["were adopted,"] its adoption would be without a cause, since there is no other adopter. For a cloth is not adopted by the cloth itself. Rather, something other than itself is the adoptable for another. And if another adopter is possible, there would be an infinite regress—that one too would be adopted by another, and that one by yet another.
Moreover, the absurd consequence of being for the sake of another would arise. For something is adopted for the sake of another cause. <s>Puruṣa</s> is accepted as the cause for the adoption of <s>Pradhāna</s> characterized by <s>sattva</s> and the rest, just as the potter is the cause for the adoption of the lump of clay for the pot. If this <s>Puruṣa</s>, being the cause of <s>Pradhāna</s>'s adoption, were [itself] adopted like <s>Pradhāna</s>, it too would have the properties of <s>sattva</s> and the rest—being adoptable, like the lump of clay. And then the adoption of <s>Pradhāna</s> for a purposeful effect would be without a cause.
If [<s>Puruṣa</s>] is adopted for the sake of <s>Īśvara</s>, or if <s>Puruṣas</s> are [adopted] for one another's sake—the entire collection of faults—being an object of experience, being non-conscious, being subject to transformation, and so forth—would follow. Therefore <s>Puruṣa</s> does not have the properties of <s>Pradhāna</s>—["and if adopted, the absurd consequence of the doctrine of a [separate] cause" is stated].
Thus it has been said: ["The cause, however, would become non-<s>Puruṣa</s>."]. And if it were adopted, the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s> would be without a cause. Nor can [<s>Pradhāna</s>] by itself know its own purpose—because self-purpose is not observed in things such as light and the like.
["In the rejection of both"]—the rejection of both rejectability and adoptability—["the absurd consequence of the doctrine of eternalism (<s>śāśvatavāda</s>)"] would arise—that is, the doctrine of the eternality of the self. Although <s>Pradhāna</s>, which is adoptable, is also eternal, nevertheless it is non-eternal in its modified form. Multiplicity, impurity, being <s>avidyā</s>, being for the sake of another—such faults belong to <s>Pradhāna</s>. If <s>Puruṣas</s> too had such a nature, the absurd consequence of no liberation would follow—because of the non-difference of bondage and liberation from their respective causes, knowledge and ignorance, from their essential natures, and the absurd consequence of no distinction between the bound and the liberated. Therefore, by the rejection of both rejectability and adoptability, the doctrine of eternalism—["that itself is right vision (<s>samyagdarśana</s>)." // 15 //]

body.text: tadetacchāstraṁ caturvyūhamityabhidhīyate –
body.translated_text: That this <s>śāstra</s> has a fourfold structure is now stated—

body.text: heyaṁ duḥkhamanāgatam ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: The suffering that is yet to come is to be avoided (<s>heya</s>). // 16 //

body.text: duḥkhamatītamupabhogenātivāhitaṁ na heyapakṣe vartate। vartamānaṁ ca svakṣaṇe bhogāruḍhamiti na tatkṣaṇāntare heyatāmāpadyate। tasmādyadevānāgataṁ duḥkhaṁ tadevākṣipātrakalpaṁ yoginaṁ kliśnāti netaraṁ pratipattāram। tadeva heyatāmāpadyate ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: Past suffering, having been undergone through experience, does not fall within the category of what is to be avoided. And present suffering, having mounted the experience of its own moment, does not become avoidable in the next moment. Therefore, only that future suffering, which—like a stroke of lightning—afflicts the <s>yogin</s>, not the other, the ordinary person—only that is to be avoided. // 16 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
yathā cikitsyavyatiriktarogādicatuṣṭayamantareṇa cikitsāśāstramārogyaprayojanaṁ caturvyūhaṁ na saṁbhavati, tathedamapi hātṛsvarūpavyatiriktaheyādicatuṣṭayamantareṇa samyagdarśanaśāstraṁ hānaphalaṁ caturvyūhaṁ na sambhavatīti, heyādicatuṣṭayapratipādanena [tadetacchāstraṁ caturvyūhamabhidhīyate ॥]
katham ? [heyaṁ duḥkhamanāgatam । duḥkhamatītam] atikrāntaṁ, vartamānājjanmano'tikrāntajanmalakṣaṇaṁ duḥkhaṁ, [tadupabhogenātivāhitam] atinītaṁ na heyapakṣe vartate ! svayameva hīnatvāt ॥
[vartamānaṁ ca] yajjanmalakṣaṇaṁ duḥkham [svakṣaṇopabhogārūḍham] svaṁ vartamānaṁ bhogaviśiṣṭaṁ kṣaṇamadhvānamupabhujyamānātmakatvenārūḍha़ṁ [tat] duḥkhaṁ [na kṣaṇāntare heyatāmāpadyate ।] svayameva bhogena hīnaṁ na hānāya kṣaṇāntaramapekṣate ॥
[tasmādyadevānāgataṁ] prāyaṇānantarabhāvijanmaduḥkhalakṣaṇaṁ [duḥkhaṁ tadevākṣipātrakalpaṁ yoginaṁ kliśnātīti tadeva heyaṁ] samyagdarśanena hānīyamucyate । bhaviṣyajjanmābhāvāyaiva yatitavyam । na vartamānaduḥkhanirodhāya ॥
vartamānajanmayiyatiṣāyāṁ hi samyagdarśanamaśakyaviniyogatvādanarthakaṁ syāt । muktabāṇavat pravṛttaphalatvādvartamānaduḥkhasya । bhaviṣyati punarapravṛttatvādbījanirodha upakalpata iti samyagdarśanārthavatvam । svaviṣayo hi samyagdarśanasya sa iti ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇa</s> (Elucidation):
Just as medical science (<s>cikitsāśāstra</s>), whose purpose is health, is not possible without the fourfold [structure] of the patient and the rest, so too this <s>śāstra</s> of right vision, whose fruit is cessation [of suffering], is not possible without the fourfold [structure] of what is to be rejected and the rest, apart from the nature of the abandoner. Through the exposition of this fourfold [structure]—what is to be rejected and the rest—["this <s>śāstra</s> has a fourfold structure."]
How? ["The suffering that is yet to come is to be avoided. Past suffering"]—that which has passed, the suffering characterized by past births relative to the present birth—["having been undergone through experience,"] having been traversed, does not fall within the category of what is to be avoided—because it has already been eliminated of its own accord.
["And present"] suffering characterized by the present birth, ["having mounted the experience of its own present moment"]—its own present moment of enjoyment having been assumed in the form of being experienced—["that"] suffering ["does not become avoidable in the next moment."] Having been eliminated of its own accord through experience, it does not require another moment for its avoidance.
["Therefore, only that future"] suffering characterized by the birth that will come after death—["that suffering, which like a stroke of lightning, afflicts the <s>yogin</s>—only that is to be avoided"]—it is said to be avoidable through right vision. One should strive for the non-arising of future birth, not for the cessation of present suffering.
For if one were to strive against present-birth [suffering], right vision would be purposeless, since it cannot be effectively applied—because present suffering, like an arrow already released, has its fruition already in motion. But regarding future [suffering], since [its fruition] has not yet commenced, the suppression of its seed is possible—hence right vision has purpose. For that [future suffering] is the proper object of right vision. // 16 //

body.text: tasmādyadeva heyamityucyate tasyaiva kāraṇaṁ pratinirdiśyate –
body.translated_text: Therefore, the cause of what has been called 'to be avoided' is now indicated—

body.text: draṣṭṛdṛśyayoḥ saṁyogo heyahetuḥ ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: The conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) and the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is the cause of what is to be avoided (<s>heyahetu</s>). // 17 //

body.text: draṣṭā buddheḥ pratisaṁvedī puruṣaḥ। dṛśyā buddhisattvopārūḍhāḥ sarve dharmāḥ। tadetaddṛśyamayaskāntamaṇikalpaṁ saṁnidhimātropakāridṛśyatvena svaṁ bhavati puruṣasya dṛśirūpasya svāminaḥ, anubhavakarmaviṣayatāmāpannaṁ yataḥ। anyasvarūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakaṁ svatantramapi parārthatvātparatantram। tayordṛgdarśanaśaktyoranādirarthakataḥ saṁyogo heyaheturduḥkhasya kāraṇamityarthaḥ। tathā coktam – tatsaṁyogahetuvivarjanātsyādayamātyantiko duḥkhapratīkāraḥ। kasmāt, duḥkhahetoḥ parihāryasya pratīkāradarśanāt।
body.translated_text: The seer is <s>Puruṣa</s>, the experiencer of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect). The seen comprises all <s>dharmas</s> (phenomena) that have risen to [manifestation through] the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>. This seen, like a lodestone, functioning merely through proximity as that which is to be seen, becomes [the seen] of <s>Puruṣa</s>, the master whose nature is seeing—since it has entered the condition of being an object of experiential action. Having obtained its existence through the form of another [i.e., <s>Puruṣa</s>], though independent [in itself], it is dependent because of being for the sake of another. The beginningless, purposeful conjunction of these two—the powers of seeing and of being seen—is the cause of what is to be avoided, meaning the cause of suffering. And thus it has been said: 'By the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction, there would be this ultimate remedy for suffering. Why? Because a remedy is seen for the removable cause of suffering.'

body.text:
vivaraṇam
tadetacchāstraṁ caturvyūhamabhidhīyata ityuktam । ekaścaturṣu vyūhaḥ pratipāditaḥ [heyaṁ du:khamanāgata] miti । idānīṁ dvitīyo vyūhaḥ [tasya] duḥkhasya [kāraṇaṁ] , hetuḥ [pratinirdiśyate ॥]
nanu nirdiṣṭamava duḥkhakāraṇamiti, tathaivopasaṁhṛtamante – [tasyaitasya mahato du:khasamudāyasya prabhavabījamavidyeti ।] satyamevam । kintu du:khasvarūpamātraṁ tatkāraṇasvarūpamātraṁ ca pūrvaṁ nirdiṣṭam । na ca tatsvarūpamātre, iti tatkāraṇaṁ nirdiśyate । [draṣṭṛdṛśyayoḥ saṁyogo heyahetuḥ ॥]
draṣṭā ca dṛśyaṁ ca draṣṭṛdṛśye । tayerdraṣṭṛdṛśyayoriti । draṣṭṛdṛśyasaṁyoga iti tu vaktavye pṛthagvibhaktigrahaṇaṁ tayorbhinnajātīyatvakhyāpanārtham । bhoktṛbhogyayoḥ svasvāminoḥ pradhānapuruṣayoriti vā sūtrayituṁ śakyata eva । tathāpi draṣṭṛdṛśyagrahaṇamanena draṣṭṛdṛśyatvenaiva saṁyogo nānyathetyevamartham ॥
[draṣṭā buddheḥ pratisaṁvedī puruṣo] vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇaḥ । pratisaṁvedituṁ śīlamasya sa pratisaṁvedī । kasya ? [buddhe] riti । [dṛśyā buddhiḥ] antaḥkaraṇaṁ pratyayarūpeṇa ॥
nanu ca śabdadayo'pi viṣayā dṛśyā evetyata āha – [satvopāruḍhāḥ saveṁ dharmāḥ] śabdādayo buddhisatvamupārūḍhā buddhipratyayākārā eva dṛśyā na svataḥ । svataśca dṛśyatve jñātājñātaviṣayatvaṁ puruṣasya syāt । sadā jñātaviṣayatvaṁ ca puruṣasya nyāyena sthāpyate । tasmādbuddhayupārūḍhā eva sarve dharmā dṛśyāḥ ॥
[tadetaddṛśyamayaskāntamaṇikalpam] ayaso'pi kriyārthenaivopakartā'yaskāntamaṇiryathā, tathā [puruṣasya] puruṣārthena dvividhena bhogāpavargalakṣaṇenopakartṛtvādayaskāntamaṇiriva [svaṁ dṛśirūpasya] cititvarūpamātrasya [svāminaḥ ॥]
kathaṁ svamityata āha – [karmaviṣayatvamāpannaṁ] karmaiva viṣayaḥ karmaviṣayaḥ, karmatvāpattireva । viṣayo dṛśirūpasya dṛśyatāmāpanna ityetat । kathambhūtaṁ satkarmaviṣayatāmāpadyata iti tadviśeṣaṇārthamāha – [anyasvarūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakamiti ॥]
anyasvarūpeṇa svaparapuruṣarūpeṇa śabdādirūpeṇa ca pratilabdhātmakaṁ pratilabdhaviśeṣarūpaṁ pratilabdhapuruṣaśabdādiviśeṣasvabhāvaṁ puruṣasvarūpeṇa labdhātmakaṁ saddṛśyatvena karmatāmāpannamapavargārthena svaṁ bhavati । śabdādyākāreṇa labdhātmakaṁ saddṛśyatvena karmatāmāpannaṁ bhogārthena svaṁ bhavati ॥
nanu kathaṁ svatantrasya svatvam । na hi kiñcit svatantraṁ svayaṁ vyāpriyamāṇamanyadapekṣate । yadapi svavyāpārānuniṣpādipuruṣārtharūpaṁ, tadapi svabhāvādeva । na puruṣaniyogakāri । tasmāt svatantrasya sataḥ svatvaṁ na yuktamityata āha – [svatantramapi] puruṣārthadvayakartṛtvena [parārthatvātt paratantram ।] tataśca svameva ॥
[tayordṛgdarśanaśaktyoriti ।] draṣṭṛdṛśyayorityupakramasya dṛgdarśanaśaktyorityupasaṁhāraḥ, buddhipuruṣasaṁyogasya buddhyutpattyanantarabhāvitvādādimattvamāśaṅkya tadanādimattvapradarśanārthaṁ kriyate । [dṛgdarśanaśaktyoranādiḥ saṁyogaḥ ।] dharmiṇāṁ nityatvāt nityasambandhopapattestacchaktyorapi draṣṭṛdṛśyatvalakṣaṇo'nādiḥ saṁyogo' [rthakṛtaḥ] puruṣārthaprayojanavaśa ityarthaḥ ॥
tathā ca satyanāditve'pi prayojananivṛttau saṁyoganivṛttirupapadyate । dharmiṇāṁ tu svarūpasaṁyogaḥ sattāmātreṇa na prayojanakṛta iti nitya eva । dharmamātrābhistvanityābhiranityaḥ saṁyogaḥ । sa tu buddhipuruṣasaṁyogo [heyahetuḥ duḥkhasya kāraṇam] ityarthaḥ ॥
[tathā coktaṁ tantre – tatsaṁyogahetuvivarjanāt] tayorbuddhipuruṣayoḥ saṁyogastasya heturavidyā tadvivarjanāt । kathaṁ vivarjanam ? vidyayā samyagdarśanena tatpratipakṣeṇa nivartanāt । tasmāttatsaṁyogahetuvivarjanāt [ātyantiko'] tyantāya prabhavati [duḥkhapratīkāraḥ ।] ko'sau ? yatsamyagdarśitvam ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
It was said that this teaching is fourfold in its structure. One of the four parts has been demonstrated: ['The suffering yet to come is that which is to be avoided.'] Now the second part—[the cause of that] suffering, its reason—[is indicated.]
Objection: The cause of suffering was already indicated; and it was concluded at the end: ['The seed and source of this great mass of suffering is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).'] Reply: True indeed. But previously only the mere nature of suffering and the mere nature of its cause were indicated. And it is not the case that the mere nature [alone constitutes the teaching]—therefore the cause is now indicated: [The conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) and the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is the cause to be avoided (<s>heyahetu</s>).]
The seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) and the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) are '<s>draṣṭṛ-dṛśya</s>'; of these two, '<s>draṣṭṛ-dṛśyayoḥ</s>.' Although it could have been compounded as '<s>draṣṭṛ-dṛśya-saṃyoga</s>,' the use of separate case-endings is for the purpose of indicating that the two belong to different categories. It could also have been expressed in the <s>sūtra</s> as 'of the experiencer and the experienceable,' or 'of the master and the owned,' or 'of <s>pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>.' Nevertheless, the use of 'seer' and 'seen' [means that] the conjunction is precisely in the capacity of seer and seen, not otherwise.
[The seer is <s>Puruṣa</s>, the perceiver of <s>buddhi</s>]—whose characteristics will be described later. One whose habit it is to perceive is 'the perceiver.' Of what? [Of <s>buddhi</s>]—the intellect. [The seen is <s>buddhi</s>]—the inner organ in the form of cognition.
Objection: Sound and the other objects too are indeed seen—therefore he says: [All <s>dharmas</s> (entities), mounted upon <s>sattva</s>]—sound and the other objects, having mounted upon the <s>sattva</s> of <s>buddhi</s>, are seen only as forms of <s>buddhi</s>'s cognition—not by themselves. For if they were seen by themselves, <s>Puruṣa</s> would have both known and unknown objects. But it is established by reasoning that <s>Puruṣa</s>'s objects are always known. Therefore, all <s>dharmas</s> are seen only as mounted upon <s>buddhi</s>.
[This seen is like a lodestone.] Just as a lodestone assists iron only for the purpose of action, so too [the seen], being of service to <s>Puruṣa</s> through the twofold <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose—characterized as enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)—is like a lodestone, [being the property] of the master whose form is mere seeing (<s>dṛśirūpa</s>), whose nature is mere consciousness (<s>cititva</s>).
How is it 'its own [property]'? He says: [Having become the object of action (<s>karmaviṣaya</s>)]—action itself is the object, hence '<s>karmaviṣaya</s>'—it is the very attainment of objecthood. Being the object of one whose nature is seeing—having attained the status of the seen. In what condition does it attain the status of being an object of action? To specify this he says: [Having recovered its being through another's form.]
'Through another's form'—through the form of one's own and other <s>Puruṣas</s>, and through the form of sound and such—having recovered its being, having obtained a specific form, having obtained the nature of the specific characteristics of <s>Puruṣa</s>, sound, etc.—when it has obtained its being through <s>Puruṣa</s>'s own form, being seen and having attained the status of action-object, it becomes 'its own' for the purpose of liberation. When it has obtained its being through the form of sound and such, being seen and having attained the status of action-object, it becomes 'its own' for the purpose of enjoyment.
Objection: How can something independent (<s>svatantra</s>) be 'owned'? For nothing independent, acting of its own accord, depends on another. And whatever has the form of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose that is not accomplished without its own activity—even that is by its own nature, not acting at <s>Puruṣa</s>'s command. Therefore, ownership is not appropriate for something independent. He says: [Even though independent], by being the agent of the twofold <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose, [it is dependent because it is for another's sake.] And therefore it is indeed 'owned.'
[Of these two—the power of seeing and the power of sight.] The opening spoke of 'the seer and the seen,' and the conclusion speaks of 'the power of seeing and the power of sight'—this is done to show that the conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> is beginningless, dispelling the doubt that it begins immediately upon <s>buddhi</s>'s origination. [The conjunction of the power of seeing and the power of sight is beginningless.] Since the substrata (<s>dharmin</s>) are eternal, an eternal connection is justified; and the conjunction characterized as seer-and-seen between those powers too is beginningless—['brought about by purpose']—brought about by the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s aim.
And thus, even though [the conjunction is] truly beginningless, when the purpose ceases, the cessation of the conjunction is justified. But the conjunction of the substrata in their own form exists by mere existence, not brought about by purpose—hence it is eternal. The conjunction through properties (<s>dharma</s>) alone, being impermanent, is impermanent. And that conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> [is the cause to be avoided—the cause of suffering]—that is the meaning.
[And thus it has been said in the <s>Tantra</s>: 'Through the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction']—of that conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, the cause being <s>avidyā</s>—through the avoidance of that. How is avoidance [achieved]? Through knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), through right vision (<s>samyagdarśana</s>), through counteracting it. Therefore, through the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction, [there is] the absolute, the remedy of suffering that leads to the ultimate. What is that? Right seeing.

body.text: tadyathā – pādatalasya bhedyatā, kaṇṭakasya bhettṛtvaṁ, parihāraḥ kaṇṭakasya pādā'nadhiṣṭhānaṁ pādatrāṇavyavahitena vā'dhiṣṭhānam, etattrayaṁ yo veda loke sa tatra pratīkāramārabhamāṇo bhedajaṁ duḥkhaṁ nā''pnoti। kasmāt, tritvopalabdhisāmarthyāditi। atrāpi tāpakasya rajasaḥ sattvameva tapyam। kasmāt, tapikriyāyāḥ karmasthatvāt, sattva kriyā nāpariṇāmini niṣkriye kṣetrajñe, darśitaviṣayatvāt। sattvaṁ tu tapyamāne tadākārānurodhī puruṣo'pyanutapyata iti ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: For example: the sole of the foot is vulnerable to being pierced; the thorn has the capacity to pierce. The remedy is: either not placing the foot upon the thorn, or placing it with the protection of a shoe interposed. One who knows this triad—in the world, undertaking the remedy therein—does not incur the suffering born of piercing. Why? Because of the power of apprehending the triad. Here too, it is <s>sattva</s> alone that is burned by <s>rajas</s> the heater. Why? Because the burning action resides in the object of action (<s>karmastha</s>)—action does not exist in the unchanging, inactive knower of the field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), because his domain has been shown [to be different]. But when <s>sattva</s> is being burned, <s>Puruṣa</s> too, conforming to its form, is figuratively said to be burned. // 17 //

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kathametaditi, prasiddhaṁ dṛṣṭāntamāha-- [tadyathā--pādatalasya bhedyatā] sukumārataratvāt । [kaṇṭakasya bhetṛtvaṁ] karkaśasvabhāvatvāt । tatsaṁyogo viśiṣṭo dukhaheturityarthasiddham । tatra kaṇṭakavyathāduḥkhasya [parihāraḥ kaṇṭake padā pādena anadhiṣṭhānam] anākramaṇam । athādhiṣṭhānakārarṇa cedasti [pādatrāṇavyavahitena vā padādhiṣṭhānam । etaddvayaṁ yo veda] bhedyabhettṛdvarye parihāradvayaṁ vā yo veda [loke sa tatrā] nyataraṁ [parihāra] mārabhate । [sa tatra pratīkāramārabhamāṇī bhedajaṁ] kaṇṭakabhedajanitaṁ [duḥkhaṁ nāpnoti ॥]
tathehāpi puruṣaḥ sattvadvāreṇa kaṇṭakasthānīyaṁ pradhānam, tayorviśeṣṭaḥ saṁyego'vidyānimitto duḥkhakāraṇam , duḥkhaparihāro'pyayam – guṇagauṇebhyaḥ pradhānamātraviśeṣebhyo dṛśyebhyo nirapekṣatā, samyagdarśanena prayojanābhāvaṁ buddhvā puruṣasyāvikriyasvāt kaṇṭakādhiṣṭhānavaccharīrārambhiṇī vā karmaṇo niyatavadanīyatvādavaśyaṁ phaladāyitvaṁ buddhvā aprārthitopanatānāṁ śabdādīnāṁ samyagdarśanavyavahitena satvena bhogaḥ । evaṁ parihāraṁ sañjānānaḥ kaṇṭakabhedaduḥkhaparihāramiva saṁsāraduḥkhaṁ nāmeti ॥
kasmādetadevamiti - tritvopalabdhisāmarthyāt । pradhānapuruṣasaṁyogatritvopalabdhisāmarthyāt । evaṁ hi vijñānasya sāmarthyaṁ dṛśyate । pādatalakaṇṭakatatsaṁyogeṣvajñānasya ca tritvānupalabdherduḥkhahetutvaṁ dṛśyata eva ।
yadyevaṁ puruṣaścenna tapyate puruṣārthaṁ pradhānaṁ pravartata ityetadanupapannam । vṛttisārūpyeṇoktottarattvāt । tadevedamucyate - darśitaviṣattvāt । apariṇāmino'vikriyattvāt darśitaviṣayattvam । tasmāt dṛśikarmaṇi sattve tapye tadākārānurodhī tadākārānuvartī । tadākārānurodhitvaṁ taddṛśisannidhau bauddhasya pratyayasya dṛśirūpāvabhāsatā । yathā lākṣārasasannidhau sphaṭikasya lākṣākārāvabhāsatā, tathā puruṣo'pi tapyata ityupacaryate ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text:
[Vivaraṇa]
'How is this?' He gives a well-known illustration: [For example—the sole of the foot is vulnerable to being pierced]—because of its extreme tenderness. [The thorn has the capacity to pierce]—because of its hard nature. That their specific conjunction is the cause of suffering—this is self-evident. Therein, the [remedy for] the suffering of thorn-piercing: [either not placing the foot] upon the thorn—not stepping upon it. Or, if there is a reason for stepping: [placing the foot with the protection of a shoe interposed. One who knows this twofold]—the twofold [nature of] vulnerable and piercing, or the twofold remedy—one who knows [this, in the world], undertakes [one or the other] remedy. [One who undertakes the remedy therein does not incur the suffering born of] thorn-[piercing].
So too here: <s>Puruṣa</s>, through the medium of <s>sattva</s>, [encounters] <s>pradhāna</s> which stands in the place of the thorn. Their specific conjunction, caused by <s>avidyā</s>, is the cause of suffering. And the remedy for suffering is also this: indifference toward the entities of the <s>guṇas</s> and their secondary modifications—the seen—as mere variants of <s>pradhāna</s>; or, understanding through right vision that there is no purpose [remaining], and understanding that because of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s immutability—as in the case of stepping on a thorn—even though <s>karma</s> initiated for embodiment must necessarily yield its fruit due to its determined nature, the enjoyment of uninvited objects like sound and the rest [occurs] through <s>sattva</s> interposed by right vision. Thus, one who knows the remedy does not incur the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>, just as one avoids the suffering of thorn-piercing.
Why is this so? Because of the power of apprehending the triad. Because of the power of apprehending the triad of <s>pradhāna</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s>, and their conjunction. For such indeed is the power of knowledge. And with regard to the sole of the foot, the thorn, and their conjunction, the ignorance's failure to apprehend the triad is seen to be the cause of suffering.
If so, if <s>Puruṣa</s> does not [itself] suffer, then the statement that <s>pradhāna</s> acts for <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose would be unjustified. [Reply:] This has been answered by the statement about conformity to modifications. That is precisely what is said here: because its domain has been shown [as such]. Because of being unchanging and immutable, its domain is that of being shown objects. Therefore, when <s>sattva</s>, the object of seeing (<s>dṛśikarman</s>), is being burned, <s>Puruṣa</s>, conforming to its form, following its form— the conformity to its form is the fact that the intellectual cognition (<s>bauddha pratyaya</s>), in the proximity of seeing (<s>dṛśi</s>), appears as having the nature of seeing. Just as a crystal, in the proximity of lac-juice, appears as having the form of lac—so too <s>Puruṣa</s> is figuratively said to 'suffer.' // 17 //

body.text: dṛśyasvarūpamucyate –
body.translated_text: The nature of the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is stated:

body.text: prakāśakriyāsthitiśīlaṁ bhūtendriyātmakaṁ bhogāpavargārthaṁ dṛśyam ॥ 18 ॥
body.translated_text: The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) has the nature of illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>), activity (<s>kriyā</s>), and stability (<s>sthiti</s>); consists of elements (<s>bhūta</s>) and sense-organs (<s>indriya</s>); and serves the purposes of enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). // 18 //

body.text: prakāśaśīlaṁ sattvam। kriyāśīlaṁ rajaḥ। sthitiśīlaṁ tama iti। ete guṇāḥ parasparoparaktapravibhāgāḥpariṇāminaḥ saṁyogaviyogadharmāṇa itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ parasparāṅgāṅgitve'pyasaṁbhinnaśaktipravibhāgāstulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśaktibhedānupātinaḥ pradhānavelāyām upardaśitasaṁnidhānā guṇatve'pi ca vyāpāramātreṇa pradhānāntarṇītānumitāstitāḥ puruṣārthakartavyatayā prayuktasāmarthyāḥ saṁnidhimātropakāriṇo'yaskāntamaṇikalpāḥ pratyayamantareṇaikatamasya vṛttimanu vartamānāḥ pradhānaśabdavācyā bhavanti। etaddṛśyamityucyate।
body.translated_text: <s>Sattva</s> has the nature of illumination. <s>Rajas</s> has the nature of activity. <s>Tamas</s> has the nature of stability. These <s>guṇas</s>, with their mutual colorings and distinctions, are transforming, possess the properties of conjunction and disjunction, build their forms through mutual support, and though having the relationship of principal and subordinate parts, have undivided powers and distinctions. Following the distinctions of powers of the same and different kinds, at the time of <s>pradhāna</s> [equilibrium] they remain in a state of proximate presence as shown [earlier]. Even in their capacity as <s>guṇas</s>, by their mere activity, they are inferred to exist as subsumed within <s>pradhāna</s>. Set in motion by the obligation to fulfill <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose, assisting by their mere proximity, like a lodestone—following the activity of any one of them without [needing] an intermediary cognition—they are denoted by the word '<s>pradhāna</s>.' This is what is called 'the seen.'

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[dṛśyasvarūpamucyate ।] nanu ca [draṣṭṛdṛśyayo] rityuktaṁ pūrvasūtre । tatra kramaprāptasannidhānaṁ dṛṣṭrasvarūpameva pūrvaṁ vaktavyam । naiṣa doṣaḥ । dṛśyasvarūpāvagamapūrvakatvāddraṣṭṛsvarūpāvabedhasya । dṛśyasya hi svātmavyatiriktadraṣṭrarthavādvyatiriktadraṣṭṛsadbhāvasiddhiḥ । ata eva prādhānyāt pūrvasūtre draṣṭuḥ pūrvanipātaḥ kṛtaḥ । tallakṣaṇe tvarthakramo vivakṣyate ॥
[prakāśakriyāsthitiśīlaṁ bhūtendriyātmakaṁ bhogāpavargārthaṁ dṛśyam ।] prakāśaśca kriyā ca sthitiśca prakāśakriyāsthitayaḥ । prakāśasyābhyarhitatvāt pūrvanipātaḥ । bahuṣu cāniyamāt sthitikriyāśabdayoraniyama iti kriyāśabdasya pūrvanipātaḥ । tā eva śīlaṁ yasya tatprakāśakriyāsthitiśīlam । prakāśanaṁ prakāśaḥ, sa śīlaṁ yasya [tat prakāśaśīlaṁ sattvam ।] nanu ca yadā prakāśanaṁ kriyā, kathaṁ । tacchīlaṁ sattvaṁ syāta 1 rajo hi tacchīlaṁ, sthitiśīlaṁ vā tamaḥ kathamiti ॥
nanu ca svarūpameva tatprakāśanaṁ sthitiśca । na । svarūpamātre śīlaśabdāyogāt । na hi mṛdaṅgaśīle mārdaṅgikaḥ । mṛdaṅgavādanaśīlo hi sa ucyate । na hi vyāpāraśūnye kvacidapi śīlaśabdaḥ · prayujyate ॥
nanu ca sthitiprakāśāvapi sattvatamasoḥ svarūpam । tadetenaiva gamyate svarūpe śīlaśabdaḥ prasaṁkṣyata iti । ucyate – na svarūpe sarvatra śīlaśabdaprayogaḥ । ihāpi rajasi duḥkhasvarūpe kriyāśīlamiti kriyayā samprayujya śīlaśabdavyapadeśaḥ । sthitiprakāśāvapi vyāpārarūpāvabhipretau ॥
atha mataṁ – kriyāpi rajasaḥ svarūpameveti – na – pradhānāvasthāyāṁ sāmyābhyupagamāt guṇānām । yadi kriyā rajasaḥ svarūpamabhaviṣyat pradhānasyāpi kriyāvatvaṁ guṇasāmyāvasthāyāmabhuviṣyat । kāryāvasthāyāṁ hi kriyāvatvamabhyupagamyate, na pradhānavelāyām । tasmānna svarūpābhiprāyeṇa śīlaśabdaprayogaḥ ॥
tatrākriyāśīlayorapi sattvatamasornityaṁ kriyāśīlena rajasā saṁyogādrajaḥ kriyayaiva kriyāvattvaṁ sthitiprakāśayorapīti tatkriyopacāreṇa [prakāśaśīlaṁ sattvaṁ sthitiśīlaṁ tama] iti vyapadiśyate । sthitiprakāśayorātmalābhasya rajaḥkriyāpūrvatvāccalatorevābhivyaktestācchīlyaṁ sattvatamaserucyate ॥
tatra [prakāśaśīlaṁ] yattatsattvam । [kriyāśīlaṁ] pravṛttiśīlaṁ [rajaḥ । sthitiśīlaṁ] varaṇaśīlaṁ niyamaśīlaṁ [tama ityete guṇāḥ parasparoparaktapravibhāgāḥ] paraspareṇoparakta: pravibhāge bhedo yeṣāṁ guṇānāṁ te [parasparoparatapravibhāgāḥ ॥]
yathā prakāśaśīlamiti sattvamucyate'traiva । rajaḥkriyoparañjanāt sarvāvabhāsasamarthasyāpi satvasya niyataprakāśatvaṁ tamauparaktatvena । tathā rajaso'pi pravṛttyabhivyaktiḥ sattvoparāgeṇa ! niyatapravṛttitvaṁ tu tamauparāgeṇa ! tathā tamase'pi sthilyabhivyaktiḥ satvoparāgeṇa ! sthitiśīlatvaṁ rajauparāgeṇa । sthitistu svata eva । rajase'pi pravṛttiḥ svataḥ । sattvasyāpi prakāśaḥ svata eva । itthamevānyeṣvapi kāryeṣu satvādīnāmitaretaroparāgo draṣṭavyaḥ ॥
[saṁyogaviyogadharmāṇaḥ ।] saṁyogaśva viyogaśva saṁyogaviyogau, tau dhamaiṁ yeṣāṁ te saṁyogaviyogadharmāṇaḥ । kasmiṁścit kāryaṁ aārambhabhmāṇe guṇapradhānabhāvenānyonyaṁ saṁyujyante । tathaivārabdhakāryavirodhidharmāntarodaye parasparaṁ viyujyante ॥
[iteretaropāśreyaṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ] -mahadādistambaparyantā mūrtaya itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitā dharmadharmilakṣaṇā yaiste itarataropāśrayeṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ ॥
[parasparato bhinnā api] -paramārthato'nyonyato'nyo'pi । [asambhinnaśaṁtipravibhāgāḥ] -atyantaṁ vyāvṛttakāryārambhābhimukhyasāmathryaprabhedāḥ ॥
etaduktaṁ bhavati – ekasmin kārya ārabdhavye'tyantavyatiṣaktaparasparaśaktayaḥ kāryārambhakāle pṛthaktvenānupalakṣyamāṇaśaktipravibhāgā iti ॥
[tulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśatibhedānupatinaḥ ।] sātvikānāṁ sattvaṁ tulyajātiḥ, rājasānāṁ rajastulyajātiḥ, tāmasānāṁ tama iti ca । parasparāpekṣayā tu bhinnajātīyatvam । tulyajātīyātulyajātīyānāṁ śaktiprabhedamanupatituṁ śīlaṁ yeṣāṁ te [tulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśaktiprabhedānupatinaḥ ।] na hi sāttvike vā rājase tāmase vā prārabdhavyasya trayāṇāṁ śaktiprabhedānupātamantareṇa kāryārambhaḥ sambhavati ॥
yadyevaṁ sarvaśaktiprabhedānupātitvadekaikasya kāryārambhe tulyai prādhānyamityata āha – [pradhānavelāyāmupadarśitasannidhānāḥ] sarve । ekaikasmin prādhānyena svakāryārambhiṇi tatkāla itarayorapi sannidhānamupasarjanabhāvenopadarśitamiti [pradhānavelāyāmupadarśitasannidhānāḥ ।] na hi sarveṣāṁ yugapat prādhānyam । samapradhānatve hi pradhānameva bhaveyuḥ, na kāryarambhitvam ॥
athecyate – kathaṁ punarekasmin prādhānyena kāryārambhiṇītarāstitvamavagamyata iti । taducyate – [guṇatve] copasarjanabhāve [ca vyapāramātreṇa] pradhāna upalakṣyamāṇena vyāpāramātreṇa । [pradhānāntarnītena] na hi pradhānasyāntarnāto vyāpāraḥ itarayorupasarjanabhāvenāsānnidhāne saṁbhaviṣyatīti pradhānavyāpariṇā [numitāstitvāḥ ॥]
[puruṣārthetikartavyatāprayuktasāmarthyāḥ] puruṣārthe bhogāpavargau tasyetikartavyatā yathā yathā arthaniṣpattistathā tathā prayuktaṁ kāryārambhaṁ prati [sāmarthyaṁ] yeṣāṁ te [puruṣārthetikartavyatāprayuktasāmarthyāḥ ॥]
[sannidhimātropakāriṇaḥ] vikārapratyayarūpasannidhimātreṇa puruṣasyepakurvantīti [sannidhimātre.opakāriṇaḥ । ayaskāntamaṇikalpāḥ ॥]
pratyayaṁ vṛttiṁ jñānamantareṇa ekatamasya vṛttiṁ sthitilakṣaṇāṁ samatāmanuvartamānāḥ । [pradhānaśabdavācyā bhavānti ।] naiva triguṇīvyatirekeṇānyatpradhānaṁ nāmāsti । ta eva guṇā: sāmyāvasthāḥ pradhānaikaśabdābhidhānīyakaṁ pratipadyante । vaiṣamyaṁ bhajante vikāraśabdābhidheyā vṛttimante bhavanti ॥
[etaddṛśyamityucyate ।]
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇa (Elucidation):
[The nature of the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is stated.] But it was said in the previous <s>sūtra</s>: 'of the seer and the seen.' There, by the order of proximity, the nature of the seer should be stated first. This is not a defect, because the understanding of the seer's nature is preceded by the understanding of the seen's nature. For the existence of a seer distinct from oneself is established by the fact that the seen has the purpose of a seer other than itself. Hence, due to primacy, the seer was mentioned first in the previous <s>sūtra</s>. But in defining it, the logical order of subject matter is intended.
[The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) has the nature of illumination, activity, and stability; consists of elements and sense organs; and serves the purposes of experience (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).] Illumination, activity, and stability are <s>prakāśa</s>, <s>kriyā</s>, and <s>sthiti</s>. Illumination (<s>prakāśa</s>) is mentioned first because of its preeminence. Since there is no fixed order among the many, and since there is no fixed order between the words '<s>sthiti</s>' and '<s>kriyā</s>,' the word '<s>kriyā</s>' is placed first. That whose nature (<s>śīla</s>) is these [three] is 'having the nature of illumination, activity, and stability.' Illumination (<s>prakāśana</s>) is <s>prakāśa</s>; that whose nature is that [is <s>sattva</s>, which has the nature of illumination.] But if illumination is an activity, how can <s>sattva</s> have that nature? For it is <s>rajas</s> that has the nature of activity; or how can <s>tamas</s> have the nature of stability?
But illumination and stability are simply the essential nature of <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s> respectively—no, because the word '<s>śīla</s>' (nature/disposition) is inapplicable to mere essence. For a drum-player is not called one 'whose nature is the drum'; rather, he is called one 'whose nature is drum-playing.' For the word '<s>śīla</s>' is never used where there is no activity.
But illumination and stability too are the essential nature of <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>—from this very [argument] it follows that the word '<s>śīla</s>' would be forced upon the essential nature. It is said: the word '<s>śīla</s>' is not used everywhere for essential nature. Here too, regarding <s>rajas</s> whose essential nature is suffering, the designation '<s>śīla</s>' is applied through conjunction with activity as '<s>kriyāśīla</s>' (having the nature of activity). Stability and illumination too are intended as having the form of activity.
If one thinks that activity too is simply the essential nature of <s>rajas</s>—no, because the equilibrium of the <s>guṇas</s> is accepted in the state of <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter). If activity were the essential nature of <s>rajas</s>, then even in the state of <s>pradhāna</s> there would be activity in the equilibrium of the <s>guṇas</s>. But activity is accepted only in the state of effects, not in the state of <s>pradhāna</s>. Therefore the word '<s>śīla</s>' is not used with the intention of essential nature.
In this regard, <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>, though not having the nature of activity themselves, through their perpetual conjunction with <s>rajas</s> which has the nature of activity, possess activity through the activity of <s>rajas</s> alone—and the same applies to stability and illumination. Thus, by the figurative attribution of that activity, [<s>sattva</s> is designated as having the nature of illumination, and <s>tamas</s> as having the nature of stability]. Since the attainment of stability and illumination is preceded by the activity of <s>rajas</s>, and since only what moves manifests, the 'nature' (<s>śīla</s>) is attributed to <s>sattva</s> and <s>tamas</s>.
Therein, [that which has the nature of illumination] is <s>sattva</s>. [That which has the nature of activity]—the nature of movement—[is <s>rajas</s>. That which has the nature of stability]—the nature of veiling, of restraint—[is <s>tamas</s>. These <s>guṇas</s> have their distinctions colored by one another]—colored by one another, with their distinctions qualified by each other.
Just as <s>sattva</s> is said to have the nature of illumination—here itself, through being colored by the activity of <s>rajas</s>, even though <s>sattva</s> is capable of illuminating everything, it has limited illumination through being colored by <s>tamas</s>. Likewise, the manifestation of the activity of <s>rajas</s> occurs through being colored by <s>sattva</s>; but its limited activity is through being colored by <s>tamas</s>. Likewise, the manifestation of the stability of <s>tamas</s> occurs through being colored by <s>sattva</s>; and its nature of stability is through being colored by <s>rajas</s>. But stability belongs to <s>tamas</s> of itself; activity belongs to <s>rajas</s> of itself; illumination belongs to <s>sattva</s> of itself. In this manner, the mutual coloring of <s>sattva</s> etc. in other effects too should be understood.
[Having the property of conjunction and disjunction.] Conjunction and disjunction are their properties. When initiating some effect, they conjoin with one another in a principal-subordinate relationship. And likewise, upon the arising of a different property that opposes the initiated effect, they disjoin from one another.
[Having forms acquired through mutual dependence]—the forms from <s>mahat</s> (the great principle) up to a blade of grass, characterized as properties and their substrates, are acquired through mutual dependence.
[Though truly distinct from one another]—in the ultimate sense, each is different from the others. [Having undivided dispositions of power]—having undivided classifications of power directed toward the initiation of effects.
This amounts to saying: when a particular effect is to be initiated, their powers are so thoroughly interwoven with one another that, at the time of initiating the effect, the classifications of power cannot be separately identified.
[Following the divisions of power of similar and dissimilar kinds.] For <s>sāttvika</s> (effects dominated by <s>sattva</s>), <s>sattva</s> is the similar kind; for <s>rājasa</s> effects, <s>rajas</s>; for <s>tāmasa</s> effects, <s>tamas</s>. Relative to each other, however, they are of dissimilar kind. Those whose disposition is to follow the classifications of power of similar and dissimilar kinds—for no effect, whether <s>sāttvika</s>, <s>rājasa</s>, or <s>tāmasa</s>, can be initiated without all three following the classifications of power.
If so, then since each follows all classifications of power, there would be equal primacy of each in every effect-initiation—to this he says: [All have their presence displayed at the time of primacy.] When one is primary in initiating its own effect, at that time the presence of the other two is displayed in a subordinate capacity. For there is no simultaneous primacy of all. If there were equal primacy, they would remain as <s>pradhāna</s> (undifferentiated primordial matter) and not initiate any effect.
If one asks—how is the existence of the others known when one is primary in effect-initiation?—to that it is said: [In the subordinate state] and [by activity alone]—by the activity that is observed, through which the principal manifests. [Absorbed within the principal]—for the activity that is absorbed within the principal would not be possible if the other two in their subordinate capacity were not present. Therefore [their existence is inferred from the activity of the principal.]
[Having powers directed by the proper procedure for the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>]—the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s> is experience (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>); the proper procedure for that is the manner in which the accomplishment of that purpose proceeds; the power directed toward initiating effects in accordance with that—those whose powers are thus directed.
[Assisting by mere proximity]—assisting <s>Puruṣa</s> by the mere proximity in the form of a modification-cognition. [Like a lodestone.]
Without a cognition—that is, without a modification, a cognition—following the one [<s>guṇa</s>] whose modification has the character of stability, maintaining equilibrium—[they are designated by the word <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter).] For there is no <s>pradhāna</s> other than the triad of <s>guṇas</s>.
