And the means for their removal has been explained in the second <s>pāda</s> (chapter). Therefore, <s>vāsanā</s> is not an obstacle to <s>kaivalya</s> when right knowledge has arisen. When <s>avidyā</s> ceases, <s>kaivalya</s> indeed comes to be. || 11 ||

body.text: nāstyasataḥ saṁbhavaḥ, na cāsti sato vināśa iti dravyatvena saṁbhavantyaḥ kathaṁ nivartiṣyante vāsanā iti।
body.translated_text: There is no coming into being of what does not exist, nor is there destruction of what exists — so how will <s>vāsanās</s>, which exist as real substances, be brought to cessation?

body.text: atītānāgataṁ svarūpato'styadhvabhedāddharmāṇām ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text: The past and the future exist in their own form, [the difference being] due to the distinction of time-paths (<s>adhvan</s>) of <s>dharmas</s> (properties). || 12 ||

body.text: bhaviṣyadvyaktikamanāgatamanubhūtavyaktikamatītaṁ svavyāpāropāruḍhaṁ vartamānaṁ, trayaṁ caitadvastu jñānasya jñeyam। yadi caitatsvarūpato nābhaviṣyannedaṁ nirviṣayaṁ jñānamudapatsyata। tasmādatītānāgataṁ svarūpato'stīti। kiṁca bhogabhāgīyasya vā'pavargabhāgīyasya vā karmaṇaḥ phalamutpitsu yadi nirupākhyamiti taduddeśena tena nimittena kuśalānuṣṭhānaṁ na yujyeta। sataśca phalasya nimittaṁ vartamānīkaraṇe samarthaṁ nāpūrvopajanane। siddhaṁ nimittaṁ naimittikasya viśeṣānugrahaṇaṁ kurute nāpūrvamutpādayatīti।
body.translated_text: That whose manifestation is yet to come is future; that whose manifestation has been experienced is past; that which is engaged in its own activity is present. And this triad is the object to be known by knowledge. If this [triad] did not exist in its own essential form, then knowledge would arise without an object. Therefore, the past and future exist in their own essential form. Moreover, if the fruit of <s>karma</s> — whether pertaining to worldly experience (<s>bhoga</s>) or to liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) — were non-existent for one who wishes [to produce it], then skillful practice undertaken with that aim, motivated by that cause, would not be possible. And an instrumental cause is capable of making an existing fruit present — not of producing something entirely new. An established cause confers a specific advantage upon its effect; it does not produce something entirely unprecedented.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
nanu caiṣāmabhāve tadabhāva ityuktam । tathā ca siddhāntahāniḥ ! katham ? evaṁ hi siddhāntaḥ [nāstyasataḥ sambhavaḥ] utpattiḥ । [na cāsti sato vināśa] iti । atha punaḥ santi vāsanāstadā, [dravyatvena] (vastusatyaḥ) [[sambhavantyaḥ] kathaṁ nivartiṣyante ।] naiva nivartiṣyanta ityarthaḥ । tatra kathamuktameṣāmabhāve tadabhāva iti । kathaṁ vā kaivatyamanivṛttāsu hetukṛtajanmasu vāsanāsvityata uttaraṁ paṭhati - [atītānāgataṁ svarūpato'styadhvabhedāddharmaṇām ॥]
evaṁ vaitat । atha vā siddhāntapakṣeṇaiva neyaṁ bhāṣyam । katham ? [eṣāmabhāve tadabhāvaḥ] iti hetvādīnāṁ vāsanānāṁ ca nātyantābhāva ucyate । kasmāt ? [nāstyasataḥ sambhavo na cāsti sato vināśa iti dravyatvena] vastutayā [sambhavantyaḥ kathaṁ nivartiṣyante vāsanāḥ ।] śabdavikalpitatve vāsanā nātyantaṁ nivartiṣyante । santyevātītasvarūpeṇetyarthaḥ ॥
[bhaviṣyadvyaktikaṁ] bhaviṣyati vyaktiḥ yasya tat [bhaviṣyadvyaktikam ।] yathā piṇḍāvasthāyāṁ ghaṭarūpam । pravṛttetikartavyatāsādhanaṁ tat [anāgatam । bhūtavyaktikamatītaṁ] bhūtā atikrāntā vyaktirupalabdhirviṣayatvāpattiryasya । yathā prabhagno ghaṭaḥ tadatītamityucyate । avyaṅgyamabhaviṣyat yasya vyañjane sādhanamupādeyam । anatītavyaktikamabhūtam । kiṁ tarhi? [vyāpāropārūḍha़ṁ tat vartamānam ।] yathā ghaṭaḥ svakriyāyāḥ ॥
[trayaṁ caitat] atītānāgatavartamānalakṣaṇakaṁ vartamāne dharmiṇi vartamāne dharmarūpaṁ [vastu] samastalokaviniścitarūpasyāvyabhicāriṇo jñānasya pramāṇabhūtasya [jñeyam] hi saṅgirāmahe । kasmāt? niścitajñānotpattiviṣayatvāt ॥
[yadi caitadvastu svarūpato nābhaviṣyat nedaṁ nirviṣayaṁ jñānamudapatsyata ।] yathā śaśaviṣāṇādi niścitajñānotpatikāraṇaṁ na bhavati । na ca tatheha niścitavastujñānotpattihetuviṣayatvaṁ na vidyate । sakalajanānubhavaviṣayamidaṁ jñānaṁ vartate । ghaṭo bhaviṣyati ghaṭo bhūta iti ca । tasmādvastveva kālatrayasambandhi । pariniścitajñānotpattiviṣayatvāt ॥
atha vā nāvastuviṣayamatīte bhaviṣyati ca ghaṭādau jñānam । śabdavikalpitatve sati niścitarūpeṇa utpadyamānatvāt, vartamānaghaṭādiviṣayajñānavat । avyabhicārācca । liṅgānumeyatvācca, dhūmena agnyādijñānavat । liṅgadarśanānantarotpattervā ॥
yadvā, atītamanāgataṁ ca vastu sat svarūpeṇa, liṅgadarśanānantarabuddhiviṣayatvāt, prasiddhānumeyavat । tasmādatītānāgataṁ svarūpato'sti ॥
kiṁ ca - [bhogabhāgīyasya] bhogahitasya yāgāde:, [apavargabhāgīyasya vā] apavargahitasya samādhyādeḥ [karmaṇaḥ phalamutpitsu] yasya nāsti tasya vādinaḥ tat [nirupākhyaṁ] prāpnoti śaśaviṣāṇavat । na hi śaśaviṣāṇaṁ bhaviṣyatītyupākhyāyate । na tatheha । kiṁ tarhi ? yāgena svargo bhaviṣyati, samādhyādinā mokṣo bhaviṣyati iti ca kuśalaiḥ atikaṭhoramatibhirupākhyāyate ॥
tasmāt nirupākhyatvāt [taduddeśena] phaloddeśena । nirupākhyatvāt [tena] phalena [nimittena kuśalānujñānam] idaṁ kuru bhaviṣyati trānenādaḥ iti svayamapratipadyamānāḥ kuśalāḥ kathamanujānīyuḥ upadiśeyurvā । kiṁ ca, dṛṣṭamātrapratipattau kuśalākuśalāviśeṣaśca prāpnoti । kuśalānāṁ vā mithyāpratipattiḥ ‘akuśalāḥ samīcīnadarśanāḥ’ iti ॥
kiṁ ca, abhāvajñānāt kuśalā api phalāya nābhisamīheran । abhāvāviśeṣācca kāraṇaniyamo nākalpiṣyata । (na) sarvato vā sarvamudapatsyata । nāpi kāraṇamupādāsyata । upādāne vā tailārthī saikatamapyupādāsyata kiṁ tilairanekāyāsaniṣpādyaiḥ । atyantāsadapūrvaṁ cedamajaniṣyata । na caitad dṛṣṭam ॥
tasmāttadbhogabhāgīyamapavargabhāgīyaṁ vā karma [nimitaṁ] kāraṇaṁ vidyamānasyaiva tasya phalasya [vartamānīkaraṇe samarthaṁ nāpūrvopajane । siddhaṁ] hi svenātmanā [nimittaṁ] sthālī kṣīradharmātañcanādi dadhyādikasya [naimittikasya] karkaśatarabhāvādyabhivyaktidvāreṇa [viśeṣānugrahaṁ kurute-nāpūrvameva dadhi utpādayati] tatheha bhogabhāgīyādikarma ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
But it was stated that 'in the absence of these [causes], there is the absence of that [effect].' And thus there would be a loss of the established doctrine! How? For the doctrine is: ["there is no origination of the non-existent"] — no production. ["Nor is there destruction of the existent."] If, then, the <s>vāsanās</s> (latent impressions) exist, ["being of the nature of substance"] (real entities), ["how will they cease?"] — they would never cease, is the meaning. Then how was it said 'in the absence of these, there is the absence of that'? And how could there be <s>kaivalya</s> if the <s>vāsanās</s> that give rise to births through their causes have not ceased? To this he reads the answer — ["The past and future exist in their own essential form, due to the difference of time-paths (<s>adhvan</s>) of the <s>dharmas</s>."]
This is indeed so. Or alternatively, this <s>Bhāṣya</s> passage should be interpreted according to the established doctrine itself. How? ["In the absence of these, there is the absence of that"] — what is said is not the absolute non-existence of the causes and <s>vāsanās</s>. Why? ["There is no origination of the non-existent, nor destruction of the existent; being of the nature of substance,"] as real entities, ["how will the <s>vāsanās</s> cease?"] Even if they are conceptually constructed by words, the <s>vāsanās</s> will not absolutely cease. They exist in their past essential form — this is the meaning.
["That whose manifestation is yet to come"] — that in which manifestation will be in the future — is ["that whose manifestation is yet to come."] Like the form of a pot in the state of a lump [of clay]. That which is the means for accomplishing what is yet to be done is ["the future. That whose manifestation has been experienced is the past"] — that whose manifestation, apprehension, and becoming an object [of cognition] have passed. Like a broken pot — that is called 'past.' That which is unmanifested is that whose means of manifestation is yet to be adopted. That whose manifestation has not passed is not past. What then? ["That which is engaged in its activity is the present."] Like a pot [engaged] in its own function.
["This triad,"] characterized as past, future, and present, in its present property-form while the property-bearer is present, ["is an object"] to be cognized by knowledge that is of unfailing nature, ascertained by the entire world and constituting a valid means of knowledge. Why? Because it is the object of the arising of certain knowledge.
["If this object did not exist in its own essential form, then knowledge would arise without an object."] Just as a hare's horn does not become the cause of the arising of certain knowledge. And it is not the case here that there is no object-nature for the arising of certain knowledge of objects. This knowledge operates within the scope of everyone's experience — [the knowledge that] 'the pot will be' and 'the pot was.' Therefore, the object is indeed related to the three times — because it is the object of the arising of certain knowledge.
Alternatively — knowledge concerning a past or future pot and the like is not without an object. Because, being of the nature of verbal conceptualization, it arises in the form of certainty, like knowledge of a present pot and the like. And because it is unfailing. And because it can be inferred through a mark (<s>liṅga</s>), like knowledge of fire from smoke. Or because it arises immediately after the perception of the mark.
Or: a past and future object exists in its own essential form, because it is the object of cognition arising immediately after the perception of the mark — like what is well-known to be inferable. Therefore, the past and future exist in their own essential form.
Moreover — ["If the fruit of <s>karma</s>, whether pertaining to experience"] — beneficial for experience, such as sacrifice — ["or pertaining to liberation"] — beneficial for liberation, such as <s>samādhi</s> — ["were non-existent for one who wishes,"] then for such a proponent, it ["would be without designation"] — like a hare's horn. For a hare's horn is not designated as 'it will be.' Not so here. Rather, 'through sacrifice, heaven will come to be' and 'through <s>samādhi</s> and the like, liberation will come to be' — this is designated by the skilled and those of extremely sharp intellect.
Therefore, since it would be without designation, ["for the purpose of that"] — for the purpose of the fruit — since it would be without designation, ["skillful instruction"] [motivated by] ["that"] fruit as ["the cause"] — 'do this and that will come from it' — those who are themselves unable to understand, how would the skilled instruct or guide [them]? Moreover, in the apprehension of merely what is seen, there would follow no distinction between the skilled and the unskilled. Or the apprehension of the skilled would be erroneous — [with the consequence that] 'the unskilled have correct vision.'
Moreover, from knowledge of non-existence, even the skilled would not endeavor towards the fruit. And since non-existence is undifferentiated, there would be no restriction of causes. Or, everything would arise from everything. Nor would anyone adopt a [specific] cause. Or, if one did adopt one, then one seeking oil would adopt even sand — why bother with sesame that requires much labor? Something absolutely non-existent, entirely unprecedented, would have arisen. And this is not observed.
Therefore, that <s>karma</s> pertaining to experience or to liberation — the ["cause"] is capable of ["making present"] that very fruit which already exists — ["not of producing something entirely new. An established cause"] — like a pot, milk, heating, and the like for curds — ["confers a specific advantage upon its"] effect — through the manifestation of harder states and such — ["it does not produce entirely new curds."] So too here with <s>karma</s> pertaining to experience and the like.

body.text: dharmī cānekadharmasvabhāvastasya cādhvabhedena dharmāḥ pratyavasthitāḥ। na ca yathā vartamānaṁ vyaktiviśeṣāpannaṁ dravyato'styevamatītamanāgataṁ ca। kathaṁ tarhi, svenaiva vyaṅgyena svarūpeṇānāgatamasti। svena cānubhūtavyaktikena svarūpeṇātītamiti। vartamānasyaivādhvanaḥ svarūpavyaktiriti na sā bhavatyatītānāgatayoradhvanoḥ। ekasya cādhvanaḥ samaye dvāvadhvānau dharmisamanvāgatau bhavata eveti nābhūtvā bhāvastrayāṇāmadhvanāmiti ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text: And the property-bearer is of the nature of multiple properties, and its properties are established according to the difference of time-paths (<s>adhvan</s>). But it is not the case that the past and future exist as substances in the same way that the present exists, having attained a particular manifestation. How then? The future exists in its own unmanifested essential form. And the past exists in its own essential form whose manifestation has been experienced. The manifestation of essential form belongs only to the present time-path; it does not belong to the past and future time-paths. And at the time of one time-path, the other two time-paths, being connected with the property-bearer, do exist — thus there is no arising from non-existence for the three time-paths. ॥ 12 ॥

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kiṁ ca, [dharmī cānekadharmasvabhāvo] 'nekadharmātmā । yathā kanakapiṇḍaḥ śāntoditāvyapadeśyarucakakuṇḍalādidharmātmakaḥ । tasya dharmiṇaḥ adhvabhedena atītādilakṣaṇabhedena [dharmāḥ pratyavasthitāḥ ॥]
[yathā vartamānaṁ] vastu [vyaktiviśeṣāpannaṁ] kuṇḍalādivyaktiprāptaṁ [dravyataḥ] kāryarūpataḥ [asti] vyāpārādhirūḍhatayā, [naivamatītamanāgataṁ ca । kiṁ tarhi? svenaiva vyaṅgyena svarūpeṇa] bhaviṣyatā [anāgatamasti । svena cānubhūtavyaktikena] atikrāntopalabdhikena [atītamasti ॥]
[vartamānasyaiva tvadhvanaḥ svarūpato vyaktiriti na sā] vyaktiḥ [bhavatyatītānāgatayoradhvanoḥ । ekasya cādhvanaḥ samaye kāledvāvadhvānau dharmisamantāgātau] virodhāt [na bhavata eveti ।] tathā cokto'śvasaṁkaraparihāraḥ ॥
yasya punaratītamanāgataṁ ca lakṣaṇaṁ svarūpeṇa nāsti, tasya dharmāṇāmadhvabhedo na prāpnoti । katham ? na hi tasya ghaṭo bhaviṣyannatīto vā vidyate । na hi kapālāni piṇḍo vā ghaṭaḥ । ityekasya vartamānasyaivādhvanaḥ. samaye trayāṇāmadhvanāṁ dharmatvena samāgamaḥ syāt । ataśca vartamāna eva ghaṭo'tīto'nāgata iti cocyeta piṇḍakapālayoraghaṭatvāt mṛdi ca ghaṭasyābhāvādbhaviṣyati ghaṭo'tīto ghaṭa iti ca piṇḍakapāle nirucyeyātām । tathā ca vivakṣato gairapyaśva iti syādadho'pi gai.auriti ॥
athocyeta, ghaṭasya pragabhāvapradhvaṁsābhāvāvatītānāgatatvenābhidhīyete iti । tato'pyeṣa pāpīyānabhyupagamaḥ । tatra yuktamapi gauraśva iti vastutvādetayoḥ । na tviha vastuvācinā śabdena ghaṭo'tīto'nāgata iti cābhāvasyābhidhānaṁ yujyate sa[tya]tvavādinām ॥
nāpi niyama upapadyate । ghaṭenaiva vyapadiśyate, ghaṭo'tīto ghaṭe bhaviṣyatīti ca । na punaḥ kulālādibhirapadiśyate kulālādayo'tītā bhaviṣyanti veti ॥
atha ghaṭasyaiva tatrānupalabhyamānatvāditi cet-na-hastiśārdūlādīnāmapi tatrānupalambhe vyapadeśaprasaṅgāt । athopalabdhapūrvasyaiva vyapadeśa iti cet-na- ghaṭakriyādiṣvapi prasaṅgāt ॥
atha ghaṭasya tena kriyādyabhāva iti cet-na-abhāvasya sambandhaviśeṣānupapatteḥ । na hi samavāyalakṣaṇaḥ prāptilakṣaṇo vā sambandho bhāvābhāvayoravakalpate । yenāsau ghaṭasya abhāvo na punaḥ kriyādīnām । anyatarasambandhe ca abhāvasya vastutvaprasaṅgaḥ । atha vastveveti cet, siddhastarhi bhaviṣyannatītaśca padārthaḥ ॥
athopacārāt siddhakapālāvasthā avayavā bhaviṣyati ghaṭo bhūto ghaṭa iti cāpadiśyeran sambandhāt, tadyathā-annaṁ prāṇā iti, atrāpi yathā kulālacakradaṇḍasūtrādiṣu ghaṭo nāsti, tathā piṇḍakapāleṣvapīti tadabhāvaviśeṣe ca kapāleṣu ghaṭe'tīta iti vyapadeśo na kulālādiṣviti niyamānupapattiḥ ॥
na cāpi vidyamānānāṁ sādhanānāṁ ghaṭādiniṣpādināmapyavidyamānairutpādyairghaṭādibhiḥ sambandha upapadyate । na cāsati sambandhe ghaṭotpādanābhiprāyeṇa kārakapravṛttiḥ ॥
athāyutasiddhaḥ samavāyalakṣaṇaḥ sambandho janyānāṁ kāraṇānāṁ ca na pratiṣidhyata iti cet-na-yutasiddhāyutasiddhatvasya samānakālabhāvināṁ vastūnāṁ darśanāt । na bhāvābhāvayoḥ kvacidapi yutasiddhatvamayutāsiddhatvaṁ vā dṛśyate ॥
tasmājjanyajanakānāmapi sambandhābhyupagamādvidyamānatvameveti, utpatteḥ prāgūrdhvaṁ ca vidyate kāryam, vastvantarasambandhāt, prasiddhaghaṭādivat । upalapsyamānatvādupalabdhatvācca, apavarakasthaghaṭadivat । uddiśya kartrā prāpyatvāt, deśāntaravat । tathā kartṛvyāpāraprāpyatvācceti ॥
kiṁ ca, na laukikā atītānāgataśabdābhyāṁ gaganakamalinavidavidyamānamarthaṁ pratiyanti pratipādayanti vā । tasmādatītamanāgataṁ ca svarūpato vidyata eva । [nābhūtvā bhāvastrayāṇāmadhvanām ।] kiṁ tarhi ? vidyamānānāmevābhivyaktiḥ ॥
tasmādvyaktirūpeṇa vāsanānāmatyantāvinivṛttiḥ । guṇarūpeṇa tu satīnāmapi kāryāsamarthatvānna kaivalyābhāvadoṣaḥ । nāpi siddhāntavirodhaḥ ॥ 12 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
Moreover, ["the property-bearer is of the nature of multiple properties"] — it has the nature of multiple properties. Just as a lump of gold has the nature of the properties of earring, bracelet, and so on — quiescent, arisen, and indeterminate. The properties of that property-bearer ["are established according to the difference of time-paths"] — according to the distinction of past and the like.
["The present"] object, ["having attained a particular manifestation"] — having reached the manifestation of earring and the like — ["exists as a substance"] — in the form of an effect — through being engaged in activity. ["Not so the past and future. How then? The future exists in its own essential form that is to be manifested."] And ["the past exists in its own essential form whose manifestation has been experienced"] — whose apprehension has passed.
["The manifestation of essential form belongs only to the present time-path; it"] — that manifestation — ["does not belong to the past and future time-paths. And at the time of one time-path, the other two time-paths, being connected with the property-bearer,"] due to mutual opposition, ["do not exist"] — [more precisely,] thus [it has been stated]. And thus the resolution of the 'horse-mixture' [objection] has been stated.
But for one who holds that the past and future characteristics do not exist in their own essential form, the difference of time-paths of the <s>dharmas</s> is not tenable. How? For him, a future or past pot does not exist. For neither potsherds nor a lump [of clay] is a pot. Thus, at the time of only one present time-path, the three time-paths would converge as properties [of the same thing]. And thus the present pot alone would be called 'past' and 'future' — since the lump and potsherds are not pots, and since there is no pot in the clay. [It would follow that] the lump and potsherds would be designated as 'the pot will be' and 'the pot was.' And thus, for one who wishes [to speak this way], a cow could also be a horse, and what is below could also be a cow.
If one were to say that the prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) and the posterior non-existence (<s>pradhvaṁsābhāva</s>) of the pot are designated as future and past — that is an even worse admission. In that case, even the designation 'a cow is a horse' would be justified, since both [absences] are real entities. But here, it is not justifiable for proponents of the reality [of things] to designate absence by a word that denotes a [positive] entity — 'the pot is past' or 'the pot is future.'
Nor is the restriction tenable — that it is designated only with reference to the pot: 'the pot is past,' 'the pot will be.' For it is not designated with reference to the potter and the like: 'the potter is past,' 'the potter will be.'
If [one argues] that [it is because] the pot is not apprehended therein — no, because there would be the unwanted consequence of [such] designation with regard to elephants, tigers, and the like, which are also not apprehended therein. If [one argues] that designation applies only to what has been previously apprehended — no, because there would be the unwanted consequence [of such designation] with regard to the pot's activities and the like as well.
If [one argues] that there is an absence of that activity in the pot — no, because a specific relation of absence is untenable. For neither a relation characterized by inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) nor one characterized by contact (<s>prāpti</s>) is conceivable between an existent and a non-existent. By which [relation] that absence would belong to the pot but not to the activities. And if there is some other relation, then absence would be a real entity. If one were to say it is indeed a real entity, then a future and past object is established!
If [one argues] that figuratively, the established constituent-state — the parts such as potsherds — would be designated as 'the pot will be' and 'the pot was' on the basis of [some] relation, like 'food is the vital breaths' — even here, just as the pot does not exist in the potter, wheel, stick, string, and the like, so too it does not exist in the lump and potsherds. And the restriction that the designation 'the pot is past' applies to the specific absence in the potsherds but not in the potters and the like is untenable.
Nor can there be a relation between existing means of production — which produce pots and the like — and non-existing things to be produced such as pots and the like. And without a relation, the activity of an agent with the intention of producing a pot is [untenable].
If [one argues] that the inseparable relation characterized by inherence between effects and their causes is not denied — no, because it is observed that things existing at the same time are [sometimes] separably and [sometimes] inseparably established. Nowhere is separable or inseparable establishment observed between an existent and a non-existent.
Therefore, from the acceptance of a relation between effects and their causes, their existence [follows]. And an effect exists both before and after its production, because of its relation with other entities, like a well-known pot and the like. Because it will be apprehended and because it has been apprehended — like a pot inside a room. Because it is to be attained by an agent who has aimed at it — like another place. And because it is to be attained through the agent's activity.
Moreover, ordinary people do not understand or communicate, by the words 'past' and 'future,' a meaning that is non-existent like a sky-lotus. Therefore, the past and future exist in their own essential form indeed. ["There is no arising from non-existence for the three time-paths."] Rather, there is merely the manifestation of what already exists.
Therefore, the <s>vāsanās</s> do not absolutely cease in their manifest form. But even though they exist in the form of <s>guṇas</s>, because of their incapacity to produce effects, there is no fault regarding the absence of <s>kaivalya</s>. Nor is there a contradiction with the established doctrine. ॥ 12 ॥

body.text: te vyaktasūkṣmā guṇātmānaḥ ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text: They — whether manifest or subtle — are of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>. ॥ 13 ॥

body.text: te khalvamī tryadhvāno dharmā vartamānā vyaktātmāno'tītānāgatāḥ sūkṣmātmānaḥ ṣaḍviśeṣarūpāḥ। sarvamidaṁ guṇānāṁ saṁniveśaviśeṣamātramiti paramārthato guṇātmānaḥ। tathā ca śāstrānuśāsanam – guṇānāṁ paramaṁ rūpaṁ na dṛṣṭipathamṛcchati। yattu dṛṣṭipathaṁ prāptaṁ tanmāyeva sutucchakam ॥ iti ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text: These properties belonging to the three time-paths — those that are present have a manifest nature; those that are past and future have a subtle nature — are of the form of the six <s>viśeṣas</s> (particularities). All this is merely a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇas</s> — thus in the ultimate sense they are of the nature of the <s>guṇas</s>. And thus the scriptural teaching — 'The supreme form of the <s>guṇas</s> does not come within the range of sight. That which has come within the range of sight is merely <s>māyā</s>, utterly trifling.' ॥ 13 ॥

body.text:
vivaraṇam
atītānāgatavartamānadharmā: kena punā rūpeṇa santīti tatpratipādanārthamāha- [te vyaktasūkṣmā guṇātmānaḥ । te khalvamī tryadhvānaḥ] atītānāgatavartamānādhvatrayopārūḍhāḥ [dharmāḥ vartamānāḥ] vartamānalakṣaṇopārūḍhāḥ [vyaktātmānaḥ] lokapratyayaviṣayībhūtasvabhāvāḥ । [atītānāgatāḥ sūkṣmātmānaḥ] lokapratyayaviṣayabhāvamaprāptāḥ [ṣaḍaviśeṣasvarūpāḥ] asmitādisvabhāvāḥ । tataśca vyaktātmānaḥ ṣoḍaśavikārāḥ kāryakāraṇalakṣaṇāḥ ॥
[sarvamidam] adhyātmikaṁ kāryakāraṇarūpaṁ vyaktātmakaṁ, yacca sūkṣmamaviśeṣalakṣaṇamasmitādi, yacca liṅgamātraṁ sūkṣmatvāviśeṣat, [sarvamidaṁ] jagat [guṇānāṁ] sattvarajastamasāṁ prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlānāṁ [sanniveśaviśeṣamātramiti paramārthato guṇātmānaḥ] guṇasvabhāvāḥ ॥
[tathā ca śāstrānuśāsanam-guṇānāṁ paramaṁ rūpaṁ] svaṁ paramārtharūpamanapāyopajanātmakamekaikasya । tacca na [dṛṣṭipathamṛcchati ।] na dṛṣṭigocarībhavati । [yatu dṛṣṭipathaṁ prāptaṁ] guṇāparimardena viṣamabhāvakṛtasanniveśalakṣaṇaṁ, [tanmāyeva] na tu māyaiva, asāratvāttu māyāvaditi । [sutucchakam] atyalpamakadaśamātrapariṇāmatvāt sāmyāvasthānāṁ guṇānām ॥ 13 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
In what form do <s>dharmas</s> of the past, future, and present exist? To explain this, he says — ['They are manifest and subtle, having the <s>guṇas</s> as their essence. These indeed, belonging to the three time-paths'] — mounted upon the three paths of past, future, and present — ['<s>dharmas</s> that are present'] — mounted upon the present characteristic — ['are of manifest nature'] — their essential nature has become the object of worldly cognition. ['Those that are past and future are of subtle nature'] — they have not attained the status of being objects of worldly cognition — ['having the nature of the six non-specifics (<s>ṣaḍaviśeṣa</s>)'] — having the nature of <s>asmitā</s> (ego-sense) and the rest. And therefore, those of manifest nature are the sixteen modifications, characterized as effects and causes.
['All this'] — the subjective realm in the form of effects and causes having a manifest nature, and what is subtle with the characteristic of the non-specific such as <s>asmitā</s> and so on, and what is the mere mark (<s>liṅgamātra</s>) due to its subtlety and non-specificity — ['all this'] universe — ['is merely a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇas</s>'] — of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>, whose natures are luminosity, activity, and inertia — ['in ultimate reality, they have the <s>guṇas</s> as their essence'] — their essential nature is that of the <s>guṇas</s>.
['And thus the teaching of the <s>śāstra</s> — the supreme form of the <s>guṇas</s>'] — the ultimate form of each individual <s>guṇa</s>, whose nature is neither diminishing nor arising. And that ['does not come within the range of vision.'] It does not become an object of perception. ['But what has come within the range of vision'] — having the characteristic of arrangement produced by the imbalanced state through the mutual friction of the <s>guṇas</s> — ['is like <s>māyā</s> (illusion)'] — not that it is illusion itself, but because of its insubstantiality it is like illusion. ['Most trifling'] — extremely small, because of being a transformation of merely one-tenth of the <s>guṇas</s> in their state of equilibrium. ॥ 13 ॥

body.text: yadā tu sarve guṇāḥ kathamekaḥ śabda ekamindriyamiti –
body.translated_text: But if everything is the <s>guṇas</s>, then how is there one sound and one sense organ? —

body.text: pariṇāmaikatvādvastutattvam ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text: The reality of a thing (<s>vastu-tattva</s>) is due to the unity of transformation (<s>pariṇāma-ekatva</s>). ॥ 14 ॥

body.text: prakhyākriyāsthitiśīlānāṁ guṇānāṁ grahaṇātmakānāṁ karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotramindriyaṁ, grāhyātmakānāṁ śabdatanmātrabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣaya iti, śabdādīnāṁ mūrtisamānajātīyānāmekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīparamāṇustanmātrāvayavasteṣāṁ caikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivī gaurvṛkṣaḥ parvata ityevamādirbhūtāntareṣvapi snehauṣṇyapraṇāmitvāvakāśadānānyupādāya sāmānyamekavikārārambhaḥ samādheyaḥ।
body.translated_text: Of the <s>guṇas</s>, whose natures are luminosity (<s>prakhyā</s>), activity (<s>kriyā</s>), and inertia (<s>sthiti</s>), those that have the nature of apprehension — their single transformation in the form of an instrument is the ear, the sense organ. Those that have the nature of the apprehensible — their single transformation in the form of the sound <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element) is sound, the object. Of those similar in type to sound and the other [subtle elements] that have physical form — their single transformation is the earth atom, consisting of <s>tanmātra</s> parts. And of those [atoms], one transformation is earth — a cow, a tree, a mountain, and so on. In the other elements too, by taking into account the properties of moisture, heat, mobility, and the provision of space, a general principle of the origin of a single modification should be understood.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yadā sarve guṇāḥ] pṛthivyādayaḥ, tadā [kathamekaḥ śabdaḥ] śaṅkhādijanitaḥ । [ekamindriyaṁ] śrotrādikamityekabuddhyālambanatvaṁ bhavet । na khalu bhavitavyam । triguṇatvena hi kāraṇena traya iti pratyayaḥ syāt । evamindriyāṇāṁ ca pratyekaṁ tritvam । tathā ca niyamo na prāpnoti । na hi grāhyatvamekasyaiva śabdasya, grāhakatvaṁ caikasya śrotrasya, iti niyama upakalpate । tathā sparśādiṣu, tvagindriyādiṣu ca yojyam । niyamaśca dṛśyate । [kāraṇaṁ] tatra vacanīyamityāha- [pariṇāmaikatvādvastutatvam ॥]
[prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlānāṁ guṇānāṁ grahaṇātmakānāṁ] satvaprādhānyāt bodhātmanāmasmitāsaṁsthānānāṁ [karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotrendriyam ।] yathā viruddhānāṁ tailavartitejasāṁ pradīpaḥ । tathā tvagādīndriyeṣu puruṣārthetikaraṇīye prayuktānāmekaikamindriyaṁ pariṇāma iti yojyam ॥
tathā [grāhyātmakānāṁ] guṇānāṁ tamaḥpradhānānāṁ [śabdabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣayaḥ ।] tathā [śabdādīnāṁ mūrtisamānajātīyānāṁ] samānām [ekaḥ] gandha [tanmātrāvayavaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīparamāṇuḥ । teṣāṁ] paramāṇūnām [ekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivī gaurvṛkṣaḥ parvata ityevamādiḥ ॥]
[bhūtāntareṣvapi] yojyam । śabdasparśarūparasānāṁ snehasamānajātīyānām [ekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ rasatanmātrāvayavaḥ jalaparamāṇuḥ । teṣāṁ paramāṇūnāmekaḥ pariṇāme jalam] ॥
śabdasparśarūpāṇāmuṣṇatvasamānajātīyānāmekaḥ pariṇāmo rūpatanmātrāvayavaḥ tejaḥparamāṇuḥ । teṣāṁ paramāṇūnāmekaḥ pariṇāmo vahniḥ salilendhano dāruśakaladīpanaśca ॥
tathā śabdasparśayoḥ praṇāmitvasamānajātīyayoḥ sparśatanmātrāvayavaḥ vāyuparamāṇurekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ । teṣāṁ paramāṇūnāmekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ vāyuḥ sapta marudgaṇāśca ॥
tathā śabdatanmātrāvayavānāmanāvṛtatvasamānajātīyānameka: pariṇāma ākāśaḥ । ityevamuktena mārgeṇa [snehauṣṇyapraṇāmitvādyupādāya sāmānyūmekavikārārambhaḥ samādheyaḥ] yojyaḥ । tasmādbahūnāmapyekapariṇāmitvādekaviṣayatvaṁ, grāhyagrahaṇaniyamaśca sarvamupapadyate ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
['If everything is the <s>guṇas</s>'] — earth and the rest — then ['how is there one sound'] — produced from a conch and the like? ['One sense organ'] — the ear and the rest — how could there be a cognition grasping them as unitary? Surely there should not be. For because of being three <s>guṇas</s>, the cognition should be of three. Likewise, each sense organ would be triple. And thus no restriction would obtain. For the restriction that only one sound is the apprehensible, and only one ear is the apprehender, cannot be established. Similarly, this should be applied to touch and the rest, and to the skin and other sense organs. Yet restriction is observed. ['The reason'] for this must be stated — thus he says — ['The reality of a thing is due to the unity of transformation.']
['Of the <s>guṇas</s>, whose natures are luminosity, activity, and inertia, those that have the nature of apprehension'] — because of the predominance of <s>sattva</s>, having the nature of cognition, having the configuration of <s>asmitā</s> — ['their single transformation in the form of an instrument is the ear, the sense organ.'] Just as a lamp is [a single entity formed from] contradictory elements — oil, wick, and fire. Similarly, in the skin and other sense organs, being employed for the accomplishment of <s>Puruṣa</s>'s purpose, each individual sense organ is a single transformation — this should be understood.
Likewise, ['of the <s>guṇas</s> that have the nature of the apprehensible,'] with <s>tamas</s> predominating, ['their single transformation in the form of sound is sound, the object.'] Likewise, ['of those similar in type to sound and the rest, having physical form,'] of similar kind — ['one'] smell — ['<s>tanmātra</s>-part transformation is the earth atom. Of those'] atoms, ['one transformation is earth — a cow, a tree, a mountain, and so on.']
['In the other elements too,'] this should be applied. Of sound, touch, and form, which are of a similar type with respect to moisture — one transformation is the <s>tanmātra</s>-part water atom. Of those atoms, one transformation is water.
Of sound, touch, and form, which are of a similar type with respect to heat — one transformation is the <s>tanmātra</s>-part fire atom. Of those atoms, one transformation is fire — kindled by water-fuel, wood-fuel, and lamp-fuel.
Likewise, of sound and touch, which are of a similar type with respect to mobility — one transformation is the <s>tanmātra</s>-part air atom. Of those atoms, one transformation is air — the seven groups of winds (<s>Maruts</s>).
Likewise, of those that are parts of the sound <s>tanmātra</s>, being of a similar type with respect to non-obstruction — one transformation is space (<s>ākāśa</s>). Thus, by the method stated, ['by taking into account the properties of moisture, heat, mobility, and the provision of space, a general principle of the origin of a single modification should be understood.'] Therefore, even though there are many constituents, because of their having a single transformation, there is a single object, and the restriction of apprehensible and apprehender is fully established. ॥ 14 ॥

body.text: nāstyartho vijñānavisahacaraḥ, asti tu jñānamarthavisahacaraṁ svapnādau kalpitamityanayā diśā ye vastusvarūpamapahnuvate jñānaparikalpanāmātraṁ vastu svapnaviṣayopamaṁ na paramārthato'stīti ya āhuste tatheti pratyupasthitamidaṁ svamāhātmyena vastu kathamapramāṇātmakena vikalpajñānabalena vastusvarūpamutsṛjya tadevāpalapantaḥ śraddheyavacanāḥ syuḥ ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text: There is no object without the accompaniment of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>); but there is knowledge without the accompaniment of an object — in dreams and the like, being merely imagined. In this direction, those who deny the essential nature of things, [asserting that] things are mere mental fabrication, comparable to dream objects, and do not truly exist — how can those who, having themselves apprehended a thing that has presented itself in its own grandeur, then deny that very thing by the force of conceptual knowledge that is not based on valid means of cognition — how can their words be trusted? ॥ 14 ॥

body.text:
vivaraṇam
nanu ca nāsyevāsau ekapratyayaviṣayaḥ śabdādiḥ । etattu sarvaṁ vijñānaparijṛmbhitameva, vijñānabhāvabhāvitvāt । kathaṁ tadbhāvabhāvitvamityāha - [nāstyartho vijñānavisahacaraḥ] pṛthagvijñānādupalabdha: pṛthagbhāvī vā । [vijñānamarthavisahacaraṁ] pṛthaktvenopalabdha pṛthagbhāvi vā [asti ।] tasmādartho vijñānavyatirekeṇa nāstīti pratijānīmahe ॥
pramāṇamapyatra bhavati- vijñānavyatirekeṇa nāsti grāhyaṁ vastu, vijñānavyatirekeṇānupalabhyamānatvāt, vijñānasvarūpavat । bāhyārthaśūnyāni jāgradvijñānāni, vijñānatvāt, svapnasamayavijñānavat । vijñānaparikalpitā vā jāgradviṣayāḥ, viṣayatvāt, svapnaviṣayavat । vijñānaṁ vā viṣayāvyatireki, vijñānatvāt, svapnavijñānavaditi ॥
yadyevaṁ syāt kiṁ naśchinnaṁ syāt ? puruṣasya dṛśyaviyogāt kaivalyaṁ prastutaṁ na siddhaṁ syāt ॥
yathā upalabhyamānasya stambhāderabhāvaḥ evamupalabhyamānatvādvijñānasyāpyabhāvaḥ । tadabhāve ca liṅgābhāvādupalabdhurapyabhāvaḥ prāpnuyāditi, kasya kaivatyam ? kena dṛśyena viyogaḥ syāt ? kena samprayoge vā bandhaḥ pratijñāyeta ? bandhābhāve cābhyudayaniḥśrayasārthapravṛttiphalatā na prasajeyata ॥
kiṁ cānyat-vijñānavyatirekeṇārtho nāstīti buvatā vijñānamartha iti caikaḥ padārthe'bhyupagato bhavati, yathā-agniranala iti । evaṁ ca sati vijñānaṁ grāhyaṁ grāhakam, arthaḥ grāhyo grāhakaśceti nāmamātre vipratipattiḥ, na punarekasya grāhyagrāhakabhāvaḥ pratyākhyāyate । tathā ca sati puruṣasyāpi grāhyagrāhakabhāvaḥ prāptaḥ । tathā'pi vipramokṣānavaklṛptiḥ, ityevamādayo bhūyāṁso doṣāḥ prāpnuvanti ॥
tasmāt [amuyā diśā] anena nyāyābhāsabalena [ye vastusvarūpamapahnuvate jñānaparikalpanāmātraṁ vastu svapnaviṣayopamam, na tu paramārthato'stīti, te] svayaṁ [tatheti] abhyupagamya [svamāhātmyena pratyupasthitaṁ vastuṁ kathamapramāṇātmakena vikalpajñānabalena vastu svayamupagṛhya] abhyupagamya [tadeva] abhyupagataṁ [apalapantaḥ] idamityabhyupetya idaṁ nāstītyapahnuvānāḥ [śraddheyavacanāḥ syuḥ ।] na hi svānubhavapratyākhyāyinaḥ śraddhānīyavacanavistārā bhavitumarhanti ॥
tatra vijñānavyatirekeṇārtho nāstīti pratyakṣavirodhinī pratijñā । saṁvedanīkārakaṁ vijñānaṁ pratīyāmaḥ । pṛthubudhnādyākāramarthaṁ pratipadyemahi । grāhakaṁ ca vijñānamavabhāsakaṁ, avabhāsanīyaścārthaḥ । svalakṣaṇabhedenārthajñānayorupalabhyamānatvānnāvyatirekagandho'pi । tataśca vyatirekeṇānupalabhyamānatvādityasiddho hetustava ॥
na ca jñānasyaiva pṛthubudhnādyākāratā । jñānasyaikasyāvabhāsyāvabhāsakatvānupapatteḥ pradīpasyeva kevalasya । bhinnayoḥ pradīpayoḥ prakāśyaprakāśakatvānupalambhādekasya ca svātmani prāptyasambhavāt, evaṁ jñānasya ॥
apicānaikāntikaśva buddhena pratipakṣavādinā ca । na cāsau nāstīti śakyaṁ pratijñātuṁ, yaṁ prati sisādhayiṣasi, sa cettadvijñānavyatiriktaḥ, tathā ghaṭādirapi sidhyati ॥
svapnajñānamapi upalabdhārthaviṣayatvāt na nirālaṁbanam । pratijñāyāḥ pratyakṣavirodho lokavirodhaśca । sarvaṁ jñānaṁ sālambanaṁ, jñānatvāt, prativādiduṣṭavākyajñānavat, svavākyaguṇajñānavacca । tataśca jñānatvādīnāṁ nirālaṁbanatvahetūnāmevamādibhiranaikāntikatā ॥ 14 ॥
body.translated_text:
<s>Vivaraṇam</s> (Elucidation)
Now, this sound and the rest is not a single object of cognition at all. Rather, all this is merely the manifestation of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), because it exists only when consciousness exists. How is its existence dependent on consciousness? He says — ['There is no object without the accompaniment of consciousness'] — found apart from consciousness or existing apart from it. ['But knowledge without the accompaniment of an object'] — found apart or existing apart — ['does exist.'] Therefore, we maintain that an object does not exist apart from consciousness.
There is also a proof here: There is no apprehensible object apart from consciousness, because it is not perceived apart from consciousness, just like the nature of consciousness itself. Waking cognitions are devoid of external objects, because they are cognitions, like dream-state cognitions. Or: waking objects are fabricated by consciousness, because they are objects, like dream objects. Or: consciousness is non-different from objects, because it is consciousness, like dream consciousness.
If this were so, what would we lose? The <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) of <s>Puruṣa</s> through separation from the seen, which is the present topic, would not be established.
Just as the non-existence of a perceived pillar and the like [is absurd], so too the non-existence of consciousness, which is perceived, [would follow]. And if that is non-existent, then due to the absence of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>), the non-existence of the perceiver too would follow — then whose <s>kaivalya</s> would there be? From what seen thing would there be separation? Or in conjunction with what would bondage be asserted? And if there is no bondage, then purposeful activity directed toward worldly prosperity and final liberation would not follow.
Moreover — by one who says 'an object does not exist apart from consciousness,' one entity is accepted under two names — consciousness and object — just as fire and flame. And this being so, consciousness is both the apprehensible and the apprehender; the object is both the apprehensible and the apprehender — the disagreement is merely about names, not that the apprehensible-apprehender relationship of one thing is denied. And this being so, the apprehensible-apprehender relationship would apply to <s>Puruṣa</s> too. And even so, the possibility of liberation would not be established — and many more such faults would follow.
Therefore, ['in this direction'] — by the force of this semblance of logic — ['those who deny the essential nature of things, asserting that things are mere mental fabrication, comparable to dream objects, and do not truly exist'] — they ['having themselves accepted'] the thing ['that has presented itself in its own grandeur, how can they, by the force of conceptual knowledge that is not based on valid means of cognition, having themselves grasped'] and accepted ['that very'] accepted thing, ['then denying it'] — having accepted 'this exists' and then denying 'this does not exist' — ['have their words trusted?'] For those who contradict their own experience cannot deserve to have their elaborate statements believed.
Regarding this — 'an object does not exist apart from consciousness' — is a proposition that contradicts direct perception. We experience consciousness as having the nature of illumination. We apprehend an object as having the form of a broad base and so on. And consciousness is the apprehender, the illuminator; and the object is what is to be illuminated. Because of being perceived as different through the distinction of their individual characteristics, there is not even a trace of non-difference. And therefore, 'because of not being perceived apart' — your reason is unestablished.
Nor does consciousness itself have the form of a broad base and so on — because it is impossible for one consciousness to be both what is illuminated and the illuminator, just as a single lamp [cannot illuminate itself]. Because two different lamps are not observed to have the relationship of illuminated and illuminator, and because one cannot reach itself — so too with consciousness.
Moreover, [your reason] is inconclusive — [as recognized] by the <s>Buddha</s> himself and by the opponent. Nor can it be maintained that 'he does not exist' — the one toward whom you wish to prove [your thesis]; if he is different from that consciousness, then a pot and the like would also be established [as different].
Dream knowledge too, because it has a previously perceived object as its content, is not without a support. Your proposition contradicts direct perception and common experience. All knowledge has a support, because it is knowledge — like knowledge of the opponent's defective statement, and like knowledge of the qualities of one's own statement. And therefore, the reasons such as 'because it is consciousness' for supportlessness are inconclusive in these and other ways. ॥ 14 ॥

body.text: kutaścaitadanyāyyam –
body.translated_text: And why is this [position of the idealists] unreasonable —

body.text: vastusāmye cittabhedāttayorvibhaktaḥ panthāḥ ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text: When the object is the same, because of the difference of minds, their paths are separate. ॥ 15 ॥

body.text: bahucittālambanībhūtamekaṁ vastu sādhāraṇaṁ, tatkhalu naikacittaparikalpitaṁ nāpyanekacittaparikalpitaṁ kiṁtu svapratiṣṭham। kathaṁ, vastusāmye cittabhedāt। dharmāpekṣaṁ cittasya vastusāmye'pi sakhajñānaṁ bhavatyadharmāpekṣaṁ tata eva duḥkhajñānamavidyāpekṣaṁ tata eva mūḍhajñānaṁ samyagdarśanāpekṣaṁ tata eva mādhyasthyajñānamiti। kasya taccittena parikalpitam। na cānyacittaparikalpitenārthenānyasya cittoparāgo yuktaḥ। tasmādvastujñānayorgrāhyagrahaṇabhedabhinnayorvibhaktaḥ panthāḥ। nānayoḥ saṁkaragandho'pyastīti।
body.translated_text: One object, having become the support of many minds, is common. That is indeed not fabricated by one mind, nor fabricated by many minds, but rather self-established. How? Because when the object is the same, there is difference of minds. With respect to an object that is the same, depending on <s>dharma</s> (merit), there is pleasurable cognition; depending on <s>adharma</s> (demerit), there is painful cognition from that very same object; depending on <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), there is deluded cognition from that very same object; depending on right vision, there is cognition of equanimity from that very same object. By whose mind, then, is that fabricated? Nor is it reasonable that an object fabricated by one mind should color another's mind. Therefore, the paths of object and knowledge — which are different as apprehensible and apprehender — are separate. Not even a trace of their commingling exists.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[kutacaitadanyāyyaṁ] gṛhyamāṇaṁ vastu nāstīti ? [vastusāmye cittebhadāttayorviviktaḥ panthāḥ । bahucittālambanībhūtaṁ] anekacittaviṣayībhūtaṁ [ekaṁ vastu] putrādikaṁ [sādhāraṇaṁ] samānam । [tat khalu] naikacittatantraṁ [bhavati ।] ekacittatantratvābhāvā [danekacittaparikalpitamapi na bhavati ॥]
[kintu svarūpapratiṣṭhaṁ] cittanirapekṣaṁ svatantratayā vyavasthitam । [katham ? vastusāmye] vastunaḥ putrāderekatve [cittabhedāt] ekasmin putrādiviṣaye viṣayiṇāṁ jñānānāmanekatvāt ॥
kathaṁ cittabheda ityāha- [dharmāpekṣaṁ cittasya vastusāmye'pi] yathā putrata eva mātāpitroḥ [sukhajñānaṁ bhavati ।] tata eva putrādeḥ [adharmāpekṣaṁ] ahitānāṁ [duḥkhajñānaṁ] upajaniṣyate ॥
[tasmodavāvidyāpekṣaṁ] kāmukānāṁ mūḍha़jñānam । [tata eva putrādeḥ samyagjñānopakṣaṁ] yogināṁ [mādhyasthyajñānaṁ] heyopādeyaśūnyamutpadyate । kauleyādīnāṁ tata eva lobhāpekṣayā bhakṣyajñānam । tata eva putrāderviraktasya kuṇapādijñānam ॥
yadi kasyaciccittena parikālpatamabhaviṣyat (na) anyacittaparikalpitenānyeṣāṁ cittamupārakṣyata । naitadyuktaṁ, atyantāsambaddhānāmadarśanāt । yadi cānyaparikalpitenāpyanyacittoparāgo'bhaviṣyat, tadā sarve'pi sarvaṁ samajñāsyanta । na cedaṁ dṛṣṭam । [tasmāt] na cittaparikalpitaṁ vastviti, [vastujñānayoḥ grāhyagrahaṇabhedādbhinnayorvivittaḥ panthāḥ । nānayoḥ saṅkaragandho'pyasti ॥]
sukhajñānālamvanībhūtaṁ putrādivastu na tajjñānaparikalpitam । tadviruddhānakacittotoparañjakatvāt, vādiprativadipratijñāguṇadoṣatadābhāsavat । vādiprativādiprabhṛtīnāmapi vijñānamātratve sādhyasādhanādivyavahāravilopaḥ syāt ॥
atha svavijñānavyatirekeṇa teṣāṁ jñānarūpāṇāmeva pṛthaktvamiti cet-astu । tadeva vastu jñānāntaraviṣayatvādarthantaraṁ siddham । sañjñāmātre vipratipattiḥ । viṣayiviṣayabhedastu na sādhyaḥ । tasmānnānayoḥ saṁkaragandho'pīti ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇam (Elucidation)
['Why is this unreasonable'] — that the object being apprehended does not exist? ['When the object is the same, due to the difference of minds, their paths are distinct. A single object'] such as a son ['which has become the support of many minds'] — the object of many cognitions — ['is common'] — shared. ['That indeed'] does not depend on a single mind. ['Because it does not depend on a single mind, it is also not fabricated by many minds.']
['Rather, it is established in its own nature'] — independent of mind, established autonomously. ['How? When the object is the same'] — when the object such as a son is one — ['due to the difference of minds'] — because the cognitions of the cognizers regarding a single object such as a son are many.
How is there difference of minds? He says: ['Depending on dharma (merit), even when the object is the same,'] just as from a son, for the parents, ['there arises the cognition of happiness.'] From that very son, ['depending on adharma (demerit),'] for enemies, ['the cognition of suffering'] arises.
['Likewise, depending on ignorance (avidyā),'] for those driven by desire, there is deluded cognition. ['From that very son, depending on right knowledge,'] for yogins, ['the cognition of equanimity'] — devoid of acceptance and rejection — arises. For dogs and such, from that very [son], depending on greed, there is the cognition of food. From that very son, for one who is dispassionate, there is the cognition of a corpse and such.
If the object had been fabricated by someone's mind, then what was fabricated by one mind would not engage the mind of another. This is not reasonable, because it is never observed among entirely unconnected things. And if the coloring of another's mind occurred even through what was fabricated by someone else, then everyone would know everything. But this is not observed. ['Therefore,'] the object is not fabricated by the mind. ['The path of the object and knowledge — of the grasped and the grasping — being different, is distinct. There is not even a trace of confusion between them.']
The object such as a son that serves as the support of the cognition of happiness is not fabricated by that cognition — because it colors many minds with contradictory [cognitions], just like the thesis and counter-thesis of a proponent and opponent, along with merits, faults, and their semblances. If even the proponent, opponent, and others were mere cognition, the conventional usage of what is to be proved, the means of proof, and so forth would collapse.
If one says that apart from their own cognition, the distinctness of those [things] is merely in the form of knowledge — so be it. That very object, being the object of another cognition, is established as something different. The disagreement is merely about terminology. But the distinction between the subject and the object is not something to be proved. Therefore, there is not even a trace of confusion between them.

body.text: sāṁkhyapakṣe punarvastu triguṇaṁ calaṁ ca guṇavṛttamiti dharmādinimittāpekṣaṁ cittairabhisaṁbadhyate। nimittānurūpasya ca pratyayasyotpadyamānasya tena tenā''tmanā heturbhavati। kecidāhuḥ – jñānasahabhūrevārtho bhogyatvātsukhādivaditi। ta etayā dvārā sādhāraṇatvaṁ bādhamānāḥ pūrvottarakṣaṇeṣu vasturūpamevāpahnuvate ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text: In the Sāṅkhya view, moreover, the object — being of the three guṇas and in motion as the activity of the guṇas — is connected with minds depending on conditions such as dharma (merit). And for a cognition that arises corresponding to its conditions, [the object] becomes the cause in that particular form. Some say: 'The object co-exists only with knowledge, because it is enjoyable — like pleasure and the like.' They too, by refuting commonality in this way, deny the very nature of the object ['in prior and subsequent moments.' || 15 ||]

body.text:
vivaraṇam
atha vastuni svarūpapratiṣṭhe'pi sukhādibhinnapratyayālambanatā na samīcīnarūpeti cet atrocyate – [vastu punastriguṇaṁ calaṁ guṇavṛttimiti dharmādinimittaṁ cāpekṣya cittaiḥ] sukhaduḥkhādibhedarūpeṇa [abhisaṁbadhyate] pariṇāmitvādanekaśaktitvācca ॥
dharmādi [nimittānurūpasya cotpadyamānasya pratyayasya tena tena] nimittena [ātmanā heturbhavati ।] satvātmanā dharmādinimittāpekṣaṁ putrādivastu sukhaheturbhavati । rajaātmanā tvadharmanimittāpekṣaṁ duḥkhaheturbhavati । tamaātmanā tvavidyāpekṣaṁ tadeva vastu mohaheturbhavati । sattāmātrātmanā samyagdarśanāpekṣaṁ tadeva mādhyasthyajñānaheturbhavati ॥
[kecidāhuḥ] eṣameva bauddhānāmanyatame bāhyamarthamabhyupagacchanta āhuḥ - [jñānasahabhūrevārthaḥ,] yathā vijñānaṁ pratikṣaṇaṁ dharmiśūnyaṁ utpadyate vinaśyati ca, tathā sahaiva jñānenārtho vijñāyate vinaśyati ca, [bhogyatvāt, sukhādivat ।] tadyathā-sukhaduḥkhādirūpaṁ bhogyaṁ vijñānasahotpattivināśamasādhāraṇam, evaṁ ghaṭādirartho'pi vijñānasamānasamayajanmavināśa eva, bhogyatvāditi ॥
te'pi tathaiva vijñānavādivat sādhāraṇatvaṁ anekasukhādicittālambanatvaṁ [bādhamānāḥ pūrvottarakṣaṇeṣu] svakīyavijñānotpatteḥ paurastyeṣu kṣaṇeṣu pāścātyeṣu ca vastu nāstīti [vastusvarūpamevāpahnuvate ॥]
tasmāt na hi vastunaḥ svarūpaṁ vijñānasahabhāvi, tadevedamiti pratyabhijñānāt । nācirajanmapralayaṁ tadevedamiti pratyabhijñāyeta, yathā vijñānam । na hi tadevādau me vijñānamiti bhavati । vastu punastadevedamiti pratyabhijñāyate । arthajñānayorekasamayabhavitve'pyeka[pariśeṣaḥ]viśeṣaḥ syāt ॥
nāpi sādṛśyāt pratyabhijñānam । grāhyagrāhakayoryugapadutpattivināśavatvāt । vyavasthite hi vastvantaradṛśye anyatatsadṛśavastudarśanena sādṛśyapratyayaḥ । evaṁ tatsadṛśaṁ vā drakṣyāmītyuttarābhilāṣaḥ । na hi tadaharniścitamaraṇasyāparedyurarthadarśanākāṁkṣā jāyate । nāpi matsadṛśa īkṣipyata ityabhilaṣati । na caivaṁ dṛṣṭam । sarvo hi svārthamīhate । bhinnasantatiṣvadarśanāt ॥
tasmādidānīṁtano'rthaḥ nedānīntanajñānasahabhūreveti, grāhyatvāt, atītārthavat । atīto vā nātītajñānasahanāśajanmā, grāhyatvāt, idānīntanārthavat । bhūtabhaviṣyajjñānagrāhyā arthā adhunā'pi santi, grāhyatvāt, adhunātanapratyayagrāhyavat ॥ idānīntanamapi vastu pūrvottarakṣaṇeṣu tathaiva ॥
atha sukhadu:khajñānādabhiranaikāntikamiti cet-na-atītānāgataṁ svarūpato'stīti sādhitatvāt । evaṁ ca sati sukhādīnāṁ ca svarūpeṇa sadbhāvāt sukhādivaditi sādhyasamāno dṛṣṭāntaḥ ॥
atha vartamānarūpaviśeṣeṇātītānāgatalakṣaṇayorarthasya sukhādivadabhāva iti cet, siddhasādhyatā । na hi kumārabhāva eva vṛddhatvaṁ vidyate ॥ 15 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇam (Elucidation)
If one objects that even when the object is established in its own nature, its being the support of cognitions differing as pleasure and pain is not proper — to this we reply: ['The object, being of the three guṇas, in motion, and consisting of the activity of the guṇas, depending on conditions such as dharma, is connected with minds'] in the form of differentiation into pleasure, pain, and the like — because it is transformable and has multiple potencies.
['For a cognition arising in conformity with its conditions such as dharma, the object becomes the cause in that particular form.'] In its sattva-nature, depending on conditions such as dharma, an object like a son becomes the cause of pleasure. In its rajas-nature, depending on the condition of adharma, it becomes the cause of suffering. In its tamas-nature, depending on ignorance, that very object becomes the cause of delusion. In its nature as mere existence, depending on right vision, that very object becomes the cause of equanimous knowledge.
['Some say'] — among these very Buddhists, those who accept external objects say: ['The object co-exists only with knowledge,'] just as cognition arises and perishes moment by moment, devoid of a substrate, so too the object is known and perishes simultaneously with knowledge, ['because it is enjoyable, like pleasure and the like.'] Just as pleasure, suffering, and such — enjoyable forms that arise and perish simultaneously with consciousness, not shared — so too an object like a pot also has birth and destruction simultaneous with consciousness, because it is enjoyable.
['They too, just like the consciousness-only advocates, refuting commonality'] — the being-supported-by-many-pleasure-minds — ['deny the very nature of the object in prior and subsequent moments.']
Therefore, the nature of the object does not co-exist [merely] with cognition, because of recognition: 'this is that very thing.' What has momentary birth and destruction could not be recognized as 'this is that,' unlike cognition. For no one thinks 'this is that very cognition I had before.' But an object is recognized as 'this is that very thing.' Even if object and knowledge occur at the same moment, there would be [at least] one distinguishing feature.
Nor is recognition due to similarity — because the grasped and the grasper both arise and perish simultaneously. For the cognition of similarity arises when, with one object remaining stable, another similar object is seen. Likewise the subsequent desire 'I shall see something similar to that.' One who is certain of dying today has no expectation of seeing objects the next day. Nor does one desire that 'one like me shall be seen.' And this is not observed. Everyone strives for their own purpose. Because this is not observed in different series [of moments].
Therefore, the present object does not merely co-exist with present knowledge — because it is graspable, like a past object. Or a past [object] does not arise and perish simultaneously with past knowledge — because it is graspable, like a present object. Objects graspable by past and future knowledge exist even now — because they are graspable, like what is grasped by present cognition. And even a present object exists similarly in prior and subsequent moments.
If one says that the inference from pleasure-knowledge and such is inconclusive: No — because the existence of the past and future in their own nature has been established. And this being so, since pleasure and such exist in their own nature, 'like pleasure and such' — the example is equivalent to what is to be proved.
If one says that in the specific form of the present, the object in its past and future characteristics is absent, like pleasure: that is proving what is already proved. For old age does not exist in the state of youth. || 15 ||

body.text: na caikacittatantraṁ vastu tadapramāṇakaṁ tadā kiṁ syāt ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: And if an object depended on a single mind, when that [mind's] means of valid knowledge is absent, what would [the object] then be? || 16 ||

body.text: ekacittatantraṁ cedvastu syāttadā citte vyagre niruddhe vā'svarūpameva tenāparāmṛṣṭamanyasyāviṣayībhūtamapramāṇakamagṛhītasvabhāvakaṁ kenacittadānīṁ kiṁ tatsyāt। saṁbadhyamānaṁ ca punaścittena kuta utpadyeta। ye cāsyānupasthitābhāgāste cāsyana syurevaṁ nāsti pṛṣṭhamityudaramapi na gṛhyeta। tasmātsvatantro'rthaḥ sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇaḥ svatantrāṇi ca cittāni pratipuruṣaṁ pravartante। tayoḥ saṁbandhādupalabdhiḥ puruṣasya bhoga iti ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text: If an object were to depend on a single mind, then when that mind is distracted or ceased, [the object] — not grasped by that [mind], not having become the object of any other [mind] — without valid cognition, with its nature unapprehended, what would it then be? And when the mind again connects with [the object], whence would it arise? And those parts of it not presented [to that mind] would not exist for it — thus if 'the back does not exist,' then 'the belly' too would not be apprehended. Therefore, the object is independent, common to all <s>Puruṣas</s>. And minds operate independently for each <s>Puruṣa</s>. From the connection of these two, there is apprehension — the experience of <s>Puruṣa</s>. || 16 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
itaśca cittatantratā vastuno nāvakalpate । ekacittatantraṁ vā vastu bhavedanekacittatantraṁ vā ? ekacittatantratve brūmaḥ – [na caikacittatantraṁ vastu tadapramāṇakaṁ tadā kiṁ syāt?] na tāvadekacittatantraṁ, [ekacittatantraṁ cedvastu syāt] yadicedamucyate, [taccitte] yaccittatantraṁ vastu tasmiṁścitte vyagre parāsakte [niruddhe vā] vinaṣṭe vā [tena] pramāṇacittena [aparāmṛṣṭaṁ] ca [anyasya cāviṣayībhūtaṁ] etacittantratayaiva, [tadā tat] vastu [apramāṇakamagṛhītasvabhāvaṁ] prāṇacittanirodhādeva [tadānīṁ kiṁ tat syāt ।] na hi kiṁcidapi syāt । vittapramāṇakaṁ tat tadabhāve na tena bhavitavyam ॥
nanu ca yathā tatpramāṇacittaṁ nirudhyate, tathaiva tadapi kṣaṇikatvānniruddhameva । kiṁ tatrābhidhānīyaṁ syāt । ucyate-na-vyavahāravilopānniyamānupapatteśca । agnirayaṁ māsprākṣīḥ, imaṁ gṛhāṇa, adaḥ pradehīti vyavahāro vilupyeta । ekacittasahakṣayatvādvastunaḥ ॥
tatsantatijamatyantasadṛśaṁ vyavahārapratipattaye bhavediti cet-atrāpi tatsantānādeva tatsamānenānyanānubhavanīyaṁ parapramāṇasya ca tadviṣayabhūtamiti ko niyacchet । na hi niyamaheturasti ॥
api ca ekacittatantratvādvyavahāravelāyāmanyata(na)redaṁpratyayaviṣayālambano nānyata(na)rapratyayo yujyate । na hi khalvapi vahucittatantraṁ vastu । tataśca gṛhāṇedaṁ prayacchada iti kathaṁ vyavaharemahi ॥
nāpyevaṁdarśanaśālinaḥ śiṣyācāryopadeśapradānādibhiranyonyaṁ vyavahareran । tasmānna caikacittatantraṁ vastu । pramāṇacittavināśe tadvyagrabhāve vā anavadhṛtasvabhāvavādvastuna: ॥
[saṁbadhyamānaṁ vā vastu punaścittena kuta utpadyeta ।] na kutaścidutpattirupapadyate tatsantānāditi hi pratyavocāma ॥
kiṁñca, [asya] vastunaḥ [anupasthitāḥ] ekasya pratyayasyāviṣayībhūtā[ye] [bhāgāste cāsya na syuḥ ।] eko hi vastubhāgo viṣayībhūtaścittatantro nānyaḥ iti । [nāsti pṛṣṭhamiti udaramapi] abhimukhībhūtaṁ [na syādeva ॥]
athāpi kākatalīyanyāyena bhūyāṁsi cittāni yugapadutpadyeran tadviṣayaṁ ca vastu tatsamānakālamunmajjatīti, tadetenaiva pṛṣṭhodarābhāvanidarśanena pratyākhyāye । nāpi kākatālīyavṛttāntenānādisamayādhīno vyavahārasāgara uttīryate । sarve ca vijñānadarśanaślāghiṣu doṣā ihāpi samānā eva ॥
[tasmāt] āha- [svatantro'rthaḥ sarvapuruṣasādhāraṇaḥ] yasminnavasthite samastalokavyavahāra upakalpiṣyate । [svatantrāṇi ca cittāni pratipuruṣaṁ pravartante । tayośca] arthacittayoḥ [sambandhādupalabdhiḥ puruṣasya bhogaḥ ।] tasmādbhoktā puruṣaḥ cittaṁ karaṇam artho viṣayaḥ karmabhūta ityeteṣāṁ bhoktṛkaraṇakarmaṇāṁ vivittaḥ panthāḥ ॥ 16 ॥
body.translated_text:
Vivaraṇam (Elucidation)
For this further reason too, mind-dependence of the object is untenable. Would the object depend on a single mind or on many minds? Regarding dependence on a single mind, we say: ['If an object depended on a single mind, when the means of valid knowledge is absent, what would it then be?'] It does not depend on a single mind. ['If an object were to depend on a single mind,'] if this is asserted, ['when that mind'] — the mind on which the object depends — is distracted, engaged elsewhere, ['or has ceased'] or been destroyed, ['and the object is not grasped by that'] cognizing mind, ['and has not become the object of another'] precisely because of its dependence on that one mind, ['then that'] object, ['without valid cognition, with its nature unapprehended,'] precisely from the cessation of the cognizing mind, ['what would it then be?'] It would be nothing at all. It has that [mind] as its means of valid cognition; in its absence, it ought not to exist.
But one might object: just as that cognizing mind ceases, so too the object itself ceases due to its momentariness — what is there to say about it? The reply: No — because of the collapse of conventional usage and the impossibility of regularity. The practical usage 'this is fire, do not touch it; take this, give that' would collapse — because the object would perish simultaneously with one mind.
If one says that what is born from its series, being extremely similar, would serve for practical conduct: even here, since what arises from that series, being similar to it, is not experienced by another, and since no one would restrict another's means of valid knowledge from having it as object — for there is no basis for such restriction.
Moreover, because of dependence on a single mind, at the time of practical activity, this-cognition having the object as support, no other-cognition would be possible. For the object does not depend on many minds. And thus, how could we engage in practical activity like 'take this, give that'?
Nor would those possessing such a view interact with each other through teaching, learning, giving instruction, and the like between students and teachers. Therefore, an object does not depend on a single mind — because with the destruction or distraction of the cognizing mind, the nature of the object would be unascertained.
['And when the object again connects with the mind, whence would it arise?'] No origin from anywhere is tenable — we have already replied to the claim 'from its series.'
Moreover, ['those parts of the object not presented'] — not having become the object of a single cognition — ['would not exist for it.'] For only that one part of the object that has become an object is mind-dependent, not another. ['If the back does not exist, then even the belly,'] which faces [the perceiver], ['would not exist.']
Or even if, by the principle of coincidence (kāka-tālīya), many minds were to arise simultaneously and the object pertaining to them would surface at the same time — that is refuted by this very illustration of the non-existence of back and belly. Nor can the ocean of beginningless conventional practice be crossed by resorting to the principle of coincidence. And all the faults that apply to those who extol the consciousness-only view apply equally here.
['Therefore,'] he says: ['The object is independent, common to all Puruṣas'] — when it is established, the entire conventional activity of the world will be accounted for. ['And minds operate independently for each Puruṣa. And from the connection of these two'] — of object and mind — ['there is apprehension — the experience of Puruṣa.'] Therefore, the experiencer is Puruṣa, the mind is the instrument, the object is the objective, having the role of the object-case — the path of these three — experiencer, instrument, and object — is distinct. || 16 ||

body.text: taduparāgāpekṣitvāccittasya vastu jñātājñātam ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: An object is known or unknown to the mind depending on whether it colors [the mind]. || 17 ||

body.text: ayaskāntamaṇikalpā viṣayā ayaḥsadharmakaṁ cittamabhisaṁbandhyoparañjayanti। yena ca viṣayeṇoparaktaṁ cittaṁ sa viṣayo jñātastato'nyaḥ punarajñātaḥ। vastuno jñātājñātasvarūpatvātpariṇāmi cittam ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: Objects, like lodestones, connect with and color the mind, which is like iron. The object by which the mind is colored — that object is known; any other is unknown. Because the object has both a known and unknown nature, the mind is transformable. || 17 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
kathaṁ cittatadviṣayayoḥ sambandhāt puruṣasya bhoga ityāha-yadvā, yasya cittavyatirekeṇa vastu nāsti, cittatantrameva vā vastu, tasya jñātājñātaviṣayatvamanupapannamityāha – [taduparāgāpekṣatvāccittasya vastu jñātājñātam । tena] viṣayeṇa [cittasyoparāgaḥ] taṁ prati [apekṣā] yasya [tat] [cittaṁ taduparāgāpekṣam,] tasya bhāvaḥ [taduparāgāpekṣatvaṁ] tasmāt [taduparāgāpekṣatvāccittasya vastu] jñātājñātam ॥
yena vastunā cittamuparajyate tat jñātaṁ, yena ca noparajyate tat [ajñātam ।] sa coparāgaścittapariṇāmāpekṣaḥ । indriyamārgeṇa cittaṁ hyākāreṇa pariṇamamānaṁ hi sambadhyate ॥
kiṁ punaścittapariṇāmanimitamityāha- [ayaskāntamaṇikalpā] ayaskāntasamānāḥ [viṣayāḥ, ayassadharmakaṁ cittam] -ayassadharmakatvaṁ ca viṣayasannidhāne vikriyata iti । viṣayāṇāmapyayaskāntamaṇikalpatvaṁ sannidhimātreṇa cittavikriyāpādanasāmarthyāt । ato viṣayā ātmākāreṇa pariṇataṁ [cittam abhisaṁbadhyoparañjayanti ॥]
[yena ca viṣayeṇoparaktaṁ cittaṁ] sa viṣayo jñātaḥ । [tato'nyaḥ('nye) punaḥ] anuparañjako (ka)viṣayaḥ(yā) [ajñātaḥ] (tāḥ) । tasmāt [vastuno jñātājñātasvarūpa] (viṣaya)tvāt [pariṇāmi cittam ।] atha punaścittatantra eva viṣayaścittameva vā viṣayaḥ, tasya vādinaḥ sarvaviṣayajñatvamaviṣayajñatvaṁ vā bhavet । ajñātasya cittasyābhāvāt । na cedaṁ dṛśyate । kiṁ tarhi ? jñātājñātaviṣayatvameva cittasya pratipadyāmahe । taccaitat sthirāvasthānānāṁ viṣayāṇāṁ prāpyabhāvādanyathā ca saṁbandhānavakalpanācittapariṇāmāpekṣameveti pariṇāmitvam ॥ 17 ॥
body.translated_text: Commentary: How does the connection between <s>citta</s> (mind) and its object result in experience (<s>bhoga</s>) for <s>Puruṣa</s>? To this he says — Or alternatively, for one who holds that no object exists apart from <s>citta</s>, or that objects are merely dependent on <s>citta</s>, the state of objects being known and unknown is untenable — thus he says: [Because <s>citta</s> depends on the coloring by that, an object is known or unknown.] By that object, the coloring (<s>uparāga</s>) of <s>citta</s> — the dependence upon that [coloring] — whose nature is such, [that <s>citta</s> depends on the coloring by that]; the state of being so is [the dependence on coloring by that]; therefore, [because <s>citta</s> depends on the coloring by that, an object is] known or unknown. That object by which <s>citta</s> is colored becomes known, and that by which it is not colored is [unknown.] And that coloring depends on the transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) of <s>citta</s>. For <s>citta</s>, transforming through the pathway of the senses into a particular form, becomes connected [with the object]. What then is the cause of <s>citta</s>'s transformation? To this he says — [The objects are like a magnet-stone,] comparable to a magnet; [<s>citta</s> is like iron] — and its iron-like nature consists in being modified in the proximity of objects. The objects too are like a magnet-stone, because they have the capacity to bring about modification of <s>citta</s> by mere proximity. Therefore, the objects [connect with and color <s>citta</s> that has transformed into their own form.] [That object by which <s>citta</s> is colored] — that object is known. [Other objects] that do not color [are unknown.] Therefore, [because objects have the nature of being known or unknown, <s>citta</s> is subject to transformation (<s>pariṇāmin</s>).] Now, if an object were entirely dependent on <s>citta</s>, or if <s>citta</s> itself were the object, then for such an advocate there would be either omniscience or complete ignorance — since an unknown <s>citta</s> would be non-existent. But this is not observed. What then? We understand that <s>citta</s> has objects both known and unknown. And this, because objects abide in a stable state and connection cannot be conceived otherwise, depends precisely on the transformation of <s>citta</s> — thus its nature as subject to transformation is established.

body.text: yasya tu tadeva cittaṁ viṣayastasya –
body.translated_text: But for one whose object is that very <s>citta</s> itself —

body.text: sadā jñātāścittavṛttayastatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvāt ॥ 18 ॥
body.translated_text: The <s>cittavṛttis</s> (mental modifications) are always known to their lord, <s>Puruṣa</s>, because of his unchangeability (<s>apariṇāmitva</s>). || 18 ||

body.text: yadi cittavatprabhurapi puruṣaḥ pariṇamettatastadviṣayāścittavṛttayaḥ śabdādiviṣayavajjñātājñātāḥ syuḥ। sadājñātatvaṁ tu manasastatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvamanumāpayati ॥ 18 ॥
body.translated_text: If the lord <s>Puruṣa</s> were to undergo transformation like <s>citta</s>, then the <s>cittavṛttis</s> that are his objects would be known and unknown, just as objects like sound and the rest are. But the fact that the <s>cittavṛttis</s> of the mind are always known leads us to infer the unchangeability (<s>apariṇāmitva</s>) of their lord <s>Puruṣa</s>. || 18 ||

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[yasya] tu svāmino bhoktuḥ [tadeva] jñātājñātaviṣayaṁ [cittaṁ] vṛttirūpeṇa [viṣayaḥ] na hi niruddhavṛttinaścetaso viṣayatvamiti, [tasya] puruṣasya sadā [jñātāścittavṛttaya: [tatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvāt] ।] tāsāṁ pratyakṣatvāt sadā jñātaviṣayatvamaprasādhyam ॥
yadvā pratyakṣagamyāścittavṛttayaḥ, upalabdhatvena śabdaliṅgānapekṣaṁ smaryamāṇatvāt, pratyakṣopalabdhaghaṭavat । niścitarūpatvācca tathaiva । saṁśayāviṣayatvācca । yadi hi sadaivāpratyakṣāścittavṛttayaḥ, tā bāhyaviṣayavat saṁśayitā api kadācit kāścana bhaveyuḥ । na hi kāśvana kadācana saṁśayamārgasaṁpātinyo dṛṣṭāḥ ॥
api ca, bhavati hi kadācijjñātaḥ sannartho jñāta iti [pratīyamānaḥ] । cittavṛtipratyakṣāgrāhyatve [tat] nopapadyate । na ca phaladvāreṇānumātuṁ tatra śakyata । phalasyānavadhāraṇāt ॥
tasmāt saṁśayasya cāviṣayatvāt, pṛthak ca viṣayācittavṛttīnāṁ svarūpamātreṇaiva smaryamāṇatvāt, sarvadā sarvvāḥ pratyakṣāścittavṛttayaḥ । tathā pratipatturavabhāsakatvāt, karaṇatvāt, abhivyañjakatvācca, pradīpādivat । na tu cakṣurādibhiranaikāntikatvam । tatrāpi pratyakṣagrāhyatvāt । yathā pradīpādyālokiviśiṣṭā ghaṭādayo gṛhyante, tathā śrotrādisvālokaviśiṣṭā eva śabdādayo gṛhyante ॥
na ca vivicyāgrahaṇādapratyakṣatvamiti śakyaṁ vaktum । yathā pradīpayoḥ parasparavyatibhinnā raśmayaḥ, na cāsyāyaṁ raśmirasya cāyamiti vivicyate, na ca tāvatā teṣāmapratyakṣatvam, [evaṁ] ihāpi cakṣurādīnāṁ tulyajātīyabāhyālokādivyatiṣaṅgādvivicyāgrahaṇam । na ca tāvanmātreṇa teṣāmapratyakṣatvam । yo hi pratyakṣāvasīyamānacittavṛtyapalāpaṁ karoti, nūnamasāvātmānamapyapālapediti sarvopalabdheścittavṛtyadhīnatvāt rūpopalabdherivāloka(pratyāyakaṁ tattvam) pratyayādhīnatvam । tasmādāha- [sadā jñātāścittavṛttayaḥ puruṣasyeti ॥]
yaccaitat sadā jñātaviṣayatvam, [tatprabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmatvāt ।] nityopalabdhṛsvarūpaprayuktaṁ hi taditi । [yadi cittavat prabhurapi puruṣaḥ pariṇameta, tatastadviṣayāścittavṛttayaḥ cittasyeva śabdādiviṣayāḥ, jñātā ajñātā api syuḥ ॥]
yattu jñātājñātaṁ śabdādiviṣayajātaṁ, tat pariṇāminaścittasya pariṇāmāpekṣaṁ draṣṭavyam । tathaivendriyāṇāmapi pariṇāmāpekṣameva jñātājñātaviṣayatvaṁ dṛśyate । na ca tathā cittavṛttīnāmanyatamāsāmapi jñātatvamajñātatvaṁ ca । nityatastajjñātā eva cittavṛttayaḥ । tasmādyadvṛttirūpeṇa [sadā jñātatvaṁ manasaḥ tat prabhoḥ puruṣasyāpariṇāmitvamanumāpayati ॥]
apariṇāmī puruṣa iti pratijñā । sadā jñātaviṣayatvāditi hetuḥ । vaidharmyeṇa cittamindriyāṇi ca dṛṣṭāntaḥ । upalabdhuśca viṣayiṇaḥ prakṛtatvāt sadā jñātaviṣayatvapratiṣedhāya muktātmavaditi dṛṣṭānto nopapadyate । muktasyāviṣayitvāt ॥ 18 ॥
body.translated_text: Commentary: [For one] who is the owner, the experiencer, [that very] <s>citta</s> — having known and unknown objects — is [the object] in the form of <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications); for <s>citta</s> whose modifications have ceased does not serve as an object. [For that] <s>Puruṣa</s>, the <s>cittavṛttis</s> are always [known, because of the unchangeability of their lord <s>Puruṣa</s>.] Since those are directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), the state of always having known objects need not be separately established. Or alternatively, the <s>cittavṛttis</s>, apprehended through direct perception by <s>Puruṣa</s> in due order, are thus always known — this should be construed in detail. He shows the means of proof for what is to be proved — [If] the lord <s>Puruṣa</s>, like a sentient being, [were also to undergo transformation, then the <s>cittavṛttis</s> that are his objects] would be [known and unknown] to <s>Puruṣa</s>. There would be the restriction: 'this is known, but this is not known' — for whom? For <s>Puruṣa</s>, were he subject to transformation. For if there were transformation, the <s>cittavṛttis</s> would not always be <s>Puruṣa</s>'s objects; rather, when <s>Puruṣa</s> is proximate to <s>citta</s>, then they would be his objects, and when not proximate, they would not — objecthood would be like that of external objects. And transformation of the capacity for direct perception and so forth cannot occur in <s>Puruṣa</s> as it does in objects; if it is conceded that there is in <s>Puruṣa</s> a transformation of perceptual capacity that does not manifest objects — that being the transformation of <s>Puruṣa</s> — then it is not proper to say that the <s>cittavṛttis</s> are always known to <s>Puruṣa</s>. [But the fact that the <s>vṛttis</s> of the mind are always known] by <s>Puruṣa</s> [leads us to infer, as a means of proof, the unchangeability of their lord <s>Puruṣa</s>. || 18 ||]

body.text: syādāśaṅkā cittameva svābhāsaṁ viṣayābhāsaṁ ca bhaviṣyatītyagnivat –
body.translated_text: An objection might arise: <s>citta</s> itself will be self-luminous (<s>svābhāsa</s>) and also illuminating objects (<s>viṣayābhāsa</s>), like fire —

body.text: na tatsvābhāsaṁ dṛśyatvāt ॥ 19 ॥
body.translated_text: That [<s>citta</s>] is not self-luminous, because it is an object of perception (<s>dṛśya</s>). || 19 ||

body.text: yathetarāṇīndriyāṇi śabdādayaśca dṛśyatvānna svābhāsāni tathā mano'pi pratyetavyam।
body.translated_text: Just as the other sense organs and objects such as sound, being objects of perception (<s>dṛśya</s>), are not self-luminous, so too the mind should be understood in the same way.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
[syādāśaṅkā-cittameva svābhāsaṁ viṣayābhāsaṁ ca bhaviṣyatīti ।] grāhyaṁ grāhakaṁ ceti । svasaṁviditākārā eva hi vṛttayaḥ । yathā pradīpaḥ prakāśayati ghaṭādīnātmānaṁ ca । kiṁ puruṣeṇa cittavṛttyupalambhinā cittavyatiriktena kalpiteneti ॥
atrocyate- [na tat svābhāsaṁ dṛśyatvāt । yathetarāṇīndriyāṇi] śre.ātrādīni viṣayāśca [śabdādayaḥ । na svābhāsāni] indriyāṇi । nāpi svābhāsāḥ śabdādayaḥ । [dṛśyatvāt । tathā mano'pi pratyetavyam ।] na svābhāsaṁ cittaṁ dṛśyatvāditi pratipattavyam ॥
nanu ca agnivadeva svābhāsatvaṁ viṣayābhāsatvaṁ ca bhavatu, yathaiva ghaṭādayaḥ prakāśyāḥ svarūpopalambhanārthamālokāntaramapekṣante, na tathā pradīpaḥ । yathā pradīpaḥ svābhāso viṣayābhāsaśca । tathā mano'pyavabhāsakatvādevaṁ bhavatu kimātmanā? na hi pradīpapratipattaye pradīpāntaramādadate laukikāḥ ॥
yadi copādīyaran anavasthaiva syāt । evaṁ vijñānasyāpi vyatiriktena grāhyatve tasya cānyena grahaṇaṁ tasya cānyenetyevaṁ prasajyata । kiṁ ca vijñānasyāvabhāsātmakatvāt grāhakasyāpyavabhāsarūpatvāt na parasparopakāryopakārakabhāvaḥ । tadyathā pradīpayordvayoḥ । tasmāt kalpito'pi vijñānasya grahītā anarthaka iti, bhavatu jñānaṁ svābhāsaṁ parābhāsaṁ ceti ॥
body.translated_text: Commentary: [An objection might arise — <s>citta</s> itself will be self-luminous and also illuminating objects.] It would be both the grasped and the grasper. For the <s>vṛttis</s> (modifications) are indeed of a self-cognized form. Just as a lamp illuminates pots and other things as well as itself. What need is there for a <s>Puruṣa</s> distinct from <s>citta</s>, imagined as a perceiver of <s>cittavṛttis</s>? To this it is replied — [That is not self-luminous, because it is an object of perception. Just as the other sense organs and objects such as sound, being objects of perception, are not self-luminous, so too the mind should be understood in the same way.] Rather, the meaning is that it is apprehended by its own faculty — that is what 'self-luminous' would mean [if accepted]. Now, it has been said that <s>citta</s> is self-illuminating like a lamp. To that he replies —

body.text: na cāgniratra dṛṣṭāntaḥ। na hyagnirātmasvarūpamaprakāśaṁ prakāśayati। prakāśaścāyaṁ prakāśyaprakāśakasaṁyoge dṛṣṭaḥ। na ca svarūpamātre'sti saṁyogaḥ। kiṁ ca svābhāsaṁ cittamityagrāhyameva kasyaciditi śabdārthaḥ। tadyathā svātmapratiṣṭhamākāśaṁ na parapratiṣṭhamityarthaḥ। svabuddhipracārapratisaṁvedanātsattvānāṁ pravṛttirdṛśyate – kruddho'haṁ bhīto'hamamutra me rāgo'mutra me krodha iti। etatsvabuddheragrahaṇe na yuktamiti ॥ 19 ॥
body.translated_text: And fire is not a valid analogy here. For fire does not illuminate its own nature as though it were previously unmanifest. And this illumination is observed in the conjunction of the illuminated and the illuminator. But there is no conjunction with respect to one's own nature alone. Moreover, if <s>citta</s> is said to be self-luminous (<s>svābhāsa</s>), the meaning of this term is that it is not graspable by anything. Just as <s>ākāśa</s> (space) is self-established, not established through another — that is the meaning. And the awareness of the activity of one's own <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) is established through direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) by all living beings.

body.text:
vivaraṇam
atrocyate-tadetaddṛṣṭāntāpaśadāvaṣṭambhena sakalalokaprasiddhamārgopārohiṇa ātmano nirākaraṇamaśakyam । kasmāt? [na cāgniratra dṛṣṭantaḥ । na hyagnirātmasvarūpamaprakāśaṁ prakāśayati,] yadi cāgniraprakāśaḥ san ātmanaiva ghaṭādivat prākāśayiṣyata, tata upāpatsyata dṛṣṭāntaḥ । na tvevam । na hi kadācidagniraprakāśaḥ ॥
[prakāśaścāyam । sa ca prakāśyaprakāśakasaṁyoge dṛṣṭaḥ । na ca svarūpamātre'sti saṁyogaḥ ।] dvayerhi saṁyegaḥ । nāsati saṁyoge svarūpāvabhāsakratvam ॥
yadapyucyate-ghaṭādivat prakāśāntaraṁ nāgnirapekṣata iti । tat prakāśyarūpābhāvāt । na tu tasya ghaṭādivat prakāśyaṁ rūpamasti । na tāvatā vyatiriktāgrāhyatvam । cakṣuṣā tulyavyatiriktena gṛhyata eva ॥
prakāśyasya ghaṭāderavatamasatiraskārāya prakāśa upādāyiṣyate । na tvaprakāśyarūpatvāt । agnerālokāntarānākāṅkṣaṇaṁ tu bhavataivābhihitaṁ-dvayoḥ pradīpayornāsti parasparopakāra iti । yatra nāma bhede'pi dvayoḥ pradīpayornāstyaprakāśyarūpatvādanyonyopakāraḥ, kimuta asati bhede'tra prakāśāntaromeva nāpekṣate iti ॥
na tu vyatiriktagrāhyatvaṁ vyabhicarati, pradīpayordṛśyatvādghaṭādivat । etena vyatiriktagrāhyatvaṁ jñānasya dṛśyatvāt pradīpādivat siddhaṁ bhavati । pradīpādivacca jñānasya prakāśasvarūpatvāt karaṇāntarānapekṣāpi siddhā । tathā ca anavasthādoṣagandhī na vidyate ॥
yadapyucyate-jñānasyāvabhāsātmakatvāt tadgrāhakasyāpyavabhāsarūpatvāt na parasparopakāryopakārakabhāvaḥ pradīpayoriva dvayoriti । nāsau doṣaḥ । cakṣuḥpradīpavadātmajñānayorjātyantaratvāt ॥
